F major with some chromatic inflections in certain versions. The B part has an Irish reel character that's fun to lean into. Let the bow arm drive.

title: Betty Baker
description:
BETTY BAKER 1. AKA and see "Indian Nation (4)." American, Reel (cut time). USA; eastern Kentucky, West Virginia. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. Although the tune called "Betty Baker" is known as a "W.Va. standard," it was played (in more or less related versions) by a number of east Kentucky fiddlers, including Manon Campbell, Clyde Davenport, Ed Haley and Hiram Stamper (1893-1992), of Knott County.  The latter also played a tune he called "Indian Nation (4)" 1 that is a version of "Betty Baker (1)."  See West Virginia versions at "Betty Baker (3)." 

Source for notated version: -  Manon Campbell (Hallie, Letcher County, Kentucky, 1977) Titon. 

Printed sources: - Titon (Old Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 5, p. 36. 

Recorded sources:   -  Augusta Heritage Records 003, Ernie Carpenter - "Elk River Blues - Traditional Tunes From Braxton County, W.Va." Copper Creek CCCD-0196, Tom, Brad & Alice - "We'll Die in the Pig Pen Fighting."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Betty Baker (Over the Hill to Betty Baker)
description:
The tune gets its full title from an old folk verse attached to it. One version of the lyric reads: "I went down for to see Betty Baker, / She was asleep and the Devil couldn't wake her; / She wouldn't stir and her mother wouldn't shake her, / Long time ago." A shorter, more localized eastern Kentucky version was remembered by oral tradition: Grover Salyer recalled a verse: "Went over the hill to see Betty Baker, / She was asleep and I could not wake her." The "Betty Baker" of the title appears to be a stock folk character — a sleepy, unresponsive woman — rather than a documented historical person.

Although the tune called "Betty Baker" is known as a "W.Va. standard," it was played (in more or less related versions) by a number of east Kentucky fiddlers, including Manon Campbell, Clyde Davenport, Ed Haley, and Hiram Stamper (1893–1992), of Knott County.

The tune exists in at least two distinct versions documented in the Traditional Tune Archive:
Betty Baker [1] — An American reel in cut time, in D Major, from eastern Kentucky and West Virginia. Hiram Stamper also played a tune he called "Indian Nation" that is a version of "Betty Baker (1)."
Betty Baker [2] — An old-time air and breakdown in G Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB form. This version was printed in Ira Ford's Traditional Music in America (1940).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bibb County Hoedown
description:
Bibb County, Georgia was named for William Wyatt Bibb, Georgia's first governor (1817). Located in central Georgia with Macon as its county seat, Bibb County was part of the fertile Georgia piedmont that supported a prosperous agricultural economy. The 'hoedown' — originally a dance where participants stamped and clapped rhythmically — became a generic term for any vigorous country dance gathering. Georgia fiddle contest traditions were distinct from both Virginia and Texas styles.

Attributed to A.A. Gray. Geographic provenance: USA (Piedmont). First documented in Gene Silberberg's *Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern* (2002). BIBB COUNTY HOEDOWN . AKA - "Bibb County Breakdown." American, Reel (cut time). C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. In the repertoire of Seven Foot Dilly and His Dill Pickles (A.A. Gray, fiddle), north Georgia, who recorded it in Atlanta in November, 1930. The group probably consisted of John Dilleshaw (guitar), A.A. Gray (fiddle), plus a second fiddle and guitar, banjo and a washtub bass. All were more or less musicians in the Skillet Lickers circle of north Georgia musicians in the 1920'… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A Georgia breakdown with a strong, county-fair energy. Keep the bow arm driving and the rhythm absolutely steady. A hoedown was literally a dance at a farm gathering — communal, informal, and exuberant. This tune should feel like a crowd of people who've been working hard and are ready to dance hard too.

title: Big Eyed Rabbit
description:
Animal-themed tunes were among the most popular in the Old-Time repertoire — 'Big Eyed Rabbit,' 'Rabbit in the Pea Patch,' 'Rabbit Where'd You Get Them Long Ears' — reflecting the rabbit's prominent place in both Appalachian hunting culture and African American trickster tales (Br'er Rabbit). The rabbit was a dietary staple and a figure of folk wisdom: always watchful, always ready to run, surviving through cleverness rather than strength.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A comic, animal-themed breakdown with a loose, swinging quality. The rabbit's wide eyes suggest wariness and speed — keep the rhythm quick and light. Don't dig the bow in; let it bounce. This is one of those tunes that sounds better played with a little carelessness than with excessive precision. Great for large sessions.

title: Big John McNeil
description:
BIG JOHN McNEIL(L)/McNEAL. AKA and see "John McNeil's Reel." Canadian, American, Scottish; Reel. Canada, widely known. USA; New England, Missouri. A Major. Standard (or infrequently AEae) tuning (fiddle). AABB (Gibbons, Messer, Sweet): AABB' (Miller & Perron): AA'BB' (Bégin, Perlman, Phillips). Though now known as a Canadian standard it originally was a reel composed (as "John McNeil") by the brilliant Scottish fiddler Peter Milne (1824-1908), one of J. Scott Skinner's teachers and early playing partners, who earned his living playing in theaters until his opium addiction (he abused laudanum, originally prescribed for rheumatism) reduced him to busking on ferry-boats crossing the Firth of Forth. He died in unpleasant circumstances in a mental institution. John McNeil was a famous Highland dancer of the mid-to-later 19th century (see note for "John McNeil's Reel" for more). The melody was in the repertoire of Cyrill Stinnett, a fiddler who epitomised the 'North Missouri Hornpipe Style' of playing, who apparently learned it and other tunes from listening to Canadian fiddlers broadcasting on the radio from Canada. Indeed, an influential recording of the tune was made 'Down-East' Canadian fiddler Don Messer with his group the Islanders, early in the 1940's-among the first of the sides the group waxed. A very similar melody, or a version, is "Lord Ramsay's Reel." Perlman (1996) notes the tune is a popular tune on Prince Edward Island, and a favorite vehicle for stepdancing in Prince County, PEI, on the western part of the island. Irish fiddler Sean Maguire recorded the melody in the 1960's under the title "Betty's Fancy (2).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Big Sandy
description:
There are actually two distinct fiddle tunes commonly associated with the "Big Sandy" name in American traditional music. Here's a full breakdown:

"Big Sandy River" is credited to Kenny Baker and Bill Monroe, composed in 1963. It is primarily a bluegrass tune, written in the key of G.

Kenny Baker was Monroe's longtime fiddler with the Blue Grass Boys, and the tune reflects that virtuosic bluegrass fiddle style. It is considered an essential bluegrass fiddle piece, frequently appearing at jams alongside tunes like Lonesome Moonlight Waltz and Monroe's Hornpipe.

The tune takes its name from the Big Sandy River, which forms the border between eastern Kentucky and West Virginia — deep in the heart of Appalachian old-time and bluegrass country.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bill Brown
description:
BILL BROWN. American, Reel (cut time). USA; Magoffin County, Ky. A Major. AEac# tuning (fiddle). AABB. An irregular tune (the 'A' part has eight repeated measures, the 'B' part four repeated measures) in repertoire of Kentucky fiddler biography:John Salyer (Salyersville, Magoffin County). It was named for the fiddler who played the tune. Jeff Titon (2001) suggests it might have been named after William H. "Bill" Brown, who was executed by hanging for the murder of Irish peddler Morris Hagerty in Morgan County, Ky., in 1855. Bruce Greene likened the tune to "Sugar in the Gourd," according to Bruce Molsky.  John Salyer

Source for notated version: - a home recording of John Salyer, 1941 or 1942, by his sons, Grover and Glen Titon. 

Printed sources: - Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 8, p. 39. 

Recorded sources:   - Berea College Appalachian Center AC003, "John Salyer: Home Recordings 1941-1942" (1993). Rounder 0361, Bruce Molsky - "Lost Boy" (1996).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bill Driver's Tune
description:
William "Bill" Driver was born in Eldridge, Laclede County, Missouri, and later relocated to Miller County, central Missouri, southwest of Iberia, where he spent most of his fiddling career.

His father, also named William Driver, was the son of a slave known only as Mandy Dixon or Dickson. William Driver Sr. was born in 1859 and adopted as a child by a family called Driver, the name he carried for the remainder of his life. When he died in 1934, Bill Sr.'s occupation was listed as Minister of the Gospel; he had been a Free Will Baptist preacher traveling the circuit.

Bill Driver is one of two African-American traditional fiddlers from the Central Missouri area who are still well-known.

A gifted musician, he had a keen ear, kept steady time, and played vigorously. His was described as "the best example of a strictly indigenous repertory" his collector knew of — whereas other Missouri fiddlers had their repertoires diluted with hornpipes, jigs, and reels from phonograph records or mail-order sheet music, Bill stuck with the music and style of his locale.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Billy in the Lowland
description:
"Billy in the Lowground" is one of the most enduring and widespread of American traditional dance tunes in the key of C, known throughout the South, Midwest, and West and even into the northern part of the United States. As with most such long-lived and widely disseminated reels, there is a tremendous variation of the core melody due to both regional style, musical style (e.g., bluegrass, western swing), and individual fiddlers' idiosyncratic renderings.

The American tune borrows motifs from British and Irish sources. Scholar Samuel Bayard traced its genealogy carefully. The tune originated in Britain as a slow 3/4 time song tune from c. 1710 or earlier, called "O Dear Mother (Minnie) What Shall I Do?" He sees the development of the tune as having then split into two branches, and during the 1740s a 6/8 "giga" or jig form was composed called variously "All the Blue Bonnets Are Over the Border." Later in the century the second branch was fashioned from the original 3/4 tune into a fast duple time (4/4) dancing air which went by several titles including "The Braes of Auchtertyre/Auchentyre," "Belles of Tipperary," and "Beaus of Albany." These latter tunes are the immediate ancestor of the "Billy in the Lowground" group of tunes in America.

The title's meaning is hotly debated. Several competing folk explanations circulate:
William of Orange: The tune is said to be Scottish in origin, and the title refers to William of Orange at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, where a "deep swampy ravine" figured in the tactics of the battle.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bitter Creek
description:
Bitter Creek could refer to several geographic features in the American West and South — there are Bitter Creeks in Wyoming, West Virginia, and elsewhere — all named because their water was alkaline, sulfurous, or otherwise undrinkable. In Appalachian folklore, 'bitter' was used to describe situations or places that were genuinely difficult — bitter cold, bitter grief, bitter labor. Old-Time tunes with austere names often preserved an unflinching honesty about the hardships of rural life.

Attributed to Oscar Harper. Geographic provenance: USA (Southwest). First documented in R.P. Christeson's *Old Time Fiddler's Repertory vol. 1* (1973). BITTER CREEK . AKA – "Bitter Creek Breakdown." American, Reel (cut time). USA; Texas, Kentucky. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB (Brody, Phillips): ABB'C (Harper): ABCDD (Devil's Box): AABBCCDD (Christeson, Songer). The tune was recorded in Dallas, Texas, for OKeh Records at the end of November, 1929, by Texas fiddler Oscar Harper (1888-1952), accompanied by guitar player Doc Harper. In 1942 Harper was recorded playing "Bitter Creek" by John Lomax for the Library of Congress [ 1 &#… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A tune with an uncompromising name — 'bitter' in Appalachian parlance meant something difficult, hard, or genuinely unpleasant. Play it with some grit and don't try to sweeten it up. The modal quality enhances the sense of hardship. A tune that tells the truth about difficult experiences without melodrama.

title: Black-Eyed Susie
description:
The black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta) is a wildflower native to eastern North America — its bright yellow petals and dark center made it one of the most recognizable flowers of the Appalachian meadow landscape. In Old-Time tradition, 'Black-Eyed Susie' refers to a young woman, likely dark-eyed and attractive. The tune appears in multiple collections from across the Appalachian region and has been recorded by dozens of artists from traditional fiddlers to modern string bands.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A cheerful courting tune that's one of the most widely-played in the Old-Time tradition. Keep it bright and forward. The A part has an insistent, questioning quality; the B part answers with more confidence. This tune is great for beginners because the form is clear and forgiving, but it has enough character to reward advanced players who add ornamentation.

title: Black-Eyed Suzy-Anna
description:
The tune's lineage is remarkably deep. Musicologist Samuel Bayard traces the history of the tune back to the British Isles, beginning with a melody called "Rosasolis," set by Giles Farnaby (c. 1560–c. 1600), which appears in the Fitzwilliam Virginal Book.

Another version of the melody is called "Morris Off" and appears in Jehan Tabourot's Orchesographie (1588); it is still used for English morris dances and has been called the earliest recorded morris tune. Still another version appears as an old Welsh harp tune in Alawon Fy Ngwlad / Lays of My Land.

Later developments of the tune were popular in England and Scotland from the early 17th century through the 18th, under the title "Three Jolly Sheep Skins"; while in Ireland a variation became known as "Aillilliu mo Mhailin" (Alas my little bag) — a humorous lament for a stolen bag of sundries.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Black Jack Grove
description:
BLACK JACK GROVE 1. AKA - "Blackjack Grove." American, Reel. USA, Kentucky. A Mixolydian ('A' part) & A Dorian ('B' part) {Phillips, Titon}: A Mixolydian ('A' part) & A Major ('B' part) {Silberberg}.  Standard or AEae (McNew) tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberbert): AABB (Phillips, Titon). Phillips notes that his source, Walter McNew, tended to blur the 'C' notes in the 'B' part of his unaccompanied version, resulting in a tonality somewhere between minor and major. Jeff Titon (2001) finds the title in tune lists from Berea College in 1915 and in the 1919 Berea fiddle contest list. The title presumably takes its name from a locale with a  grove of blackjack oak trees.  

McNew learned "Black Jack Grove" from his father John McNew (b. 1888), a telegraph operator and depot agent for the L & N Railroad, who would play his fiddle between dispatches during the graveyard shift at his train depot. Walter learned the tune from his father, and thought that his father in turn had it from a man known to the family as 'Uncle' Garrett Bow, who used to visit with the elder McNew at the train depot where the two would swap tunes through the night 1 McNew was also highly influenced by neighboring Madison County, Ky., fiddler Doc Roberts, whom he knew and held in awe. 

See also "Blackjack", recorded in the field from the playing of Hobert Bowling by John Harrod and Mark Wilson (heard on Rounder 0544/Field Recorder Collective FRC731). For the musically unrelated Texas tune of the same name, see "Black Jack Grove (2)."

Source for notated version: - Walter McNew (1912-1998, Mt. Vernon, Rockcastle County, central Ky.) Milliner & Koken, Phillips, Titon

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Black Sally Goodin
description:
BLACK SALLY GOODIN. Old-Time, Breakdown (cut or 2/4 time). USA, Missouri. G Major (Christeson): D Major (Pete McMaham). Standard or GDad tuning (fiddle). ABC. "Black Sally Goodin'" is on Missouri fiddler and teacher Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. The title probably does not refer to an African-American female named Sally Goodin', but rather that the tune was played by Black fiddlers and absorbed into white fiddlers' repertoire. Describing it as 'Black Sally Goodin' differentiated the melody from other "Sally Goodin'" tunes and helped avoid confusion. 

Source for notated version: - African-American fiddler Bill Caton (or Katon) via his friend Vee Latty (Callaway County, north-central Missouri), who was recorded in the field in the 1950's Christeson. Bill Caton (or Katon) was an African-American fiddler who played regularly over WOS, accompanied on guitar by Ola Gaithright. Unfortunately no commercial or field recordings survive of Caton's playing.

Printed sources: - R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; No. 134, p. 95. Bill Shull (Cross-Tuning Your Fiddle), 1994;

Recorded sources:   - Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association 001, Pete McMahan - "Ozark Mountain Waltz." JL 9601, Kim & Jim Lansford - "New Harmony".

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Black Satin
description:
Satin — a smooth, glossy woven fabric with a silky texture — was a luxury textile associated with formal dress, ballrooms, and high-status social occasions in 19th-century American culture. 'Black Satin' as a tune name evokes the world of formal social dancing: polished floors, fine clothes, and carefully executed dance figures. The tune's smooth melodic character suits the material it's named for.

BLACK SATIN . American, Reel. G Major. GDad tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. The tune was in the repertoire of the Perry County (Tenn.) Music Makers-Nonnie Presson and Bulow Smith on zither and gtr., who recorded several sides for Vocalion Records in 1930. Nonnie learned the tune from a local banjo player, Will Warren. A tune called "Black Satin" (DDad tuning) was in the repertory of fiddler George Mert Reves (1884?-1992?), of Dennard, Arkansas, although he had lived much of his life in the Oklahoma … (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A smooth, elegant tune that should sound like its name — silky and polished. Keep the bow arm relaxed and the tone round and warm. No roughness here. This is a tune for showing off clean intonation and smooth bow changes. Play it at a moderate tempo where the elegance can register.

title: Black Widow Romp
description:
The tune was written by Chris Romain (also sometimes spelled Romaine), from the DC area. He can often be found at Clifftop (the renowned Appalachian String Band Music Festival in West Virginia) with the other Roustabouts at the Elvis Shrine.

In Dan Levenson's "Buzzard Banjo" tab book, the tune is credited as being written by Chris Romaine. Some sources credit it to both Chris Romaine and Dan Levenson — a common occurrence in the old-time community where arrangers and compilers sometimes get co-credited alongside the original composer.

It appears to be a newly written tune, meaning it's a modern composition in the old-time style rather than a tune with deep historical roots stretching back generations. New fiddle tunes have always been written and are still being written today in the old-time tradition, so "Black Widow Romp" fits squarely in that living, evolving practice.

Geographic provenance: USA (Southeast). (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Blake's March
description:
"Blake's March" was written by Norman Blake. Norman L. Blake (born March 10, 1938) is a traditional American stringed instrument artist and songwriter, born in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and raised in Sulphur Springs, Alabama.

He grew up listening to old-time and country music on the radio — the Carter Family, the Skillet Lickers, Roy Acuff, and the Monroe Brothers — and learned guitar at age 11 or 12, then mandolin, dobro, and fiddle in his teens. When he was 16, he dropped out of school to play music professionally.

Though probably best known for his fluid renditions of classic fiddle tunes transcribed for guitar, Blake has also written songs that became bluegrass and folk standards, such as "Ginseng Sullivan," "Slow Train through Georgia," and "Church Street Blues."

Norman Blake's tune "Blake's March" was recorded on Original Underground Music from the Mysterious South (available on the compilation Natasha's Waltz) by the Rising Fawn String Ensemble: Norman Blake, Nancy Blake, Peter Ostroushko, Carl Jones, and Larry Sledge. It's a sprightly fiddle tune in the key of G.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Blue Eagle
description:
BLUE EAGLE. American, Reel (cut time). USA, Texas. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. A regional Texas tune not well known in other parts of the South. The tune has been attributed to fiddle player Orville Burns (b. 1921, Oklahoma, later moved to Texas), whose father suggested the name to him. The Blue Eagle was the depression-era symbol of a thunderbird, employed by companies to show compliance with the National Industrial Recovery Act.

Source for notated version: - Lewis Franklin (Texas) Devil's Box, Phillips; Gary Lee Moore (Seattle) Silberberg.

Printed sources: -  Stephen F. Davis (The Devil's Box), vol. 14, No. 3, Sept. 1980; p. 34. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 30. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 13.

Recorded sources: - County 707, Lewis Franklin - "Texas Fiddle Favorites."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Blue Goose
description:
The snow goose (Chen caerulescens) has a blue-gray 'blue morph' phase that gave it the folk name 'blue goose' in many parts of North America. Migratory waterfowl — geese, ducks, herons — were important food sources and harbingers of seasonal change in Appalachian culture. The Blue Goose was also a common name for country stores and roadhouses throughout the rural South, suggesting a warm, unpretentious gathering place.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A tune with the unhurried, heavy quality of a goose in flight — keep the tempo moderate and the bow arm grounded. The Blue Goose was a real bird and a real brand, and the name suggests something solid and unpretentious. Don't rush this one. Let the open string drones carry.

title: Blue Mule
description:
BLUE MULE. AKA - "Old Blue Mule." AKA and see "Austin Breakdown." American, Reel (cut time). USA; Arkansas, Missouri. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AA'BB'C (Beisswenger & McCann). "Blue Mule" was recorded for the Library of Congress by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph in the early 1940's from Ozarks Mountains fiddlers, where it is a regionally popular tune formerly seldom heard in other parts of the country. The tune may have had origins in a hornpipe and is structurally similar. Mark Wilson sees resemblance with the tunes "Nancy's Got a Pretty Dress On" and "Austin Breakdown," while Drew Beisswenger (2008) finds Absie Morrison's "Irish Washerwoman (2)" (a reel version) similar, particularly with the ending cadences. There is some speculation it may have derived from the play-party song "Skip to My Lou." "Blue Mule" is usually heard played in two strains. Source Glen Rickman (1901-1982) believed the tune to have been played during the Civil War, and identified his additional third part as the one a "Rebel" cousin had played Beisswenger & McCann. 

Guthrie Meade gives two early 78RPM recorded sources: Bob Miller's Hinky Dinkers (1930) and Jess Hillard & His West Virginia Hillbillies (1933). It was in the repertoire of Missouri fiddlers Art Galbraith (1909-1993, who said it was learned from older members of his family) and Bob Holt (1930-2004), and by Bill (Willie) Bilyeau for the Library of Congress.

Printed sources: -  Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 112. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 13.

Recorded sources: - Rounder 133, Art Galbraith - "Dixie Blossoms" (1981). Rounder 0435, Bob Holt. Rounder 8041, Art Galbraith & Gordon McCann - "The Land of Yahoe."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Boating Up The Sandy
description:
The Big Sandy River, forming the border between West Virginia and Kentucky, was a major transportation route in the early 19th century. Before roads and railroads, flatboats and keelboats moved goods along river systems throughout Appalachia. 'Boating up' the river — working upstream against the current — was grueling labor that required organized crews working in rhythm. Work songs and fiddle tunes that matched the rhythm of physical labor were a practical necessity on early American waterways.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A river tune with a powerful, upstream-pulling quality — 'boating up' meant poling or pulling a flatboat against the current. Put that muscle into the bow arm. The rhythm should feel like steady, rhythmic labor. The Sandy River (probably the Big Sandy, West Virginia/Kentucky) was a major commerce route in the early 19th century.

title: Boatman
description:
BOATMAN 1 (Boate Man). English, Country Dance Tune (6/8 or 6/4 time). D Major (Fleming-Williams): C Major (Barnes, Chappell, Karpeles, Sharp). Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Chappell): ABB (Sharp): AABB (Barnes, Fleming-Williams, Karpeles). The air was first published (with directions for a country dance) by John Playford in the first edition of The English Dancing Master (1651) and again in his Musick's Recreation on the Viol, Lyra-way (1661), and it was retained in the series of editions of the Dancing Master through the 10th edition of 1698, published at the time by John's son, Henry Playford. A song to the tune was published by poet and playwright Wikipedia:Allan_Ramsay_(poet) (1686-1758) and published in his Tea-Table Miscellany (1724) and is titled "The Bonny Scot." Anne Gilchrist1, however, believes there was an original song, now lost (which may have been adapted by Ramsay). Ramsay's verses begin:

The air to Ramsay's verses was published by London singer and song collector William Thomson in his Orpheus Caledonius (1725), who ascribed it to David Rizzio (1533-1566) in his first edition, although this was removed in the second edition of 17332.

Printed sources: -  Barnes (English Country Dance Tunes), 1989. Chappell (Popular Music of the Olden Times, vol. 1), 1859; pp. 308-309. Fleming- Williams & Shaw (English Dance Airs; Popular Selection, Book 1), 1965; p. 7. Karpeles & Schofield (A Selection of 100 English Folk Dance Airs), 1951; p. 18. Raven (English Country Dance Tunes), 1984; p. 37. Sharp (Country Dance Tunes), 1909; p. 43.

↑ Anne G. Gilchrist, "Some Additional Notes on the Traditional History of Certain Ballad-Tunes in the Dancing Master", Journal of the English Folk Dance and Song Society, vol. 3, No. 4, Dec., 1939, p. 275).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Boatman Tune
description:
| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Tune Name | The Boatman Tune |
| Key | D |
| Tuning | Standard (GDAE) |
| Tradition | Old-Time / North Carolina Fiddling |
| Known Performer | Lauchlin Shaw |
| Recorded | 1989 |
| Recording Event | Festival of American Fiddle Tunes |
| Recorded By | James T. Newberry |
| Collection | Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes |

"The Boatman Tune" is documented in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes, associated with North Carolina old-time fiddling, and is played in the key of D in standard GDAE tuning. The known recorded performance is by fiddler Lauchlin Shaw, captured in 1989 at the Festival of American Fiddle Tunes by recordist James T. Newberry.
Lauchlin Shaw is the primary fiddler associated with this tune in the archival record. He was a North Carolina fiddler whose repertoire was part of the broader documentation effort captured in the Milliner-Koken Collection, one of the most important archives of American old-time fiddle tunes.
The Festival of American Fiddle Tunes (held in Port Townsend, WA) has been a crucial gathering place for preserving regional fiddle traditions, and Shaw's 1989 concert recording is how this tune entered the wider old-time community's awareness.
The tune's name — "Boatman Tune" — suggests a likely connection to the boatman/riverman culture of the American South and Appalachia, a rich source of folk song and fiddle tune naming conventions (cf.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bob Tailed Mule
description:
Bob Tailed Mule comes from Kenner "KC" Kartchner — an Arizona fiddler born in 1886. Kartchner was an employee of the U.S. Forest Service from 1913 to 1956, and he was deeply rooted in the frontier culture of the American Southwest.

There are recordings of KC and his daughter Merle playing this and other of his tunes that are truly worth hearing.

The tune comes from the playing of Kenner "KC" Kartchner of Arizona fiddle fame. He was born in the late 1800s and played it on fiddle in cross A (AEae), sometimes referred to there as "The Italian" tuning.

The primary recorded source is a Jim & Kim Lansford recording on Vigortone Records — "Call Your Dogs" (2003) — learned from a 1943 field recording of Snowflake, Arizona fiddler Kenner Kartchner.

Geographic provenance: USA (Southwest). First documented in Stacy Phillips's *Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 1* (1994). (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Bob Walters' Hornpipe
description:
"Bob Walters' Hornpipe" comes from the playing of Bob Walters (1889–1960) of Burt County, east Nebraska. It is in cut time (C|), key of D, and is described as being played "Very Quick." It originated as an untitled piece captured in a 1954 field recording by Dwight Lamb — and the tune is played almost as a reel, with a little swing.

The tune was given its name posthumously by the old-time fiddle community to honor the man from whose playing it was documented. The recording was made by Dwight Lamb and the tune appears in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes, Old Time Fiddling From the State of Nebraska, and the Gettysburg Collection. The tune was passed down "by way of Keith Stubbs."

Robert E. "Uncle Bob" Walters was born on June 16, 1889, in Decatur, Burt County, Nebraska. His grandfather, Ike Walters, and his father, William Wilson "Wilse" Walters, were both noted fiddlers.

His brothers Sant, Harold, and Hiram all played fiddle as well as rhythm instruments. The entire family spent many hours honing the craft of old-time music. Bob married Goldie Brockway in 1910 and their home was soon filled with music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bob Walters Tune 113
description:
The title "Bob Walters Tune 113" is almost certainly a catalog or index reference from *R. P. Christeson's The Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory**, not a name Walters himself gave the tune. The 245 fiddle tunes in Christeson's book are indexed by tune number, and those numbers on reference sites correspond directly to the tune numbers in the Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory book. Many of Walters' tunes had no formal name. Walters had an extensive repertoire of tunes learned from many different sources — at one time he had written down over three hundred tunes for which he knew the names, and he played many others for which there were no titles. Untitled tunes were often cataloged simply as "Tune [#]" or attributed generically to their source fiddler — hence "Bob Walters Tune 113."

Transcriptions of Walters' music outnumber all others in R. P. Christeson's two volumes of The Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory*.

Robert E. "Uncle Bob" Walters was born on June 16, 1889, in Decatur, Burt County, east Nebraska. His grandfather, Ike Walters, and his father William Wilson "Wilse" Walters were both noted fiddlers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bone Yard
description:
A 'bone yard' in American rural parlance was either a cemetery, a place where animal carcasses were disposed of, or a junkyard of discarded machinery — all suggesting the aftermath of death and the long decomposition of material things. The name gives this Old-Time tune a memento mori quality unusual in the fiddle repertoire. Modal tunes with dark titles often preserved older folk practices of naming music for the full spectrum of human (and animal) experience, not just its bright moments.

Attributed to Garry Harrison. Geographic provenance: USA (Central). (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A tune with a spare, skeletal quality — play it without much ornamentation, letting the bare structure show. The modal quality and open string drones give it an austere, almost eerie feeling. Keep the bow arm relaxed but the rhythm precise. This is a tune that sounds better late at night than at midday.

title: Booth Shot Lincoln
description:
John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in Washington, DC on April 14, 1865 — five days after General Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Lincoln died the following morning. The assassination shocked the nation and transformed Reconstruction policy. That this event became the title of a fiddle tune reflects how deeply it penetrated popular consciousness — and how Old-Time music encoded American history in its repertoire. The tune circulated in both Northern and Southern communities with very different emotional valences.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: The most historically charged title in the Old-Time fiddle canon. Play it with the weight that event deserves — an event that changed American history on April 14, 1865. The minor-tinged quality should feel somber without being melodramatic. A tune that makes audiences stop and think.

title: Boston Boy
description:
BOSTON BOY. AKA and see "Take Me Back to Georgia," "Ladies in the Ballroom (2)," "Rattlesnake Bit the Baby." Old-Time, Bluegrass; Breakdown. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. The tune was a favorite of "Uncle Pen" Vanderver, a fiddler made famous by Bill Monroe's famous song (and Monroe's uncle). The 'A' part of "Boston Boy" is similar the 'C' part of "Texas Gales/Gals." 

Recorded sources: Rounder CD 0371, Mac Bendord and the Woodshed All-Stars - "Willow" (1996).

Jane Keefer's Folk Music Index: An Index to Recorded Sources 1

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bound to Have a Little Fun
description:
'Bound to Have a Little Fun' belongs to the category of Old-Time tunes that are essentially mission statements — announcing their purpose in the title. In the context of pre-radio Appalachian life, where entertainment had to be created rather than consumed, the determination to have fun was not trivial. Dance gatherings, music sessions, and community events were hard-won pleasures that required planning and effort. The tune celebrates that determination with unabashed joy.

Attributed to Adison Wallace. Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). BOUND TO HAVE A LITTLE FUN . American, Reel (cut time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. The tune was popularized by the playing of Kentucky fiddler Bruce Green, who learned it from Gusty Wallace. Gustace "Gusty" Wallace was born in Hart County, Kentucky, on November 24, 1890, but lived in Metcalf County, Kentucky, when Bruce Green visited him in the 1970's. Wallace claimed it was the first tune he ever learned, and that he had it from his father, Adison Wallace. The second strain c… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A tune whose title is its entire philosophy — play it with that determined, unrepentant joy. The rhythm should feel irrepressible. This is not a tune for careful, reserved playing; it's a tune for maximum enjoyment. If the bow arm isn't having fun, start over. A perfect session closer when everyone is warmed up.

title: Box the Fox
description:
BOX (THE) FOX. AKA and see "Double Hornpipe," "Blockhouse Dutchman." American, Reel. USA, central and southwestern Pa. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1894) gives that 'box the fox' means to rob an orchard, i.e. steal apples, in British and Irish usage. See also the similar first strain of the Trois copains' "Reel Ti'phonse," recorded in Montreal in 1939.

Source for notated version: - Issac Morris (Greene County, Pa., 1930's) Bayard.

Printed sources: -  Bayard (Dance to the Fiddle), 1981; No. 299B, p. 253.

Recorded sources: - Folkways Records, Bruce Hutton - "Old Time Music, It's All Around." Rounder 0132, Bob Carlin - "Fiddle Tunes for Clawhammer Banjo" (1979. Learned from Washington D.C. revival musician Bruce Hutton, who had it from a Pa. source). Revonah Records RS-924, "The West Orrtanna String Band" (1976. Identified as a "popular breakdown" in the York County, Pa., area for many years).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Boy In The Gap
description:
"Boy in the Gap" is an Irish reel in D Major, in standard AABB fiddle tuning. It is a lively dance tune in 4/4 time, typically played at a moderate to fast tempo.

The most colorful and widely accepted explanation comes from Irish accordion master Paddy O'Brien's notes to his tune collection:

Before the founding of the Gaelic Athletic Association (G.A.A.) in 1884, hurling was played openly in fields and byways. The boy in the gap was the goalkeeper — the last defender — in a game where one parish would take on a rival parish. If the ball went past him, his job was to retrieve it and whack it as far as possible into the territory of the opposing team, which might number more than a hundred. These sports contests more often than not turned into ferocious faction fights.

Another interpretation: a "gap" in this context is simply an opening in a hedge or stone fence — making "the boy in the gap" whoever was posted to guard or stand in that opening.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Boys Around The World
description: Boys Around The World is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Boys My Money's All Gone
description:
BOYS, MY MONEY'S ALL GONE 1. American, Reel (cut time). A Dorian or Mixolydian/Dorian. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Charlie Bowman Old-Time versions of "Money in Both Pockets" are sourced to a February, 1929, recording by East Tennessee fiddler Charlie Bowman 1 (1889-1962) and His Brothers, called "Moonshiner and His Money", which was Columbia Records first entree into recording early country music. "Moonshiner and His Money" was a skit with music, along the lines of the Skillet Licker's successful similar recordings. There were two tunes played in between banter, "Money in Both Pockets (3)" and "Boys My Money's All Gone (1)."

Source for notated version: - East Tennessee fiddler Charlie Bowman Phillips.

Printed sources: -  Kaufman (Beginning Old Time Fiddle), 1977; p. 97. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), vol. 1, 1994; p. 35. Reiner (Anthology of Fiddle Styles), 1979; p. 97.

Recorded sources: - Columbia 15387-D (78 RPM), Charlie Bowman and His Brothers (1929). County Records 507, Charlie Bowman - "Old Time Fiddle Classics." County CD 3511, Charlie Bowman = "Rural String Bands of Tennessee" (1997).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Brandywine
description:
BRANDYWINE. American, Reel (cut time).  G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB.  "Brandywine" was perhaps named after the famous mountain music festival held in southeastern Pennsylvania.  The tune is played by both bluegrass and old-time musicians, although the versions can differ.  Bluegrass fiddler Kenny Baker's version is similar to the version played by old-time musicians in the second strain, which is similar to the first strain in old-time versions.

Printed sources: -  Songer and Curley (Portland Collection, vol. 3), 2015; p. 42.

Recorded sources: - County 2705, Kenny Baker - "Master Fiddler."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Brasstown
description:
"Brasstown" is an Old-Time reel composed by fiddler Donna (of Fiddling Demystified), and along with the Celtic air Raven's Wing (co-written with guitarist Max Cohen), it has made its way into the fiddling canon.

The tune is featured in Donna's original tune collection, Hand Made Tunes, a collection of 39 original tunes with fully-styled bowings and chords and bonus viola and cello transcriptions. Two are Max Cohen originals, three are co-written with Max, and another is her Irish twist on a Jane Rothfield Old-Time tune.

The tune is named after Brasstown, North Carolina, a small mountain community in the western part of the state that has a long and rich musical heritage. Its most famous institution, the John C. Campbell Folk School, was founded by Olive Dame Campbell, who collected the music of the region, including ballads and fiddle tunes. Today, people from all over the world travel to the Folk School to begin their day with Morningsong and attend classes in everything from mandolin playing to blacksmithing.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Breaking Up Christmas
description:
In Appalachian tradition, 'Christmas' extended from December 25 through January 6 (Old Christmas or Epiphany) — a twelve-day season of visiting, feasting, and dancing. 'Breaking up Christmas' was the final community dance that ended this extended holiday, marking the return to ordinary work life. The tradition was strongest in Virginia and North Carolina; folklorist Patrick Mullen documented the custom in detail. The tune carries both the festivity of Christmas and the melancholy of its ending.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: One of the most evocatively named tunes in the Old-Time tradition — 'breaking up Christmas' refers to the end of the holiday season, when neighbors gathered one last time for dancing and music. Play it with the festive, slightly bittersweet energy of a party ending. A strong, driving tempo is traditional.

title: Breezy Point
description:
"Breezy Point" is credited to Jane Rothfield, appearing as an original composition on her album In the Moment.

The album features a mix of traditional old-time tunes and songs alongside original new compositions. Jane leads on fiddle throughout, and also showcases her touch on banjo and a strong, clear singing voice.

The concept behind the project was to replicate the experience of playing with a group of musicians who are well versed in traditional idioms and willing to let the music surge in spontaneity. This means "Breezy Point," while an original composition, is firmly rooted in the old-time tradition and written to feel at home in that style.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Briar Picker Brown
description:
"Briarpicker Brown" comes from the fiddle playing of Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas, who died in 1974 at the young age of 39 and was from Emerson, Kentucky (Lewis County).

He played some bluegrass and country music but favored old-time fiddle tunes. He died unexpectedly in 1974 at the age of 39, and Kitty Puss is his only commercial recording.

The melody is known as a Kentucky tune in modern times, largely due to an influential recording by Buddy Thomas. However, Thomas had learned the tune from an elderly Portsmouth, Ohio, fiddler named Morris Allen. The tune structurally resembles West Virginia fiddler Clark Kessinger's "Everyone to the Puncheon," and Allen was in fact a friend of Kessinger.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: British Field March
description:
The story of "British Field March" is really a story about three people across roughly a century of American history — a war-era fifer, an Appalachian fiddler, and a folklorist.

The tune was learned from Quince Dillion, a fifer in the Mexican War, and an old man when Henry Reed was a boy. The tune is sourced to the repertoire of fifer Quince Dillon, who said it was a British field march from the War of 1812. A relative, William Dillon, was a soldier and fifer in the American Revolutionary War.

So the Dillion family had deep roots in American military fife-and-drum culture spanning from the Revolution through the Mexican-American War.

In calling this piece "British Field March," Quince said that it was the march used by the British to retreat in the Battle of New Orleans, where Andrew Jackson and his American forces routed the British contingent.

First documented in Stacy Phillips's *Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 2* (1995). (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Brown Button Shoes
description:
BROWN BUTTON SHOES. American, Reel (cut time). USA, northeastern Ky. G Major ('A' part) & C Major ('B' part). Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB (Phillips): AA'BB' (Reiner & Anick). The tune was also in the repertoire of Portsmouth, Ohio, fiddler and instrument repairer Jimmy Wheeler (1917-1987), who learned it either from his father or Acey "Aaa" Neal. Jeff Goehring says it was one of the "not-strictly Kentucky"  tunes "popular among Portsmouth area fiddlers of an earlier era" 1.  Joe Stamper (Lewis County), another northeastern Kentucky fiddler, played a distanced version of the tune (which he also called "Brown Button Shoes"). 

Source for notated version: - Joe Stamper & Morris Allen via Buddy Thomas (Ky.) Reiner & Anick, Phillips. 

Printed sources: - Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 38. Reiner & Anick (Old Time Fiddling Across America), 1989; p. 102. 

Recorded sources:   -Rounder 0032, Buddy Thomas (northeast Ky.) - "Kitty Puss: Old Time Fiddle Music From Kentucky" (1976).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Brownie's Reel
description: Brownie's Reel is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Buck Mountain
description:
BUCK MOUNTAIN. American, Reel. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB' (Phillips, Silberberg): AA'BB (Songer). Buck Mountain is in northwestern Albermarle County, Virginia, the only peak in its vicinity and a fairly prominent local feature. The tune is sourced (by Pete Vigour) to a fiddler from Woodridge, in southern Albemarle County, Virginia, by the name of Napoleon Bonaparte "Uncle Nip" Chisholm, active in the 1930's. "Uncle Nip" derived his nickname from his drinking habits, says Vigour, and not from a shortening of his given name. The tune was popularized regionally by a group called the Virginia Vagabonds, formed in 1932, whose guitar player, Earl Smith, was related to Chisholm and learned the melody from him (the elderly fiddler was perhaps his great uncle). Remarkably, the Virginia Vagabonds survived as a band, with some original and near-original members, into the 21st century. Fiddler Armin Barnet, the source for the tune in The Portland Collection and who is credited with popularizing it among 'revival' fiddlers, went to graduate school in Charlottesville, N.C., in the early 1970's and picked up the tune from regional players. The Vagabonds, however, played the tune in the key of G Major with the parts reversed from the printed versions, and with a more old-fashioned feel, says Vigour.

Source for notated version: - Pete Sutherland (Vermont) Phillips; Armin Barnett (Seattle) via Sally White (Scio, Oregon) Songer; Gary Moore (New Jersey) Kuntz; Peter Boveng Silberberg.

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 39. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 18. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 41.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Buckskin Reel
description:
Buckskin — deer leather tanned using the deer's own brain — was the primary clothing material for Native American peoples and early European frontiersmen throughout North America. Daniel Boone, Davy Crockett, and other frontier heroes were depicted in buckskin in popular imagery. By the 19th century, 'buckskin' had become synonymous with frontier self-reliance and practical craftsmanship. Tunes with frontier-clothing names — buckskin, linsey-woolsey, homespun — evoked the aesthetic of practical self-sufficiency.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A frontier-energy tune — buckskin (tanned deer leather) was the quintessential clothing material of the American frontier. Play it with the direct, unadorned quality of buckskin itself: no frills, just function. The rhythm should be solid and dependable. A good all-purpose session tune that works at any tempo.

title: Buckwheat Batter
description:
BUCKWHEAT BATTER.  American, Jig (6/8 time). A Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Though West Virginia's Tweedy Brothers 1928 recording shared the name Buckwheat Batter with modern Canadian versions (see "Buckwheat Batter (2)"), the tune is different than Messer's and predates Messer's recording. Buckwheat Batter is in the repertoire of Western Maryland fiddler Shawn Craver and is similar to the Tweedy recording.

Printed sources: -  E.F. Adam (Old Time Fiddlers Favorite Barn Dance Tunes for the Violin), 1928.

Recorded sources: - Gennett 6604 (78 RPM), 1928, Tweedy Brothers (W.Va. brother band Harry, Charles and George, who played twin fiddles and piano). Gennett 3292 (78 RPM), 1926, Tom Owen's Barn Dance Trio of WLS (Paul Tyler says that Owens, a caller, was a native of Missouri).

 Hear the Tweedy Brothers' 1928 recording at youtube.com 1

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bug In The Taters
description:
"Bug in the Taters" was recorded by Al Hopkins and His Buckle Busters on May 14th, 1927, in New York City. It was paired with "Boatin' Up Sandy" and released as Brunswick #182.

The recording was made for Brunswick Records, with fiddler Charlie Bowman credited on the label. For this session, the lineup included Bowman and Elvis "Tony" Alderman on fiddles, Jack Reedy on banjo, Elbert Bowman on guitar, and John Hopkins on ukulele. Dance calls were vocalized by Al Hopkins.

Only Bowman is credited on the label for this tune, but on the flip side, "Boatin' Up Sandy," both Bowman and Alderman are credited with the fiddling.

Al Hopkins and His Buckle Busters were the same group as The Hill Billies. The group's releases on Vocalion were credited to The Hill Billies, while their Brunswick releases went under the Buckle Busters name — in many cases, the same recordings appeared on both labels. "Bug in the Taters," however, is only known to have been released on Brunswick, making it distinctly a Buckle Busters track.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Bull at the Wagon
description:
BULL AT THE WAGON. American, Reel (cut or 2/4 time). USA; Texas, Oklahoma. A Major. Standard or AEae (Lewis Brothers) tunings (fiddle). AABBCC. Recorded in El Paso, Texas, by the Lewis Brothers (Dempson, b. 1891, on fiddle and Denmon on guitar [1]) for Victor in July, 1929, who are the source for the reel. Oklahoma fiddler Earl Collins learned his version from the Lewis Brothers (or, as some say, from Tom Sauber), but altered it somewhat, especially in the 'A' part. See also the related tunes "Karo" and "Red Bird." 

The Lewis Brothers were originally from San Antonio, Texas, although the family relocated to Crow Flat, New Mexico, in 1902, when they were still boys. Denmon Lewis (1894-1977) played the guitar but also played the fiddle. In 1969, when interviewed by Charles Faurot for liner notes to County Records 517 ("Texas Farewell: Texas Fiddlers 1922-1930") at the age of 75, he still worked daily on his cattle ranch in Otero County, New Mexico. Isaac Dempson "Demp" Lewis (1890-1960) was the duo's primary fiddler on recordings but they both played the instrument for local dances and organized dances at Liberty Hall, El Paso. It was through an entrepreneurial woman who ran some of these dances that they were introduced to the Victor A & R representative, who had the duo record four sides on July, 11th, 1929 (all of which were released), including their most famous tune, "Bull at the Wagon." 

Source for notated version: - Dempson Lewis (Texas) [Brody]; Earl Collins (Oklahoma) [Milliner & Koken, Phillips]; Hank Bradley (Seattle) [Silberberg].

Printed sources: -  Brody (Fiddler's Fakebook), 1983; p. 58. Fiddler Magazine, vol. 21, No. 3, Fall 2014; p. 27. Clare Milliner & Walk Koken (The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 86.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bull of the Woods
description:
In Southern logging camp culture, the 'bull of the woods' was the woods foreman — the authority figure who commanded the logging crew and set the pace of work. Logging was one of the most physically demanding and dangerous occupations in Appalachia, and the social hierarchy of the logging camp was intensely masculine. Tunes named for logging figures and activities — 'Bull of the Woods,' 'Lumberjack Polka,' 'The Logger's Boast' — commemorated this important regional industry.

Attributed to Paisley Hagood. Geographic provenance: USA (Deep south). BULL OF THE WOODS. American, Reel (cut time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. The tune is sourced to Limestone County, north-central Alabama fiddler and farmer Paisley Hagood (1905-1977) (see note for " annotation:Old Abbott " for more on Hagood). "Bull of the Woods" refers to a foreman of a lumber or railroad crew in Canada and parts of the United States. In the northwest the term refers to someone important or self-important, which probably was in more general usage and must have bee… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A powerful, dominant-energy tune — the bull of the woods was the biggest, strongest man on a logging crew, and this tune should feel like him. Keep the bow arm heavy and confident. The rhythm should be absolutely unshakeable. A great tune for demonstrating strong tone production and a commanding presence.

title: Bummer's Reel
description:
BUMMER'S REEL [1]. AKA and see "Fletcher's Delight," "Levantine's Barrel," "Reilly's Own," "Tullamore Piper (The)."  American, Reel (cut or 2/4 time). USA; Pennsylvania, Vermont. G Major (Howe): A Major (Bowman). Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB.  The tune was printed by S.S. Stewart (Phila., Pa.) in a piano/banjo arrangement (by Thomas J. Armstrong)  in 1884. Stewart was a music publisher as well as a banjo manufacturer. Bayard (1981) finds no particular antecedents from the British Isles or Europe, and believes it may be an American composition that perhaps derived from Irish tradition; at any rate he says it was a great favorite with Pennslvania fiddlers. He did find an Irish tune, "Bean an Tighe ar Lar" (Woman of the House), with an 'A' part that was similar to the 'A' part of "Bummer's Reel," but with a different 'B' part. O'Neill maintains the piece is similar to "Cows Are a-Milking (The)," while Bayard finds another Irish tune with similarities under the title "Maighstreas an Ti" (Lady of the House). Some versions of "Bummer's Reel," keeping in mind that many American variants have considerable differences, are similar to the American tune "Peaches and Cream." R.P. Christeson (1973, p. 109) gives a tune, "Breakdown No. 155" from Bob Walters (Burt County) [Nebraska], and identifries the parent tune as "Bummer's Reel." A version also appears in Howe's collection, c. 1860.

Source for notated version: - Harvey Thompson (Pa.) [Christeson]; Harry Daddario (Union County, Pa.) [Guntharp]; Bayard (1981) gives 10 versions from 10 different southwestern Pa. fiddling and fifing sources; Elmer Barton (Vt.) [Phillips].

Printed sources: -  Bayard (Hill Country Tunes), 1944; No. 49 (appears as an untitled reel). Bayard (Dance to the Fiddle), 1981; No. 247A-J, pp. 206-209. A.S.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: A Bunch Of Chickens
description:
Bunch of Chickens is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown from Indiana, USA, played in G Major with standard fiddle tuning, in an AABB form.

The notated version is sourced from John Summers of Indiana, as transcribed by Phillips in Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, Vol. 1 (1994), p. 42.

It was also recorded on Rounder 0194 — John W. Summers, "Indiana Fiddler" (1984). This makes John W. Summers the primary known carrier and recording source of the tune. The Rounder Records release is the earliest documented recording.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Burt Anderson's Tune
description:
BURT ANDERSON'S TUNE. American, Reel (cut time). C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. "Burt Anderson's Tune" is from the playing of Cumberland Plateau fiddler Clyde Davenport, born in 1921, of Monticello, the county seat of Wayne County, south-central Kentucky (on the border with Tennessee).  The title was perhaps originally 'Byrd Anderson'.

Source for notated version: - 

Recorded sources:   -  

See also listing at:

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bye Bye My Honey I'm Gone
description:
"Bye Bye My Honey I'm Gone" was a "coon song" written in 1885 or 1886 by Virginia songwriter and journalist Monroe H. "Rosey" Rosenfeld (c. 1861–1918), the son of German immigrants and the man credited with coining the phrase "Tin Pan Alley."

It was set to a schottische melody — a popular mid-tempo dance form of Central European origin — giving it the bouncy, lilting feel that would eventually translate so naturally to fiddle playing.

> ️ Note: The term "coon song" refers to a deeply racist genre of the 19th-century popular song industry. The original lyrics reflected the ugly racial caricatures common to that era.

The song was recorded in the infant cylinder recording medium in 1897 by comedian and singer Billy Golden, and the composition was adapted as a patriotic song in 1918, also with the title "Goodbye, My Honey, I'm Gone," with words and music credited to James Reese Europe, Noble Sissle, and Eubie Blake.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: By The Waterfall
description:
Waterfalls were sacred and recreational sites in Appalachian culture — sources of water power, swimming holes in summer, and objects of aesthetic wonder. The Appalachian mountains contain hundreds of significant waterfalls, from Looking Glass Falls in North Carolina to Blackwater Falls in West Virginia. In the Romantic tradition that permeated 19th-century American culture, waterfalls represented the sublime — the overwhelming power and beauty of nature that humans could witness but not control.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A meditative, flowing tune — let the bow arm mirror the water's movement. Long, smooth strokes work better than short, detached ones. The waterfall setting suggests both beauty and power; the music should have both qualities. Play slowly enough to hear the individual notes sustain and blend. A tune that rewards patience.

title: C&A Breakdown
description: C&A Breakdown is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cacklin Hen
description:
"Cluck Old Hen" (Roud 4235), also known by variants like "Cacklin' Hen," is a popular Appalachian old-time tune usually in the mixolydian or dorian mode. It is played either as an instrumental or with lyrics, which vary from one version to another.

Important distinction: "Cacklin' Hen" and "Cluck Old Hen" are titles that are similar and sometimes confused; however, "Cacklin' Hen" generally refers to a different tune played in the key of G Major.

The earliest text found dates to 1886, appearing in the article "South Texas Negro Work-Songs," included in Rainbow in the Morning (Dallas, 1926, reprinted 1965 & 1975).

It was one of the first country music recordings ever made, in 1923, by north Georgia musician and entertainer Fiddlin' John Carson (1868–1949), who called it "Old Hen Cackled and the Rooster's Going to Crow." A year later, Chattanooga fiddler Jess Young added a part in the key of C in his recording of the same name (Taylor's Kentucky Boys and the Short Creek Trio also released their versions on 78 RPM).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Caliche Creek
description:
Caliche (pronounced ka-LEE-chee) is the hardpan calcium carbonate layer found just below the surface in arid and semi-arid soils across the American Southwest, Great Plains, and parts of Texas. For farmers and ranchers, caliche was a genuine obstacle — too hard to plow through, impeding drainage and root growth. Creeks flowing through caliche country had a distinctive milky appearance. The tune likely originated in the Texas fiddle tradition, which developed its own distinct character from Appalachian styles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A Southwest-inflected tune — caliche is the calcium carbonate crust that forms in arid soils of the American Southwest and Great Plains. Play with a slightly different character than Appalachian creek tunes: drier, more open, with less of the lush mountain sound. A tune that feels like a different landscape.

title: Calico
description:
CALICO. AKA and see "Want to go to Meeting and Got No Shoes." American, Reel (cut time). USA; Mississippi, south-central Kentucky. A Mixolydian ('A' part) & A Major ('B' part). AEae or GDgd tuning (fiddle). ABB. There is an Appalachian fiddle tuning called 'Calico' tuning, or AEac#, but source Bowles' tune plays much easier in when the instrument is tuned in AEae or GDgd. A different "Calico (2)", often called "Marcus Martin's Calico" and a different tune, is played in AEac#, or 'Calico' tuning.

Calico is an all-cotton fabric woven in plain, or tabby, weave and printed with simple designs in one or more colors. Calico originated in Calicut, India, by the 11th century, if not earlier, and in the 17th and 18th centuries calicoes were an important commodity traded between India and Europe. 

A tune by this name was learned by south-central Kentucky fiddler Jim Bowles (1903-1993) from local musicians, although his cross-tuned version was supposedly not widely known outside his area. Jim Nelson maintains that Bowles learned the tune from Thomas Page (Titon, 2001). Titon says the melody is similar to Marcus Martin's "Citaco."  The tune was recorded by Herbert Halpert for the Library of Congress from the playing of Lauderville County, Mississippi, fiddler Stephen B. Tucker in 1939. A rhyme sung to the tune goes:

Don't care where in the world I go,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Calico Corn
description:
Calico corn — also called Indian corn, flint corn, or ornamental corn — is a heritage variety of maize with multi-colored kernels in patterns of purple, red, yellow, blue, and white. It was grown by Native American peoples throughout North America and adopted by European settlers who used it for food (cornmeal, hominy), animal feed, and decoration. The autumn harvest of calico corn was a communal activity that culminated in corn-shucking parties — community events with music, food, and dancing.

Attributed to Gib Ingram. Geographic provenance: USA (Central). First documented in Garry Harrison and Jo Burgess's *Dear Old Illinois* (2007). Calico corn is also known as Indian corn, and has kernels that have red, yellow, and brownish red striping and mottling.

Recorded sources : - Field Recorders Collective FRC 607 - "The Indian Creek Delta Boys" (2015). Marimac 9059-CD, Lynn `Chirps' Smith - "Midwestern Harvest" (1994).

See also listing at: Hear a version from Chirps Smith at the Old Towne School of Folk Music's Fiddle Tune Archive [1] Hear a learning version from Paul Tyler at the Old Towne School of Folk Music's Fiddle Tune … (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A cheerful, harvest-time breakdown — calico corn (multi-colored Indian corn) was both a food crop and a decorative autumn staple. Keep the rhythm bright and energetic. This is a tune for the harvest dance, played after the corn is in the crib and the hard work is done. Let the bow bounce.

title: California Cotillion
description:
CALIFORNIA COTILLION. Old-Time, Cotillion or March. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. "California Cotillion" comes from the Ballard Branch Bogtrotters' recording for the AFS/Library of Congress, around 1941. Galax, Va., fiddler Eck Dunford remarked to the collector Lomax that he learned "California Cotillion" from a fellow Galax musician, Hicks Ring, who had moved to Nebraska, then returned with "tunes he learned from the Germans." The name California was given to the land on the Pacific coast of North America, supposedly by Cortez, who officially called it Santa Cruz. Cortez mistakenly thought the rather parched bit of real estate was an island (i.e. Baja California) and he and his men began to refer to it as California after a Spanish romance book about an island populated by women. 

Source for notated version: - Jere Canote [Phillips].

Printed sources: - Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 27.

Recorded sources:   -

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Camp Chase
description:
Camp Chase in Columbus, Ohio was a Union prisoner-of-war camp that held Confederate soldiers from 1861 to 1865. At its peak it held 8,000–9,000 prisoners in conditions that were desperately overcrowded; approximately 2,260 Confederate soldiers died there, mainly from disease. The camp cemetery still exists in Columbus. Tunes named for Civil War camps — Camp Chase, Camp Douglas, Andersonville — carried the weight of that experience for the communities that lost men to those places.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A reflective, minor-tinged tune named for one of the Civil War's notorious Northern prisoner-of-war camps. Play it with restraint and gravity — this is a tune about confinement and suffering. The melody has a quality of quiet endurance. Let the phrases breathe and don't rush the resolution.

title: Camp Meeting on the Fourth of July
description:
Camp meeting revivals were a central institution of 19th-century American religious life — outdoor gatherings lasting days or weeks where preachers, musicians, and thousands of worshippers camped together for an extended period of communal prayer and conversion. The Fourth of July was often chosen for camp meetings because it maximized attendance. The combination — patriotism and evangelical religion — captured two of the most powerful currents in 19th-century American culture and the music that expressed both.

First documented in Gene Silberberg's *Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern* (2002). CAMP MEETING ON THE FOURTH OF JULY . American, March. D Major. Standard or DDad (tuning). AB. James Bryan has said that the tune was originally played as a processional for evening services at camp meetings in Arkansas in the 19th century. Bryan's source was Tom Jackson, who learned it from Coleman Barwick, an old-time fiddler from Blountsville, Alabama. (Not to be confused with similarly-titled melodies "4th of July at the County Fair" or "At a Georgia Camp Meeting").

Additional notes Sourc… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A joyful, celebratory breakdown combining two great American institutions: the camp meeting revival and Independence Day. Play it with maximum energy and enthusiasm. This tune should feel like 300 people clapping and singing in a field. Don't hold back — this is a tune about unreserved collective joy.

title: Carroll County Blues
description:
CARROLL COUNTY BLUES. Old-Time, Country Blues or Two-Step. USA; Mississippi, Missouri. A Major (Brody, Phillips): G Major (Beisswenger & McCann, Reiner & Anick). Standard tuning (fiddle). AAB (Brody, Reiner & Anick): AA'B (Beisswenger & McCann, Phillips). "Carroll County Blues" was the Mississippi fiddle and guitar duo Narmour and Smith's biggest hit recording. The original melody is said to have been composed by fiddler Will Narmour (1889-1961) and was named for his home county, Carroll County, north-central Mississippi, but whether Narmour actually composed it is in dispute. Narmour, however, did record the tune with a man named Shell (Sherril) Smith, whose wife, it has been written, recalled that Narmour may have heard the tune either being whistled by a black farmer (according to David Freeman), or hummed by a black field hand (remembers Henry Young). This farmer claimed authorship and called the tune "Carroll County Blues." Narmour and Smith then "worked the tune out," presumably meaning that they arranged it for fiddle and guitar. Narmour is known to have been friendly with black bluesman Mississippi John Hurt, who lived in nearby Avalon.  It has also been maintained, ostensibly by older community members in Avalon, that Narmour's mentor, Gene Clardy, an older local fiddler, was the one who composed "Carroll County Blues." However, the story about the black farmer is also disputed, and, further, it may be that Gene Clardy neither wrote nor played the tune.

Gary Stanton, in his article "All Counties Have Blues: County Blues as an Emergent Genre of Fiddle Tunes in Eastern Mississippi" (North Carolina Folklore Journal, vol. 28, no. 2, Nov.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Catlettsburg
description:
Division Street, CatlettsburgCATLETTSBURG. American, Reel (cut time). USA, eastern Ky. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'.  There are Catlettsburgs in Ohio and Kentucky, although the title probably honors a small town in Boyd County at the confluence of the Ohio and Big Sandy rivers in the far northeastern part of the state by the West Virginia border.  It was named for an early pioneering family, Alexander and Horatio Catlett, who settled the area at the end of the 18th century. The town was also early known as Mouth of Sandy and Big Sandy Landing. Alexander's son opened a post office using the name 'Catlettsburg' in 1810, although the town itself wasn't established until 1849 when the then owner of the former Catlett farm subdivided the land into individual town lots. By the end of the 19th century Catlettsburg enjoyed economic success as a result of the timber industry1, although by 1920 the boom times had passed. 

"Catlettsbury" is one of several tunes regionally influential fiddler wikipedia:Ed_Haley (1885-1951) named for places he frequented and played, perhaps (as his son Lawrence suggested) because people there liked that particular tune2. Haley also lived in the Catlettsburg-Ashland area of Boyd County, KY, from at least 1920 until his death in 1951 [Brandon Kirk].

Source for notated version: - Ed Haley (eastern Ky.) [Phillips].

Printed sources: -  Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 100. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 44.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cauliflower
description:
CAULIFLOWER.  American, Reel (cut time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). ABC. The tune seems unique to Portsmouth, Ohio, fiddler and instrument repairman Jimmy Wheeler's (1917-1987) repertoire.

Printed sources: -  Field Recorders Collective FRC 4001, "Jimmy Wheeler" (2004).

Recorded sources: - Hear Jimmy Wheeler's recording at Slippery Hill [1]

Back to Cauliflower (1)

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cello
description:
CELLO. American, March (?. 4/4 time). USA; Ohio, Michigan. A Minor ('A' part) & C Major ('B' part). Standard tuning (fiddle). AAB. The title is pronounced with a soft 'C', as in "celebrity." Al Smitley collected the tune from an elderly fiddler by the name of Ray Shepard whom (in May, 2000) was still playing in his 80th decade. Smitley says: "Shepard grew up in southern Ohio and it was there that he learned the tune.  He moved to Michigan (south of Saline) when he was a young man." Origins are obscure, but it may have been a minstrel tune or a part of a quadrille. 

Source for notated version: fiddler Al Smitley of Michigan's Ruffwater Stringband [Johnson]. 

Printed sources: Johnson (The Kitchen Musician's No. 7: Michigan Tunes), vol. 7, 1986-87; p. 12.

Retrieved from "https://tunearch.org/w/index.php?title=Annotation:Cello&oldid=325047"

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Centennial Foxtrot
description: Centennial Foxtrot is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: (Old) Chattanooga
description:
(Old) Chattanooga is a traditional fiddle tune from the Walden's Ridge / Sequatchie Valley area near Chattanooga, Tennessee. As music historian Charles Wolfe described it: "The hills and hollows of Walden's Ridge and the Sequatchie Valley stretch northeast from Chattanooga toward Knoxville in a bewildering pattern of rugged terrain and isolated grassy valleys. Though the mountains are not as spectacular as the Smokies further to the east, they have their own beauty; and though their culture is not as well documented, it has its own richness and variety. This is especially true of the music of the area."

It was in these mountains, near Chattanooga, TN, where Blaine Smith (1915–1997) spent most of his life. He started learning fiddle from his mother and uncle as a child and could play well by the age of ten.

Blaine Smith learned this tune from Bob Douglas in the 1920s. He also learned it from Bob Douglas's father. It was also known to other fiddlers and bands in the area.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Charlestown Gals
description:
The tune circulates under several names:
Charlestown Gals (Appalachian/old-time spelling)
Charleston Gals
Charleston Girls

These are generally considered the same tune or close relatives in the folk tradition.

The tune apparently originated in the minstrel tradition and appears in sheet music from the mid-1840s. This places it squarely in the antebellum American popular music scene, when minstrel songs were the dominant commercial entertainment form.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Charlie Wyler's Tune
description:
Unfortunately, after two thorough searches across old-time fiddle databases, tune history archives, the Fiddle Hangout forums, Slippery Hill, Smithsonian Folkways, and general old-time music resources, no documented information about a tune called "Charlie Wyler's Tune" could be found. The name does not appear in any indexed old-time tune repertory, fiddler biography, or online discussion.

This is actually very common in the old-time tradition. The majority of the old-time fiddle repertoire consists of very old tunes with no known authorship, and many of them have rich historical significance but exist only in local or regional oral traditions. Many important figures in old-time fiddling are known only in local oral histories.

Tunes named after specific fiddlers (e.g., "Charlie Wyler's Tune") are a classic example of the folk process at work. A neighbor, student, or admirer hears someone play something distinctive, names it informally after that person, and it circulates locally—sometimes never making it into any published collection or recording archive. Despite the fact that the majority of the old-time fiddle tradition consists of very old tunes with no known authorship, new fiddle tunes have always been written and are still being written today.

| Resource | Why It Helps |
|---|---|
| [The Session (thesession.org)](https://thesession.org) | Huge community-sourced tune database with discussion threads on obscure tunes |
| [Slippery Hill](https://www.slippery-hill.

title: Chase The Banshee
description:
The Fiddler's Companion classifies "Chase the Banshee" as an Irish Polka. However, players note it's hard to hear the Irish polka feel in most recordings — it has taken on a distinctly American old-time character as it passed through hands.

The clearest attribution in the old-time community points to the Flanagan Brothers, an influential Irish-American recording and performing group active in the 1920s–30s. Multiple old-time tune archives list the source as "Flannagan Brothers via Chirps Smith." The tune appears to have traveled from an Irish-American context into the American Midwestern old-time tradition.
