The earliest documented recording connection in the old-time world links it to the Coleman Archive, an Irish traditional music repository: fiddler Kevin McHugh (born 1925, Foxford, Co. Mayo) recorded it for the Coleman Music Center release "The Coleman Archive, vol. 2: The Home Place" (2005).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chase the Squirrel
description:
CHASE THE SQUIRREL [1]. AKA and see "The Maid That Dare Not Tell." American, Reel. USA, southwestern Pa. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). ABA. The title is a floating one, and this tune Bayard (1981) identifies as a composite made from combining or fusing strains from other tunes. The 'A' part is very reminiscent of "Shepherd's Hey" (see note for that tune). A tune with some similarities, esp. in the 'A' part, is "The Eighth of January" in Ford (1944). 

Source for notated version: George Strosnider (elderly fiddler from Greene County, Pa., 1930's) [Bayard]. 

Printed source: Bayard (Dance to the Fiddle), 1981; No. 16, p. 23.

Back to Chase the Squirrel (1)

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: (Old) Cheat Mountain
description:
Cheat Mountain in Randolph County, West Virginia rises to 4,848 feet — one of the highest peaks in the state. The Cheat River (which the mountain takes its name from) was reputedly named for its treacherous nature, which 'cheated' travelers who tried to ford it. Civil War skirmishing occurred on Cheat Mountain in 1861 in one of Robert E. Lee's first campaigns as a Confederate general. The area remained remote and wild well into the 20th century, home to a rich fiddle tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A mountain breakdown with a slightly deceptive quality built into its name — the Cheat Mountain area of West Virginia was wild, remote, and treacherous country. Play it with a slightly unpredictable energy. The rhythm should feel secure but not completely square. This tune rewards fiddlers who can play with confident looseness.

title: Cherry River Rag
description:
CHERRY RIVER RAG. American, Country Rag (cut time). USA, northeastern Ky/W.Va. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. Apparently Ashland, Ky., fiddler wikipedia:Ed_Haley was the only one to record this tune (at least prior to John Hartford), named for the Cherry River, part of the Kanawha-New River drainage basin of West Virginia. There are two forks of the Cherry, North and South, parts of which are today prime recreation areas. 

A shift to the second or third position on the violin will facilitate this tune.

Source for notated version: - Ed Haley (northeastern Ky.) [Phillips, Reiner & Anick].

Printed sources: -  Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 104. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 30. Reiner & Anick (Old Time Fiddling Across America), 1989; p. 97.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Chickadee's Polka
description:
CHICKADEE'S POLKA, THE. American, Polka. USA, New Hampshire. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. Composed by Peterborough, New Hampshire, accordion and piano player Bob McQuillen, October, 1975. McQuillen is one of the modern founding fathers of the contra-dance revival. 

Printed sources: Miller & Perron (101 Polkas), 1978; No. 79. McQuillen (Bob's Note Book #2); No. 44. 

Alcazar Dance Series FR 203, "New England Chestnuts" (1980).

Back to Chickadee's Polka

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Chicken Polka
description:
CHICKEN POLKA. AKA and see "Kyckling Polka." American, Polka. The melody was in the repertoire of northwest Pennsylvania fiddler Jehile Kirkhuff. It is of Swedish origin and is a novelty tune whose first strain is in imitation of the fowl. 

Back to Chicken Polka

Retrieved from "https://tunearch.org/w/index.php?title=Annotation:Chicken_Polka&oldid=325300"

	Manage cookie preferences

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Chicken Reel
description:
CHICKEN REEL [1]. AKA - "Performer's Buck." American, Reel (cut time). USA, Widely known. D Major. Standard or ADae tunings (fiddle). AABB (Brody, Ford, Phillips, Ruth, Spadaro, Sweet, Thede): AABBC (Bayard {Ireland}): AABBAACC (Krassen {Higgins}): AABBCDDAABBC'C' (Krassen {Summers}). "Chicken Reel" was composed by nineteen-year-old Joseph M. Daly (1891-1968) as a piano composition, and published in Boston in 1910.  It translated well to the fiddle (once moved to the key of 'D' from Daly's original key of 'C') and became a popular fiddler's piece.  The long glissando followed by quick eight notes is imitative of the jerky movements of the fowl.  Daly may have either adopted an existing folk melody or "composed" it from folk strains (Fuld, 1966, 1971). It was characterized as a "Performer's Buck" (i.e. buck dance). Regarding those folk strains, Bayard (1981) vaguely states that the tune may have been of Scottish or Irish in origin, and makes general reference to tunes in O'Neill without citing them. Though the tune is usually played in two parts several fiddlers have added variations. Miles Krassen states Indiana fiddler John Summers, whose roots were in the northern (US) tradition, had B and C parts which were probably composed by him and identifies the latter as a strain commonly found in hornpipes. Bayard collected another 'C' part from southwestern Pa. fiddler Walter Ireland and generally found the versions from that area of the country had little of the pronounced sliding that accompany the tune in the South. The melody was in the repertoire of Arizona fiddler Kenner C. Kartchner since the early 20th century and Bronner (1987) notes it was commonly played for dances in New York state at that time (often in combination with the tune "Black Cat").

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Chicken Under the Washtub
description:
The tune was written and recorded by Vivian Williams, a Pacific Northwest fiddler and folk music figure, who titled it "Chicken Under the Washtub." It is therefore a composed tune rather than a tune of anonymous traditional origin — though it was written in the old-time style.

The tune was later recorded by Jason Carter with the Del McCoury Band, lending it significant credibility in the bluegrass/old-time world — though as Williams noted, Carter "added a lot of blue feathers to the original chicken," and the original features a very mild chicken squawk incorporated into the melody.

There is reportedly "a long story behind the title," though Williams did not elaborate publicly in the forum discussion where this information surfaced. The title itself evokes a classic piece of rural American folk humor — hiding a chicken under a washtub being a well-known trope of country life and storytelling.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chief Logan
description:
The tune is named after Chief Logan (c. 1725–1780), also known as Tahgahjute, a prominent leader of the Mingo people (a splinter group of the Iroquois/Haudenosaunee who settled in the Ohio Valley region). Logan was famous for his initially peaceful relations with European settlers in western Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Ohio — and later for his devastating raids in retaliation for the Yellow Creek Massacre of 1774, in which his family was killed by colonial militia. His story culminated in "Logan's Lament" — an eloquent speech delivered at the end of Lord Dunmore's War (1774) — which became one of the most famous pieces of Native American oratory in early American history. Thomas Jefferson praised and reprinted it in Notes on the State of Virginia.

Logan's story was deeply embedded in the Appalachian and Ohio Valley frontier consciousness, which is the cultural heartland of old-time fiddle music, making him a natural subject for a commemorative tune.
Type: Old-time fiddle tune, typically in a major key (often A or D), with a driving, modal-flavored feel common to Appalachian fiddle traditions.
Form: Standard AABB 32-bar structure (two 8-bar parts, each repeated), typical of reels and breakdowns.
Regional tradition: Associated with West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Ohio old-time traditions — the very territory where Logan lived and died.
Related tunes: It shares melodic and structural DNA with tunes from the mid-Appalachian fiddle repertoire.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chiggers In The Bedsheets
description: Chiggers In The Bedsheets is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chinese Rag
description:
CHINESE RAG. AKA and see "Chinese Breakdown [1]." Old-Time. USA, Ga. (c. 1922). A version of "Chinese Breakdown."

Retrieved from "https://tunearch.org/w/index.php?title=Annotation:Chinese_Rag&oldid=325333"

	Manage cookie preferences

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cincinnati Breakdown
description:
The tune most commonly called "Cincinnati Breakdown" in old-time circles exists in a somewhat murky area of folk tune nomenclature. It travels under several related names — including "Cincinnati Hornpipe" and "Cincinnati Rag" — and the exact identity can shift depending on the regional tradition and the player. This naming fluidity is extremely common in old-time music.

Cincinnati, Ohio was a significant commercial and cultural hub in the 19th century, sitting at the crossroads of the Midwest and the upper South. It was a major river city on the Ohio River, and its name got attached to several fiddle tunes, likely because:
Tunes were often named after nearby cities or notable places by the fiddlers who played them
Most old-time fiddle tunes are in the public domain and have no known authorship, yet many have rich historical significance.

The most historically traceable "Cincinnati" tune is the Cincinnati Hornpipe, documented by old-time fiddler and educator Dan Levenson:
There is very little information on this version of the tune. It was first heard played by Chirps Smith at the Kent State Folk Festival in Kent, OH (around 1997), though no recording was made at that time.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cindy
description:
CINDY [1]. AKA and see "Cindy in the Summertime," "Cindy in the Meadows,"  "Get Along Home Cindy," "Git Along Cindy," "J'etais au Bal," "Old Time Cinda," "Run along Home Cindy, "Run along Home Sandy."  American, Song and Breakdown. USA; Arkansas, North Carolina, Tennessee, Kentucky, Georgia, Mississippi, Oklahoma. D Major (most versions): G Major (John Brown): A Major (Fuller/Leftwich). Standard or ADae tuning (fiddle). AB (Brody): AABB (Phillips/1989 {the 'B' part is 'crooked' in Phillip's version}): AA'BB (Phillips, 1994). A widely known frolic tune, appearing in many folk music collections and even old elementary school songbooks. The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954, and was recorded for the Library of Congress in 1939 by Mississippi fiddler John A. Brown. A very popular Cajun version of the tune, probably borrowed from the American song, is "J'etais au Bal" (I Went to the Dance Last Night).  Verses set to the tune are many, including several "floaters":

Cindy in the summertime, 

Can't have Cindy all the time, 

Don't want Cindy at all.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cleveland's March to the Whitehouse
description:
The tune refers to Grover Cleveland, the 22nd (and 24th) President of the United States. Cleveland is the only U.S. president to have served two non-consecutive terms (1885–1889 and 1893–1897). Folklorist Mike Yates (2002) believes the tune dates to one of Cleveland's election campaigns — most likely either 1884 or 1892, both of which were dramatic, hard-fought races that would have inspired folk composers of the day.

The tune is fairly well known in the Blue Ridge mountain area of western Virginia and North Carolina — a hotbed of old-time fiddling tradition. Like many tunes of its era, it was passed down orally through local fiddle communities rather than via formal notation or commercial recording.

The original composer is unknown — consistent with the old-time tradition. The great fiddlers do not play a tune the same way every time, and two fiddlers seldom agree on the same version, even of "traditional" tunes. "Cleveland's March" almost certainly emerged from the political campaign culture of the Gilded Age, when local fiddlers commonly wrote or renamed tunes to celebrate candidates and current events.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Climb the Golden Stairs
description:
CLIMB THE GOLDEN STAIRS. Old-Time, Breakdown. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. Though the titles are similar, the melodic material for this tune and the minstrel piece "Climbing Up the Golden Stair" is quite different. 

Source for notated version: Jere Canote [Phillips]. 

Printed sources: Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 54. 

Back to Climb the Golden Stairs

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Clyde Durst's Tune
description:
CLYDE DURST'S TUNE. American, Reel (cut time). USA, Missouri. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB. It is on Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. 

Source for notated version: Cyril Stinnett (Mo.) [Phillips]. 

Printed sources: Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 54.

Recorded sources: MSOTFA 007, Charlie Walden - "Draggin' the Bow" (1985).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: The Coast Is Clear
description: The Coast Is Clear is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Colonel Crockett
description:
This is one of the trickier cases in old-time tune history: there are actually (at least) two different tunes called "Colonel Crockett," and they are not the same melody.

Tune #1 — The Knauff "Virginia Reels" Version (Pre–Civil War)
The melody appears under this title in George P. Knauff's Virginia Reels, Volume III (Baltimore, 1839). This is an American reel, making it one of the earliest documented appearances of the name in print. There are actually two different tunes under the title "Colonel Crockett" in different editions of Virginia Reels, which adds to the confusion surrounding the tune's identity.

Tune #2 — The Bruce Greene / Kentucky Version
This version is an old-time breakdown in A Dorian, standard tuning, in AABB form — drawn from the playing of Kentucky fiddler Bruce Greene. According to the Fiddler's Companion, this "Colonel Crockett" (from Bruce Greene) is a version of "The Route." It is also known under the aliases "The Route" and "Jenny on the Railroad."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Coming Down From Denver
description:
"Coming Down from Denver" is an American reel (in 2/4 and cut time), played in A Major, rooted in the fiddle traditions of Missouri and Nebraska. It appears on Charlie Walden's list of "100 Essential Missouri Fiddle Tunes." When that list was being assembled, "Comin' Down From Denver" came up again and again from other musicians as a must-have.

The tune is far older than the "Denver" title suggests, and its print trail goes back well before Colorado was even a state:
The tune was published as early as 1864 by Howe in Boston under the title "Lardner's Reel", while a violin music collection published by George H. Coe in 1876 has it under the title "Old Gray Mare."
Blackface minstrel troupe leader James Buckley published a version as "King of all Reels" in 1860.
The 'A' part of the tune parallels "Lardner's Reel" but the 'B' part shows some modification.

So the melody circulated widely under many names throughout the 1800s long before it acquired its "Denver" identity.

The tune's survival and spread into the 20th-century old-time scene is most strongly tied to Missouri fiddler Cleo Pursinger (1909–1971):
Pursinger often played the tune in contests, including his appearances at Weiser, Idaho in the 1960s. Somewhat inexplicably, when he announced the tune, he gave it a title that included two alternate titles for the old melody: "Coming Down from Denver on a Trip to Galway Here and There."
Where "Trip to Galway" enters the picture is unknown.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Coming Up The Pike
description:
The tune's fuller name is "Coming Up the Turnpike," with "Coming Up the Pike" being the common short-form alias.

It is an American Reel rooted in the traditions of Arkansas and Missouri, played in C Major in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB part structure.

The tune is firmly planted in Ozark Mountains fiddle tradition. It was recorded for the Library of Congress in the early 1940s by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, from Ozarks fiddlers — among them William Bilyeu (1943) and Delbert McGrath (1942).
The Bilyeu Family (Ozark, MO): A prominent fiddling family from the Ozarks region who appear to be central to the tune's preservation and transmission.
Art Galbraith (1909–1993): Galbraith, who lived near Springfield, Missouri, learned the tune from one of several fiddlers in the Bilyeu family of Ozark, Missouri. He is the source for the notated (written-out sheet music) version of the tune.

title: Coon Dog 1
description:
The tune is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown, also known as "Coon Dog." It uses standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB form (two repeated parts).

The tune is known by the "Old Coon Dog" title in eastern Kentucky and central Appalachia, according to Jeff Titon (Old Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes, p. 66). It is deeply rooted in northeastern Kentucky hill country traditions, with multiple distinct (but related) versions circulating across the region.

Note that there were several tunes extant in northeast Kentucky and elsewhere that were called "Coon Dog" or "Old Coon Dog."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Coon Dog 2
description:
"Coon Dog" is not a single tune but rather a family of related but musically distinct old-time breakdown tunes that share the same name. There were several tunes extant in northeast Kentucky and elsewhere that were called "Coon Dog" or "Old Coon Dog." The Traditional Tune Archive catalogs at least four distinct numbered variants (Coon Dog 1–4), which is why you see designations like "Coon Dog 2."

The tune is known by the "Old Coon Dog" title in eastern Kentucky and central Appalachia, according to Jeff Titon (Old Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes, p. 66).

Coon Dog [1] is also known as "Raccoon's Tail" and "Lynchburg Town," and has roots in Oklahoma as well as the broader old-time tradition. Its notated source comes from fiddler Bill Grant of Delaware County, Oklahoma, as documented by Marion Thede.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cora Dye
description:
CORA DYE. American, Reel. USA, Illinois G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB.  According to the book Dear Old Illinois, this tune originally came from a woman named Cora Dye, who played the tune on the guitar.

A recording of farmer and dance fiddler Jim Reed playing it was taken June 14, 1972. The note from Dear Old Illinois says: "Learned by Mr. Reed from its namesake, a Benton area musician who was said to have played it on the guitar."

Source for notated version: - Jim Reed (Benton, Ill., 1972) [Harrison & Burgess], Laurie Andres (Seattle) [Silberberg].

Printed sources: -  Harrison & Burgess (Dear Old Illinois), 2007; Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 26.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cornhusker Frolic
description: Cornhusker Frolic is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Corn In The Crib
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Tune Name | Corn in the Crib |
| Key | G Major |
| Form | AABB (standard old-time two-part form) |
| Primary Source Fiddler | Blaine Smith |
| Genre | Old-Time / American Fiddle Tune |

The tune "Corn in the Crib" is catalogued in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes in the key of G, and is attributed to Blaine Smith. It also appears in the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource collection, listed as "Corn In The Crib" and credited to Blaine Smith, dated November 23, 2017.

Beyond these specific attributions, the tune's exact origins in terms of time and place are not well-documented in the historical record — which is typical of the old-time tradition as a whole. Most of the old-time fiddle repertoire is in the public domain and has no known authorship, though many of these tunes carry rich historical significance.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cotton Picker's Drag
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Full / Alternate Title | Cotton Picker's Rag (also called Cotton Picker's Drag) |
| Genre | Old-Time / Country Rag |
| Origin | USA — Missouri |
| Key | B Major |
| Tuning | Standard (GDAE) |
| Structure | AA′BB′ |

The tune was possibly composed by Missouri fiddler Ben Tinnon (1891–1975), leader of the band known as the Grinnell Giggers.

The band's curious name has a colorful regional backstory: as music historian Charles Wolfe explains, the name was taken from the practice of fishing with "gigs" (three-pronged forks) for a trash-fish called the grinnell, which could be found in the backwater pools left from the annual flooding of the Mississippi River in the Missouri/Arkansas border region.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cowboy's Dream
description:
There are actually two distinct fiddle tunes that go by the name "Cowboy's Dream," each with its own lineage. Here's a full breakdown:

| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Genre | American Reel (cut time) |
| Key | D Major |
| Region | Ohio (east/southeast) |
| Structure | AABB (or AABB') |
| Earliest Known Carrier | John W. Hutchison (1915–1979) |

John McCutcheon identifies "Cowboy's Dream" as an Ohio tune, although its origins are somewhat obscure.

The clearest thread of the tune's history traces back to a single fiddler:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cowhide Boots
description:
COWHIDE BOOTS. Old-Time, Breakdown. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB' (Phillips). Carthy Sisco's recording has the parts reversed from the usual order. The tune is to sourced to fiddler biography:Lyman Enloe (1906-1998), who was born into a musical family in Cole County, Missouri, on the northern edge of the Ozarks. He moved to central Missouri and played with a number of influential fiddlers, including Tony Gilmore.  

Sources for notated versions: - Armin Barnett (Seattle) [Phillips]; Carthy Sisco (learned from a tape of Lyman Enloe) [Silberberg]. Sisco (b. 1921), originally from Arkansas, lives in Washington state.

Printed sources: - Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 59.  Shull  (Uncle Pink and other Central Missouri Fiddle Tunes from Lyman Enloe). Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 27. 

Recorded sources:   -  MSOTFA 004, Lyman Enloe - "Rugged Road" (1976). Voyager CD 362, Carthy Sisco - "Rugged Road."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cranberry Rock
description:
CRANBERRY ROCK. American, Reel. USA, West Virginia. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. An irregular tune with similarities to "Billy in the Lowground (1)."

Source for notated version: - Burl Hammons (1908-1993, Pocahontas County, W.Va.) and Mel Marshall [Milliner & Koken, Phillips].

Printed sources: -  Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 131. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 59. Susan Songer with Clyde Curley (Portland Collection vol. 3), 2015; p. 54.

Recorded sources: - Reed Island Rounders - "Goin' Home" (2002).  Appalachian Music Group, "Chance McCoy and the Appalachian String Band" (2008).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Crapshooter's Rag
description:
Crapshooter's Rag is an Old-Time, Country Rag tune from Texas, USA. It is played in standard fiddle tuning with an AB structure.

The tune exists in two closely related but distinct versions: "Crapshooter's Rag" and "Texas Crapshooter" — and the authorship question is genuinely murky.
The Traditional Tune Archive credits "Texas Crapshooter" to composers Larken Williams & Hugh Farr, sourced from Hugh (1903–1980) and Karl (1909–1961) Farr of Rochelle, Texas, and Encino, California, transcribed from a 1930s radio broadcast.
One prominent old-time fiddling authority, Dave Reiner, noted that he believed it was Hugh Farr's brother-in-law, Larken Williams, who wrote Texas Crapshooter, "although Hugh definitely made it popular."
Another source noted that Farr "did not write Texas Crapshooter" and that another name was involved — the exact authorship remaining a point of debate among players.
The open question among researchers and players has long been: is this an old tune that pre-dates Hugh Farr's rendition, or could he have written it? The sheet music in the Phillips book credits Hugh Farr, "but that may just be for the version."

Hugh Farr's rendition of Texas Crapshooter has been described as "manic" — "very fast and intricate and in F" — and widely considered one of the most demanding versions of the tune.

Geographic provenance: USA (Southwest). First documented in R.P. Christeson's *Old Time Fiddler's Repertory vol. 1* (1973).

title: Creal Springs Breakdown
description:
"Creal Springs Breakdown" is a relatively obscure old-time fiddle tune named after the small town of Creal Springs, Illinois. Here is a full picture drawn from what the historical record offers:

Creal Springs is a small city in Williamson County, Illinois, located on the north slope of the Shawnee Hills in the southern part of the state.

The town was founded by Edward G. Creal (1835–1891) and boomed as a summer resort after mineral springs were discovered on his farm. Between 1890 and 1903, Creal Springs was one of the most popular spots in the Midwest, with four daily trains serving the town.

The town had a lively cultural life that could easily have fostered local music. The Creal Springs Seminary — later renamed the Creal Springs College and Conservatory of Music — operated from 1884 to 1916 and included a music department.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Creighton's Hornpipe
description:
CREIGHTON'S HORNPIPE. Old-Time, Hornpipe. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune was learned by Lotus Dickey and his brother Cyprien from a volume called The Young Violinist's Favorite No. 1 by biography:A.S. Bowman, printed in Chicago in 1891. The brothers bought the collection from a Sears catalog at the time they talked their father into buying them a fiddle. Albert Bowman, born around 1844,  was a journeyman violinist, bandleader and composer in Philadelphia and southeastern Pennsylvania. 

Source for notated version: -  Lotus Dickey (Indiana) [Phillips]. 

Printed sources: -  Bowman (The Young Violinist's Favorite No. 1), 1891; p. 15. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), vol. 2, 1995; p. 187. 

Recorded sources:   -  Marimac Recordings ‎9030, Lotus Dickey ‎– Fiddle Tunes From Orange County, Indiana Volume II" (1992).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Crockett's Honeymoon
description:
CROCKETT'S HONEYMOON. AKA - "George Ainley's Tune." AKA and see "Honeymoon Reel (1)," "Maid Who Left the Mountains (The)." Old-Time, Breakdown. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB (Songer): AA'BB' (Phillips). The name "Crockett's Honeymoon" (or, sometimes, "Crockett's Wedding") appears to have originated in the 1970's, attached (perhaps by George Ainley) to an untitled tune contained in a medley on a 1920's recording by Crockett's Kentucky Mountaineers. The alternate title "George Ainley's Tune" comes from the recording by the Fat Meat Boys. A similar American tune is "Maid Who Left the Mountains (The)," which may be the original ancestor to these variants. It has a similar title to the Irish reel called "Maid Who Left the County (1) (The)," which itself has a cognate tune entitled "Honeymoon Reel (2) (The)".  "Honeymoon Reel (1)", a close variant of the Irish "Honeymoon Reel (2) (The)" was printed as long ago as 1883 in the Boston, Massachusetts, publication Ryan's Mammoth Collection. The "Maid" and "Honeymoon" titles thus appear to weave in and out of each other in both Irish and American tradition. See also the cognate "Lady Mary Drummond's Reel" from Alexander's 50 New Scotch & Irish Reels & Hornpipe (c. 1826).

Source for notated version: - Ruthie Dornfeld (Seattle, Washington) [Phillips]; Ron Andrico (Portland, Oregon) [Songer].

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 62. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 56.

Recorded sources: - Brunswick 291 (78 RPM), Crockett's Kentucky Mountaineers - "Medley of Old Time Dance Tunes." Rounder CD 0397, Scott Nygaard - "Dreamer's Waltz" (1996). Varrick VR-038, Yankee Ingenuity - "Heatin' Up the Hall" (1989).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Crook Brothers Breakdown
description:
The tune's name traces back to one of the most storied acts in early country music. The Crook Brothers had more than 63 years on the Grand Ole Opry, and cut their first record with RCA in 1928. The band was built around Herman Crook and his brother Matthew Crook, who were both harmonica players — the group's defining sonic signature. In 1931, Matthew left to work for the Nashville Police Department, and Herman, maintaining that he could not find a good enough harmonica player, for the first time added a fiddle to the band.

For a time, Kirk McGee was the fiddler, and when he quit to join the Dixie Liners, he was replaced by Floyd Ethridge, who remained with the group through the 1930s. Ethridge was a native of McEwen, Tennessee, and came from the same West Tennessee–Dickson County area that spawned Arthur Smith and Howdy Forrester. He had performed with a young Arthur Smith at local square dances and fiddling contests, and had a fondness for playing in a fast, high style, relying on quick fingering of the E string.

The brothers recorded four instrumentals for RCA-Victor in 1928, which sold well, but those were surprisingly the only recordings by the Crook Brothers until 1962. Eventually, the deaths of so many old-time musicians resulted in the remaining members of the Possum Hunters and the Crook Brothers combining into one band, which continued to play on the Opry until Herman Crook died in 1988.

"Crook Brothers Breakdown" is not part of the Crooks' recorded output, at least not under that title.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Crow Creek
description:
"Crow Creek" is an Illinois fiddle tune, rooted in the old-time hoedown tradition of the American Midwest. "Here in the State of Illinois this tune is known as Crow Creek." Its precise authorship is murky, as is common with folk tunes passed orally through generations, but the trail leads back to one source in particular.

The most credible attribution points to Stelle Elam, an Illinois fiddler. The Dear Old Illinois book credits the tune to Stelle Elam, though beyond that, detailed biographical information is hard to come by. The tune is described as "this somewhat odd version" coming from the playing of Stele Elam, and recordings of hers are preserved on archive.org.

The tune entered wider circulation through the important regional collection Dear Old Illinois. It appears on Track 5 of CD 1 in the triple-CD collection of the same name. It is catalogued as Hoedown #53 in the Dear Old Illinois book, where it is notated in the key of D.

The tune has circulated in more than one key, which has caused ongoing debate in the old-time community:
The tune has been published in A, but many players have always played it in D—some tracing this preference back to at least 1981.
Both keys appear in play: "N5CP is in D and this one is in A," though some players perform it in cross E tuning (EBEB).
There's also debate about resolution: "Some folks play it in D. Some folks don't resolve the A part (ever). Some resolve it sometimes and not others."

title: Crow Little Rooster
description:
CROW LITTLE ROOSTER. American, Reel (cut time). A Major. Standard or AEae tuning (fiddle). AB.  Sourced to Oklahoma brothers Max (1916-2001) and Earl (1911-1975) Collins, members of a large family that included several well-regarded fiddlers. The family was originally from Branson, Missouri, but moved to Pottawatomie County, Oklahoma. Earl Collins eventually removed to southern California, but Max reminded in Oklahoma.

Source for notated version: -  

Printed sources: -  Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 29.

Recorded sources Swing Cat 1618, Hart & Blech - "Devil of a Row" (1999).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cuckoo's Nest
description:
'Cuckoo's Nest' is among the oldest tunes in the English-speaking world's folk repertoire, with documented appearances dating to at least the early 18th century across multiple traditions simultaneously. In England, it survives as a Cotswold Morris dance tune associated with villages including Bledington, Ilmington, and Longborough — some scholars date its Morris use to the mid-17th century. In Scotland, it appears as a reel under the same name, with attribution theories pointing to Scottish origins. It crossed the Atlantic with Scots-Irish immigrants and entered the American old-time repertoire, where it appears in regional collections throughout the 19th century. The cuckoo of the title carries both ornithological meaning (the cuckoo was the harbinger of spring in British folk tradition) and bawdy implication — 'cuckoo's nest' was a common euphemism in 18th-century popular songs, and the playful energy of the tune suits both readings. Its universality — Morris dance, Scottish session, Appalachian breakdown, New England contra dance — makes it one of the most cross-traditional tunes in the English-speaking world.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: D major with a bright, rollicking quality that has made it a crowd-pleaser across three centuries and two continents. The AABB structure is symmetrical and easy to pick up, which is why it works in so many different dance contexts. The American old-time version tends to drive harder and sit lower in the bow arm than the English Morris or Scottish session versions. Learn all three if you can — the interpretive differences reveal how the same melody can serve completely different musical communities.

title: Cuffy
description:
CUFFY. AKA - "Cuffey." American, Reel. USA; southwestern Va., western North Carolina. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Brody). Known as a tune and tune-name peculiar to the Franklin/Floyd County area of southwestern Va., say Tom Carter and Blanton Owen (1976); also known as a Surry County, North Carolina, regional tune (says Kerry Blech). It was, for example, in the repertoire of N.H. 'Nicky' Mills, of Boone's Mill, Virginia, south of Roanoke (as identified by Joel Shimberg). Mills was apparently the source for the tune among modern 'revival' fidders. A rather taciturn individual, he valued his privacy and when Armin Barnett visited him he abjured the younger fiddler not to let anyone know about him: "If anyone asks about me, tell them I'm dead." Which Armin did, until it was true. Shimberg doubts whether the tune was current in North Carolina prior to its being disseminated by Barnett. Armin was the source for the tune for the Highwoods String Band, who recorded an influential version on their album "No. 3 Special," after which it was in the common repertoire of "revival" fiddlers of the 1970's and 1980's. 

The name 'Cuffy' has a long history in America as a slave name, especially on the minstrel stage where it was regularly employed by blackface dancers and musicians. "For example," says Hans Nathan (Dan Emmett and Negro Minstrelsy, Univ. of Oklahoma Press, 1962, pg. 44), "{the period actor} Edwin Forrest lent his great talents to a personification of Cuffee, a Kentucky Negro, opposite the black Miss Philisy, in the play The Tailor in Distress; or, A Yankee Trick. Performing in Cincinnati in 1823, Forrest probably enlivened his act with singing and dancing.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Curmudgeon's Fancy
description: Curmudgeon's Fancy is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cut Knife Hill
description:
CUT KNIFE HILL. Canadian, Reel. E Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). "Cut Knife Hill" was composed by Métis fidler John Arcand, born in 1942 near the Debden-Big River region of northwestern Saskatchewan.  The title references a battle near what is now Battleford, Saskatchewan, during the North-West Rebellion of 1885, in which a band of Cree were attacked by surprise by the Canadian military.  

Source for notated version: - 

Recorded sources:   -  

Back to Cut Knife Hill

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Cutting At The Point
description:
"Cutting At The Point" is a relatively obscure old-time fiddle tune with no widely published, single-source origin story. Like the majority of old-time tunes, its composer and precise origin are unknown or disputed.

"Most of the old-time fiddle repertoire is in the public domain and has no known authorship" — yet many of these tunes carry rich historical significance.

Fiddle tunes are part of an oral (or aural) tradition, and with lots of variations, nobody knows exactly where most of them came from.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Damon's Winder
description:
Back to Damon's Winder 

DAMON'S WINDOW/WINDER. AKA - "Damon." AKA and see "Rocky Mountain Goat," "Railroading Through the Rocky Mountains." American, Reel (cut time). D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. A version of  "Marmaduke's Hornpipe", although some versions have a 'C' natural note instead of a 'C' sharp in the third and fourth measures. Kerry Blech explains a 'winder' is a type of dance-set in Kentucky where the figure winds about ('winder' is sometimes erroneously converted to 'window' in tune title). It was recorded in 1934 under this title by Kentucky fiddler J.W. Day under his pseudonym, Jilson Setters, and was in the repertoire of several central and east-central Kentucky fiddlers. See also related tunes "Devil in Georgia (2) (The)," "Hell Among the Yearlings," "Mud Fence," "Ride the Goat Over the Mountain," "Railroading Through the Rocky Mountains," "Rocky Mountain Goat," "Swiss Chalet," "Grand Hornpipe (1)," and "Cricket on the Hearth." The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.

Source for notated version: -  

Recorded sources:   -

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dance All Night
description:
DANCE ALL NIGHT. AKA- "Dance All Night with a Bottle in Your Hand," "Danced All Night with a Bottle in My Hand," "Give the Fiddler a Dram (1)," "Give Me a Bottle of I Don't Know What."  American, Song/Reel (cut time). USA: West Virginia, Virginia, western North Carolina, north Georgia, Alabama, Nebraska.  G Major (most versions): D Major (Silberberg). Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Brody, Christeson, Phillips) or AABAACCB (Kuntz, Brody). A fairly wide-spread song/instrumental Guthrie Meade thinks the tune has some relation to "Buffalo Gals." Rosenbaum (1989) points out that the 78 RPM recording by Gid Tanner and the Skillet Lickers [1] for Columbia was very influential, especially in Georgia (in fact, the melody is known as a north Georgia tune). His source, Georgian  Lawrence Eller, learned the tune/song from family tradition and Rosenbaum concludes (apparently on the strength of the floating verse about hanging Jefferson Davis) from this that the lyrics bespeak Unionist loyalties in parts of the southern Appalachians. 

Dance All Night with a bottle in my hand,

Bottle in my hand, bottle in my hand;

Dance All Night with a bottle in my hand,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dance Around Molly
description:
DANCE AROUND MOLLY. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA; Missouri, North Carolina. A Major. Standard or AEae (Art Stamper) tunings (fiddle). AABB (Phillips, Silberberg): AA'BB' (Beisswenger & McCann). A traditional dance tune collected in Missouri and North Carolina. "Well-known tune among Missouri fiddlers" (Frank Maloy), and indeed, it has been recorded by (and is associated with) several fiddlers from that state. It is on Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'.   Howard Marshall says the reel is associated with fiddlers from the north and central part of Missouri, such as Jake Hockemeyer, Johnny Bruce, Cleo Persinger, Taylor McBaine, Pete McMahan, and Charlie Walden. Howard says: "All the fiddlers I've known credit Jake Hockemeyer with the best version anywhere and it was one of Jake's fiddle contest "money tunes." I played backup guitar for Hockemeyer in several contests in the 80s when he played the tune to good effect even though by that time his arthritis problems were getting him down. The tune is what I'd call a hornpipe." The melody has lost some currency in modern times among contest players in the state. 

Tommy Magness (1916-1972) with Bill Monroe (mand.) Bill Wesbrooks (bass) and Clyde Moody (gtr.), early 1940's. Photo courtesy of James Monroe."Dance around Molly" was played by Tommy Magness over WSM in the 1940's and the composition is often credited to him--certainly he popularizing it, as his 1951 recording was highly influential. According to one story in circulation, Magness composed the tune one night after a gig when eating in a restaurant with his band. A waitress named Molly started bantering with the band and got them to play a tune so she could dance to it.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dandy Lusk
description:
DANDY LUSK.  AKA - "Dandy Lusk's Tune." American, Reel (cut time). USA, Kentucky. G Major. DGad tuning (fiddle). AABB. A slightly 'crooked' tune. Fernando "Dandy Lusk" (b. 1890's) was a child of Letcher County, southeast Kentucky, fiddler Elvina "Viney" Campbell Lusk (b. 1870's), who, like his mother, played the fiddle. He died unrecorded save for a 1952 recording made at his home with clawhammer banjo player Lee Sexton (also from Letcher County). Elvina and Fernando were aunt and cousin of fiddler Manon Campbell (1890-1987) who was recorded by folklorists, and who also learned some of his repertoire from the Lusks.

Printed sources: -  Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 146.

Recorded sources: - MM-0030-CD, Clare Milliner & Walt Koken - "Just Tunes" (2003).

See also listing at:

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Darling Nellie Gray
description:
DARLING NELLIE GRAY. AKA - "Nelly Grey," "Old Nelly Grey." American, Air and Dance Tune. B Flat Major (Jarman): G Major (Perlman, Sweet): D Major (Johnson). Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Johnson, Sweet): AA'B (Perlman): AABB (Jarman). An abolitionist song composed by Benjamin Russell Hanby in 1856, while a student at Otterbein college, Ohio. Hanby was moved by the plight of a runaway slave named Joseph Selby, along with the efforts of Hanby's father to raise money to gain the freedom of Selby's beloved. The popular song became a rallying anthem for the abolitionist movement. It begins:

One night I went to see her, but she's gone the neighbors say, 

And the white man had bound her with his chain.

They have taken her to Georgia for to wear her life away

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Davey Come Back and Act Like You Oughta
description:
Erynn Marshall is an old-time fiddler who resides in Galax, Virginia, and has played for over 30 years, performing and teaching at music camps and festivals across North America, Europe, Australia, and China. She has won 1st place in fiddle at both the Clifftop and Mt. Airy Fiddlers Conventions.

The tune appears as the opening track on Erynn Marshall's album Calico, released December 13, 2012. She has recorded 9 CDs in total.

The tune is credited as "Arranged by Erynn Marshall" — suggesting it may be a traditional piece she shaped into its current form, rather than an entirely original composition. It is classified as an A Modal tune, which is a hallmark of the Appalachian old-time tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dean Reed's Favorite (Oh How She Lied)
description: Dean Reed's Favorite (Oh How She Lied) is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Devil Eat The Groundhog
description:
Devil Eat the Groundhog comes from Kentuckian Owen "Snake" Chapman (1919–2002), who learned it from his elderly father, Doc Chapman, born in 1850.

Doc Chapman's father is said to have helped Abe Lincoln build fences. Snake got his nickname from an Italian worker who visited the family home, giving Owen cookies and affectionately calling him "Blacksnake," the name of his pony.

Owen "Snake" Chapman hailed from Canada, Pike County, in southeastern Kentucky.

The tune comes with one of the best backstories in old-time music — and "Devil" is not the supernatural kind:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dickey's Discovery
description:
DICKEY'S DISCOVERY. AKA and see "Brisk Young Soldier," "King's Lament." Old-Time, Breakdown. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. A modern title for an older tune, named for Indiana fiddler Lotus Dickey (1911-1989) who 'discovered' it in 1985.  Later he remembered he had learned it (along with a number of other tunes) from fiddler Allen Downey, who came to Dickey's southern Indiana district from Robinson, Illinois (although Dickey said it was Robinson County, there is no such county in the state, although there is a town called Robinson 1).  Dickey's contemporary, Southern Illinois fiddler Mel Durham, had a version of the tune that he called "King's Lament" after George King, a blacksmith and a fiddler in Johnsonville, Illinois.  Harvey Taylor's (1894-1987, Effingham, Illinois) "Brisk Young Soldier" is cognate it the first strain of the tune but the second strains differ. See also the related "Crow Creek." 

Source for notated version: -  Lotus Dickey (Orange County, Indiana) [Phillips].

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 70. 

Recorded sources:   -Marimac 9020, Lotus Dickey - "Fiddle Tunes from Orange County, Indiana, vol. 1," (1989). Marimac 9022, Volo Bogtrotters - "Backside of Buncombe" (1989).  Vigortone Recordings, Lotus Dickey - "Down the Pike and other Fiddle Tunes from Orange County, Indiana" (2013. Reissue of Marimac 9020).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dick Sand's Hornpipe
description:
Dick Sands was a celebrated stage performer of step dancing in the United States during the latter half of the 19th century (1860s on), who also sang and did "Irish character" performances.

A publication by J.F. Finn (New York, 1879/1880) bears his name: Dick Sands' Irish Jig, Clog and Dance Book, described as "a history of the personal, political and professional sentiments and peregrinations of Dick Sands with complete and practical instructions in the art of clog-dancing."

He was closely associated with P.T. Barnum's shows. Barnum did have fairy-tale and nursery rhyme themes in his shows, and his circus parade featured floats based on these themes, including a mother goose float that perhaps Sands was associated with.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dill Pickle Rag
description:
DILL PICKLE RAG. AKA - "Dill Pickles." Texas Style, Old-Time; Country Rag. USA; Texas, Tennessee, Virginia, Arkansas, Missouri. G Major ('A' and 'B' parts) & C Major ('C' part): sometimes then goes to F Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). ABC (Silberberg): AABBCCAA (Brody): AA'BB'AA'CAA'BB'AA'C'AA' (Phillips). A novelty rag composed in 1907 by Kansas City native and resident Charles L. Johnson [1] (1876-1950), a publisher and prolific composer (under his own name and aliases), especially of cakewalk and ragtime pieces for piano. Johnson also was an accomplished string player who joined several guitar and mandolin societies, and who started several string orchestras. See also his "Hen Cackle Rag." 

Charles L. Johnson (1876-1950)

"Dill Pickles" is one of his most famous compositions (and a personal favorite of the composer), recorded over thirty times on 78 RPM recordings. The piece obtained its title when Johnson was working at Carl Hoffman Music Company. Johnson was polishing his newly composed piece at work, when the company's bookkeeper inquired as to its title. Noticing that the clerk was carrying a carton of pickles for his dinner, Johnson relied, "I'll call it Dill Pickles Rag" (Jasen and Tichenor, Rags and Ragtime: A Musical History, 1978, p. 39). It was fairly quickly absorbed into old-time tradition due to the many available recordings. The title appears in a list of "traditional" Ozark Mountain fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954. 

"Dill Pickle" was learned by itinerant West Virginia fiddler John Johnson (1916-1996), originally from Clay County, from fiddler Dorvel Hill who lived in a coal-mining town called Pigtown, not far from the town of Clay, W.Va.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dinah
description:
DINAH. AKA and see "Go to Sleep John Dinny." American, Reel (cut time). A Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Krassen). A member of a large and widespread tune family that includes "Heel Flies (1)," "Rock Along John to Kansas," "Seneca Square Dance," "Old Raccoon," "Coon Dog," and others. Samuel Bayard collected a vocal version of the tune in southwestern Pa. (see Bayard, Dance to the Fiddle, 1981; Appendix No. 25, pp. 582-583), but said it was known also as a dance tune. The alternate title comes from a ditty sung to the tune:

It’s go to sleep, John Dinny,

It’s go to sleep I say,

It’s go to sleep, John Dinny,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dirty Sheets
description: Dirty Sheets is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dixie Banner
description: Dixie Banner is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dixie Blossoms
description:
DIXIE BLOSSOMS. AKA - "Chicken Pie." American, Country Rag, Two-Step or Song Tune. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. The tune was remembered by fiddler Art Galbraith as dating to around 1916, and was "a perennial favorite of his mother" (Reiner & Anick). Beisswenger & McCann add that it was played by a cousin for Galbraith's who fought in World War 1. Galbraith also recalled "Byron Kelly, an old bass player, the only black man left in Christian County, used to be a professional, he liked this one a lot"1. "Dixie Blossoms" is a composition by ragtime and song composer Percy Wenrich (1887-1952) who composed it in 1906 as "Dixie Blossoms March-Two-Step." He was also the composer the music of "Put on Your Old Grey Bonnet" (1909) and the ragtime melody "Peaches and Cream" (1905), among many others, and was known for incorporating "folk" elements in his tunes2. Wenrich was born in Joplin, Missouri (he was known as "The Joplin Kid"), but moved to Chicago in 1901, and in 1909 removed to New York where he had a long and successful career in Tin-Pan-Alley. However, his early influences were from his mother, an accomplished amateur pianist, and from the booming club and music scene in Joplin, home to several important ragtime composers and performers, black and white. A similar tune is "Chicken Pie," collected in Reynolds County, Missouri, however, it is not the "Chicken Pie" in Marion Thede's book, which is an unrelated tune.

Source for notated version: - Art Galbraith (1909-1993, near Springfield, Missouri) [Beisswenger & McCann, Phillips, Reiner & Anick].

Printed sources: -  Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 38. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 41. Reiner & Ancik (Old Time Fiddling Across America), 1989; p. 122.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dixie Hoedown
description:
DIXIE HOEDOWN. American, Reel (cut time).

Recorded sources: - Rounder 11661-0133-2, "Art Galbraith, James River Fiddler: Dixie Blossoms" (2007, extended reissue of 1981 LP).

Back to Dixie Hoedown

title: Doc Corn's Tune
description:
The tune comes from an Illinois fiddler named John Ray "Doc" Corn, documented on a recording made on his birthday in 1976. The tune was also recorded by Lynn "Chirps" Smith, another respected old-time fiddler.

John Ray "Doc" Corn was the grandfather of at least one musician active in the old-time community — described as "a good fiddler and a very fine gentleman."

He was born in Hamilton County, Illinois in 1893, and died in Franklin County, Illinois in 1984 — making him a product of a truly deep layer of Midwestern old-time fiddle tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dogs in the Dishes
description:
DOGS IN THE DISHES. American, Breakdown or Reel. USA, southwestern Pa. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. The first strain is shared with "Blockhouse Dutchman."

Source for notated version: - Irvin Yaugher (Fayette County, Pa., 1944; learned from fiddler Bill Lowry) [Bayard].

Printed sources: -  Bayard (Dance to the Fiddle, March to the Fife), 1981; No. 107, p. 62.

Back to Dogs in the Dishes

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dog Treed A Possum Up A White Oak Tree
description:
"Dog Treed a Possum Up a White Oak Tree" is a traditional old-time fiddle tune rooted in downstate Illinois. It is classified as a reel in D Major with an AABB structure, played in standard fiddle tuning.

The tune's primary origin traces to a single central Illinois fiddler:
"Dog Treed a Possum Up a White Oak Tree" is an Illinois fiddle tune learned from the late fiddler Howard Sims, who came from a family of fiddlers in Modesto, Illinois.
Howard Sims lived (approximately) 1896–1977, and was based in Modesto, Illinois.
Sims was a farmer from outside Modesto. He kept the fiddle up over the years and was a regular in the senior division (over 70) at the state fiddle contest, then held in Shelbyville.
His gravesite is located in Pulliam Cemetery in Modesto.

The tune passed through a clear line of fiddlers in central/southern Illinois:
The tune was learned from Howard Sims by Ivan Dodge, who played tunes together with Sims for forty years before the latter died.
It was also documented by Chirps Smith and associated with fiddlers Bill Rintz and Ivan Dodge.
Noted Midwestern fiddler Chirps Smith and Garry Harrison were doing extensive tune collecting from older southern Illinois fiddlers in the 1970s, which is likely how the tune was more widely preserved.
One modern performer learned it from Steve Rosen, their first fiddle teacher.
There are three Howard Sims tunes on the Dear Old Illinois CDs: Old Mose, Stump-Tail Dog, and Dog Treed a Possum Up a White Oak Tree.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Doney
description:
The tune was recorded in 1939 by Abbott Ferriss and Herbert Halpert for the Library of Congress, from the playing of Mississippi fiddler Charles Long, of Quitman, Clarke County, Mississippi. This is the most well-documented early recording of the tune in the old-time fiddle tradition.

The tune shares the same "fine phrase" (A-part) as "Goodbye Liza Jane (2)" as recorded by Georgia musician Fiddling John Carson, although Long's B-part ("coarse phrase") is different from the usual "Liza Jane" song air. This overlap points to a broader family of related Southern fiddle tunes and song-airs that were in common circulation in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

The word "dony" or "doney" is generally thought to have been a 19th-century slang term for a sweetheart or a woman, particularly in the frontier and Southern United States, among both Black and white communities. It was associated with Cockney and British circus slang, and sometimes considered somewhat vulgar, though it derives from common Italian and Spanish roots (likely from the Italian donna or Spanish doña, meaning "woman" or "lady"). This etymology suggests the word traveled to America via immigrant and traveling-show communities.

title: Don Tremaine's Reel
description:
DON TREMAINE'S REEL. Canadian, American; Reel. Canada, Ontario. D Major. Standard tuning. AABB (Brody, Phillips, Songer): AA'BB' (Kaufman). Composed by Barrie, Ontario, fiddler Graham Townsend, (copyright 1961) and named for the announcer of the CBC television show "Don Messer's Jubilee." The melody is a past favorite at New England contra dances.

Source for notated version: - Tom McCreesh and Jay Ungar (N.Y.) [Phillips].

Printed sources: -  Brody (Fiddler's Fakebook), 1983; p. 88. Kaufman (Beginning Old Time Fiddle), 1977; p. 18. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), vol. 1, 1994; p. 73. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 63.

Recorded sources: - Banff Records RBS 1083, Graham Townsend - "Famous Canadian Fiddlers vol. 1" (1960). Folkways FTS 31098, Ken Perlman - "Clawhammer Banjo and Fingerstyle Guitar Solos." Front Hall 01, Fennigs All Stars- "The Hammered Dulcimer" (1973). Voyageur Recordings VRLP 310-S, Gerry and Bobby Robichaud - "Down East Fiddling" (1973).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Dora Dean
description:
Dora DeanDORA DEAN. American, Country Rag (cut time). F Major ('A' part) & D Minor ('B' part). Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'BB'. This 'raggy' melody was composed by the great Black entertainer and comedian Bert Williams (1874-1922) and published in 1896 ("Oh have you seen Miss Dora Dean, She's the sweetest gal you ever seen"). Mark Wilson remarks that it was a popular piano piece around the turn of the 20th century; widely popular at the time, it was coined “The Greatest Coon Song Ever Written”.  The song was composed in honor of vaudeville entertainer named Dora (Babbage) Dean, an African-American woman who possessed great style, poise and personality, and flaunted in front of white crowds in ways that were unheard of by a Black performer.  Along with her partner and husband, Charles Johnson, she is credited with helping to popularize the Cakewalk dance. Their song-and-dance act took them abroad for months on end, touring Europe and even Australia. They performed in Hungary and Russia, even for England’s King Edward VII.

Say, have you seen Miss Dora Dean?

She is the finest gal you’ve ever seen;

I’m a-goin’ try  and make this gal my queen,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Down in Little Egypt
description:
DOWN IN LITTLE EGYPT.   American, Reel (cut time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. The tune was in the repertory of fiddler<tspan x="0" dy="1.2em">Noah Beavers (1897-1990), of Elkville, southern Illinois, collected by fiddler Lynn "Chirps" Smith. Beavers had no name for the tune, but Smith christened it "Down in Little Egypt" after the old nickname for southern Illinois, Little Egypt. </tspan>

Recorded sources: - Vigortone Recordings, Lynn "Chirps" Smith - "Down in Little Egypt" (2016).

Back to Down in Little Egypt

Retrieved from "https://tunearch.org/w/index.php?title=Annotation:Down_in_Little_Egypt&oldid=413612"

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Down The River
description:
"Going Down the River" is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in AABB form. It is associated with Kentucky, North Carolina, and Missouri.

"Going Down the River" was recorded for Victor Records in Memphis, Tennessee, in September 1928 by the Arkansas group Dr. Smith's Champion Hoss Hair Pullers, although it was not released by Victor until 1929. It featured the twin fiddling of Brian Lackey and Clark Duncan on the cut.

However, a very similar version had been recorded a year earlier by The Hill Billies (Tony Alderman & Charlie Bowman, fiddles) as "Boating Up Sandy", one of many different tunes by that title.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dr. Brown
description: Dr. Brown is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Drunken Hiccoughs
description:
"Drunken Hiccoughs" (also spelled "Drunken Hiccups") goes by a remarkable range of aliases, including "Drunkard's Hiccups," "Clinch Mountain," "Devil's Waltz," "Frosty Morning," "Jack of Diamonds," "Rye Whiskey," and "Way Up on Clinch Mountain." It is classified as an Old-Time and Texas-Style tune in 3/4 time — functioning as an air, waltz, jig, and song tune.

Folklorist Paul Clayton identifies the tune as "old and of English origin," and scholar Samuel Bayard associates it with the Scottish "Todlin Hame" tune family.

Bayard (1981) believed the piece was a vocal song before it became an instrumental, and identified a wide sweep of British Isles and American songs that use the same melody, including "Johnnie Armstrong," "Tod(d)lin' Hame," "The Wagoner's Lad," "Clinch Mountain," "Rye Whiskey," "Jack of Diamonds," and "Saints Bound for Heaven." Related instrumental variants from the British Isles include "Drunk at Night and Dry i' the Morning" and "Lude's Lament."

The tune is documented across a wide swath of America: Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Texas, and Arizona.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Drunken Hiccups
description:
DRUNKEN HICCUPS [1]. AKA- "Drunkard's Hiccups," "Drunken Hiccoughs." AKA and see "Clinch Mountain," "Cuckoo (5) (The)" (Ford), "Devil's Waltz," "Frosty Morning (3)," "Jack of Diamonds (3)," "Lame Beggar (The)" (Ire.), "The Mocking Bird" (Pa.), "My Name is Dick Kelly" (Ire.), "Rye Whiskey (1)," "Livre de Tabac (Un)" (A pound of tobacco), "Way up on Clinch Mountain." Old-Time, Texas Style; Air, Waltz, Jig, and Song Tune (3/4 time). USA; Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Texas, Arizona. A Major. AEac# (Brody, Jarrell, Reiner & Anick, Shumway): AEae (Ford) tunings. AABCC (Brody, Ford, Thede): AA'BB'CC'DD' (Reiner & Anick, Shumway). Paul Clayton identifies the tune as "old and of English origin," and Samuel Bayard associates it with the Scottish "Todlin Hame (1)" tune family. Arizona fiddler Kartchner called it a "favorite from the South," and, with the left-hand pizzicato passages (meant to suggest a hiccup), it was often a favorite showcase tune. Bayard (1981) states it was a vocal piece before it was an instrumental one, and identifies the following duple and triple time songs from the British Isles and America as using variants tune: "Johnnie Armstrong," "Todlin Hame (1)," "Bacach," "Robie donua gorach"/"Daft Robin," "Wagoner's Lad (The)," "Clinch Mountain," "Cuckoo (5) (The)," Rye Whiskey (1)
"Jack of Diamonds (3)," "Saints Bound for Heaven," "Separation," "John Adkins' Farewell. Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Duck River
description:
DUCK RIVER. AKA and see "Drum Tune,." "Dubuque," "Old Dubuque," "General Lee," "Hell on the Nine Mile," "Sally in the Green Corn." Old-Time, Breakdown. USA; Magoffin Count, Ky. D Major. Standard or ADae tunings (fiddle). AABB. Jeff Titon (2001) says the specific "Duck River" tune seems to be particular to the Salyer family, although it is part of a fairly common tune family. West Virginia fiddler Israel Welch played a version of this tune he called Forks of Cheat. Titon says the tune family to which "Duck River" belongs also includes "Ma Ferguson,"  "Nancy Dawson (2)," "Nancy Dalton," and "Hell Up Coal Holler (2)." See also "Mabel," "Possum Up a Gum Stump," and "Drum Tune."

Source for notated version: - John Morgan Salyer (1882-1952, Salyersville, Magoffin County, Ky., 1941) [Milliner & Koken, Phillips, Titon]; Alan Garren (Portland, Oregon) who learned it from the Bruce Greene recording [Songer].

Printed sources: -  S. Johnson (The Kitchen Musician No. 2: Occasional Collection of Old-Timey Fiddle Tunes for Hammer Dulcimer, Fiddle, etc.), 1982 (revised 1988, 2003); p. 8. Milliner * Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 173. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 2),  1995; p. 45. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 67. title: Duck's Eyeball
description:
DUCK'S EYEBALL [1]. AKA and see "Wait in the Kitchen (Till the Cook Comes In)." American, Reel. The title comes from one of the silly verses sung to the tune. Kerry Blech calls it a variant of "Richmond." "Duck's Eyeball" was in the repertoire of western Virginia fiddler Luther Davis (as "Right in the middle of a duck's eyeball"). It may have sometimes been called "Duck's Asshole." Tommy Magness recorded the tune in 1948 (along with many others in his older traditional repertoire) for a private recording for fiddler Roy Acuff on an old home disc recorder (Charles Wolfe, Classic Country, p. 148, 2001). John Hartford (in notes to Rounder 1131/1132, 1997) remarks that the tune is similar to a pair of northeast Kentucky fiddler Ed Hayley's "Stonewall Jackson" and his "Green Mountain Polka." "It also resembles Frazier Moss's 'Denver Belle' and Charlie Acuff's 'Wait in the Kitchen 'Till the Cook Comes In.' Curly Parker said the old time name was 'Swiss Galoplane.' Clark Kessinger called it 'West Virginia Special.'"

Back to Duck's Eyeball (1)

title: Dull Chisel
description:
"Dull Chisel" is a modern old-time tune by the late Illinois fiddle player Garry Harrison. His tune "Red Prairie Dawn" is possibly better known and is widely played by old-time players, but "Dull Chisel" has become the tune that truly spread through the community.

"Dull Chisel" was composed by the late Garry Harrison and appeared on his ca. 2000 CD Red Prairie Dawn. The CD went out of print some years ago, after which Garry made it available for free download on the web.

"Dull Chisel" was formed originally inside the mind of the late fiddler Garry Harrison and released on his album Red Prairie Dawn; in short order it found its way into jams and festivals all over — which is a rare thing. Most of the tunes that have become old-time jam staples are centuries old, but every now and then a tune of recent vintage and singular appeal works its way into the mix.
"Dull Chisel" is an original fiddle tune played in AEAE tuning.
It has two parts.
It is in the key of A, and is structured as a 4/4 reel.

A lot of people play it differently from the original in one or both of two ways: the high part was the A part in Garry's recording, but the low part is often played first in jams. Neither of these is necessarily a bad thing, but the way the tune is getting socialized is perhaps somewhat different from how the author wrote it.
Jack Burgess and the Stanly County Boys recorded a nice medley of "Road to Westfield" and "Dull Chisel," which appeared on their Patchwork Kimono CD (2003).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dunbar
description:
DUNBAR. American, Reel. USA, Kentucky. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Titon): AABB (Songer). Mark Wilson and Guthrie Meade (1976) remark that this tune is related to "Billy in the Lowground (1)", although it appears to have been a regional tune, perhaps, as its name suggests, from the area around Dunbar, West Virginia, near Charleston. "Dunbar" is one of several tunes regionally influential fiddler Ed Haley named for places he played, perhaps (as his son Lawrence suggested) because people there liked that particular tune1. Jeff Titon (2001) remarks that he knows of no other source musician who played the melody besides the regionally influential fiddler Ed Haley [1] (1885-1951), of Ashland, Ky. Ed Haley Originally, the name Dunbar was a Gaelic term meaning 'the fort on the hilltop'.

Source for notated version: - Ed Haley (1883-1951, Ashland, Boyd County, Ky., 1946) [Milliner & Koken, Titon]; Bruce Schwarz (Ketchikan, Alaska) [Songer].

Printed sources: -  Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of  American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 178. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 68. Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 36, p. 69.

Recorded sources: - Rounder 1010, Ed Haley - "Parkersburg Landing" (1976).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: The Dusty Miller
description:
"The Dusty Miller" is one of the most fascinating tune names in Anglo-American folk music — not a single tune at all, but a family of at least eight distinct melodies sharing the same name, each with its own regional roots, fiddlers, and story.

The oldest documented "Dusty Miller" is a popular and widespread late 17th-century tune in the old triple-time hornpipe metre, published in Scotland in 1730 in a volume labelled Dances, Marches, in Robert Bremner's Scots Reels (c. 1765), in Edinburgh fiddler and writing master David Young's McFarlane Manuscript (c. 1741), and in the Gillespie Manuscript of Perth (1768).

William Chappell (Popular Music of the Olden Time, 1859) identifies the tune not as Scottish but as English, noting it can be found in the first volume of Walsh's Compleat Country Dancing Master (1718) and other English collections — though most of those are later than the 1730 Scottish publication.

Chappell maintained that "Dusty Miller" is related to a melody from the Blaikie Manuscript (1692) for the lyra-viol entitled "Binny's Jig," which has a similar first strain and nearly identical melodic contour.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Eadle Alley
description:
EADLE ALLEY.  American, Reel (cut time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. The source for "Eadle Alley" is Braxton County, West Virginia, fiddler Melvin Wine (1909-2003), who said it 'was an old tune some cousins of mine used to play'. His cousins were the Allen family, who he said were 4th generation descendants of an Irishman. He did not know the meaning of the title or what it referred to.

Recorded sources: - HJM003MRR, Haints Old Time String Band - "Shout Monah" (2009).

See also listing at:

title: Ebb and Flow
description:
"Ebb and Flow" is a modern tune written by Carl Jones — it is not an ancient anonymous folk tune, but a composed piece in the old-time/traditional style that has been adopted widely into the folk session repertoire.

It comes from an album by Beverley Smith and Carl Jones, and is described as "a lovely tune written by Carl Jones that has gone viral in sessions around the UK."

Notably, the B part is beautifully crooked — meaning it has irregular or asymmetric phrasing, a hallmark that makes the tune especially distinctive and memorable to players.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Echoes Of the Ozarks
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Title(s) | Echoes of the Ozarks / Echoes from the Ozarks / Echoes of the Hills |
| Genre | American Country Rag |
| Region | USA, Missouri |
| Key | D Major (most commonly; also played in G, A, Bb, and B) |
| Structure | AB or AABB form |

The tune's roots go back further than its earliest recording. It is melodically similar to the popular song "Little Old Log Cabin in the Lane," written in 1871 (and popularized by Fiddlin' John Carson's 1923 recording), and appears to be, in fact, a song tune.

Going even deeper, the melody is traced to an 1874 song called "I'se Gwine Back to Dixie." Ira Ford (1940) and R.P. Christeson both mention that their versions have similarities with "The Yellow Rose of Texas." The tune thus sits at a rich crossroads of 19th-century American song traditions, absorbed and re-shaped by Ozark fiddlers over generations.

Missouri fiddler Sam Long (1876–1931), originally from Scranton, Kansas, but who also lived in Missouri and Oklahoma, recorded the tune (via acoustic, not electronic methods) in 1926, and despite the rather poor quality of the sound it sold well in the Mid-west and West.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Eli Green's Cakewalk
description:
Sadie G. Koninsky (August 1879 – January 2, 1952) was an American composer, music publisher, and music teacher who lived most of her life in Troy, New York. A prolific composer, she is thought to have authored over 300 pieces of music, including waltzes and marches. As a child, she received classical training in violin.

In 1896, a young woman named Sadie Koninsky from Troy, New York walked into a large New York City music publisher with a letter of introduction and a tune she had written. She was a department store clerk and ran a music counter. Dave Reed Jr., a well-known lyricist of the time, wrote some words, and Eli Green's Cakewalk became a hit. Who Eli Green actually was remains a mystery.

"Eli Green's Cakewalk" became a popular hit when it appeared in 1898 and was also the first cakewalk published by a woman. Its only real competition that year was At a Georgia Camp Meeting, written by Kerry Mills — also a cakewalk. Miss Koninsky never wrote another hit.

The original dance had African-American roots dating back to the early days of slavery in the South. On Sundays, when there was little work on the plantations, enslaved people would gather to do a high-kicking, prancing couple's "walk around," accompanied mostly by banjos, fiddles, and drums. It evolved in the 1890s into the dance that became wildly popular in fashionable ballrooms throughout the country.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Emmett Lundy's (Richmond) Cotillion
description:
Emmett Lundy was born in Grayson County, Virginia on May 9, 1864, one of nine children of Churchwell and Caroline Ward Lundy. From family records, the Lundys emigrated from England in 1687, and Emmett's great-grandfather John Lundy moved to Grayson County around 1787, acquiring land near Dalhart, just south of the present town of Galax.

As a young man, Emmett became absorbed in the music he heard around the community at dances, log rollings, pumpkin peelings, and other excuses for having a little fiddle music.

In his late teens, Lundy started the fiddle and immediately took up with an older fiddler named Green (for Greenberry) Leonard. Green Leonard lived in Old Town, just a few miles north of the Lundy home place. Leonard was a pretty old man when Lundy met him, probably born in the early decades of the 19th century. Although he was never recorded, Emmett and others declared Leonard as the best fiddler in the region. The older musician didn't like to share his tunes, but Lundy "caught" them anyway by hanging around Greenberry Leonard as much as he could.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Evening Shade
description:
EVENING SHADE. American, Reel (cut time). USA, Tennessee. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune is credited to Arthur Smith (1898-1971), born in Humphreys County, middle-eastern Tennessee, and is a slower tempo than the usual breakdown speed, and a change of pace from the usual blazingly fast Arthur Smith breakdowns. On a home recording by Arthur Smith's son, Ernest, the tune is entitled "Evening Shade Falling," although on Smith's LP it is listed simply as "Evening Shade." Arthur Smith

title: Fair Morning Hornpipe
description:
FAIR MORNING HORNPIPE. USA, West Virginia. Old-Time, Breakdown. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. A simple reel from the repertoire of Rush Fork, Clay County, W.Va., fiddler Wilson Douglas [1](1922-1999). Paul Mitchell finds that Cape Breton fiddler Joe MacLean recorded an almost completely identical tune, which he called "Nancy."
