The tune was "universally known to Pennsylvania fifers and some fiddlers," according to scholar Samuel Bayard (1981), who was not able to trace it back to British Isles antecedents — meaning it appears to be a distinctly American composition, likely originating in the Pennsylvania tradition rather than being transplanted from older European sources.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hooker's Hornpipe
description:
HOOKER'S HORNPIPE [2]. American, Hornpipe or Reel (2/4 time). USA; north Missouri, Nebraska. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The low part is reminiscent of Clayton McMichen's tune "McMichen's Reel." Hooker may refer to a fiddler, the Civil War general Joe Hooker, or, as Howard Marshall points out, to a laborer on a riverboat, a petty thief or pickpocket, a one-masted fishing boat, loggers, etc. "Hooker's Hornpipe [2]" is on Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'.

Source for notated version: - Bob Walters (Burt County, Nebraska) [Christeson]; Taylor McBaine [1] (1910-1994, central Mo.) [Phillips].

Printed sources: -  R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers' Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; p. 87. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 201.

Recorded sources: - Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association 002, Taylor McBaine (b. 1910, Columbia, Mo.) - "Boone County Fiddler." Voyager 340, Jim Herd - "Old Time Ozark Fiddling." Voyager VRCD 344, Howard Marshall & John Williams - "Fiddling Missouri" (1999. Learned from Taylor McBaine and Jimmy Gilmore of Jefferson City).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hop High Ladies
description:
'Hop High Ladies' is the American old-time descendant of 'Miss McLeod's Reel,' a Scottish reel that dates to the early 19th century or earlier. The primary melodic difference between the two is telling: the Scottish original ends phrases on the dominant (a harmonically open, questioning gesture), while the American version resolves to the tonic (settled, complete). This subtle shift transforms the feel of the tune from one of anticipation to one of satisfaction — fitting, perhaps, for the communal American dance tradition that adapted it. The tune's famous command — 'Hop high ladies, step lively too / Hop high ladies, the cake's all through' — connects it to the cakewalk tradition of Southern community dances, where the best dancers won a prize. Early recordings include versions by New England fiddlers, Appalachian string bands, and Midwestern dance orchestras, showing how thoroughly the tune permeated American folk music culture.

First documented in Viola "Mom's *Pioneer Western Folk Tunes* (1948). HOP HIGH LADIES (THE CAKE'S ALL DOUGH) . AKA and see " Billy Boy (2) ," " Did You Ever Go to Meetin' Uncle Joe Uncle Joe? " " Did You Ever See the Devil Uncle Joe? " " Gigue américaine ," " Green Mountain (1) ," " Hop Light Ladies ," " Knickerbocker Reel ," " McCloud's Reel ," " Miss McCloud's Reel ," " McLeod's Reel ," " Mrs. MacLeod of Raasay ," " Miss McLeod's Reel (1) ," " Miss MacLeod's Reel ," " Old Tom Kittypuss ," " Sally's Hornpipe ," " Uncle Joe ," " Walk Jaw Bone (1) ," " Whitewash… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: D major with a light, skipping quality that matches the 'hopping' of the title. The American version should feel grounded and complete — land on the tonic. The Scottish Miss McLeod's version, if you know it, will feel different by comparison. Good for singalongs: 'Hop high ladies the cake's all through / Hop high ladies, step lively too.' In dance contexts, the caller can work with the clear four-bar phrases. Keep the tempo brisk but not rushed.

title: Hopping Rabbit (Saut du Lapin)
description:
"Saut de/du Lapin" translates as "Leap of the Rabbit" or "Rabbit's Jump." It's rendered variously in English as Bunny Hop, Hop of the Bunny, Rabbit's Leap, or The Jumping Rabbit. There is also a subtle French nuance: "de Lapin" vs. "du Lapin" — the "du" form would specify a particular rabbit, rather than the more general sense.

It is a French-Canadian reel, rooted in the rich Québécois fiddle tradition. Many French-Canadian tunes have origins in Scotland, Ireland, Wales, and England, brought to the Americas by early settlers.

There are actually two distinct tunes that carry the name "Saut du Lapin," documented separately in the Traditional Tune Archive:

The notated version traces back to French-Canadian violinist Joseph Bouchard (1905–1980), passed on via Québec button accordion player Philippe Bruneau, and subsequently transmitted to American fiddlers Ruthie Dornfeld (Seattle) and Lisa Ornstein.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Horny Ewe
description:
"The Horny Ewe" (sometimes spelled Horney Ewe, and pronounced "Horny-O") is a tune by West Virginia fiddler Ernie Carpenter.

It appears consistently attributed to Carpenter across multiple old-time tune reference sources:
It is catalogued in the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource directly under Ernie Carpenter's name.
It is also included in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John S. Lamancusa, again attributed to Ernie Carpenter, notated in the key of A.

The tune is short, rhythmic, and a little crooked — meaning it has an irregular or non-standard phrase length, a hallmark of certain West Virginia old-time fiddle styles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Huckleberry Blues
description:
HUCKLEBERRY BLUES. AKA and see "East Tennessee Blues." Old-Time, Country Blues/Rag. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle).

Dykes Magic City Trio

Source for notated version: 

Recorded sources: Old Homestead OHCS 191, "Dykes Magic City Trio" (eastern Tennessee) {originally recorded for Brunswick, 1927}.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Huntin' for the Buffalo
description:
"Hunting for the Buffalo" goes by several alternate titles including "Hunting the Buffalo" and "We're Gonna Hunt the Buffalo." It's classified as an American Reel (cut time), rooted in Arkansas. It is typically played in A Major, using either standard or the unusual BEgb fiddle tuning.

The most important name in the tune's traceable history is Jimmy Driftwood — a legendary Arkansas musician. Mike Seeger plays a version learned from singer, songwriter, and fiddler Jimmy Driftwood (1907–1998, born John Morris of Timbo, Arkansas), who had the tune from his two fiddler uncles who lived in Indian Territory for years.

Jimmy said he learned it from an uncle who was half-Cherokee and spent his early years living in the Indian Territory, but that he wasn't sure where the tune came from originally.

Mike Seeger first heard this tune from Ramona Jones, but didn't learn it until he heard a solo fiddle recording done by Jimmy Driftwood — the same musician who wrote "Tennessee Stud" and wrote the lyrics for "Battle of New Orleans," combining them with the fiddle tune "Eighth of January."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Hut In The Bog
description:
"Hut in the Bog" is a reel — a 4/4 time dance tune — rooted in the Irish traditional music tradition. There are actually two reels called "The Hut in the Bog," which causes some confusion in the folk music world. One of them is a traditional Irish reel with four known settings and has been added to over two hundred tunebooks.

The tune is supposedly a composition of Sligo fiddler Paddy Killoran, who called his version "On the Road to Lurgan" and recorded it on the Milestone at the Garden record, in Em.

However, the attribution is disputed. The tune is also known by the title "Killoran's Reel," but it is incorrectly claimed as a Paddy Killoran composition in some sources. The name "Hut in the Bog" itself may have come later — it's believed the tune was never called "The Hut in the Bog" until it was given that title — possibly mistakenly — on Mary Bergin's first solo recording.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Iberia Breakdown
description:
IBERIA BREAKDOWN. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, Missouri. The source for this tune was biography:Bill Driver, an African-American fiddler from Iberia, Miller County, central Missouri, one of collector R.P. Christeson's sources in the mid-20th century. The title is Christeson's, given to a tune he collected from Driver that did not have a title. Bill Driver (1881-1986) 

Source for notated version: - 

Recorded sources:   -Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers' Association, Bill Driver (et al) - "Old Time Fiddler's Repertory" (1976).

See also listing at:

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Icy Mountain
description:
ICY MOUNTAIN. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, West Virginia. D Mixolydian. Standard or AEae tunings (fiddle). AABB. There is a song collected in Kentucky by this title given by Roberts (p. 105), which is a variant of "My Home's Across the Smoky Mountains" or "My Home's Across the Blue Ridge Mountains;" it seems unrelated to this breakdown piece. However, the tune in circulation by this title was collected from Ward Jarvis (b. 1894), originally of Braxton County, West Virginia (later of southeastern Ohio, where he moved in the 1940's to work in the timber industry), who learned it from a Clay County (W.Va.) left-handed fiddler by the name Frank Santy. 

Source for notated version: Ward Jarvis [Milliner & Koken].

Printed sources: Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; pp. 310-311. Spadaro (10 Cents a Dance), 1980; p. 15. 

Recorded sources: Front Hall 017, Michael, McCreesh, & Campbell - "Dance Like the Waves of the Sea" (1978). Rounder 0132, Bob Carlin - "Fiddle Tunes for Clawhammer Banjo" (1980). CD2001, "The Rough Deal Stringband."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: I Don't Love Nobody
description:
I DON'T LOVE NOBODY [1]. AKA – “I Don’t Want to Get Married,” “I Love a Nobody, "Piece (1).” American, Country Rag (cut time). USA; widely known. C Major ('A' part) & A Minor ('B' part). Standard tuning (fiddle). AAB (Phillips): AABB (Brody): ABC (Beiswenger/McCann). This popular tune has been covered by many old-time fiddlers, but also has been played in bluegrass, contest and Western Swing style.  Charles Wolfe (1983) remarks that it was issued by no less than six labels in the early 1930's, and prior to that it was recorded by Georgia fiddler Gid Tanner (1924), Earl Johnson (1927), and the Dixie String Band (1924). One early recording, by the Red Headed Fiddlers (with A.L. “Red” Steely on fiddle and Red Graham on banjo), resulted in the song being released as “Fatal Wedding.” The tune was recorded for the Library of Congress by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph from Ozarks Mountains fiddlers in the early 1940's, and 20th century Ozarks fiddler Art Galbraith noted that he heard many fiddlers play the tune1. Lyrics to the melody begin:

I was born in Kentucky, lived there all of my life,

Thought I'd better be lucky, never had no wife;

I once thought I'd get married, I asked a little girl to wed,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Illinois Rickett's Hornpipe
description:
The specific "Illinois Rickett's Hornpipe" variant traces directly to a single fiddler and a single place. "Illinois Rickett's Hornpipe" is from Dick Reid of Clayville, Illinois. It was collected and documented by the old-time band Volo Bogtrotters, whose members were active in gathering tunes from older Illinois fiddlers. Members of the band and their friend Garry Harrison were active in collecting tunes from older fiddlers in Illinois, and that collecting was an important source for the tunes they played. The Illinois prefix in the tune's name signals what old-time collectors call a local variant — a well-traveled tune that picked up distinct regional character in central Illinois.

The Ricketts being referred to in the title was a circus promoter, one John Bill Ricketts, a Scots immigrant who came from England in 1792 and flourished in America through the 1790s till about 1800, when his Philadelphia enterprise was destroyed in a fire on Dec. 17, 1799. He delighted his audiences by dancing hornpipes on the backs of galloping horses.

He reportedly also hired another famous American hornpipe dancer, John Durang, to produce pantomimes for him. Alan Jabbour (in American Fiddle Tunes) says that circuses under his name appeared in New York City, Philadelphia, Norfolk, Charlestown, Albany, Boston, Hartford, and Montreal.

Both Ricketts and Durang had hornpipes named for them that have endured in American tradition, in both the North and the South, right up through the twentieth century.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: I Love My Wife As Well As Anybody...
description:
The full name of the tune is "I Love My Wife As Well As Anybody, But When My Back's Turned, She's Hugging Everybody." It appears in lists of old-time tunes and is well known in the community primarily for its outrageously long, comedic title — a hallmark of the old-time tradition.

This is a Southern Appalachian old-time breakdown/dance tune, a genre defined by:
Tunes passed down orally and by ear across generations
Humorous, vivid, or satirical titles often telling a story in themselves
A strong tradition of fiddle-and-banjo pairing at dances and jams

One of the things old-time players love most about these tunes is their names — titles like "Nail a Catfish to a Tree" or "Spider Bit the Baby" are part of the fun.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: I'm Gonna Have My Mustache Blacked When I Get There
description:
(also listed as "I'm Gonna Get My Mustache Blacked When I Get There")
Regional origin: At least one YouTube source identifies it as a West Virginia tune.
Published source: It appears in the Milliner-Koken book, a respected old-time fiddle tune collection, though details on its documented backstory within that book are not widely discussed online.
Transmission lineage (Tater Joe's listing): The tune is attributed to Taylor Kimbell via Palmer Loux, suggesting it was passed down through that chain of fiddlers.
Community discovery: The tune first circulated more widely in the modern old-time community via a clip from a dance in Southern Illinois, with players immediately drawn to both the title and the melody.
Notable players: The tune has been played and promoted by fiddlers like Billy Mathews, documented at events like the Heritage Day Festival in Springfield, MO.

The tune is a relatively obscure old-time piece with West Virginia roots, documented in the Milliner-Koken collection, and traceable through the Kimbell → Loux fiddling lineage. Its quirky, humorous title (a hallmark of many old Appalachian and Southern tunes) has made it a favorite wherever it's been heard, but deep historical documentation on its composer or exact origin remains scarce — typical of many orally transmitted old-time tunes.

Want a ABC notation, sheet music source, or YouTube performance links? I can help track those down.

title: Indian Corn
description:
"Indian Corn" comes from the fiddling of Willie O. Ault, from the small town of Hidalgo, Illinois. Willie was an old fiddler who was "collected" and field recorded by Garry Harrison back in the 1970s, when Willie was in his 80s. Garry Harrison has been described as a "modern-day John James Audubon of fiddle tunes" for his work preserving these regional Illinois tunes.

Harrison's mentor, Lynn "Chirps" Smith, was in an old-time string band with Garry called The Indian Creek Delta Boys when they were in their late teens and early twenties — they attended the same high school.

When fiddler Rhys Jones (of Bigfoot String Band) was learning tunes from Chirps as a teenager, he had access to those field recordings including the ones of Willie Ault. However, the tape was mislabeled — "Indian Corn" was listed as "Ol' Woodward's Tune," and for years everyone mistakenly called it by that name.

So the tune we now call "Indian Corn" was known to many as "Ol' Woodard's Tune," while the title "Indian Corn" was actually assigned to a completely different tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Indian Ate the Woodchuck
description:
(Redirected from Indian Ate the Woodchuck)

Back to Indian Ate the Woodchuck (1)

INDIAN ATE/EAT THE WOODCHUCK [1]. American, Reel. USA; Arkansas, Kentucky, Tennessee. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AAAA'BB (Phillips): AABCC (Titon). Jeff Titon (2001) gives its provenance as eastern Kentucky and explains the confusion of titles between the substitution of 'eat' and 'ate' and 'woodchuck', 'woodpecker', 'woodcock' and 'woodhen'. The melody was in the repertoire of Kentucky fiddlers John Salyer (1882-1952), Estill Bingham (1899-1990), Owen "Snake" Chapman, and bluegrass fiddler Kenny Baker (who called it "Indian Killed a Woodcock"). Baker's tune is similar to the tune J.P. Fraley of Rush, Kentucky, plays idiosyncratically called, "Sail away Ladies (4)" (not the tune usually known by that title, and one he obtained from Ed Hayley (1883-1951), who did call it by the "Indian" title--see "Indian Ate the Woodchuck (2)"). Titon seems to think that the Baker/Fraley tune is distanced from the Hayley and Salyer versions, however, and he points out that "Indian Ate the Woodchuck" (and variants) is something of a floating title, noting the similarity, for example to the unrelated "Indian and the Woodhen." Salyer's version is a two-part one that is not as "busy" or 'notey' as Haley's tune. The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954. African-American fiddler Frank Patterson recorded the tune under the title "Indian and the Woodchuck" for the Library of Congress around 1942.

Source for notated version: - John Salyer (recorded 1940-41, Salyersville, Magoffin County, Ky.) [Milliner & Koken, Phillips]; Ed Hayley (Ashland, Boyd County, Ky.) [Titon]; Mark Gaponoff [Silberberg].

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Indians Over the Hill
description:
INDIANS OVER THE HILL. AKA - "Indians are over the Hill (The)."  Old-Time, Breakdown. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Sourced to John Scotland Hannah (1920-?), who made his living as a coffin maker. Hannah was born in Logan County, West Virginia, but was collected at his home in later life in Columbus, Ohio. His grandfather was originally Eastern Kentucky, and migrated to West Virginia sometime around the 1870's. According to Kerry Blech, Hannah's grandfather taught the tune "Lost Indian" to Ed Haley when Haley was a young man. Hannah played the tune down-tempo, more like a march, although it has been accelerated in the playing of modern fiddlers. 

Sources for notated versions: Jeff Goehring [Milliner & Koken]; John Scotland Hannah [Milliner & Koken]. 

Printed sources: Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; pp. 322-323. 

Recorded sources: Field Recorders Collective FRC601 - "Jeff Goehring with friends & family". 5-String Productions 5SP04003 , Jane Rothfield - "In the Moment."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Indian War Whoop
description:
The title "Indian War Whoop" seems to be fairly wide-spread up and down the Mississippi River region, with tunes by that title collected from the Deep South (Louisiana, Mississippi) north to the Missouri/Ozarks. It also is a fairly old title, by American standards, and first appears in print in Knauff's Virginia Reels (1839) (Indian War Whoop (4) [1]). Ming's "Indian War Whoop" is a different tune than Mississippi fiddler Frank Kittrell's "Indian War Whoop." "Indian War Whoop" was recorded on a 78 RPM by Monroe, north Louisiana, fiddler Hiter Colvin (Indian War Whoop (2)).

Source for notated version: - s

Printed sources: -  s

Recorded sources: - County 528, Floyd (Hoyt) Ming & His Pep-Steppers - "Mississippi Breakdown: Traditional Fiddle Music of Mississippi, vol. 1." Folkways FA 2952, Floyd Ming and his Pep-Steppers - "Anthology of American Folk Music, vol. 2: Social Music" (1952). Rounder 0320, Bob Carlin & John Hartford - "The Fun of Open Discussion." Victor 21294A (78 RPM), Floyd Ming and His Pep-Steppers" (1928).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Irish Hornpipe
description:
IRISH HORNPIPE [1]. American(?), Hornpipe. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Despite the title, the tune does not sound characteristically Irish to my ears, but rather more like the standard 19th century British or American stage hornpipes typical in the Elias Howe publications. It may have been assigned an Irish provenance due to its printing in Patrick O'Flannagan's Hibernia Collection (1860), another of Boston publisher Howe's volumes. Cape Breton fiddler Angus Chisholm recorded the hornpipe in the mid-20th century, pairing it with two of Dan R. MacDonald's compositions, "Miss Marguerite MacNeill" and "Miss Joan MacDonald]]." 

"Irish Hornpipe" is on Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. There are similarities in the first strain with the Irish reel "Hand Me Down the Tackle," but perhaps not enough to establish a cognate relationship.

A genericly titled "Irish Hornpipe" was recorded by Joseph Samuels for Edison Records (50900 {78 RPM}) in 1920 (appears as one of tunes of "Miss Johnson's Party Melody").

Printed sources: -  Cole (1000 Fiddle Tunes), 1940; p. 103. O'Flannagan (The Hibernia Collection), 1860; p. 11. Ryan's Mammoth Collection, 1883; p. 139.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Irish Polka
description:
The polka itself is not Irish in origin — it is Bohemian (Czech). The polka's origin story first appears in the periodical Bohemia in 1844, in which it was attributed to a young Bohemian woman named Anna Slezáková. As told by Čeněk Zíbrt, the music teacher Josef Neruda noticed her dancing in an unusual way to accompany a local folk song in 1830, and Neruda put the tune to paper and taught other young men to dance it.

Historians believe the polka evolved as a quicker version of the waltz, and associate the rapid spread of the polka across Europe in the mid-1800s with the Romantic movement, which emphasized an idealized version of peasant culture.

The polka found favor and spread across Europe from 1844 onwards. A leading dance master from New York, Allen Dodworth, claimed he had introduced the polka to New York society in 1843, having just returned from Paris where he learned the dance. The form ultimately found its way into Irish traditional music and was especially popular in the South-West of the country.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Irish Reel
description:
"Irish Reel" is both a genre label and a specific tune title found in the old-time fiddle canon. Fiddle tunes are primarily instrumental melodies, most of which originated for dancing. The terms reel and jig refer both to the type of dance and to the type of tune played to accompany the dance.

Importantly, reels originated in Scotland and were introduced to Ireland in the late 18th century. So the genre itself has a Scottish root that was adopted and transformed into a distinctly Irish tradition before crossing the Atlantic.

The origins of the Scots-Irish lie primarily in the Lowlands of Scotland and in northern England. They were relocated to Ireland's northern province of Ulster starting in 1606, primarily to strengthen royal control over the North of Ireland. Most of the Scots-Irish emigrants settled initially in Pennsylvania. From there, many followed the Great Wagon Road to make their homes in the Appalachian Mountains — Virginia, Tennessee, Kentucky, and the Carolinas.

Once in Appalachia, much of the work on the American frontier — barn raising, molasses making, corn husking, and apple peeling — was done communally. At the end of the workday, people danced the old Scottish and Irish reels and jigs, with the music provided by a fiddle or fiddles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jake's Best Reel
description:
JAKE'S BEST REEL. American, Reel. USA; Nebraska, Missouri. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune is a version of "Old Jake Gillie."

Source for notated version: - Bob Walters (Burt County, Nebraska) [Christeson].

Printed sources: -  R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, vol. 2), 1984; p. 56.

Recorded sources: - Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers' Association, Cyril Stinnett (1912-1986) - "Plain Old Time Fiddling." Rounder 0429, Dwight Lamb - “Joseph Won a Coated Fiddle” (1999. The Lamb and Walters families were close when Dwight was younger, and Lamb became a protege of Bob Walters, absorbing much of his repertoire).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jake's Got A Bellyache
description:
"Jake's Got the Bellyache" comes to us from West Virginia fiddler Edden Hammons. The recording is in the key of A Modal, played in ADAE tuning, and was captured in 1947, appearing on The Edden Hammons Collection, Vol. 2.

The notation in the Traditional Tune Archive credits it as: Source: Alan Jabbour, from Edden Hammons — transcribed by Andrew Kuntz. This means the tune was collected and preserved by folklorist Alan Jabbour, who recorded and documented Hammons' playing.

It is an American Reel in cut time, in A Mixolydian mode, played in ADae fiddle tuning, with an AAB structure.

title: JayBird
description:
"Jaybird" is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown, American March and Reel, and also has English/Scottish roots (Morris and Sword Dance tradition). It has been documented primarily in New England, Pennsylvania, and possibly Missouri, played in D Major in standard or ADae fiddle tuning.

Folklorist Samuel Bayard collected numerous versions — most called "Jaybird" — from southwestern Pennsylvania fifers and fiddlers in the mid-20th century, where it was played as both a march and a reel. He identified "Jaybird" as a derivative of the British air "The Ladies Breast Knot."

This gives the tune a transatlantic lineage: a British melody that crossed the Atlantic and took root in American folk tradition, picking up new names, lyrics, and regional variations along the way.

Researcher Joel Shimberg found the first strain of the tune in Leah Jackson Wolford's book The Play Party in Indiana (pre-1920), as a melody for a play-party called "Down in Jaybird Town" — Wolford notes it was also played as a fiddle tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jaybird Died of the Whooping Cough
description:
Jaybird Died of the Whooping Cough,

Squirrel died of the colic;

'Long come a red bird sittin' on a fence,

Call all the young girls to frolic.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jefferson City
description:
JEFFERSON CITY. AKA - "Bill Caton's Hornpipe," "Bill Katon's Tune," "Jeff City," "Old Jeff City." AKA and see "Caton's Hornpipe." Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, Missouri. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB (Beisswenger & McCann): AA'BB' (Phillips). The tune is associated with African-American fiddler Bill Caton (sometimes Katon), from around Tebbetts, south Calloway County, Missouri, born in the 19th century. The capital of Missouri, Jefferson City, is south, across the Missouri River, from Caton's area. Missouri fiddler Howard Marshall writes: "Mr. Katon was well-known in central Missouri and frequently played dances throughout the area, played over live radio programs, and played for both white and black people's dances...Mr. Katon's name was spelled with a "C" and also with a "K." I have been told he preferred "K." He is buried in the old Tebbetts community cemetery high on a river hill north of Tebbetts in Callaway County MO."  "Jefferson City" (also called  "Old Jeff City" and "Jeff City" by Caton) appears in R.P. Christeson's Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory, vol. 1 (1973), as an un-named hornpipe. Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden calls it "Bill Caton's Hornpipe" and it is on his list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. Iowa fiddler Dwight Lamb also played the tune, but Theodosia, Missouri, fiddler Alton Jones (who can be heard on Rounder 0437) played a somewhat distanced version from that usually heard. Mr. Marshall also remarks: "...It's a square dance tune. The fine part of the tune is striking, as it needs some pretty keen and specific bowing that in a manner that is rarely heard. I learned the tune from the late Jimmy Gilmore of Jefferson City MO and Pete McMahan of Columbia Mo., both of whom were fans of Bill Katon's music.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jeff Davis
description:
JEFF DAVIS [1]. American, Reel (cut time). C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). ABBBBIn the repertoire of Bert Layne (Ga.) of the Skillet Lickers. The title refers no doubt to the only President of the Confederate states, Jefferson Davis.

Source for notated version: - Blaine Smith [Phillips]. Blaine Smith was recorded in the field in his home in Flat Top, Tennessee, when he was age 63. He played in a band with his mother-in-law, Florrie Stewart (who was age 75), and Willie Brandon (age 48). They had played for years for dances, until they died out in his area. He played an oversize fiddle, like a viola, that a neighbor had given him for tearing down an old house, and played in a straight-forward, unornamented style.

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 123.

Recorded sources: - Pine Breeze 003, Blaine Smith - "A Bottle of Wine and a Gingercake: Traditional Music from Southeast Tennessee" (1977). Marimac 9054, The Ill-Mo Boys - "Fine as Frog Hair" (1995).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jeff Davis County Reel
description:
"Jeff Davis County Reel" is grouped alongside "Jefferson Davis' Reel" in lists of presidential fiddle tunes, both referencing Jefferson Davis, President of the Confederate States of America, 1861–1865. Like many old-time fiddle tunes of the Civil War era and post-war South, its title memorializes a prominent political figure — a common naming convention in American folk music of the 19th century.

The tune is transcribed in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John S. Lamancusa, where it is listed in the key of C, attributed to fiddler Casey Driscoll. This appears to be the primary documented source fiddler for the tune in the modern old-time revival tradition. Beyond this attribution, no earlier field recording or named 19th-century originator has been publicly documented in available sources.

There is a closely related tune, simply called "Jeff Davis", which sheds light on the broader "Jeff Davis" tune family:
It comes "from the playing of fiddler Baine Smith (born c. 1914, east Tenn.)", and its first strain resembles "Four Cent Cotton," while the second strain is reminiscent of "Casey Jones."
It is documented as an American Reel in cut time, recorded on Blaine Smith – "Bottle of Wine and a Ginger Cake" (1977).
It was also in the repertoire of Bert Layne (Ga.) of the Skillet Lickers, and "the title refers no doubt to the only President of the Confederate states, Jefferson Davis.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jenny Comb Your Hair
description:
JENNY COMB YOUR HAIR. American, Reel. USA, Missouri. A Minor. Standard tuning (fiddle). ABB. The tune is sourced to Missouri fiddler Cyril Stinnett, from whom his protege, Dwight Lamb, had it.

Cyril Stinnett (1912-1986)

Source for notated version: - Cyril Stinnett (1912-1986, Oregon, Missouri) [Christeson].

Printed sources: -  R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, vol. 2), 1984; p. 90.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jenny Get Around
description:
JENNY GET AROUND. Old-Time, Song and Breakdown. USA, Kentucky. A Major. AEae tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune is known as an eastern Kentucky tune, popular with both fiddlers and banjo players. Jeff Titon (2001) says the tune is related to one of the "Liza Jane" melody types, and points out similarities between the 'A' part of "Jenny Get Around" and the 'B' part of Clyde Davenport's "Liza Jane." Mark Wilson points out relationships between "Jenny..." and the "Sugar Hill" tune family. Titon calls it a regional eastern Kentucky tunes and finds it listed twice on the Berea, Kentucky, tune lists of 1915. However is is known in the Ozarks as well. It is often sung, with banjo accompaniment and was collected as a song by John and Alan Lomax, who printed it in their book Our Singing Country (1941, pp. 63-65).

Source for notated version: - John M. Salyer [1] (1882-1952, Salyersville, Magoffin County, Ky., 1941) [Milliner & Koken, Titon].

Printed sources: -  Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 331. Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Music), 2001; No. 74, p. 103.

Recorded sources: - Berea College Appalachian Center AC003, "John M. Salyer: Home Recordings 1941-1942, vol. 2" (1993). Jim Martin Productions JMP201, Gerry Milnes (et al) - "Gandydancer." June Apal 0051, Lee Sexton - "Whoa Mule" (1988). June Apal 0055, Morgan Sexton - "Rock Dust" (1989). Mudthumper Music MM-0030, Clare Milliner and Walt Koken - "Just Tunes."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jenny In The Cotton Patch
description:
A "jenny" is a mule — a female donkey or mule used for farm work. So the image in the title is a simple, rural one: a mule that has wandered into the cotton field.

The clearest lineage for this tune traces through three generations of Kentucky and Tennessee fiddlers:

1. Will Phipps — Phipps was an old-timer, born in 1812, from Rock Creek, Tennessee, who was supposed to have been buried with his fiddle in his coffin. He is the earliest known source of the tune.

2. Will Davenport — The tune was learned by Monticello, south-central Kentucky, fiddler Clyde Davenport from his father, Will Davenport, who himself had it from Will Phipps.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jenny Run Away in the Mud in the Night
description:
The tune is originally from an old recording by North Carolina fiddler Marcus Martin (1881–1974). He was born in Macon County and recorded by the Library of Congress and several folklorists; he is remembered for his beautiful and unusual tunes, including "Lady Hamilton" and "Jenny Run Away in the Mud in the Night."

Growing up farming, he learned to play fiddle from his father, Rowan Martin, and then worked a series of odd jobs around western North Carolina — logging, textiles, postal service, and more. Throughout his life, Martin played square dances around Macon and Cherokee Counties, accompanying Bascom Lamar Lunsford and others; he was featured for many years at Lunsford's Mountain Dance and Folk Festival in Asheville.

Martin's fiddle style makes heavy use of cross-tuning (GDGD, GDGB, DDAD, GDEB, or GDAD), and he also played banjo, harmonica, and mountain dulcimer.

title: Jimmy Johnson
description:
JIMMY JOHNSON. American, Reel (cut time). USA; Virginia, West Virginia. A Major. AEae tuning (fiddle). AAB. "Jimmy Johnson" is a common West Virginia tune, and elsewhere, under different titles. It was in the repertory of W.Va. fiddlers Melvin Wine (1909-2003) and Ernie Carpenter (1909-1997, who learned it from his father Shelt Carpenter). Glen Smith

It was said to have been Wine's favorite tune.

Source for notated version: - Glen Smith (Galax, Va.) [Phillips] {who said he learned the tune from Johnny Johnson}; Melvin Wine (W.Va.) [Milliner & Koken]; Ward Jarvis [Milliner & Koken].

Printed sources: -  Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; pp. 337-339 (two versions). Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Music, vol. 1), 1994; p. 125.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jimmy Shank
description:
The tune is catalogued as JIM SHANK(S), with aliases including "Jimmy Shenk" and "Jimmy Shanks."

It is an American Reel played in cut time, in the key of A Major, using AEae cross-tuning on the fiddle. The tune follows an AA'BB' structure.

It is a southern Kentucky / Tennessee tune, found in the repertoire of fiddler Bruce Greene, drawn from his field recording of Tennessee fiddler Sam Dyer.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: John Brown's March
description:
JOHN BROWN'S MARCH [1]. Old-Time, March (2/4, 4/4 or cut time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB (Songer, Welling): AA'AA'BB (Phillips).   

Sources for notated versions: - Pete Sutherland (VT) [Phillips]; Alan Jabbour via Alan Garren [Songer]; Harlan Coble (Guilford County, North Carolina Piedmont) [Milliner & Koken]. 

Printed sources: - Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 341. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), vol. 2, 1995; p. 70. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 112. Welling (Welling's Hartford Tune Book), 1976; p. 2.

Recorded sources:   -PearlMae Music 004-2, Jim Taylor - "The Civil War Collection" (1996. Learned from banjoist Sheila Adams, who had the tune from Tommy Jarrel and Scott Ansley).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Johnny Cope
description:
JOHNNY COPE [1] (Seanin Ua Copa). AKA and see "Fye to the Coals in the Morning," "General Coope," "Hey Johnny Cope," "Sir Iain Cope." Scottish (originally), Canadian; Reel, Hornpipe or March; American, March or Polka (2/4 or cut time); Irish, Hornpipe. Canada, Prince Edward Island. G Mixolydian/Minor (Aird, Gatherer, Johnson, O'Neill/1915): A Mixolydian (Gunn): A Dorian (Cranford, Doyle): A Minor (Howe, Johnson/2003, O'Farrell): B Minor (Miller & Perron). Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Bayard): AABB (Johnson/2003, Miller & Perron, O'Neill/1850, Perlman, Doyle, Roche, Winstock): AABBCC (Gunn): AABBCCDD (Aird, Gatherer, O'Farrell): AABB'CCDDEEFFAABB' (Johnson): AABBCCDDEEFFGGHH (Howe). The tune is still played by Scottish regiments as their reveille. It is a satirical melody which commemorates the 1745 Jacobite rebellion when Sir John Cope (d. 1760) and the English were defeated by the Scots under Bonnie Prince Charlie at the Battle of Prestonpans, on the 22nd of September, 1745. In 1745, when Prince Charles landed in the highlands, Sir John was commander in chief in Scotland and he bravely resolved to march into the Highlands to oppose him. Cope was ill-prepared and outnumbered however, and soon retreated in the face of opposition in order to regroup. The rebels meanwhile secured Edinburgh and when they learned that Cope was marching to the city's relief they marched to meet him. Both armies neared each other at Prestonpans late in the day, separated by marshy ground, and it was resolved to wait until the next day to begin hostilities.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Johnny Don't Get Drunk
description:
"Johnny Don't Get Drunk" is an American reel played in cut time, also known by several alternate titles including "John John Don't You Come Home Drunk," "Johnny Johnny Don't Get Drunk," "Don't Come Home Drunk Johnny," and "Jimmy Don't Come Home Drunk." It is played in D Major in standard fiddle tuning.

It is a fun, peppy tune that is often played for contra dances.

The tune is documented across the USA, particularly in Kentucky, Virginia, Missouri, and Nebraska. The melody is regarded as a Missouri tune and is one of the "100 essential Missouri tunes" listed by Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden. However, it is widely disseminated throughout the greater Appalachian and Midwest regions.

The tune's precise origin is murky — no single composer has ever been identified. A few theories exist:
Temperance song connection: Scholars see similarities between this tune and the Irish reel "Miss Monaghan's Reel." Folklorist Jeff Titon (2001) believes the tune may have been derived from a temperance song.
Radio transmission: Owen Chapman (b. 1919) said he thought he might have learned it after hearing it played on the radio.
No definitive answer: As one YouTube commenter noted, there is "nothing reliable about the history of this tune" and the origins remain a subject of speculation.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Johnny Don't Come Home Drunk
description:
Back to Johnny Don't Come Home Drunk

|:[A2A2]-|"D"[A2A2][AA][AB] [A2A2][AA][AA]|[FA][A2A2][AB] [A2A2][A2A2]-|[A2A2][AA][AA] [AA][AB][AA][AA]|"A7"[F2A2][E4A4][A2A2]-|

JOHNNY, DON'T COME HOME DRUNK. AKA - "John John Don't You Come Home Drunk," "Johnny Don't Get Drunk," "Johnny Johnny Don't Get Drunk," "Don't Come Home Drunk Johnny," "Jimmy Don't Come Home Drunk." American, Reel (cut time). USA; Kentucky, Virginia, Missouri, Nebraska. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (most versions). The melody is known as a Missouri tune and is one of  '100 essential Missouri tunes' listed by Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden. However, it is widely disseminated throughout the 'greater Appalachian' and Mid-west regions. Some see similarities between this tune and the Irish reel "Miss Monahan/Miss Monaghan’s Reel." Jeff Titon (2001) believes the tune may have been derived from a temperance song. Source Owen "Snake" Chapman (b. 1919, Kentucky) said he thought he might have learned it after hearing it played on the radio.  See also the related "My Wife Died on Saturday Night."

Source for notated version: - Bob Walters (Burt County, Nebraska), recorded in 1954 [Christeson, Milliner & Koken]; Art Stamper (Ky.) [Phillips]; Stuart Williams [Songer]; Owen "Snake" Chapman (Whitesburg, Letcher County, Ky., 1990) [Titon]; Carthy Sisco [Silberberg].

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: John Rawl Jamieson
description:
JOHN RAWL JAMIESON. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, Ky. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune was known under this title by northestern Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas (1934-1974), who told Mark Wilson (Rounder Records) that it was named after an elderly man "who lived bock on Shouls on a ridge." The tune was also called by the 'Jamieson' title by Morris Allen, a mentor and sometime playing partner of Thomas. 

Source for notated version: Buddy Thomas [Milliner & Koken].

Printed sources: Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 344. Songer (Portland Collection, vol. 2), 2005; p. 104. 

Recorded sources: Kate Lissauer - "Walk Talk Chicken" (2005). Rounder 0032, Buddy Thomas (northeastern Ky.) - "Kitty Puss: Old-Time Fiddle Music From Kentucky"

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: John Short's Tune
description:
JOHN SHORT'S TUNE.  American, Polka. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Fiddler 'Chirps' Smith remarks that the tune was collected by members of the Allen Street String Band from a musician named Erwin Thompson (1915-2015) of Godfrey, Madison Co, IL . Smith also found reference to a fiddler named John W. Short (1839-1927) from Mt. Vernon, Jefferson County, Illinois, who was remembered as 'loving to play at every occasion'. It is possible Short was the source for the tune. 

Curiously, the first few bars closely resemble those of "King of Prussia's March (2)," although the rest of the tune differs.

Recorded sources: - Vigortone Records 2001, The Ill-Mo Boys - "Laugh and Grow Fat" (2001. Learned from fiddler Erwin Thompson, Godfrey, Illinois).

Back to John Short's Tune

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Johnson Gal
description:
Johnson Gal(s) is an American Reel in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning.

The tune is documented in Arkansas and Mississippi. The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist and folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.

A tune by this name was in the repertoire of fiddler Archibald Alexander Shaw of Harnett County, N.C., located in the Sandhills section between the coastal plain and the piedmont — though Evelyn Shaw states it was not played in other parts of the state, but was unique to Shaw's area.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Joke on the Puppy
description:
"The Joke on the Puppy" is an old-time breakdown. The tune is usually known as "Rye Straw," but has several titles, and structurally various versions contain anywhere from two to four distinct parts.

It is rooted in the USA, specifically western North Carolina, eastern Tennessee, north Georgia, and Mississippi. It is typically played in ADae cross-tuning on the fiddle.

The melody was known throughout the South and Midwest under a variety of mostly related titles, but appears to have first been published in the 1876 collection by blackface minstrel performer and composer George H. Coes of Boston, Massachusetts, as "Whoop from Arkansas," and later by Missouri physician W.H. Morris (Old Time Violin Melodies, 1927) as "Acrobat."

The title "Rye Straw" appears in two of the lists of fiddle tunes in the Berea Tune Lists, collected from informants from east Tennessee and east Kentucky as a student project in 1915 under the auspices of Prof. John F. Smith.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Julianne Flanigan
description:
"Julianne Flanigan", fiddled by North Georgian Lowe Stokes, is excerpted from a 1928 skit recording (Paramount 3105), titled "Barn Dance on the Mountain, Part 2", recorded under the name The Lookout Mountain Revelers.

This is the oldest documented source of the tune, placing its commercial debut firmly in the late 1920s Southern string band era.

Lowe Stokes was a prominent North Georgia fiddler of the era. He also appeared on recordings by Gid Tanner and His Skillet Lickers (Columbia 15404, 1929), a session that featured three fiddlers: Lowe Stokes, Gid Tanner, and Lowe Stokes again. This places Stokes squarely in the heart of the Atlanta-area commercial old-time recording scene of the late 1920s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: JulieAnn Johnson
description:
"Julie Ann Johnson" comes from Grayson County fiddle legend Emmett Lundy (1864–1953). Lundy, a Galax, Virginia-area fiddler, recorded this tune — one of the few recordings he ever made.

Lundy was recorded in the field in 1941 by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax, along with John Work and Joseph Liss. The recording is archived at the Library of Congress as AFS 4940-A4, A5 (1941).

Greenberry Leonard (b. 1808) of Old Town township of Grayson County, Virginia, was Lundy's mentor and was considerably older. The younger fiddler characterized Leonard as "an old mountain boomer" on his AFS field recordings. This places the tune's roots potentially as far back as the early-to-mid 1800s in the Virginia Blue Ridge mountains.
An American reel in D Major.
Played in standard (Lundy) or ADae cross-tuning on fiddle.
A distinctive harmonic quirk: "It has no 'G' chord in it." This modal, two-chord character is a hallmark of its old Appalachian style.
The tune follows an AA'BB' structure.

Although the Emmett Lundy recording is the sole source for modern versions, there are glimpses of an earlier history of this tune.

title: Jump Fingers
description:
JUMP FINGERS. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA; Nebraska, Missouri. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune was one of  '100 essential Missouri tunes' listed by Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden. Described as a "parlor novelty piece" by Mark Wilson. Composition credit is claimed by George "Jeffie" Pounds, who was playing the tune in a barber shop that happened at the same time to be patronized by Nebraska fiddler Bob Walters. Walters listened to it a few times, then played it expertly himself, causing the exasperated Pounds to rush out of the shop (see liner notes to Rounder CD0375). 

Bob Walters and R.P. Christeson (2nd & 3rd from left)

Bob WaltersSource for notated version: George Pounds via Bob Walters (both Burt County, Nebraska, fiddlers) [Christeson, Milliner & Koken]; Lonnie Robertson (1908-1981, Springfield, Mo.), learned from Bob Walters  [Beisswenger & McCann].

Printed sources: Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 117. R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; p. 41. Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 351.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Jump Jim Crow
description:
JUMP JIM CROW. American, Reel (cut time). USA, West Virginia. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Phillips). "Jump Jim Crow" is an Appalachian fiddle tune that can be traced to blackface minstrelsy.  While distanced from the old song "Jim Crow", the derivative reel still echoes the melody of the original.   The origins of the Jim Crow song, character and dance come from a black entertainer named John 'Picayune' Butler, who was perhaps originally from Martinique, but who made his home in New Orleans. He is said to have started his career sometime in the 1820’s, and by 1850 his fame was such that he was known throughout the Mississippi and Ohio River regions, even to Cincinnati. According to T. Allston Brown (Early History of Negro Minstrelsy, 1913) it was around 1830 that an entertainer named George Nichols first sang a song about ‘Jim Crow’, first as a clown, and then in blackface. "He first conceived the idea,” notes Brown, “from...a banjo player, known [along the river route] from New Orleans to Cincinnati as Picayune Butler".   The title "Jump Jim Crow" was included in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954. The set of lyrics below is from "Sketches and Eccentricities of Col. David Crockett of W. Tennessee," 1833, by J.S. French  {quoted by Charles Wolfe, The Devil's Box, Sept. 1982, p. 38}.

My old misses she don't like me,

Because I don't eat the blackeyed pea.  ...  (x2)

My old misses long time ago,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kanawha March
description:
KANAWHA MARCH. American, March (cut time). USA, West Virginia. D Major {Phillips}: G Major ('A' part) & D Major ('B' part) {Silberberg}. Standard tuning (fiddle). One part (Phillips): AB (Silberberg). A local West Virginia tune recorded for the Brunswick label by Kanawha County fiddler Clark Kessinger (1896-1975) in the late 1920's.

Source for notated version: - Clark Kessinger (W.Va.) [Phillips]; Barry Schultz [Silberberg].

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 71. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 79.

Recorded sources: - Brunswick 238 (78 RPM), Kessinger Brothers (1928).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Katie Bar the Door
description:
KATIE BAR THE DOOR. AKA and see "Katy Bar the Door." Old-Time, Breakdown. D Major (Silberberg): C Major (Milliner & Koken). Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Milliner & Koken). From the banjo playing of Roscoe Parrish (1897-1984), Galax, Carroll County, Virginia. This ditty is sung with the tune. 

The Indians jumping all around your house,

Source for notated version: Roscoe Parish (Galax, Virginia) [Milliner & Koken]. 

Printed sources: Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of Amercian Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 355. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 81.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Katy Did
description:
KATY DID [1].  American, Reel (cut or whole time). USA; north Georgia, northeast Alabama. C Major ('A' part), A Aeolian ('B' part). Standard tuning (fiddle). AAB (Silberberg): AABB (Brody, Reiner & Anick): AA'BB' (Phillips). A tune by this name was mentioned in reports (1926-31) of the De Kalb County (northeast Alabama) Annual (Fiddlers') Convention (Cauthen, 1990). In the 'B' part the 'E' chord played during the accompaniment may be either major or minor. North Georgia fiddler Lowe Stokes recorded the tune in this third session, in 1929, with guitarist Mike Whitten. Stokes' "Katy Did" was backed with "Take Me Back to Georgia," and some confusion of titles existed because many labels were reversed on the 78 RPM record; thus some fiddlers called "Katy Did" by the name "Take Me Back to Georgia"; furthermore, both tunes are in the key of 'C' major. However "Take Me Back to Georgia" is instead related to "Boston Boy"/"Ladies in the Ballroom (2)"/"Rattlesnake Bit the Baby."  Fiddlin' John Carson used the minor mode second strain of "Katy Did [1}" as part of his recording of "Billy in the Lowground (1)." Compare also Stokes 1929 "Katy Did" with the western North Carolina "Grey Eagle (6)."   The Hometown Boys. Lowe Stokes is on right, with guitar

Source for notated version: - Lowe Stokes (north Ga.) [Brody, Stecher/Fiddler Mag, Milliner & Koken, Phillips]; Howie Meltzer [Silberberg].

Printed sources: -  Brody (Fiddler's Fakebook), 1983; p. 154. Larsen (Fiddler Magazine), vol. 25, No. 3, Fall 2018; p. 32. Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of Ameriand Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 356. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), 1994; p. 130. Reiner & Anick (Old Time Fiddling Across America), 1989; p. 112. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 82.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kelton Cotillion
description: Kelton Cotillion is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kennedy Rag
description:
KENNEDY RAG. American, Country Rag. USA, Alabama. F Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB. Composed by fiddler Charlie Stripling [1] (1896-1966), who named it for the community of Kennedy in southeastern Lamar County, where he had relocated, but near his birthplace in Pickens County, west Alabama.  Kennedy had a population 277 at that time of release of the recording in 1929 on the Vocalion label (a subsidiary of Brunswick Records).  The town had just completed construction of the Kennedy High School in 1927, although when it burned in 1984 it was not replaced and students now attend Lamar County schools. 

The Stripling Brothers, Charlie Stripling fiddle    "Kennedy Rag", described  by Charlie Stripling as a "ragtime breakdown", was one of ten numbers recorded by the brothers in Chicago, Ill., in 1929,  based on the success of their initial 1928 Brunswick recording of "Lost Child (The)" and "Black Mountain Rag."

Source for notated version: - Charlie Stripling (Alabama) [Milliner & Koken, Phillips]; Lee Stripling (1921-2009,Seattle), learned from his father Charlie [Silberberg].

Printed sources: -  Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 357. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 71. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 82.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kentucky Whiskey
description:
KENTUCKY WHISKEY. Old-Time, Breakdown. A Major. AEae tuning (fiddle). AABB. The name Kentucky is derived from the Iroquois phrase kenta ke, meaning 'grass land' (Matthews, 1972). 

Source for notated version: 

Recorded sources: Front Hall Records FHR-037, Mark Graham - "Natural Selections" (1987). Rounder CD0403, The Freight Hoppers - "Where'd You Come From, Where'd You Go?"

Back to Kentucky Whiskey

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kickin' Up the Devil on a Holiday
description:
The tune was published by Thomas F. Briggs in his Briggs' Banjo Instructor (1855, Oliver Ditson Co., Boston). It may have been composed by Briggs and is often credited to him, although no composer credit is given with the tune itself in the volume. The frontispiece of the volume declares that tunes were "composed and arranged by Briggs," but there are clearly tunes by many composers in the contents — the declaration is taken to mean Briggs takes credit for the banjo arrangements for tunes that don't bear his name.

The original title — "Kick Up Dee Debbel on a Holiday" — indicates the tune was intended for the blackface minstrel stage. This dialect spelling was a common minstrel-era stylistic convention and places the tune squarely in the mid-19th-century American parlor/minstrel tradition.

It is an American reel, in D Mixolydian, standard fiddle tuning, with an AB two-part form.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kiowa Special
description:
KIOWA SPECIAL. American, Reel (cut time). D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). ABB'. Kiowa refers to the name of a Native American Indian tribe, currently settled in southwestern Oklahoma. Oklahoma fiddler Earl Collins (whose family was from Arkansas) is generally considered the core source for the tune.

Source for notated version: - Howie Meltzer [Silberberg].

Printed sources: -  Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 83.

Back to Kiowa Special

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: L&N Rag
description:
"L&N Rag" is an old-time, country rag tune in C Major from Kentucky, also known by the alternate title "Sleeping Lulu."

Alex Hood and the Railroad Boys — who recorded the tune in 1930 — came from Corbin, an eastern Kentucky railroad hub where many people worked for the lines. In their case, that line was the Louisville & Nashville (L&N) Railroad, which gave the tune its name.

Another old-time group, Walker's Corbin Ramblers, also made Corbin home at the time — in fact, mandolin player John Walker was a member of both groups.

The "L&N Rag" featured the playing of Emory Mills on fiddle, while banjoist Alex Hood and Vocalion A&R man Bill Brown provided live spoken commentary during the recording.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lacy Brown
description:
"Lacy Brown" is an old-time breakdown tune from the USA, specifically traced to Kentucky. It is played in A Major using AEae cross-tuning on the fiddle — a distinctive open tuning common to many Appalachian fiddle tunes that gives the melody a ringing, resonant quality.

The tune is almost exclusively associated with John Morgan Salyer, a fiddler from eastern Kentucky.
Salyer was born in 1882 and died in 1952, hailing from Salyersville, Magoffin County, Kentucky.
The source for the notated version of the tune is John M. Salyer (recorded in Salyersville, Magoffin County, Ky., 1942), as documented by Jeff Titon in Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes (2001), No. 77, p. 105.
A home recording of the tune was released on Berea College Appalachian Center AC003, "John M. Salyer: Home Recordings, vol. 1, 1941–1942" (1993).

Salyer's home recordings from 1941–42 are the primary (and essentially sole) documented source for this tune, making it a deeply personal piece tied to one regional master fiddler.

According to scholar Jeff Titon (2001), the tune is related to "Grey Eagle" — another well-known old-time breakdown. This is a common phenomenon in the old-time tradition, where tunes share skeletal melodic material but diverge through regional and personal stylistic interpretation.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ladies on the Steamboat
description:
"Ladies on the Steamboat" is an old-time, breakdown fiddle tune. It is typically played in the key of G (standard GDAE tuning) and has a driving, rollicking quality characteristic of Kentucky and Appalachian fiddle styles.

The tune is credited to and first recorded by Burnett & Rutherford, though it is likely they learned the tune from the influential blind fiddler from Eastern Kentucky, Ed Haley.

More specifically, Dick Burnett of Monticello, Wayne County, Kentucky, who recorded the tune in 1927 (for Columbia Records) with fiddler Leonard Rutherford (c. 1900–1954), recollected he might have learned the tune from Haley.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 1
description:
"Lady of the Lake" is one of the most beloved — and most confusing — tune titles in the old-time fiddle canon. The Fiddler's Companion lists nine distinct tunes entitled "Lady of the Lake," including two jigs, two reels, three hornpipes, and two breakdowns, with keys ranging from A Mixolydian to G Major to D Major. Here's the full story focused on Lady of the Lake No. 1 — the G-major reel that became the dominant version in modern old-time circles:

John Hartford points out that Sir Walter Scott's epic poem "Lady of the Lake" (1810) was popular on the American frontier, and broad familiarity with that title may have aided the name's dissemination across multiple unrelated tunes. In fact, there are several unrelated tunes that have been called "Lady of the Lake," a situation which stems from association with the very popular country dance of the same name — and the title is also associated with Scott's 1810 romantic narrative poem.

The title and tune are at least as old as Church of Ireland cleric James Goodman's mid-19th century music manuscripts. Goodman (1828–1896) was an uilleann piper and Irish-language speaker who collected locally in County Cork and elsewhere in Munster, and also obtained tunes from manuscripts and printed collections. The melody and title appear in English and Scottish publications later in the 19th century, and (as "Billy the Barber") in Boston publisher Elias Howe's c. 1867 1000 Jigs and Reels.

This is likely the version most people mean today when they say "Lady of the Lake" in an old-time jam.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 2
description:
Here is a comprehensive deep-dive into the history and origin story of the old-time fiddle tune "Lady of the Lake 2" — plus crucial context about why the numbering system exists in the first place.

"Lady of the Lake" is actually a family of at least nine distinct tunes listed in the Fiddler's Companion — including two jigs, two reels, three hornpipes, and two breakdowns — spanning keys from A Mixolydian to G Major to D Major. The numbering (Lady of the Lake 1, 2, 3, etc.) comes primarily from scholarly tune collections like *Phillips' Traditional American Fiddle Tunes and the Milliner-Koken Collection, which catalogued distinct melodies that had all attracted the same name over time.

There are several unrelated tunes that have been called "Lady of the Lake," a situation which stems from association with the very popular country dance of the same name. The title is also associated with Sir Walter Scott's popular romantic narrative poem "Lady of the Lake" (1810).

John Hartford points out that Sir Walter Scott's epic poem "Lady of the Lake" (1810) was popular on the American frontier, and broad familiarity with that title may have aided dissemination. Notably, "Scott's Favorite" is the tune that shares the page in Knauff's 1839 volume — suggesting the association was made in editor Knauff's mind.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 3
description:
Here is a deep-dive into the history and origin story of the old-time fiddle tune family known as "Lady of the Lake," with specific focus on "Lady of the Lake 3" (per the Phillips/Fiddle Hangout numbering).

"Lady of the Lake" is actually a family of at least nine distinct tunes in the Fiddler's Companion, including two jigs, two reels, three hornpipes, and two breakdowns, with keys ranging from A Mixolydian to G Major to D Major.

There are several unrelated tunes all called "Lady of the Lake," a situation which stems from association with the very popular country dance of the same name. The title is also associated with the popular romantic narrative poem "Lady of the Lake" (1810) by Sir Walter Scott.

John Hartford points out that Sir Walter Scott's epic poem "Lady of the Lake" (1810) was popular on the American frontier, and broad familiarity with that title may have aided dissemination.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 4
description:
> Quick context: "Lady of the Lake" is not one tune — it's a whole family of distinct tunes that share the same name. The Fiddler's Companion lists nine distinct tunes entitled "Lady of the Lake," all with aliases. The confusion is so endemic that in old-time jam circles, the running joke is the "Which one?" punchline muttered in unison when a fiddler asks if others would like to play "Lady of the Lake."

This is the version most closely associated with the New England contra dance scene, and its chain of transmission is unusually well-documented thanks to researcher Gary Stanton.

Gary Stanton of Fredericksburg, VA sleuthed the dissemination of the tune in modern old-time circles, finding that it is originally sourced to two unnamed renderings — one as a schottische, one as a polka — in the key of G, recorded and transcribed from the playing of Glen Lyn, Virginia, fiddler Henry Reed.

Henry Reed recorded it twice for Alan Jabbour — once as a "polka" and once as a "schottische" — but never had a name for it.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lady of the Lake 5
description:
Here is a deep dive into the history and origin story of "Lady of the Lake (5)" — the American old-time reel in the key of G — based on research from the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), The Session, and Fiddle Hangout discussions.

It is classified as an American Reel, associated with New England, in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning. The New England contra-dance "Lady of the Lake" is set to this melody, although other tunes have also been used as vehicles for the steps.

Researcher Gary Stanton of Fredericksburg, Va., sleuthed the dissemination of the tune in modern old-time circles, finding that it is originally sourced to two unnamed renderings — one as a schottische, one as a polka — in the key of G recorded and transcribed from the playing of Glen Lyn, Va., fiddler Henry Reed.

Crucially, Henry Reed didn't have a name for it — the tune was simply unnamed in his repertoire.

title: Lady On The Green
description:
| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Genre | Old-Time, Breakdown / Reel |
| Key | A Major |
| Tuning | Standard fiddle tuning |
| Form | AABB |
| Region | USA — Nebraska |
| Time Signature | 2/4 |

"Lady on the Green" is sourced to Bob Walters of Burt County, Nebraska, recorded around 1950. Walters was a traditional Great Plains fiddler whose repertoire was documented as part of a broader effort to preserve Midwestern old-time fiddle music.

The notated version of the tune comes directly from Bob Walters (Burt County, Nebraska), as transcribed by Christeson.

The tune has a deeper backstory than just the Nebraska plains. "Lady on the Green" is a replica of "Hell on the Wabash," published in 1862 by Firth and Pond in a drummers' and fifers' tune book. This ties it directly to the American Civil War era military music tradition, suggesting the melody traveled from fife-and-drum corps into civilian old-time fiddling — a common migration path for American folk tunes. The tune is also known by the alternate title "Hell on the Wabash (2)" and classified as an old-time breakdown.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lafayette
description:
It is an American Reel in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AB two-part form.

The melody was popularized on the Grand Ole Opry by fiddler Kirk McGee (1899–1983) of Williamson County, Tennessee. McGee is the central figure in bringing this tune to wide public attention, and it was recorded on Folkways FW3 1007 — Kirk McGee (fiddle) & Arthur Smith (banjo) — "Milk 'em in the Evening Blues" (1968).

Jon Pankake, who wrote the liner notes for that Folkways album, interviewed McGee in 1965 and was told that "Lafayette" was an old Civil War tune, although McGee did not mention a source for his own version. This places the tune's roots potentially in the mid-19th century, though no definitive composer or single point of origin has been documented.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Lantern In The Ditch
description:
Howard Marshall (writing to the newsgroup FIDDLE-L) states that Bob Walters had the tune from Casey Jones, and that Casey's father, John Henry Jones, composed the melody in the late 1920s.

Marshall's source for this information is Leana Hughes, one of Jones's daughters, who explained that Casey and she were walking home with their father from a dance at night, with a lantern to light the way. Somehow the lantern was dropped into a ditch, extinguishing it, and they had to travel the rest of the way in the dark. John composed a tune soon afterwards, giving it the title to commemorate the incident.

The composer was a Missouri fiddler named John Jones, who made up the melody as he and two of his children, Casey and Lena, were walking home at night after playing for a dance. The tune was thus born out of a very literal — and very dark — experience on a rural Missouri road.

The tune is an American Reel (in cut time), rooted in Iowa, Missouri, and Nebraska, in the key of D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Last of Callahan
description:
"Last of Callahan" (also known as "Callahan (1)," "Callahan Reel," and "Last of the Callahans") is an American reel in cut or 2/4 time, in D Major, found across Arkansas, Oklahoma, West Virginia, Virginia, and Kentucky. The piece is known simply as "Callahan" in Patrick County, southwestern Virginia, where it is regarded as one of the older pieces in the fiddler's repertoire, predating the "string band" genre tunes that featured banjo/fiddle combinations. Folklorist Bobby Fulcher (1986) describes it as belonging to a group of archaic tunes characterized by cross tunings, elaborate bowings, and eccentric melody lines — tunes meant not for dancing, but for "interesting listening."

The tune is inseparable from one of American folk music's most dramatic origin stories — a condemned outlaw's final performance on the gallows.

The core story: they had this man Callahan up to be hung. He had his casket brought to the scaffold, and when asked for a last request — being a fiddler — he said he'd like to play one more tune. They gave him his fiddle and he sat on the end of his casket and played. He declared that if anyone could play that tune better than he could, he'd give them his fiddle. The story goes that nobody tried, and he busted his fiddle over the end of his casket.

Elderly sources swear the Callahan story "really happened" in Clay County, Kentucky, though other locales also claim the honor.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Last Of Harris
description:
"Last of Harris" is sourced to John M. Salyer (1882–1952), of Salyersville, Magoffin County, eastern Kentucky — and he appears to be the tune's sole known carrier. Jeff Titon (2001) says Salyer was the only source musician for this tune.

The tune is known from a 1941–42 home recording made by his sons Glen & Grover Salyer, documented in the Berea College Appalachian Center collection (AC 003), released as John Salyer: Home Recordings 1941–42 (1993). This is considered the earliest known recording of the tune.
American Reel (cut time) · G Major · Standard fiddle tuning · ABB form.
The tune is sometimes played in CGDA tuning (a fourth lower than GDAE), a practice common among old Kentucky fiddlers of the pre-Civil War era.

Bruce Greene communicated to Titon that he perceived similarities between "Last of Harris" and Doc Roberts' "I've Got a Gal Named Susie" (recorded 1928) — suggesting possible shared melodic ancestry, though the tunes are not considered the same.

The title has no documented explanation, but two competing stories circulate:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Last of Sizemore
description:
Eastern Kentucky fiddler Hiram Stamper told folklorist Jeff Titon that the title refers to a soldier named Sizemore who, for some unknown reason, was taken up a hollow and shot, during or just after the Civil War. This is the only known oral account of the tune's name, and it gives the piece a haunting, narrative weight that fits the mournful, modal quality of the melody.

The tune is squarely rooted in Eastern Kentucky — one of the richest pockets of old-time fiddling tradition in Appalachia. Appalachian old-time music is made up of distinct regional traditions, and the Eastern Kentucky tradition is one of the most prominent, associated with figures like J. P. Fraley and Lee Sexton.

Two master fiddlers are most closely linked to "The Last of Sizemore":

1. Hiram Stamper (1893–1992), Knott County, Kentucky
   The tune comes from the repertoire of Hiram Stamper (1893–1992) of Knott County, Kentucky. Stamper was a remarkably long-lived tradition bearer. Like John Salyer, Stamper cared little for new music and stayed with the old-time tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Laughing Boy
description:
"Laughing Boy" comes from Texas and is deeply rooted in the Texas contest fiddling tradition. It is known as a Texas tune, played by Benny Thomasson and others in AEAc# tuning, but was popularized by Kenny Baker (in standard tuning) in his 1968 recording, which made it far more widespread.

The question of authorship has a compelling oral history angle: John Hartford remarked that fiddler Texas Shorty (Jim Chancellor) thought Thomasson may have composed it. While definitive proof of composition is elusive — as is common with traditional tunes — Benny Thomasson (1909–1984) is universally credited as the primary source.

The tune is most closely associated with Benny Thomasson, a legendary Texas contest fiddler. The transcription sourced from Slippery Hill is attributed directly to Benny Thomasson (1909–1984, Texas), recorded in AEAc# tuning. He recorded it multiple times:
County 703, Texas Hoedown (1965); County 724, Legendary Texas Fiddler (2005); and Voyager VRCD 345, "Say Old Man Can You Play the Fiddle?" (1999).

The notation in the Traditional Tune Archive was transcribed by John Hartford from the playing of Jim "Texas Shorty" Chancellor, who learned it from Texas fiddler Benny Thomasson.

title: Laughing Marge
description:
"Laughing Marj" is a New Mexico tune written by Tom Adler, composed about his wife. It appears on his CD Sweet Nell, alongside another tune, "Kerry Shuffle," by mandolin player Rob Pine.

So unlike many old-time fiddle tunes of anonymous or deeply communal origin, "Laughing Marge" has a known, relatively modern composer — Tom Adler, a New Mexico-based musician.

The tune gained traction at old-time festivals — one player noted coming back from Clifftop (the prestigious Augusta Heritage Old-Time Week / Clifftop festival in West Virginia) with it on their list, calling it "a great tune." This is a hallmark of how newer compositions enter the old-time canon: they spread organically through festival jams and word of mouth.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lazy Kate
description:
"Lazy Kate" is actually not one tune but at least three distinct regional variants catalogued in the Traditional Tune Archive, each with its own geographic origin and fiddling lineage. Here's the full picture:
Origin: The tune was described in Adams' book as a typical Ozark Mountain tune of about 1840.
Documented tradition: It appears in a list of traditional Ozark Mountain fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.
Essential status: "Lazy Kate" is one of the '100 essential Missouri tunes' listed by Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden.
Fiddlers on record: The primary sources for notated versions come from Bob Walters (Burt County, Nebraska) [Christeson] and Becky Miller [Phillips].
Print sources: Found in R.P. Christeson's Old-Time Fiddlers Repertory (vol. 1, 1973, p. 3) and Phillips' Traditional American Fiddle Tunes (vol. 1, 1994, p. 138).
E.F. Adam connection: This version of "Lazy Kate" is found in Old-Time Fiddlers' Favorite Barn Dance Tunes ©1928 by E. F. Adam — one of the earliest known printed sources.
Band: The Leake County Revelers were the best-known Mississippi band of their era, hailing from Sebastopol, MS, with Will Gilmer on fiddle, Dallas Jones on guitar and most lead vocals, R.O. Moseley on banjo-mandolin, and Jim Wolverton on banjo.
Recording history: The tune was originally recorded by the Mississippi string band the Leake County Revelers for Columbia Records in December, 1930 (Columbia, 1576D).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lead Out
description: Lead Out is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lightning Hornpipe
description: Lightning Hornpipe is a reel in the key of Bbb from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lily of the Valley
description:
"Lily of the Valley" is an American reel in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.
