The tune is most closely associated with Luther Davis, a fiddler from the Galax, Virginia area — one of the most celebrated regions for old-time fiddling in Appalachia.

A booklet accompanying recordings of three Galax-area musicians titled "The Old-Time Way, the Music and Times of Luther Davis, Roscoe Parish, and Leone Parish" was written in 1986 by Andy Cahan and Alice Gerrard, who spent extensive time with them. The 27 pages on Luther Davis (1887–1986) give a real feeling of what it was like to spend time with him — he was described as a hard-working, generous country man whose life was also filled with music.

Luther Davis, when he was near 90, could still play "Lily of the Valley" and many other beautiful and unusual fiddle tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Litchfield
description: Litchfield is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Billy Wilson
description:
"Little Billy Wilson" is a great three-part dance tune that first appeared on a recording by Texas fiddler Eck Robertson called "Brilliancy Medley", which contains two of the three parts of "Little Billy Wilson." It is an American reel in A Major, playable in standard or AEae (cross) tuning.

The tune derives from the playing of fiddler Eck Robertson (1887–1975, Amarillo, Texas), recorded using AEae tuning. His recording was made in Dallas, Texas on October 11, 1929, as part of the "Brilliancy" medley, and the side was issued in 1930 on Victor V40298.

A three-part version was synthesized by fiddler and musicologist Joel Shimberg and entered "revival" tradition, although it was based on Grand Ole Opry early star Uncle Jimmy Thompson's "Billy Wilson (2)" 1926 version.

The source of the contemporary versions is fiddler Joel Shimberg, who assembled an arrangement of the tune — the most common structure played today — by combining parts from Eck Robertson and parts from a recording of Alabama fiddler Bill Owens.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Black Mustache
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Full Title | Little Black Mustache (also known as "Black Mustache") |
| Genre | American Reel |
| Key | C Major (one version); D Major (another arrangement) |
| Tuning | Standard fiddle tuning |
| Region | Mississippi (Deep South old-time tradition) |

The tune is closely associated with Gene Clardy, a fascinating and tragic figure in Mississippi fiddle history.
Gene Clardy was a fiddler from the Avalon, Mississippi area, and was a mentor to Willie Narmour — the renowned old-time fiddler of the Narmour & Smith duo.
Clardy was credited in local lore with the composition "Carroll County Blues", which became a hit for Narmour and Smith and others.

Clardy's life ended in one of the more dramatic and grim stories in old-time music lore:
Gene Clardy was murdered in the 1930s while playing a dance. He had finished his night's work and was wrapping up, when one of the audience members demanded he continue playing. Clardy refused and was slain — he was 43 years old in the 1930 census.
"Little Black Mustache" was recorded by Clardy and Stan Clements of Grenada County, Mississippi, in 1930.

Key recorded sources include:
County 3514 — Gene Clardy & Stan Clements, Mississippi Fiddle Bands, Vol. 2
Document 8028 — Gene Clardy, Mississippi String Bands, Vol. 2
Musical Traditions MT 104 — The Nations Brothers (Mississippi), "Where the Southern Crosses the Dog: Mississippi Fiddle Music 1928–35"
Harry Bolick recorded the tune, releasing it as part of his album "Carroll County, Mississippi" (2004).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Dutch Girl
description:
LITTLE DUTCH GIRL [1]. AKA and See "Goin' Down the River." Old-Time, Breakdown. USA; Missouri, Oklahoma. A Major (Thede). AEae (Collins) or Standard tunings (fiddle). AABBCC. Thede suggests, without offering any evidence, that the tune originated in Dutchtown, Missouri, although the title could reference any girl of German extraction. Certainly the title was not uncommon; "I'm a Little Dutch Girl" is the name of an Ozarks play-party piece. There are at least two tunes called "Little Dutch Girl" in the Ozarks region, both connected with the Collins family, and Thede mentions the tune was brought to Oklahoma from southern Missouri. The version, printed by Thede, is from Willie Collins, the father of Earl (who is the source for "Little Dutch Girl (2)"). Thede gives the following lyric, sung to the tune. 

Boat begin to rock, her heart began to quiver,

I up with a rock and knocked her in the river.

Little Dutch Girl, if you don't do me better,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Little Hornpipe
description:
LITTLE HORNPIPE. American, Hornpipe or Reel. USA, Pa. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AAB. "In this tune we again have a piece with an unstable and changeable second strain. A Greene County tune in the Bayard Coll. (No. 243) has this first part and an entirely different second. But it is not improbable that the two halves of (this tune) really belong with each other, since when taken together they make up a tune which gives strong indications of being derived from the well-known 'Durang's Hornpipe (1),' a fiddle tune popular among country musicians everywhere. Almost any popular collection of country dances contains a version of 'Durangs;' a good set is in Ford, p. 53; another is in Adam, No. 19" (Bayard, 1944).  

Source for notated version: Mrs. Sarah Armstrong, (near) Derry, Pennsylvania, November 18, 1943 [Bayard]. 

Printed sources: Bayard (Hill Country Tunes), 1944; No. 34.

Back to Little Hornpipe

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Little Pine Siskin
description:
"Little Pine Siskin" is a modern old-time tune by John Reischman. Reischman is a mandolinist and bandleader based in British Columbia, Canada, best known as the leader of John Reischman and the Jaybirds.

Walk Along John is Reischman's first solo instrumental album in thirteen years, and it's also a celebration of his seminal influence in the world of bluegrass and "new acoustic music," a movement he contributed to with Tony Rice in the 1980s.

"Little Pine Siskin" was recorded on his *2013 album Walk Along John, and John also teaches it in his Melodic Mandolin Tunes course on Peghead Nation.

His compositions run the gamut, and "Little Pine Siskin" is described as sitting on the old-timey end of his compositional range — alongside more bluesy, modal, and waltz-styled pieces on the record.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Princess Footsteps
description:
| Attribute | Detail |

| Genre | Old-Time, Reel |
| Key | C Major |
| Tuning | Standard |
| Region | Mississippi, USA |
| AKA | "Little Prince's Footsteps," "Third Party" |

This is an old-time reel originating from Mississippi, USA. The original title may in fact have been "Little Prince's Footsteps" — the gender shift in the name appears to be a drift over time.

The source for the notated version comes from the playing of Mississippi fiddler Alvis Massengale (b. 1897) of the band the Newton County Hillbillies, whose members included Andrew Harrison on guitar and Marcus Harrison on mandolin. The group recorded the tune along with several others in December 1931 in Jackson, Mississippi.

title: Little Whiskey
description:
LITTLE WHISKEY. American, Reel (cut time). USA, Missouri. A Major ('A' part) & A Mixolydian ('B' part). Standard or AEae tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune is known as a "tie-hacker" tune, one that was carried to the Mid-West by railroad workers. In the case of "Little Whiskey" the source was Nile Wilson [1] (1912-2008) of Bucklin, Missouri, whose people formerly were 'tie-hackers' from Illinois.  Wilson learned "Little Whiskey" from his great-uncle Charlie Davis, but many members of his family played:

He acquired his interest in the violin and much of his repertoire from his fiddling grandfathers, Isaac Roby Wilson and Tom 

Davis, and from his father, William Randolph "Dolph" Wilson. As a child, Nile was surrounded by traditional violin players, 

from his brother Orley and his uncle Lester Wilson to his great uncle Charlie Davis and numerous neighbors and friends. His

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Liverpool Hornpipe
description:
LIVERPOOL HORNPIPE [1], THE (Crannciuil Liberpuil). AKA and see "Gigue du vieux fermier," "Grove (1) (The)," "London Hornpipe (5)," "Louisville Hornpipe," "Brilliancy" (Christeson), "Manchester Hornpipe (7)," "Processional Morris (1)" (Mellor), "Reel des régates," "Tom Jolly's Hornpipe." English, Scottish, Irish, Canadian, American; Hornpipe. USA; Maine, Massachusetts, New York, southwestern Pa., Texas, Arkansas, Missouri. Ireland; Sliabh Luachra region of the Cork-Kerry border. England; Shropshire, Lincolnshire. Canada; Cape Breton. D Major (most versions): G Major (Lees). Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Hardie): AABB (most versions): AA'BB' (Moylan): AABBCC (O'Neill/1915, 1001 & 1850). The Irish musicologist Father Henebry criticized this piece for its "purposeless vapidity," although it has been printed endlessly in collections since the mid-19th century and has been quite popular with fiddlers and fifers. Caoimhin Mac Aoidh also says it is generally considered a fiddler's tune in Ireland and points to the many versions recorded by both Sligo and Donegal masters. The title appears in a list of tunes in his repertoire brought by Philip Goodman, the last professional and traditional piper in Farney, Louth, to the Feis Ceoil in Belfast in 1898 (Breathnach, 1997). "Liverpool Hornpipe" was entered into the mid-19th century music manuscript collection of County Cork uillean piper and Church of Ireland cleric James Goodman, and also entered into Book 3 of the large c. 1883 music manuscript collection of County Leitrim musician and piper Stephen Grier.  

A minor-key variant collected in Wales appears as "Processional Morris (1).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Loggieville Two Step
description:
"Loggieville Two-Step" was composed by New Brunswick fiddler and composer Matilda Murdoch (1920–2019), of Miramichi. She learned to play the fiddle as a child and played and performed throughout her life, and her compositions numbered into the hundreds. She wrote over 200 tunes and could outlast many younger players at jam sessions well into her 80s.

Loggieville is a village in New Brunswick, now part of the city of Miramichi — and Matilda Murdoch lived in that same community her entire life. The tune is essentially a musical love letter to her home village.

It is a Canadian two-step in 2/4 time, from New Brunswick, written primarily in D Major for its 'A' and 'B' parts, in standard fiddle tuning. The transcription commonly circulated today is based on the recording of Ivan Hicks (Friendly Fiddling, The Maritime Way), with a 'C' part added by the Puslinch Fiddle Orchestra.

Many of her tunes were "covered" by other musicians, including Don Messer — one of Canada's most celebrated fiddlers and television personalities. She was inducted into the Order of Canada and the Order of New Brunswick, and received a lifetime achievement award from Music New Brunswick in 2016.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lost Girl
description:
LOST GIRL [1]. American, Reel (cut time). USA, Magoffin County, Kentucky. G Major (Silberberg, Titon): C Major (Phillips/McNew, Songer). Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Songer, Titon): AA'BB (Phillips). The melody is nowadays known as a Magoffin County, Kentucky, melody, associated with the playing of John Salyer and Walter McNew (of neighboring Rockcastle County, Ky.). However, it was not confined to the Kentucky borders. Jeff Titon (2001) writes that the tune is thought to have come to Kentucky from Virginia (an older Galax, Va., fiddler, Emmett Lundy, for example, played a version), but that it is not a common tune in Kentucky, although different versions exist. A "Lost Girl" tune was played at the Berea, Kentucky, fiddlers contests in 1919 and 1920 by H.F. Green and by Anderson Bowling, according to records of the events reviewed by Titon, although what version (or tune) they may have played is not known. 

Further afield, the title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountain fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954 (although it is not known to what music this title was applied to in that region i.e. it may or may not be related to the Kentucky tune). Texas fiddler Lake N. Porter played a cross-tuned "Lost Girl (2)", and although his melody is not musically related to the Appalachian tune, the title may have been in circulation in fiddling tradition.  

"Lost Girl" is usually played in G major (c.f. Emmett Lundy, John Salyer), although versions in C major are not uncommon (c.f. Walter McNew, and Oregon's Foghorn Stringband on their album "Weiser Sunrise", for example). See also the related "Old Beech Leaves," and John Salyer's own "Lost Boy, a variant or elaboration of "Lost Girl.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Lowery's Quadrille
description:
LOWERY'S QUADRILLE. Old-Time, Quadrille. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). ABC (Silberberg): AABB'CC (Phillips). Often played slower than a breakdown, although it is sometimes heard played at dances, although modified to fit 48 bars (i.e. AABC, etc.). The source of 'revival' versions is Indiana fiddler John Summers, whom Kerry Blech says had the tune from a western Ohio fiddler. Joel Shimberg (who spend time with and recorded Summers), however, says Summers learned it from his friend Fred Waver, of Upland, Indiana, or perhaps from Fred's father, also a fiddler. "The senior Weaver," says Joel,  "learned it from a (local I think) fiddler, who didn't have a name for it, but who was named (Mr. Weaver thought) Lowery." The tune features plucked or pizzicato notes at the end of the 'C' part.  

Source for notated version: Armin Barnett (Seattle, Washington) [Phillips]; Barry Shultz [Silberberg].  

Printed sources: Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), vol. 2, 1995; p. 82. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 94.

title: L'ville
description:
"L'ville" is a relatively modern old-time fiddle tune with a modest but documented footprint in the old-time music community. Here's a summary of what the available sources tell us:

The tune is also known as "Snake Hunt (L'Ville)", appearing under that combined name in old-time fiddle repertoire lists. The "L'ville" abbreviation almost certainly stands for "Louisville" (a common Southern nickname for Louisville, Kentucky or another L-named town), though no source explicitly confirms the referent.

L'ville and Money Creek are attributed to Fred Campeau, listed alongside other modern composed old-time tunes such as Snake River Reel (Peter Lippincott) and Squirrel Heads & Gravy (Chris German).

Fred Campeau appears in old-time music circles as a composer of original tunes in the traditional style — the kind of "new old-time" tune that gets picked up and circulated at jams and festivals.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

Preludes of an unvarying sort are quite unusual in our traditional music" (Bayard).

title: Magpie
description:
MAGPIE. American, Reel (cut or 2/4 time). USA, North Carolina (Piedmont region). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Brody, Kaufman). Collected by Eric Olson, Bobbie and Tommy Thompson in 1968, and even earlier by Alan Jabbour (1966, see Library of Congress AFS 13,036), from fiddle/banjo duo Harlan Coble and William Alonzo "Lonnie" Corsbie (Guilford County, north-central N.C.). Tom Carter also collected a D Major version from Piedmont fiddler Earl Shatterly. The 'A' part of the tune is quite similar to that of "Evans Hornpipe." The tune was very popular among young old-time musicians in the "revival" of the 1970's.

Printed sources: -  Brody (Fiddler's Fakebook), 1983; p. 181. Kaufman (Beginning Old Time Fiddle), 1977; p. 51. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 96. Songer (Portland Collection, vol. 2), 2005; p. 123.

Recorded sources: - Ken Perlman & Alan Jabbour - "Southern Summits." June Appal 028, Wry Straw - "From Earth to Heaven" (1978). Rounder 0010, "Fuzzy Mountain String Band" (1972). The Cedar Point String Band (Frank George, David O'Dell, Bob Roark).

title: Marching Jaybird
description:
MARCHING JAYBIRD. AKA - "Walking Jaybird." AKA and see "Jaybird March." G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune was in the repertoire of North Carolina African-American banjo and guitar players Etta Baker and her sister-in-law, Lacey Phillips, played fingerstyle and popularized through Phillip's 1956 recording. It is known as a banjo piece today, although it did was not always so. Etta Baker learned the tune from her brother-in-law, who himself had obtained it from his father. It was played in Baker's North Carolina community, where it functioned as "an old dance, sixteen hands-up, circle to the right. That was a very special piece played with violins." Stephen Wade records in his book The Beautiful Music All Around Us: Field Recordings and the American Experience (2012) that "Marching Jaybird" is a 'mirror' of "Spanish Fandango." 

Etta Baker & her sister Cora Phillips

Perhaps like the social dances in the American southwest also called fandangos, Etta 

Baker described hearing it at "a happy gathering that the older people had, like corn

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Marion Reece's Cumberland Gap
description:
William Marion Reece (1874–1939) was a fiddler and fife player, farmer, blacksmith, and fiddle-maker from western North Carolina, who lived in various communities including Mabel, Cove Creek, and particularly Zionville, in Watauga County — rugged country north of Boone and a few miles from the state line with Johnson County, Tennessee.

He played the older Watauga County repertoire very well according to the older fiddlers of the area, performed in both standard and cross-tuning, and was fond of drone notes.

He was a blacksmith from Zionville, NC — a skilled craftsman as much as a musician.

Reece came from a large extended family and was probably a descendant of Valentine Reece, who came to the western side of the Blue Ridge from Germany before the American Revolution with his wife Christina Harmon (Harmann).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Martha Campbell
description:
MARTHA CAMPBELL [1]. American, Reel (cut time). USA; eastern Kentucky, Indiana. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): ABB (Brody): AABB (Krassen, Phillips): AA'BB' (Phillips, Reiner & Anick). "Martha Campbell" is well-known as a Kentucky tune, once regionally associated with the northeastern and central part of the state, but now wide-spread. "Martha Campbell" was of the first tunes recorded by Kentucky fiddler Doc Roberts (1897–1978), in 1925, who remastered the tune in 1929 in an electrically recorded version for the Sears label. Music historian Charles Wolfe (1983) believed the tune related to Roberts' "Brickyard Joe (1)"
, and stated the Kentucky fiddler probably learned the tune from African-American fiddler Owen Walker of Madison County, Ky., a mentor, around 1915. Jeff Titon (2001) is also of the opinion that "Martha Campbell" may have had an African-American provenance, and the process of aural transmittal of the tune from source fiddlers appears to be from black to white. He reports that Ky. fiddler Darley Fulks spoke of hearing the melody for the first time in the 1920's, from "colored fiddlers" and notes that Fulk's version, unique to him, included a bass part that Fulks maintained African-American fiddlers included in their renditions. "Martha Campbell" was also recorded in the field by the Lomax's from the playing of white Virginia fiddler Emmett Lundy in 1941, when he was 80 years old. Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Massa Bill
description:
MASSA BILL. AKA and see "Never Get Your Money Back," "Mossy Bill." Old-Time, Breakdown. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABBCCDD. The tune is cognate with "Kansas City Rag." The "Massa Bill" title is from one of the cuts in the recording "I'm Old But I'm Awfully Tough" (1977), played by fiddler Frank Reed (1904-c. 1985) of Randolph County, north-central Missiouri. Reed also played the tune on his own album, "Old Tyme Fiddling" (1976), but there the title was given as "Mossy Bill." Commenting on Reed's having learned tunes from black fiddler Walt Dougherty of Higbee, Missouri, fiddler Howard Marshall (in liner notes to Voyager VRCD 344), says that that he was from an area of the state that was "once a slave-holding region culturally like bluegrass Kentucky or the Virginia and North Carolina tidewater and piedmont, [where] it was common for white and black musicians to play fiddle music together at house dances or fish fries, but this kind of interchange between black and white vanished in recent years."

Source for notated version: - 

Printed sources: - Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 150.

Recorded sources:   - MFFA 1001, Frank Reed & Alva Lee Hendren – "I'm Old But I'm Awfully Tough" (1977. Various artists).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Mays Fork
description:
The web searches did not return any specific results about a fiddle tune called "Mays Fork" — neither its history, origin story, nor any associated fiddler. Here's what can be said with confidence, along with some helpful context:

"Mays Fork" is not a widely documented tune in major old-time music databases, discographies, or published collections available on the open web. This is actually quite common in old-time fiddling. "There is no outright way to get fiddle tune history perfect, because there is way more than one straight story for any given tune." For instance, all anyone knows about "Soldier's Joy" is that "a grandpa wrote it" — and whose grandpa exactly remains a mystery.

"Mays Fork" is almost certainly named after a geographic location — a creek, hollow, or fork of a river. The titles of many old-time fiddle tunes "add a colorful and evocative dimension," conjuring up people and places that are part of the texture of Appalachian frontier culture. Mays Fork is the name of a real creek/community in Randolph County, West Virginia, which points to a possible West Virginia or central Appalachian origin.

The Appalachian old-time fiddle repertoire began with reels and jigs from the British Isles. Because tunes were generally played and passed on by ear rather than printed music, variations appeared — and sometimes the variations became so different from the original that they were essentially new tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Merriweather
description:
MERRIWEATHER. AKA - "Meriwether," "Weriwhether." Old-Time, Breakdown. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Known as a Kentucky tune, although Bobby Fulcher (1986) says the tune only rarely shows up in traditional Kentucky fiddlers' repertoires. Most modern version are modeled after the "Meriwether" of W.L. "Jake" Phelps of Todd County, Kentucky, recorded in the field in 1973 by fiddler Bruce Greene. Phelps was not originally from the Appalachian part of the state but rather from Purchase, on the western side. Although no one knows for certain what the title refers to, it is likely it refers to the name of a prominent 19th century Todd County family named Meriwether (note spelling). Kentucky fiddler Clyde Davenport recorded the tune for County Records in 1986, although it is likely he learned the tune from Greene. Titon (2001) finds the tune related to the Irish reels "Tom Ward's Downfall" and "Mourne Mountains (1)," and opines that it is a "rare, appealing, and well-constructed tune."

Source for notated version: - Ky. fiddler Bruce Greene (who learned it from Phelps in 1973) [Phillips]; W.L. "Jake" Phelps (b. 1882, Elkton, Todd County, Ky., 1973) [Milliner & Koken, Titon].

Printed sources: -  Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 415. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 151. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 133. Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 103, p. 132.

Recorded sources: - Berea College Appalachian Center AC001, Bruce Green - "Celebration! Old Time Music at Berea." County 786, Clyde Davenport (Monticello, Ky.) - "Clydeoscope: Rare and Beautiful Tunes from the Cumberland Plateau" (1986. Probably learned from Bruce Green, says Titon).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Messenger
description: Messenger is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Methodist Preacher
description:
METHODIST PREACHER. American, Reel (2/4 time). USA, Kentucky. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). One part (Fiddler Magazine): ABCDC (Brody): ABCDDC (Phillips). The composition is sometimes credited to Kentucky mandolin player wikipedia:Bill Monroe (1911-1996), the 'Father of Bluegrass," however it would appear that it predates Monroe in the tradition (he is said to have learned it from his "Uncle Pen", Pendleton Vandiver). Likely, Monroe adapted the existing tune to his own style, and the tune was further refined by bluegrass fiddler Kenny Baker. Monroe's family lived near the town of Rosine, Kentucky, and would come to town on Saturday afternoons to trade or on Sunday mornings to attend the Methodist church (later celebrated by Bill in song as "The Little Community Church"--Monroe sang in the church's youth choir when aged 12-13).

The tune ends on the 'D' part in Monroe's version. 

Source for notated version: - Bill Monroe (Ky.) [Brody]; Kenny Baker [Phillips]; Richard Greene [Fiddler Magazine].

Printed sources: -  Brody (Fiddler's Fakebook), 1983; p. 187. Fiddler Magazine, vol. 3, No. 2, Summer 1996; p. 24. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), vol. 1, 1994; p. 152.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Minnie Put The Kettle On
description:
"Minnie Put the Kettle On" (also known by the alternate title "Minnie Put the Skillet On") is classified as an American Reel in cut time, played in D Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

The tune's most documented source is Uncle Dick Hutchison (1897–1986), an old-time fiddler from Disney, in northeast Oklahoma. Uncle Dick Hutchison is the source for the notated version of the tune, as transcribed and published by Clare Milliner & Walt Koken in The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes (2011), pages 420–421.

Hutchison's recording appeared on the album "Old Time Fiddlin'" (recorded in the 1960s). His recording is preserved and accessible at Slippery Hill, an online archive of traditional fiddle music.

A second notable version comes from Ray Curbow, an Ozarks fiddler. Curbow's version is a three-part, "crooked" (i.e., extra beats) tune — a hallmark of certain regional old-time styles where the phrase lengths don't fall into perfectly regular measures. Curbow's recording appears on Rounder 0436, "Traditional Fiddle Music of the Ozarks, Vol. 2: On the Springfield Plain."

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Mississippi Echoes
description:
| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Tune Title | Mississippi Echoes |
| Performed By | Ray Brothers |
| Key | C |
| Tuning | Standard (GDAE) |
| Recorded Year | 1930 |
| Source Recording | Mississippi String Bands Vol. 2 — Document CD DOCD-8028 |
| Collection | Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes; Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Mississippi |

"Mississippi Echoes" is a fiddle tune in the key of C, recorded by the Ray Brothers around 1930, and preserved on Mississippi String Bands Vol. 2 (Document CD DOCD-8028). It appears in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and the compilation Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Mississippi.
The Ray Brothers were a Mississippi-based string band active in the late 1920s–1930s, part of a rich regional tradition of Southern fiddle and string band music documented during the early commercial recording era.
The tune's exact composer or origin story is not well-documented in available public sources — this is common for old-time fiddle tunes, which were often passed down orally and credited to the performing group rather than an individual composer.
The Milliner-Koken Collection (compiled by Wayne Milliner and Walt Koken) is one of the most comprehensive archives of American fiddle tunes and is a reliable reference for tunes like this one.
The Document Records label (DOCD-8028) specializes in reissuing rare pre-war recordings, making it the best starting point for hearing the original performance.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: (Missouri) Spotted Pony
description:
One of the most popular tunes in the Missouri Ozarks tradition, 'Spotted Pony' has roots in the late 19th century — fiddlers of the early 20th century reported learning it from their grandparents' generation. Folklorist Vance Randolph documented it in his 1954 list of traditional Ozark Mountain fiddle tunes, the most comprehensive survey of the regional repertoire. At least three distinct tunes share the name 'Spotted Pony,' circulating across Missouri, Arkansas, and Texas, which suggests the title was applied to multiple melodies in different communities rather than tracing back to a single source. The image of a spotted pony — piebald, pinto, colorful — was a common metaphor for something lively and unpredictable in Southern rural culture. The tune's rhythmic drive and clear structure made it a staple of Midwestern dances and contests, and it remains one of the tunes most likely to appear in an Ozark-style old-time session.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: C major with a rolling, confident structure. The tune sits well under the fingers in first position and has a natural momentum that carries dancers. Multiple versions exist — some with slightly different A parts, some in different keys — so it's worth knowing which version your band plays before the jam. The rhythm should feel light-footed, like the pony of the title. A bright, up-bow stroke on the strong beats gives it energy.

title: Molly In The Window
description:
"Molly in the Window" was written by Riley (of the band The Onlies), and named for Seattle banjo player Molly Tenenbaum, who was seen sitting in a window at the Festival of American Fiddle Tunes. This makes it a modern composition in the old-time style — not an ancient, untraceable folk tune — but one with a very specific and charming origin story rooted in the living old-time music community of the American Northwest.

This origin is actually very typical of how the old-time repertoire grows. Most of the old-time fiddle repertoire is in the public domain with no known authorship, yet new fiddle tunes have always been written and are still being written today.

The old-time style originates from the colonization of North America by immigrants from England, France, Germany, Ireland, and Scotland, who brought their native fiddling traditions with them, mixed with influence from African-American music. New tunes composed within this community naturally absorb those traditions.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Molly Put the Kettle On
description:
"Molly Put the Kettle On" is an old-time breakdown fiddle tune derived from a well-known song and nursery rhyme from Great Britain dating back to the 1790s or early 1800s, with a Roud Folk Song Index number of 7899.

The tune associated with this rhyme, called "Jenny's Baubie," is known to have existed since the 1770s. Collector John Glen (1891) found an early printing of the tune in Dale's Variations for the Pianoforte (1794) and remarked it had become at that time "very popular with young ladies."

A song with the title "Molly Put the Kettle On or Jenny's Baubie" was published by Joseph Dale in London in 1803. It was also printed with "Polly" instead of "Molly" in Dublin about 1790–1810 and in New York around 1803–07.

The nursery rhyme is mentioned in Charles Dickens' Barnaby Rudge (1841), which is the first record of the lyrics in their modern form.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Molly's Tune
description:
"Molly's Tune" comes from Kentucky fiddler Owen "Snake" Chapman. Chapman had a rich repertoire of old-time tunes, including pieces like "Chapman's Hornpipe," "Snake Chapman's Tune," "Coburn Fork of Big Creek," and others — and was an active performer well into the early 1990s, with a documented concert at Seedtime 1990.

"Molly's Tune" is catalogued under the attribution of Snake Chapman in the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource, one of the key databases for documenting the origins of old-time fiddle tunes.

The tune has circulated in the contemporary old-time community through recordings and performances. Versions of "Molly's Tune" have been recorded by players such as Jeff Norman on Buckeye Banjo (in open tuning aEADE), illustrating how the tune has spread beyond fiddle into other string band instruments.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Monkey In The Dog Cart
description:
"Monkey on/in a/the Dog Cart" is an American reel, played in whole or cut time. It is in C Major, uses standard fiddle tuning, and follows an AA'BB form.

The tune is related to the "Liza Jane" tune family and was recorded for the Library of Congress by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph from Ozarks Mountains fiddlers in the early 1940s.

However, that's not where the tune really took root. The tune appears to have not been associated with Ozarks fiddling prior to the Mississippi band the Leake County Revelers' recording, which seems to be the primary source for the tune and its title.

The Leake County Revelers were formed in Sebastopol, Mississippi, in 1926, and consisted of Will Gilmer on fiddle, Dallas Jones on guitar, R.O. Moseley on mandolin, and Jim Wolverton on banjo. They recorded "Monkey on a Dogcart" for Columbia in 1927.

title: Moon Behind The Hill
description:
The tune was popularized by West Virginia fiddler Melvin Wine (1909–2003), who played it as a two-step at a moderately brisk walking pace, though it has since been recorded at faster speeds.

Wine played the tune in the key of G in standard GDAE tuning, and the tune is preserved in collections including the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and Old Time Fiddling from the State of West Virginia, with notes from the collection of Gerry Milnes.

This is one of the best "how I learned a tune" stories in old-time music. Fiddler Erynn Marshall asked Wine about it and recorded his answer: Wine recalled that he picked it up while walking from Fairmont to Clarksburg along the road — a thirty-mile walk. Halfway there, a companion suggested stopping at a nearby dancehall to rest and watch the dancing. When they went inside, there was nobody there but a fiddler, a guitar player, and the bouncer. They were playing an unfamiliar tune, and Wine asked what it was called — "Moon Behind the Hill" — and asked them to play it again.

In other words, Wine learned the tune entirely by ear from an anonymous roadside dance musician, a perfectly emblematic moment of old-time oral tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Morgan on the Railroad
description:
"Morgan on the Railroad" is an old-time breakdown/reel with roots deep in Madison County, Kentucky. It is classified as an Old-Time breakdown from the USA, in the key of D Major. There are actually two distinct versions of the tune documented, both traceable to the same African-American source fiddler.

The tune's known origin points to a single, remarkable figure. The primary documented source is Buck Barnes (1902–1994), a Madison County, Kentucky, fiddler who lived at the mouth of Jack's Creek, overlooking the Kentucky River. He supposedly obtained the tune from African-American fiddler Jim Booker, who lived in the same area and who played for a time with an integrated string band, Taylor's Kentucky Boys.

This makes Jim Booker a significant figure in the tune's transmission — a Black fiddler whose music spread into the broader old-time tradition through his neighbors and fellow musicians.

Buck Barnes (1902–1994) learned the tune from Jim Booker. Another fiddler from the same region, John Masters, plays the same melody under the title "Muddy Creek (2)", although he also supposedly learned it from Booker.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Morelli's Lesson
description:
Great question — here is what research turns up about "Morelli's Lesson" as an old-time fiddle tune, along with important context about why detailed documentation is scarce.

"Morelli's Lesson" is catalogued in the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), formerly known as The Fiddler's Companion — a semantic index of North American, British and Irish traditional instrumental music, with annotations, containing over 55,000 tunes. Its listing there places it firmly within the canon of documented traditional tunes, but the archive's entry page does not surface detailed origin notes publicly.

The name "Morelli" in a fiddle tune title is characteristic of the old-time naming convention where tunes were associated with a specific fiddler, teacher, or local character — often someone who popularized or composed the tune in a region. The title "Morelli's Lesson" suggests it may have been:
A tune taught by or attributed to a fiddler named Morelli, possibly an itinerant music teacher or a locally celebrated player
Or a "show piece" or instructional tune (the word "lesson" in fiddle tune titles often literally referred to a pedagogical exercise or a tune used to demonstrate technique)

The old-time fiddle repertoire consists mostly of tunes in the public domain with no known authorship, though many have rich historical significance. Fiddle tunes are like any other oral (or aural) tradition — lots of variations, and nobody knows exactly where they came from.

title: Mother's Reel
description:
"Mother's Reel" is also known as "Reel de mon maton (Le)" and "Reel du régiment." It is classified as a Canadian and New England reel. The tune is primarily in C Major (A and C parts) and G Major (B part), played in standard fiddle tuning.

The composition has long been attributed to Maritime fiddler Don Messer (1909–1973). However, the attribution is contested:

Messer can claim arranger credits only, as it is a version of the reel recorded in 1929 by Montreal fiddler Joseph Allard (1873–1947), who called it "Reel de mon maton", later re-released as "Reel du régiment."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mountain Hornpipe
description:
The Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org) has the most complete scholarly record of this tune. Here's a full breakdown:

"The Mountain Hornpipe" goes by a striking number of aliases, including "Ice on the Pumphandle," "Mountains of Kerry," "Old Skeddadalink" (West Virginia title), "Doug's Favorite," "Douglas's Favorite Hornpipe," "Shape's Hornpipe" (Pa.), "Hopple's Tune" (Pa.), "Reel Maginot," and "Woody's Hornpipe." It is classified as English/Irish/American — a Hornpipe, Old-Time, and Breakdown — rooted primarily in southwestern Pennsylvania and West Virginia, most often in G Major.

The tune is a hornpipe of perhaps Irish provenance, though it has a long history in the United States. Folklorist Samuel Bayard (1981), who found several versions in the repertory of southwestern Pennsylvania fiddlers, considered it to be "at least a little older" than the 1840s or 1850s — and indeed it was published by Elias Howe in Boston as early as 1851, continuing in Howe's publications and their derivatives for roughly ninety years.

The tune's Irish roots are reinforced by its appearance in one of the most important Irish tune collections: it was included in *O'Neill's Music of Ireland: 1850 Melodies (1903), as No. 1745.

title: Muddy Creek
description:
"Muddy Creek" comes from Eastern Kentucky fiddler John Salyer. More specifically, the tune is sourced from the playing of John Morgan Salyer (1882–1952), of Salyersville, Magoffin County, eastern Kentucky, and was recorded in 1941.

"Muddy Creek" is known as a "crooked" G tune — meaning it is a lyrical tune with odd phrase lengths that don't repeat in the regular way that square dance tunes do.

It is classified as an American Reel in cut time, in the key of G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning. Its structure is described as AAB (per Titon) or AABB' (per Phillips).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Muddy Creek (aka Morgan on the Railroad)
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Genre | Old-Time, Reel (cut time) |
| Key | G Major (Muddy Creek) / D Major (Morgan on the Railroad [1]) |
| Region | Eastern & Central Kentucky |
| Character | "Crooked" tune — irregular phrase lengths |

The most significant piece of the puzzle is the original source: the tune was learned from African-American fiddler Jim Booker, and both Jim Woodward and John Masters, who learned the same tune from Booker, called it "Muddy Creek."

A functionally different version, "Morgan on the Railroad [2]," was played by Jessamine County, central Kentucky fiddler Jim Woodward (1909–1987), although it derives from the same ultimate source as "Morgan on the Railroad [1]" — namely, African-American fiddler Jim Booker.

title: Mud Fence
description:
"Mud Fence" was in the repertoire of William H. Stepp (1875–1947), a fiddler from Salyersville, Magoffin County, Kentucky, who was recorded for the Library of Congress in 1937 by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax. This recording (Library of Congress AFS 01600 B02) is the earliest known documentation of the tune and remains the definitive reference version.

The tune is played in the key of D with ADAE tuning (cross/open tuning) and is classified as a crooked tune — meaning it has an irregular or unusual phrase structure.

It is a member of a broader tune family that includes "Damon's Window/Damon's Winder," "Devil in Georgia (2)," "Grand Hornpipe (1)," "Railroading Through the Rocky Mountains," "Ride the Goat Over the Mountains," "Rocky Mountain Goat," and "Swiss Chalet." Although widespread in Appalachia under various titles, as "Mud Fence" it is specifically associated with eastern Kentucky.

Fiddler J.P. Fraley (1924–2011), of Denton, northeast Kentucky — some fifty miles north of Salyersville — had a distanced but related version of William Stepp's tune, learned from a local fiddler named Del Carpenter, whom Fraley described as "an old-fashioned frontier kind of character." Fraley's version was recorded and released on Rounder 0037, J.P. & Annadeene Fraley – "Wild Rose of the Mountain" (1973).

title: Nail that Catfish to the Tree
description:
Despite sounding like a very old tune passed down through generations, "Nail That Catfish to the Tree" was actually written by Steve Rosen. Rosen is a banjo player for the Volo Bogtrotters, and the tune was recorded on their self-titled album. Steve lives in Evanston, IL and, when not playing, teaches at The Old Town School of Folk Music in Chicago.

It is a modern composition, dating to approximately 1985, written by Volo Bogtrotters member Steve Rosen, who wrote the tune on a fishing vacation to Florida.

Of the curious title, Steve himself says: "I wrote this tune on a fishing vacation in Florida. Catfish are hard to clean because of their tough skin, and an old black man told me to 'nail its head to a tree and pull its skin off with pliers.'"

A more colorful version of the story also circulates: Steve was reportedly on the banks of the Mississippi River watching a fisherman haul out a huge channel catfish after a tremendous struggle. Steve exclaimed, "I wonder how you skin one of those monsters?" The fisherman, without missing a beat, replied, "There's only one way to skin a channel cat — you've got to nail that catfish to the tree." He then proceeded to describe slicing around the gills and using vice grips to pull the skin off from head to tail.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy
description:
The "Nancy" name covers a rich and overlapping cluster of old-time and traditional fiddle tunes. Here is a thorough breakdown of the most important ones, their origins, and the key fiddlers associated with each:

The name "Nancy" is attached to several distinct tunes in the Anglo-American fiddle tradition, each with its own lineage. Below are the major ones:

This is arguably the most well-known fiddle tune simply called "Nancy" in the traditional music world.
Composer: Tom Clough, a member of a celebrated Northumbrian piping family. Clough was a member of a Northumbrian family with a musical tradition that stretched back some 250 years. His playing has been described as crisp, staccato, and highly rhythmic. He was active in the Northumbrian Pipers Society, and was one of the first Northumbrian pipers to be recorded.
Origin stories: Several stories are associated with the tune: the first has it that the music is supposed to depict Tom's first wife Nancy tripping up and down the stairs. A second is that a squeaky wheelbarrow was the inspiration for the melody, and finally it has been said to have been written for a favourite sheep.
Melodic relationship: The tune is a variation of "My Love is but a Lassie Yet."
Crossed the Atlantic: Paul Mitchell finds an almost identical tune in the late West Virginia fiddler Wilson Douglas's repertoire, called "Fair Mountain Hornpipe." A more direct adaptation of Clough's Nancy is the American clawhammer banjo version of the same tune popularized by Howie Bursen and Ken Perlman, who were familiar with several British recordings.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy Blevins
description:
There was an actual Nancy Blevins. She was apparently born in 1852. Family history records her as: "Nancy Blevins (11/5/1852 - 1/30/1939), daughter of Alvis and Martha Blevins," married on 4/27/1871 in Ashe County, North Carolina.

Nancy Blevins began as an original little dance tune in the 1800s, named for the North Carolina fiddler who composed and fiddled it. The real person Nancy Blevins was still an active fiddler in the 1920s. Research by Carl Barron confirmed her identity: a family history recalled that "Nancy used to play the fiddle and would play at the Healing Springs Hotel."

The tune's story comes down to us largely through Albert Hash (1917–1983), the celebrated Virginia fiddler who became the tune's primary popularizer. Kilby Spencer (Hash's nephew) and Albert discussed it in a c. 1970s taped interview, wherein Albert said he learned the tune from Jim Reedy, who learned the song from his father, Bob Reedy.

Kilby provided this account from his uncle Albert: "…my granddad's cousin was a young lady, I guess getting to be about grown and she played the fiddle. Her name was Nancy Blevins and she had made up this tune and called it Nancy Blevins. And she would play it and he was wearing a dress. The little boys wore dresses, maybe til four years old sometimes….it was back just after the Civil War for he said he could remember dancing to that tune with a dress on."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy Dalton
description:
"Nancy Dalton" is an old-time breakdown in D Major, playable in standard or ADae tuning (the latter associated with Isham Monday and Jeff Titon), and follows an AABB form.

"Nancy Dalton" is rooted in the USA — specifically south-central Kentucky — and comes from fiddlers such as Jim Bowles, Isham Monday, and Pat Kingery.

The tune was in the repertoire of Monroe County, south-central Kentucky, fiddler Jim Bowles (1903–1997), who learned it from local musicians. His recording of "Nancy Dalton" appears on Railroad Through the Rocky Mountains (Marimac Recordings, 1994).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy Rollins
description:
The tune most commonly called "Nancy Rollins" circulates under several closely related spellings — "Nancy Rowland," "Nancy Rollin," and occasionally "Nancy Rollin's" — all referring to essentially the same traditional fiddle tune. The title appears (as "Nancy Rowland" and "Nancy Rollins") in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph (1892–1957), published in 1954, and Randolph described it as a well-known dance tune.
Genre: Old-Time Reel (Breakdown)
Key: G Major, standard tuning
Form: AABB (16-bar tune)
It's a great 16-bar tune in the key of G played in standard tuning, and is a standard at old-time sessions today.

The tune's origins predate any recording by decades. The tune is mentioned in a passage in Missouri physician William Percival King's Stories of a Country Doctor (1891), in his chapter called "Old Time Dances and Parties," describing community barn-raisings. This places the tune firmly in the post–Civil War rural American social dance tradition.

"Nancy Rowland" appears alongside other well-known dance tunes of the era such as "The Arkansas Traveler," "Cotton Eyed Joe," hornpipes, and other staples of the frontier dance floor.

One of the most colorful pieces of lore surrounding the tune comes from Arkansas. Randolph noted that "Nancy Rollin" was also the name of a bawdy song, for which he was not able to obtain the words. Fiddler Lon Jordan (born c.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Natchez Under the Hill
description:
The title refers to a real and notorious location. Marion Thede (1967), quoting Cushman, explains the name — Natchez Under the Hill was, in the late 1700s and early 1800s, the premier rendezvous point for the rough-and-tumble men who navigated the keelboats and flatboats on the Mississippi River. The city of Natchez was an excellent market for products of the "upper country," so hundreds of heavily laden boats congregated there — to the great dread of the law-abiding inhabitants on the upper bluff. The wild boatmen, knowing no restraint, spent their leisure hours in "drinking whiskey, yelling, fiddling, dancing, and fist-fighting."

As scholar Chris Goertzen noted in George P. Knauff's Virginia Reels and the History of American Fiddling (2017), Natchez "on the hill" and Natchez "under the hill" were very different environs divided by income and social class — the latter being the disreputable waterfront district referenced in nearly all the tune titles.

This old-time breakdown fiddle tune was first published in the US in George P. Knauff's Virginia Reels, Volume I (1839), under the title "Natchez on the Hill." Mark Wilson notes it was mentioned in print some twenty years before even that publication. The title appeared again in a humorous dialect story called "The Knob Dance," published in 1845 and set in Eastern Tennessee.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Natural Bridge Blues
description:
"Natural Bridge Blues" was composed by Tennessee fiddler Tommy Magness (1911–1972), who played with Bill Monroe, Roy Acuff, and Fiddlin' Arthur Smith. It sits at the crossroads of Old-Time, Bluegrass, and Country Blues traditions, and is associated with the USA/Missouri repertoire.

The tune is in A Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, and follows an AA'B form. It is built on a blues progression — making it an early example of the blues-influenced fiddle writing that was gaining popularity in the 1930s–40s.

The tune is named for Virginia's Natural Bridge, a limestone formation 215 ft. high and 90 ft. long — the remains of the roof of a cave or tunnel through which a creek once flowed. It was a sacred site for indigenous populations and was considered at one time to be one of the seven natural wonders of the world. Thomas Jefferson purchased the land surrounding the formation, calling it "the most Sublime of nature's works," and built a cabin there used by guests and visitors.

Magness first recorded the melody as a member of Roy Hall's Blue Ridge Entertainers. "Natural Bridge Blues" was recorded with the group in Atlanta, Georgia, and released on Bluebird Records. This was released as Bluebird B-8863 (78 RPM) by Roy Hall and His Blue Ridge Entertainers in 1941.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ned Landry's Tune
description:
Ned Landry (Frederick Lawrence Landry) was born in Saint John, New Brunswick, Canada on 2 February 1921, and died 25 August 2018 — a Canadian fiddler, composer, and singer. His career spanned more than seven decades.

Ned's musical career began at the very early age of four with the harmonica, and his love of music led to his first fiddle, which was provided by his aunt Rose Sullivan. Unable to read music, his talents showed through his keen ears and understanding of the intricacies of various instruments — but his main love was the fiddle.

Though as a boy he taught himself to play the violin, Landry first appeared in 1934 on Don Messer's CHSJ radio show 'Backwoods Breakdown' as a harmonica player.

His radio career began in the early '30s at CFBO in Saint John, and it was while playing on the radio that his talents were noted by Don Messer — thus his professional career began at five dollars per show, first with the harmonica and eventually as second fiddle.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Needle Case
description:
"Needle Case" is also known as "Needlecase" and "Needle in the Case." It is classified as an American Reel in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, and is associated with the southwest Alabama region.

One of the earliest known references to the tune appears in the Clarke County Democrat of May 9, 1929, which described it as a "popular old-time tune" predicted to be "rendered in a most approved fashion" at an upcoming fiddle contest in Grove Hill, Alabama. This places the tune firmly in the Deep South old-time tradition by at least the late 1920s.

Tennessee musician Sam McGee popularized the tune with his finger-picked banjo recording, while Vermont fiddler Pete Sutherland later adapted it as a fiddle tune.

Community discussion attributes the tune to Sam McGee, who was from Franklin, TN, about twenty miles from Nashville. However, it is not entirely clear whether McGee actually composed the tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Never Mind the Weather When the Wind Don't Blow
description:
This tune belongs to one of the most traveled tune families in all of Anglo-American folk music. It is a derivative of the British Isles' "Miss McCloud's Reel" and a relative of the folksong "Billy Boy" (also known as "Charming Billy").

The Scottish/Irish ancestor — "Miss McLeod's Reel" (also spelled MacLeod's, McCloud's) — has a very long documented history. "Miss MacLeod" was popular as long ago as 1779 in Ireland, where it was played at a "cake dance" (where the prize was a cake) in Connacht, and O'Neill (1913) notes it was one of six tunes played by Galway pipers for a traveling visitor.

As the tune crossed the Atlantic and spread through American fiddle culture, it splintered into a wide family of related tunes and song-dances, picking up new titles and lyric verses along the way.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Broom
description:
"New Broom" is an American reel in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning (GDAE). It is primarily associated with the Texas and Oklahoma fiddle traditions, though it was picked up and spread by fiddlers across multiple regions.

The exact composer is unknown — this is a traditional tune with murky origins, but there are two main theories about the title:

1. African-American / Minstrel Roots: Charles Wolfe (1991) thinks the title might be associated with an old African-American banjo song, perhaps of minstrel origins, called "Sweep dat Kittle Wid a Bran' New Broom."

2. Political Metaphor: Kentucky fiddler Jim Bowles (1903–1993) called the tune "Democrats a-Rising," associating the title "New Broom" with the political analogy of a new administration 'sweeping' out the old. This reflects the well-known saying referenced in the tune's community: "The new broom sweeps clean, but the old broom knows the corners…"

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Five Cent Piece (Buffalo Nickel)
description:
The tune is also known as Buffalo Nickel, New Five Cent Piece, New Five Cents Piece, and Ruffled Drawers. It is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown, rooted in the USA — Cumberland Plateau border region of Kentucky/Tennessee, western North Carolina, and Missouri. It is played in D Major.

Scholar Mark Wilson says the tune is called "Buffalo Nickel" in the Ozarks, dating that title to around 1913 — though the melody itself may be older, known under different titles. From what researchers can tell, somebody wrote lyrics to the melody in the early 1900s, but the tune had been around longer than that.

The "Buffalo Nickel" name refers to the iconic U.S. coin first minted in 1913, which is likely when that particular name got attached to the pre-existing melody.

"New Five Cents" was in the repertoire of Kentucky fiddler Isham Monday (1879–1964), who played the tune in ADae tuning, but who tuned his fiddle so low it sounded below C. Monday is one of the most important figures associated with the tune's preservation. He was born in 1879 and was playing professionally before the turn of the (last) century; he played with an almost flat bridge and really worked those drones, playing multiple strings almost constantly — a very archaic sound. The definitive notated version from Monday was collected at Tompkinsville, Monroe County, Kentucky, in 1959 (published in Jeff Titon's Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes, 2001).
Drew Beisswenger (2008) points out the second strain is similar to the second strain of "Grey Eagle," as played by Missouri fiddler Ike Helton.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Jordan
description:
"New Jordan" is a traditional old-time fiddle tune that appears in the repertoire of Appalachian and Southern fiddle traditions. It is sometimes also referred to simply as "Jordan" and is associated with the broader canon of old-time American folk music.

The tune draws its name and spiritual character from the biblical River Jordan, a common metaphor in American folk and gospel traditions symbolizing the crossing from earthly life into heaven. Many old-time tunes with "Jordan" in the title carry this sacred connotation, blending secular dance music with religious imagery — a hallmark of Southern Appalachian musical culture.

The tune has been associated with and recorded by several prominent old-time fiddlers. It appears in the repertoire of fiddlers from the Virginia and North Carolina mountain traditions, regions known as fertile ground for old-time tune preservation.
Key/Mode: Typically played in D major or A major
Structure: Standard AABB 32-bar form common to old-time reels and dance tunes
Feel: Has a driving, modal quality with a spiritual or hymn-like melodic contour in parts
Usage: Played at square dances, fiddle conventions, and jam sessions

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The New Leaf
description: The New Leaf is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Mexico Polka
description:
"New Mexico Polka" was learned by New Mexican fiddler Antonia Apodaca while she was living in Wyoming, from a Hispanic-American fiddler named Costales whom she heard playing for dances in Worland, Wyoming. Costales called the tune the "New Mexico Polka" — possibly because he learned it in New Mexico, or from another New Mexican living in Wyoming.

The tune's exact compositional origin is unknown — like many old-time folk tunes, it likely passed through oral tradition across the Hispanic-American communities of the Southwest and beyond.

The tune was documented on the album Tonie's Tunes, released as a free download in celebration of the life and legacy of Antonia Apodaca (November 1, 1923 – January 25, 2020). Lone Piñon, an acoustic conjunto from New Mexico whose music celebrates the diversity and integrity of their region's cultural roots, released the album in her honor.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: New Money
description:
"New Money" is an indigenous east-central Kentucky tune recorded by Doc Roberts (1897–1978). He learned it from Elza (also spelled Elzic or Elzie) Stone of Mt. Sterling, Montgomery County, Kentucky — at a fiddle contest — according to researcher Richard Nevins.

Roberts was born on Curtis Pike in Madison County, Kentucky, and recorded extensively with Gennett, ARC, and Paramount.

The tune was captured on Gennett 6775 (78 RPM) by Doc Roberts in 1927. It has since been reissued on multiple compilations:
Fiddlin' Doc Roberts Vol. 1, 1925–1928 (Document Records, 1999)
Way Down South in Dixie: Old Time Fiddle Band Music from Kentucky, Vol. 3 (Morning Star, 1980)
Kentucky Mountain Music: Classic Recordings of the 1920s & 1930s (Yazoo 2200, 2000)

"New Money" comes from Kentucky fiddler Doc Roberts and is a lyrical tune in the key of C in standard tuning, with a bit of a ragtime flavor.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Newt Payne's Tune
description:
Newt Payne was born in 1904 on South Pittsburg Mountain, just north of the town of South Pittsburg, Tennessee. He spent much of his adult life working as a miner in the nearby town of Orme, Tennessee, and died in 1977.

A glance at the map shows that South Pittsburg and Orme are just a few miles from the spot where Tennessee, Georgia, and Alabama meet — and Newt is sometimes referred to as a "Georgia fiddler."

He came from a musical family and played fiddle and banjo throughout his life, but never recorded commercially, nor did he become well-known outside his local community.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ninth of January
description:
Bob Holt (1930–2004) said he learned this Missouri square dance tune from his father, who told Bob that he heard it being played at square dances when he was growing up.

It came from the playing of fiddler Charlie Deckard, and both Bob and his father had always known it as "Charlie Deckard's Old Time Eighth of January."

The name "Ninth of January" — one day off from the famous "Eighth of January" — has a great origin story rooted in a live square dance moment:

The story goes that Bob played this tune for a square dance and was asked what tune it was. Bob said it was "The Eighth of January." The person who asked shook his head and said, "That's not the..." — essentially arguing it wasn't the correct tune. The tune is Holt's version of Charlie Deckard's playing of "The Eighth of January." It was different enough to provoke objections from those who knew the fairly common "Eighth of January" tune, saying it was not correct. Finally, Holt simply gave it a similar but different name.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nine Miles Out Of Louisville
description:
Nine Miles Out of Louisville is an old-time breakdown from the northeastern Kentucky tradition, played in G Major in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB two-part structure.

The source for the notated version is Buddy Thomas (active 1935–1974, northeastern Kentucky).

Buddy Thomas, described as "the great northeastern Kentucky fiddler who died a young man of 39," grew up deeply impoverished in rural Kentucky. He learned his music from sources such as his mother's whistling, relatives and friends like Perry Riley and Jimmy Wheeler, and a collection of 78 rpm records gotten in trade.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nixon's Farewell
description:
"Nixon's Farewell" was composed on the occasion of President Nixon's resignation in the mid-1970s by Curtis (Curt) Bouterse of San Diego, California. Bouterse was a San Diegan and a prominent, important part of the San Diego Folk Festival scene.

Right after Nixon's resignation in 1974, Bouterse figured something that monumental ought to be noted in music. His initial reaction was that the situation resembled the old "Somebody on the Gallows" or "What'shisname's Farewell," and he played around with various lonesome and lone melodies without success. He then imagined a song with the refrain, "And you won't have Old Dick Nixon to kick around anymore," and eventually came up with the tune — occasionally singing "jig words": "Nixon's gone, Nixon's gone" to the ascending melodic run.

The tune is classified as an American Reel (cut time), in D Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

The tune fits so naturally into the old-time tradition that many people assume it is a traditional tune and never realize it was composed less than 50 years ago — a testament to how all of Bouterse's tunes "just sound so traditional."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: None Of Your Business
description:
The primary source for the reel "None of Your Business" is Noah Beavers, a fiddler from Elkville, in southern Illinois, who was recorded in the field in 1979 when he was 81 years old. This makes Beavers the oldest known documented carrier of the tune, and it is strongly associated with the southern Illinois old-time tradition.

It is classified as an American Reel (cut time), in C Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABBC part structure — notably a 5-part tune, which is less common than the typical 2- or 3-part reels.

Known recordings and publications include:
Lynn "Chirps" Smith – "Midwestern Harvest" (1994, Marimac 9059-CD)
Noah Beavers – "Dear Old Illinois, CD 3" (2007, Pickaway Press)
Foghorn Trio – "Sud de la Louisiane" (2010)

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: North Carolina Breakdown
description:
"North Carolina Breakdown" was composed by Tennessee's Fiddlin' Arthur Smith (1898–1971). Despite the tune's name pointing squarely at North Carolina, it is firmly a product of Tennessee. It is classified as an American Reel in the key of G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning.

Ernest Smith, Arthur's son, believes his father wrote "North Carolina Breakdown" around 1937, about the same time as "Smith's Breakdown." That places the tune's composition squarely in the late pre-WWII era, a fertile period for old-time string band recordings and radio broadcasts across the rural South.

Smith's recording of the tune was released by Nashville's Starday label in 1962 — meaning it circulated in the oral tradition for roughly 25 years before receiving an official commercial release.

The tune has a notable variant called "Tarheel Breakdown," and is also considered similar to — if not directly descended from — "Whistling Rufus." The connection to "Whistling Rufus" is significant: "Whistling Rufus" is explicitly listed as a related melody to "North Carolina Breakdown" in the Fiddler's Companion, suggesting Smith may have drawn on or reworked that earlier tune's melodic DNA.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oak Ridge Stomp
description:
"Oak Ridge Stomp" appears in old-time fiddle tune catalogs and repertoire lists, but like a large portion of the tradition, its specific origin and composer are not definitively documented.
The tune appears in the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle catalog, listed among D-tuning tunes, catalogued as of July 12, 2014 — with no attributed composer or source fiddler listed next to it, unlike many other tunes in the same collection which name specific players (e.g., "Polecat Blues — Benton Flippen," "Old Buck — Tommy Jarrell").
It also appears in beginner/intermediate old-time repertoire lists alongside tunes like "Soldier's Joy," "Over the Waterfall," "Peacock Rag," and "Pig Ankle Rag" — suggesting it circulates widely in the old-time jam and festival community.
The old-time fiddle repertoire is largely in the public domain, and most tunes have no known authorship — many of these tunes, however, have rich historical significance.
Despite the fact that the majority of the old-time fiddle tradition consists of very old tunes with no known authorship, new fiddle tunes have always been written and are still being written today.
In the 1920s and 1930s, many string bands recorded fiddle tunes for record companies, and these early recordings became common source material for contemporary fiddle players and string bands to learn tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oh My Little Darling
description:
"Oh My Little Darling" is classified as an American Reel, played in A Major/Mixolydian, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AA'BB' structure.

The tune was recorded in the field by Herbert Halpert during his 1939 collecting trip for the Library of Congress (catalog: AAFS 3115 B1), from the playing and singing of Alabama farmer Thaddeus C. Willingham, recorded in Gulfport, Mississippi. Willingham performed it as a vocal and banjo piece — making this the foundational documented version of the tune.

A version of the tune was played as an instrumental by fiddler Charles Long in 1929 under the title "My Little Dony." Long was a Mississippi fiddler from Quitman, Clarke County, Mississippi, and his version was recorded in 1939 by Abbott Ferriss & Herbert Halpert for the Library of Congress. His recording was later reissued on the Mississippi Department of Archives and History album Great Big Yam Potatoes: Anglo-American Fiddle Music from Mississippi (1985).

So the tune appears to have circulated in the Deep South — Alabama and Mississippi — in at least two forms (as a song and as a pure fiddle instrumental) by the late 1920s/early 1930s, with no single known composer. Like most old-time tunes, it is traditional and anonymous in origin.

title: Oklahoma News
description:
"Oklahoma News" comes from old-time Kansas fiddler Bert Payne. The tune has been passed down through the community via fiddlers Howard Rains and Tricia Spencer.

This attribution is corroborated by multiple sources in the old-time community. The tune is catalogued and credited as "Oklahoma News — Bert Payne via Spencer and Rains."

Like most old-time fiddle tunes, "Oklahoma News" was transmitted orally and by ear rather than through written notation. Because tunes were generally played and passed on by ear, not printed music, variations of those tunes appeared. Sometimes the variations became so different from the original that they were essentially new tunes.

The key transmission chain for "Oklahoma News" is:
Bert Payne (originating Kansas fiddler) →
Howard Rains & Tricia Spencer (carriers/teachers) →
Widespread old-time community adoption

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oklahoma Redbird
description:
The primary source for this tune is Lyman Enloe (1906–1997), who was originally from Miller County, in the Missouri Ozarks region, and "Oklahoma Redbird" was one of his favorite tunes.

"Oklahoma Redbird" is considered one of the 100 essential Missouri tunes listed by Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden. The tune is generally credited to Enloe, according to R.P. Christeson, although there are versions that predate his 1976 recording.

The tune's origins are murky, with a fascinating folk-process story of name migration and melodic kinship:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oklahoma Rooster
description:
"Oklahoma Rooster" is an American reel in cut time, from the southwestern U.S., typically played in D Major in standard fiddle tuning, with an AA'BB' structure. It's a traditional American fiddle tune in D, with an interesting switch to the B chord at the start of the second section — a movement some describe as imitating the cry of a rooster.

The tune appears in Gems of the Ballroom (c. 1890s) as the fourth change of the "Ten Strike Quadrille." This links it firmly to 19th-century American parlor and dance music, well before it took on the "Oklahoma Rooster" name. It closely resembles a tune called "Tenstrike," which was part of the Ten Strike Quadrille, and may have descended from the old Gems of the Ballroom books. The tune is also listed under the alternate title "Ten Strike" in traditional tune archives.

The tune was in the repertoire of the late Disney, Oklahoma, fiddler John "Uncle Dick" Hutchison, who played it in the key of C.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Abe
description:
The title "Old Abe" almost certainly references Abraham Lincoln, a nickname ("Honest Abe" / "Old Abe") that was widely used during and after his presidency (1861–1865). It was common in the 19th-century old-time tradition to name fiddle tunes after public figures, presidents, and folk heroes — tunes like "Lincoln's Grand March", "Old Zip Coon", and "Jefferson and Liberty" are part of the same tradition.
The tune is part of the American old-time / Appalachian fiddle tradition and circulates in several regional variants. Like many old-time tunes, its precise composer is unknown — it was passed down orally and through community jam sessions rather than sheet music.
It appears in various tune books and collections associated with the Southern and Midwestern fiddle traditions, though no single canonical source or named fiddler has been definitively credited with composing it.
Tunes named "Old Abe" sometimes overlap or get confused with other Lincoln-era pieces, as multiple regional tunes with that title may exist independently.
Typically in AABB form (two repeated 8-bar parts), standard for old-time fiddle tunes.
Often played in the key of A or D, depending on the regional tradition and the fiddler's preference.
The tune has a lively, rhythmic character typical of breakdown or reel style tunes.
It is played at old-time jams, fiddle contests, and sessions across the U.S., particularly in Appalachian and Ozark music communities.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Aunt Jenny With Her Nightcap On
description:
American Reel, rooted in the USA — primarily West Virginia and Kentucky — in G Major, standard fiddle tuning (GDAE).

The best-documented version of this tune comes from Estill Bingham (1899–1990) of the Hensley Settlement, Pineville, Bell County, Kentucky, near the Cumberland Gap — where Kentucky, Tennessee, and Virginia meet.

Bingham was the youngest of thirteen children and took up the fiddle at age seven.

He learned this tune from his father, Noah, in southeastern Kentucky.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Baldy Kickin' Up
description: Old Baldy Kickin' Up is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Beech Leaves
description:
The source for "Old Beech Leaves" is Logan County, Kentucky, fiddler Sid Hudnall (1891–1984), recorded in 1975 by field collector Bruce Greene. Mr. Hudnall appears to have been a very private person who left little in the way of a digital footprint.

Greene, writing for Fiddler Magazine in 1997, described the encounter: "many times I strayed off the main roads as I roamed the state, to stumble onto a piece of the past that should no longer be there, yet somehow was. That was how I met fiddler Sid Hudnall, who lived with his ancient mother in an isolated farmstead, called Happy Valley because there they had escaped the curse of civilization all their lives."

"Old Beech Leaves" is a fun breakdown that was learned from Bruce Greene, who got it from Sid Hudnall of Lewisburg, KY, who in turn got it from James Wallace James, an itinerant music teacher.

So the transmission chain is:
> James Wallace James (itinerant teacher) → Sid Hudnall (Logan Co., KY fiddler) → Bruce Greene (field collector) → the wider old-time community

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Billy Hell
description:
"Old Billy Hell" comes from the playing of Estill Bingham (1899–1990) of Bell County, Kentucky. Bingham is the sole source for this tune, according to folklorist Jeff Todd Titon (2001). Bingham is the only source musician known to have been recorded playing it.

The known recording is attributed to Estill Bingham, captured in G major, standard GDAE tuning, around 1986 or 1987, recorded by Bob Butler, and preserved in the Digital Library of Appalachia. It is referenced in the collections Old Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes and Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Kentucky.

A 1989 field recording by Bruce Greene also exists and is held at the Berea Digital Archives.

The tune is in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB form. It is described as a "slightly crooked" tune — meaning its phrase lengths don't divide into perfectly even bars, a hallmark of the oldest layers of Appalachian fiddle tradition. The tune notation shows metric irregularities, with sections shifting between C| (cut time) and 6/4 time signatures mid-tune, which accounts for its delightfully quirky, "crooked" character.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Blackberry Blossom (Garfield's)
description:
This version of "Blackberry Blossom" is not the tune common in the bluegrass world that comes from Arthur Smith — it is much older, and is sometimes called "Garfield's Blackberry Blossom" to differentiate it from the bluegrass tune.

The tune was simply labeled "Blackberry Blossom" on older recordings, but picked up the name "Garfield's Blackberry Blossom" (possibly originating with John Hartford) to distinguish it from the related, later tune by Arthur Smith.

It is not entirely clear whether the earlier melody of Garfield's Blackberry Blossom evolved into Arthur Smith's version, or if the two were always separate tunes. However, the two melodies share almost no similarities besides a vague resemblance in the first measures.

The most colorful (and debated) origin story comes from Kentucky folk tradition:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Old Blue Tick
description:
