"The Old Blue Tick" is an old-time breakdown from Missouri, USA. It is played in G Major / A Major, with fiddle tuning in GDgd or AEae, and follows an AABB form.

The title refers to a dog — specifically, a Blue Tick Coonhound, the distinctive American hunting breed known for its mottled blue-gray coat and use in raccoon and small-game hunting. It's a classic example of old-time tunes named after animals, hunting culture, and rural Southern/Midwestern life.

The notated version of the tune was sourced from August Merrill of St. James, Missouri. He was recorded playing the tune in G in November 1973 in St. James, MO, as part of the R.P. Christeson Collection, which became the album Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Missouri.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ol' Bob
description:
A tune from the Kentucky oral tradition associated with Gusty Wallace (1890–1985), a fiddler from Hart County who spent most of his life in Sulphur Well, Metcalfe County, and was recorded by Bruce Greene in 1975. Wallace's version has the irregular phrase lengths and restless multi-part structure (ABCC') that characterize the deeper strata of Appalachian fiddling, where tunes evolved through decades of ear-to-ear transmission with no written score to anchor them. The most widely circulated modern version comes from Garry Harrison's CD 'Red Prairie Dawn,' featuring clawhammer banjo by Paul Brown — a recording that became a primary teaching source for many players entering the tradition in the 2000s. Fiddlers describe it as 'a damned addictive sort of a tune': the irregular bar lengths catch the ear and the melody refuses to leave. The name likely refers to a specific horse or person in the central Kentucky community that gave birth to it, after the old custom of naming tunes for local figures.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: The irregular measures are structural, not errors — Gusty Wallace played them that way because that is how the tune lives. Don't try to regularize the phrasing. Learn to feel where the extra beat falls and let it land. G major with open-string drones gives it a warm, full resonance. Once it gets into your bow arm, it is genuinely hard to shake.

title: Old Buzzard
description:
Old Buzzard is classified as an American Reel, originating from central Kentucky, played in G Major in standard fiddle tuning. Its structure is AABB'C — an unusual three-part form.

The tune was recorded by Kentucky fiddler Doc Roberts (1897–1978) in 1927 in Richmond, Indiana, backed by African-American guitarist John Booker. It was released on Gennett Records 6336 and is now part of several reference collections including the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and Old Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes.

Roberts learned the tune from Owen Walker, an older African-American fiddler from Madison County, Kentucky — a friend and neighbor — who was born in 1857.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Catville Quadrille
description:
"Old Catville Quadrille" is an American fiddle tune in jig or quadrille form, written in 6/8 time. Musicologist Paul Gifford notes that the first change of this quadrille is a variant of the tune known as "Whalen's Breakdown" (in 2/4 time) and the first strain of "Bride of the Wind(s)" (in jig time).

John Pattee was from New Boston, Michigan, which was originally named "Catville" — and his recording of the "Old Catville Quadrille" can be better understood in that light. The tune's name is essentially a nostalgic nod to his hometown's former identity.

"Colonel" John A. Pattee was born June 5, 1844, in Huron, Wayne County, Michigan. His parents came from Ohio, and he started playing the fiddle at seventeen.

Pattee was not really a "colonel," having adopted the conceit for the stage, but he was a genuine Civil War veteran of the 24th Michigan Infantry Regiment. He served in the Iron Brigade as a private at Gettysburg.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Cow Crossing the Road
description:
The tune is attributed to Bert Edwards of Mount Airy, North Carolina, and is classified as a Country Rag in cut time (C|), played at a moderate tempo. It is recorded on his album Bert's Bambaree: Old Time Fiddle Pieces.

Mount Airy, NC is deeply significant in old-time music — it is the hometown of legendary fiddler Tommy Jarrell and the heart of the Round Peak fiddle tradition, making it fertile ground for distinctive and idiosyncratic tunes like this one.

The tune is written in two parts: the A-part in the key of C, and the B-part in the key of F — an unusual two-key structure that gives the tune its quirky, rambling character. This kind of modal or key-shifting structure is a hallmark of old-time fiddle tunes that evolved from oral/aural tradition rather than formal composition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Cumberland
description:
"Old Cumberland" is recorded in the key of D, standard GDAE tuning, with the composer credited as Pat Conte, performed by fiddler Jon Bekoff on a 1990 tape from Wendy, originating from Vermont.

This makes "Old Cumberland" a relatively modern composition (or at least a modern documentation) — not a deep-roots traditional tune with centuries of oral history behind it, unlike many core old-time standards.

"Old Cumberland" almost certainly draws its name and melodic DNA from the broader Cumberland Gap fiddle tune family. That cluster of tunes has a rich, well-documented history:
The Cumberland Gap is a pass in the Appalachians between upper Tennessee and Kentucky. It is through this passage that Daniel Boone in 1773 led a group of pioneers into Kentucky along his famous Wilderness Road — an association that may have helped popularize the title for a fiddle tune, as there are actually several different tunes all called "Cumberland Gap."
Folklorist Alan Jabbour has written that the tune dates "well back" in the 19th century, and while it bears melodic resemblance to some Irish reels in part, its derivation is yet to be determined.
Bascom Lamar Lunsford maintained that "Cumberland Gap" was a speeded-up version of the ballad "Bonny James Campbell," while musicologist Mike Yates finds that Niel Gow's "Skye Air" carries a "faint suggestion" of the Appalachian standard — though Yates admits there seem to be no early printings of the tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Flannigan
description:
The tune was brought north to Kentucky by a fiddler named Brack Flannigan, originally from Texas, who settled in the Gallatin/Grant County area of Kentucky.

The Blue Ridge Mountaineers' fiddler, Frank Miller, had the tune from his uncle John Hall, who had learned it from Flannigan. Miller and his cousin (John's son, Jarvie Hall) were the only two fiddlers known to have played the tune. Having no name for it, they simply called it after their original source.

It was recorded by a Grant County, northeast Kentucky band called the Blue Ridge Mountaineers in 1929 in Richmond, Indiana — one of only two sides the group ever recorded.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Grey Bonnet
description:
It is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in G Major, standard tuning, with an AB (two-part) structure.

The tune is Scottish in origin, according to ethnomusicologist Samuel Bayard (1981), and is related to a family of tunes with titles including "The Marquis of Hastings' Strathspey," "Loudon's/Louden's Bonnie Woods (and Braes)," and "Lord Moira('s Welcome to Scotland)." This means "Old Grey Bonnet" is an Americanized descendant of a Scottish strathspey/dance tune that crossed the Atlantic with immigrant settlers.

The given title, as well as its alternates, appear to be floating titles — meaning the same melody has traveled under several different names across different regions.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Grimes
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Tune name | Old Grimes (AKA "Dubuque") |
| Key | D major |
| Tune family | Dubuque / Duck River family |
| Related tunes | Sweet Ellen, Dubuque, Duck River |
| Origins | Unknown — likely generations old |
| Notable recordings | Norman Blake (1992), Chris Eldridge & Julian Lage (Mount Royal, 2017) |

The name "Old Grimes" traces back to a well-known poem, not a fiddler. Old Grimes was originally a poem by Albert Gorton Greene (1802–1866), a lawyer, poet, and judge from Providence, Rhode Island. While he was a student at Brown University, Greene borrowed a verse from Mother Goose and added almost a dozen more of his own; the poem was first published in the Providence Gazette on January 16, 1822. Originally sung to the tune "John Gilpin was a Citizen," it lends itself equally well to "Auld Lang Syne."

The poem even made it into American popular culture through Laura Ingalls Wilder — Pa Ingalls plays "Old Grimes" in Little House in the Big Woods. Pa's lyrics in the book aren't in Greene's poem; their origin is unknown.

The fiddle tune called "Old Grimes" is a distinct entity from the poem — it's a traditional American instrumental melody. It is likely generations old; however, like most enduring fiddle tunes, its specific origins are unknown.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Joe
description:
"Old Joe Clark" is the ubiquitous, quintessential old-time fiddle tune, possessing the same venerable status as a handful of others, albeit most often played as a 'learning piece' or introduction to the genre. It is a US folk song — a mountain ballad — that was popular among soldiers from eastern Kentucky during World War I and afterwards.

Joseph Clark, born September 18, 1839, in Clay County, Kentucky, is frequently identified as the song's inspiration. He served in the 7th Kentucky Infantry Regiment (Union) during the Civil War, enlisting in 1861 and being discharged in 1862 due to disability, then operated a country store and ran a government-licensed moonshine still amid the region's rugged economy.

After his wife Elizabeth left him in 1864, Clark reputedly fathered a whole clan of children by various women. Originally a farmer, he then opened a small store and supplemented his income by running a licensed moonshine still selling whisky and brandy.

Oral narratives depict Clark as a wild, shiftless mountaineer with a penchant for dancing, gambling, and feuds, earning him numerous enemies in his community. The Kentucky State historical marker at Sexton's Creek describes him as "Joe Clark born 1839, lived here; a shiftless and rough mountaineer of that day. His enemies were legion; he was murdered in 1885. In the moonshining days of the 1870s he ran a government supervised still."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Ladies Pickin' Chickens
description:
"Old Ladies Pickin' Chickens" is an American Reel, associated with the Missouri and Iowa old-time fiddle traditions. It is played in D Major (A part) and A Major (B part).

The tune is most strongly associated with Dwight "Red" Lamb, an Iowa fiddler who is widely credited as the source of the tune in the old-time community. The Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers' Association recorded it with Dwight Lamb (b. 1934) on a release titled "Old Ladies Pickin' Chickens." Bob Bovee and Gail Heil also recorded it on Train on the Island Records (TI-12) for their album "For Old Time's Sake," having learned it directly from Iowa fiddler Dwight "Red" Lamb.

Multiple online fiddle resources (Tater Joe's, The Traditional Tune Archive) consistently attribute the tune to Dwight Lamb, making him the recognized originator or at least the primary transmitter of the piece.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Man and Old Woman
description:
"Old Man and Old Woman" (also titled "The Old Man and the Old Woman") is a beloved tune in the North American old-time and Canadian fiddle traditions. Its origins are French-Canadian, and its spread across the continent is a fascinating story of radio, recording, and oral tradition.

Although originally a popular song air, the melody is most often heard as a reel in modern times. It is listed on JC's Tunefinder under both "le viellard et la vielle dame" and "le bonhomme et la bonne femme" in the key of D — and is attributed to Mary Travis, dite "La Bolduc," the first author-composer-singer of French Canada, from Newport, Gaspésie, Québec.

However, there is reason to suppose that she may have simply put lyrics to an existing tune, as she sometimes did.

La Bolduc's 1930 recording on Starr 15700A (78 RPM) gave the tune wide dissemination, and it can be heard played by fiddlers throughout Canada.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Melinda
description:
"Old Melinda" is classified as a breakdown (2/4 time), notated in the Christeson Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory. It follows an AABBCC structure in Christeson's version, with some variant forms noted by other transcribers. "Old Melinda" is recognized as one of the '100 essential Missouri tunes' listed by Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden.

The most well-known early recording is by fiddler Bob Walters, captured in the key of C (standard GDAE tuning) in 1948, later released on the Old Time Fiddlers' Repertory University of Missouri LP (1976). It is referenced in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Nebraska.

Nebraska fiddler Bob Walters (1889–1960) announced the tune as "Old Malindee" on his recording. The tune is also known simply as "Malindy" in Ozark County — Lonnie Robertson introduces it as "Gonna play Malindee" on his CD.
Fiddle/mandolin player Eric Christopher learned the tune from an old recording of Russell "Casey" Jones, a fiddler who regularly played live on KFNF, the radio station in Shenandoah, Iowa — the same station where jazz bassist Charlie Haden (of the Ornette Coleman Quartet) played on air with his family band as a teenager.
Casey Jones (1910–1967), from northwest Missouri, also recorded the tune — it appears on his Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers' Association release "Rocky Road to Jordan.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Missouri
description:
"Old Missouri" is a traditional tune title found in old-time and contest fiddling circles, but — like many tunes in the genre — it does not have a single documented composer or origin story. Its roots are woven into the broader fabric of Missouri's fiddling tradition, which itself is a rich, multi-layered history.

Missouri fiddling is a unique style and repertoire of traditional folk violin playing practiced in Missouri, United States.

The Scotch-Irish settlers from Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Virginia are credited with providing most of the fiddle traditions found in Missouri. In the Springfield/Greene County Ozark area particularly, the settlers were mostly Ulster Scots from Northern Ireland.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Mose
description:
"Old Mose" is a terrific, if somewhat obscure, tune that came to us from Illinois fiddler Howard Sims. The liner notes from the Dear Old Illinois collection offer this brief biography: "Howard Sims (1896–1977), Modesto — Mr. Sims was a farmer from outside Modesto. He was in good practice to play the fiddle, as he had kept it up over the years. He was a regular in the senior division (over 70) at the state fiddle contest, then held in Shelbyville. His style was melodic with few bow ornaments, favoring fairly dense pieces."

The tune reached the broader old-time community through fiddler Garry Harrison (1954–2012), who collected it from Sims. Howard Sims can be heard playing the tune on the great collection Dear Old Illinois: Traditional Music of Downstate Illinois, as recorded by Garry Harrison. Harrison and fellow collector Chirps Smith were active in the 1970s doing tune-collecting work from older southern Illinois fiddlers. Sims contributed three tunes to the Dear Old Illinois CDs: Old Mose, Stump-Tail Dog, and Dog Treed a Possum Up a White Oak Tree.

The tune is classified as an American Reel (cut time), played in C Major in the Sims tradition, or alternatively in G Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AB or AABB structure. It is sometimes played in the key of G.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Pards
description: Old Pards is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Parnell Reel
description:
"Old Parnell Reel" is listed as an alternate name (AKA) for the tune "Hotfoot" (also known as "Hot Foot Rag") — an American Country Rag or Reel.

"Hotfoot" / "Old Parnell Reel" is a variant of the venerable tune "I Don't Love Nobody," and is closely associated with the playing of Texas fiddler Benny Thomasson.

This places it in a lineage of related tunes that circulated widely through the Texas contest fiddle tradition — a tune family known for its rolling, syncopated feel in the key of C.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Piss
description:
"Old Piss" is an American March or Reel from southwestern Pennsylvania, in the key of D Major. It was played by southwest Pennsylvania fifers and was collected by well-known musicologist Samuel Bayard, published in his book "Dance to the Fiddle, March to the Fife: Instrumental Folk Tunes in Pennsylvania."

The title has a fascinating and still somewhat mysterious origin story. Fiddler Paul Kirk writes regarding the origin of the title: "One was told to me from some friends in Bradford, PA, and that story goes that the title is an homage to a general whose surname was something like Pisselli, and that he was known as 'Old Piss' for short."

In a Banjo Hangout discussion forum from 2021, participant "matchbookholder" writes, "I did a little research and found that Christian R. Pisle of Franklin County (South Central PA – Chambersburg) was a Captain in the 21st Pennsylvania Cavalry, Company I, in late 1863." So the tune title referring to an officer's nickname remains a very good possibility.

The fact that Bayard was a noted authority on fife music, and wrote that "Old Piss" was one of the best-known tunes among southwest Pennsylvania fifers, lends tremendous credibility to "Old Piss" being a Civil War era (or possibly older) march.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Plantation
description:
Based on my searches, I wasn't able to surface strong, well-sourced results specifically about the history and origin of an old-time fiddle tune definitively titled "Old Plantation." This is not uncommon — many old-time tunes share similar names, exist under multiple regional variants, or have murky, undocumented origins passed down through oral tradition.

Here's what I can share based on general knowledge of old-time fiddle tradition:
"Old Plantation" is a name that appears in several old-time and Southern Appalachian fiddle repertoires, sometimes as a distinct tune, sometimes as a regional nickname for related pieces.
Plantation-themed tune titles were common in 19th–early 20th century American folk and minstrel music, reflecting the cultural landscape of that era.
Tunes with this type of name typically trace to the mid-to-late 1800s, a period when Southern rural fiddle music was heavily intertwined with minstrelsy, dance music, and cross-cultural exchange between Black and white musicians.
Many "plantation" tunes were collected during the early 20th century folk revival by figures like John Lomax, Alan Lomax, and Bascom Lamar Lunsford, though specific collector attribution for "Old Plantation" is unclear.
Old-time tunes of this name tend to be in modal or mixolydian tonality, often in the key of A or D, with a driving, dance-oriented feel suited to flatfooting or square dancing.
Like many old-time pieces, it likely exists in multiple regional versions with melodic variation across families and communities.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Reunion
description:
"Old Reunion" appears in The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes, compiled by Clare & Walt Koken, a well-regarded reference anthology of traditional American fiddle music. The version they documented came from the Tie Hacker Hoe-Down recording, released on a Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association (MSOTFA) CD (CD 202).

A notable recorded performance of the tune features Nile Wilson playing "Old Reunion."
Missouri Roots: The tune's association with the Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association and their "Tie Hacker Hoe-Down" recording strongly suggests it has roots in the Missouri/Ozarks old-time fiddle tradition, a region known for preserving older regional tunes.
"Tie Hacker" Reference: "Tie hackers" were laborers who hand-cut railroad ties from timber, a culture closely associated with Ozark and Appalachian communities — suggesting this tune was part of a working-class rural musical culture.
The Milliner-Koken Collection: This collection is one of the most authoritative compilations of American fiddle tunes and tends to document tunes with regional or historical significance, lending credibility to "Old Reunion" as a genuine traditional piece rather than a composed novelty.
The original composer or fiddler who created or first popularized the tune is not clearly documented in available sources.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Savannah
description: Old Savannah is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Sport
description:
There are three separate, unrelated fiddle tunes all called "Old Sport," each with its own origin story. Here's what's known about each:
An American reel in A Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.
This version has no relation to "Old Sport (2)" and "Old Sport (3)." WM B. Houchens recorded "Miller's Reel And Old Sport Reel" (SILVERTONE 4055-A) in 1924.
Houchens' recording matches the notation of "Old Sport" in Ryan's Mammoth Collection — one of the foundational American fiddle tune collections, published in 1883. The tune appears in Ryan's Mammoth Collection on page 53.
The tune has gained some currency among Cape Breton musicians. Massachusetts fiddler Frank Ferrel notes the tune was a favorite of Cape Breton fiddler Joe Cormier. Ferrel and J.P. Cormier played it at Joe's memorial service.
Notable recordings include Natalie MacMaster's "My Roots Are Showing" (Rounder, 2000), and Frank Ferrel's "Maritime Melodies" (2016).

This is the version most associated with the Appalachian old-time tradition and the name "Albert Hash."
Also known as "Callahan (1)" and "Last of Callahan," it is an American reel (cut time) from southwestern Virginia, in A Major.
It is played in standard tuning (Northcutt) or AEae cross-tuning (Hash), with an AAB structure.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Tom of Oxford
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Tune type | English Morris Dance Tune (4/4 time) |
| Key | G Major (standard form); D minor (archaic form) |
| Structure | ABCBCB (full form); AABB (session reel form) |
| Origin | Bampton, Oxfordshire, England's Cotswolds |
| Earliest known print | c. 1713 |
| Also known as | Old Oxford, Owld Ocsffordd, Peace and Plenty or Old Oxford |

"Old Tom" is the name of a famous bell in Christ Church College, Oxford, which hangs in Tom Tower — designed by Christopher Wren. Old Tom, or Great Tom, dates from the sixteenth century and is still sounded each night — 101 times — to signify the 100 original scholars of the college (plus one added in 1663).

In more recent years, "Old Tom" has also become the name of a pub on the opposite side of the road on St Aldate's, where informal pub sessions have taken place during the Oxford folk festival.

The tune was first published in Daniel Wright's An Extraordinary Collection of Pleasant and Merry Humours etc. (c. 1713), followed in 1719 by John Young in his Second Volume of the Dancing Master, 3rd edition, as a "Longways dance for as many as will" under the title "Peace and Plenty or Old Oxford."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Time Billy in the Lowground
description:
First, an important distinction: there are two different fiddle tunes that share this title.

1. "Billy in the Lowground" — the well-known old-time/bluegrass breakdown in C Major, ubiquitous at jams across America.
2. "Old Time Billy in the Lowground" — a distinct, older, "crooked" (irregularly metered) tune in G, played in Franklin County, Kentucky in the 19th century.

The tag "Old Time" was added to this version to avoid confusion with the later 20th-century tune which had "borrowed" the title. There is no musical relation to the key of C tune usually played under the title "Billy in the Lowground," beyond perhaps an attempt to enhance the value of the melody by linking it with the more popular tune.

The primary source for "Old Time Billy in the Lowground" is Kentucky fiddler Kelly Gilbert (1895–1991), who said it was originally known to local fiddlers simply as "Billy in the Lowground," but that the "Old Time Billy..." appellation was added when recordings of the C-major tune began to circulate. Gilbert told researchers Guthrie Meade and John Harrod that he had learned the tune from his mentor Lewis Goins, and that it was played in Franklin County in the 19th century — Goins' father was a fiddler who had six sons, all of whom were fiddlers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Time Fire on the Mountain
description:
"Fire on the Mountain" is a popular American fiddle tune that has numerous variants (some quite distanced from each other) and is widely disseminated throughout the South and Midwest. It is a traditional old-time fiddle tune dating to at least the early 19th century.

Samuel Bayard records the tune's earliest American publication date as 1814 or 1815 in Riley's Flute Melodies (where it appears as "Free on the Mountains"), and as "I Betty Martin" in A. Shattuck's Book, a fiddler's manuscript book dating from around 1801.

Wilkinson's version is nearly identical to the tune as it appears in the 1841 music manuscript collection (with the title "Fire upon the Mountains") of Dublin dentist and music collector Henry Hudson (1798–1889), whose informant was a man named James Barton.

Mike Yates (2002) summarizes that "'Fire on the Mountain(s)' is one of a broad family of early 18th century (or earlier) tunes that shades into one another and are as old as 'Hey Betty Martin, Tip Toe.'"

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Tune
description: Old Tune is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Voile
description: Old Voile is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ole Bull Hornpipe
description:
Ole Bull Hornpipe is an American hornpipe in F Major, played in standard fiddle tuning with an AABB structure. The tune is named for the Norwegian violinist Ole Bornemann Bull (1810–1880).

Norwegian violinist and composer Ole Bull (1810–1880) was among the most celebrated musicians of the nineteenth century — a violin star who toured the world, especially popular in the United States, which he visited multiple times.

Bull began playing the violin at age five, influenced by French-trained violinists of the Bergen Harmonic Society as well as by Norwegian peasant fiddlers. His debut as a soloist came in 1819, and by 1828 he was made conductor of the Musical Lyceum.

An arresting and colorful personality, he developed a highly individual playing style which fused classical schools with folk techniques associated with his native Hardanger fiddle. Adoption of the latter instrument's low bridge and round, heavy bow enabled him to achieve extraordinary polyphonic effects and to play in 4-part harmony.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: One-Eyed Cat
description:
"One-Eyed Cat" is a tune composed and copyrighted by Dave Landreth. Landreth is primarily known as a banjo player in old-time circles. He taught at the Folk School in St. Louis and was described by students as "a fantastic guy and one helluva banjo player."

The tune has a genuine, personal backstory straight from Dave Landreth himself:

"One-Eyed Cat" was inspired by a stray cat Dave found one winter that had been seriously injured. He took it in, and he and the cat both ended up recovering together, reportedly staying in bed for months through illness. The cat — originally named Jack — survived for a few years before eventually being hit by a car. Dave wrote this tune for the sorry old cat.

Dave Landreth confirmed that the tune was originally titled "One-Eyed Jack" — named directly after the cat — but he changed it to "One-Eyed Cat" for what he described as a politically correct reason. (The name "One-Eyed Jack" carries slang connotations that made the rename prudent.)

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: One More River To Cross
description:
Here's what's known about the old-time fiddle tune "One More River to Cross", drawing from the Traditional Tune Archive and related sources:
The tune is rooted in the American old-time tradition, and Mark Wilson (1981) notes that the tune bears a distant resemblance to a Negro spiritual of the same name — suggesting it may have absorbed or been influenced by that well-known spiritual tradition, though the fiddle tune likely developed as its own distinct piece.
It is categorized as a traditional spiritual, composed anonymously, which is typical of old-time tunes passed down orally through regional fiddle communities.

The tune was in the repertory of West Virginia fiddler and bagpiper Franklin George, West Virginia fiddler Wilson Douglas, and Indiana fiddler John Summers. These players represent the core regional carriers of the tune — primarily the Appalachian / Upper South fiddle tradition.
The tune is played in standard fiddle tuning and follows an AABB form — the classic two-part structure common to most old-time fiddle tunes.
Franklin George is a particularly notable figure, being both a fiddler and bagpiper from West Virginia — an unusual combination that hints at Scots-Irish cultural crossover common in Appalachian music.
Wilson Douglas was a celebrated West Virginia tradition bearer, known for preserving a deep repertoire of regional tunes.
The spiritual of the same name has long been associated with themes of crossing the Jordan River into the afterlife, and also with the Underground Railroad — the fiddle tune may carry echoes of those symbolic meanings.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: On The Banks Of The Kaney
description: On The Banks Of The Kaney is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ora Lee
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Key | G |
| Tuning | GDAD (also playable in GDAE) |
| Form | Reel (single/double); possibly old square dance tune |
| Origin | United States (Southern Appalachian / Tennessee–Alabama tradition) |
| Tempo | Slower than a standard breakdown |

The history of "Ora Lee" traces through a tight but fascinating chain of oral tradition:

1. Edward Winter (Tennessee) — The tune's earliest known source is an older Tennessee fiddler named Edward Winter. Almost nothing else is documented about Winter, and researchers have not been able to turn up much information about Edward Winter or much information about the tune.

2. James Bryan (Alabama) — Ora Lee is heard on Banging and Sawing, a seminal set of recordings featuring Bob Carlin's banjo and several great fiddlers, including James Bryan of Alabama. James Bryan learned this tune from an older Tennessee fiddler, Edward Winter.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Over The Stump And Back Again
description:
The best documented account of this tune's name and backstory comes from the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), which draws on the folklorist Samuel Bayard's seminal 1944 collection, Hill Country Tunes.

"Over the Stump and Back Again" is an American Breakdown or Reel, played in D Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB form.

The tale of how this tune got its name is a perfect window into how old-time folk music worked — names were often spontaneous, vivid, and rooted in local life.

The story Mrs. Armstrong tells about this tune illustrates the extremely casual way in which a country dance tune can acquire a new name.

title: Oyster Girl
description:
There are at least three or four distinct tunes that go by the name "Oyster Girl," with different origins and traditions. Here's how they break down:

The source for this old-time fiddle tune seems to be Nebraska fiddler Bob Walters, and the tune was published in R.P. Christeson's Old Time Fiddler's Repertoire. The Traditional Tune Archive specifically credits the source as Bob Walters of Burt County, Nebraska, 1951.

Old-time fiddler and teacher Ken Kolodner learned the tune from Sammy Lind of The Foghorn Stringband.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Oyster River Hornpipe
description:
"Oyster River Hornpipe" is also known simply as "Oyster River" and "Oyster River Reel," and is classified as both an American and Irish reel or hornpipe. It is typically played in G Major (with some versions adding a C part in D Major) in standard fiddle tuning.

The title most likely refers to Oyster River, New Hampshire. The hamlet of Oyster River Plantation was the scene of a devastating massacre during King William's War in 1694, when Abenaki Indians, incensed at abuses from the English population and encouraged by the French, killed and captured nearly 100 settlers. Whether the tune is directly commemorating this event or simply took the name of the local waterway is unknown — no single composer has ever been identified.

The tune has a remarkably well-documented paper trail going back to the early 19th century:
"Oyster River" was entered in the anonymous music manuscript dated 1826–1859, probably originating from Maine, entitled Melodist: A Collection of Music in Two Volumes (No. 29, p. 17), which included dance tunes as well as songs.
The Melodist is a musician's manuscript, probably by a fiddler, that contains tunes and songs from a variety of American and European sources. The inscription on the inside cover reads, "This is from the Bridge family of Augusta, Maine (Horatio Bridge, friend of Hawthorne's)." However, entries were in different hands, indicating several contributors.
Elias Howe published it in his Second Part of the Musician's Companion in 1843 (p. 47).
Patrick O'Flannagan included it in The Hibernia Collection (Boston, 1860), p. 7.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ozark Mountain Waltz
description:
The title "Ozark Mountain Waltz" has been applied to two different tunes in the old-time fiddle tradition, which has created some historical overlap and confusion. Here's what's known about each:

"Ozark Waltz" was originally recorded in Memphis, Tennessee, in June 1930, by the Morrison Twin Brothers String Band of Searcy County, Arkansas, featuring the twin fiddles of Abbie (1876–1965) and Absie (1876–1964) Morrison — who were themselves twins — backed up on guitars by Abbie's sons Claude and Lawson.

The brothers got their break after a recording company representative heard them play in Little Rock.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paddy On The Pike
description:
"Paddy on the Pike" is a regional West Virginia name for the broader tune family known most widely as "Paddy on the Turnpike" (a "pike" being short for turnpike, i.e., a toll road). The tune is said to be a traditional Irish fiddle tune that traveled to and took root in the United States.

The tune has deep Irish roots. It appears in O'Neill's Music of Ireland: 1850 Melodies (1903) under two separate entries (Nos. 1196 and 1555). It also appears in Henebry's A Handbook of Irish Music (1928) and Irish Music (1903). The Irish title is sometimes rendered as "Páidín Ar An Bhóthar Dola" (roughly, "Little Paddy on the Toll Road"). It has been in various tune books since Howe published it in 1864 in the key of D.

The specific name "Paddy on the Pike" is most closely associated with the mountain fiddlers of West Virginia. The primary carrier of this version is:

The notation for "Paddy on the Pike" is drawn from the playing of Wilson Douglas (1922–1999, Clay County, central W.Va.), recorded on Boatin' Up Sandy (Marimac AHS CS 01, 1989), played in AEae cross-tuning.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paddy On The (PA) Turnpike
description:
"Paddy on the Turnpike" is an Irish reel with a long history in America and the British Isles. It is quite popular and widespread and is played throughout Britain and Ireland and in nearly every North American fiddle tradition. Variants abound, with tonalities that span major mode through Dorian mode, and many versions mix modes. Some attempts have been made to sub-classify the "Turnpike" tunes depending on key or mode, but variants even within traditions are often idiosyncratic to the fiddler or the local area, making them difficult to categorize.

Scholar Samuel Bayard (1981) identifies "Paddy on the Turnpike" as a descendant of a once well-known Scottish song air known usually as "Waulkin' o' the Fauld." The modal character of the tune (sets appearing in more than one mode), its wide diffusion, and the plentitude of names attached to it indicate the tune has some "respectable" age—although Bayard points out it has not been traced before the early 18th century.

The tune has also been called "Jenny on the Railroad" and has been in various tune books since Howe published it in 1864 in the key of C. An early appearance in print is in Ryan's Mammoth Collection, aka 1000 Fiddle Tunes (1882). It appears as "The Mills are Grinding" in The Roche Collection of Traditional Irish Music (1912). The first known recording was made by Patrick J. Gaffney in 1923.

In SW Pennsylvania, western Maryland, and WV, fiddlers normally play it in A Dorian from way back.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paddy Won't You Drink Some Good Old Cider
description:
"Paddy Won't You Drink Some Good Old Cider" is an American reel tune that can be sung with lyrics, first recorded by Fiddling Bob Larkin & His Music Makers on February 22, 1928. The tune is credited as [Traditional] — no single composer is known — placing it firmly in the oral tradition of American old-time music.

The tune belongs to a whole family of cider-and-stillhouse themed old-time pieces. Related tunes include several titles referencing cider or hard cider making: "Stillhouse/Old Stillhouse is Burning Down," "Paddy Won't You Drink Some Good Old Cider," and "Down to the Still House to Get a Little Cider." Researcher Kerry Blech traces the earliest recorded version in this family to "Down to the Stillhouse to Get a Little Cider" by Ernest Stoneman & The Blue Ridge Corn Shuckers, recorded as part of a skit called "A Serenade in the Mountains" (Victor 21518 {78RPM}, 1928).

The tune is also catalogued under "Paddy Won't You Drink/Sip Some (Good Old) Cider" and appears as early as *Ira W. Ford's Traditional Music in America (Folklore Associates, 1940/1965), p. 41a.

The tune is closely related to "Cider Mill" (also called "Down to the Cider Mill"), a Blue Ridge dance tune popular in Patrick County and the Galax, VA / Mt. Airy, NC areas, later brought into wide circulation by Mt. Airy, North Carolina fiddler Tommy Jarrell and others.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pagosa Hornpipe
description: Pagosa Hornpipe is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Party Tune
description: Party Tune is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pat 'Em On The Back
description:
Here's what is known about the old-time fiddle tune "Pat 'Em On The Back", drawn from the Traditional Tune Archive and related sources:
It is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning.
The notated version of the tune is sourced from Owen "Snake" Chapman (1919–2003), of Chapman's Holler, Canada, Kentucky. He is the key figure associated with this tune's documentation and transmission.
Chapman recorded the tune on the June Appal Records release "Fiddle Ditty" (JA0061, 1990). June Appal was an Appalachian-focused record label known for preserving traditional mountain music.
The tune was printed in *Phillips' Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1 (1994), on page 181. This is one of the standard reference collections for old-time fiddle repertoire.
The accompaniment to the 'A' part begins on a V7 chord, giving the tune a slightly unusual harmonic entry — a characteristic quirk that distinguishes it from more straightforward breakdown patterns.

Owen "Snake" Chapman was a traditional fiddler from the coalfields of eastern Kentucky, representing a regional style of Appalachian old-time music. His nickname "Snake" and his community of Chapman's Holler suggest deep roots in the mountain hollow culture of Kentucky. The tune itself — "Pat 'Em On The Back" — follows the breakdown tradition: high-energy, dance-driven, and passed down orally through generations of players before being formally notated.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pegleg
description: Pegleg is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Perrodin Two Step
description:
Perrodin Two Step is a Cajun two-step in 4/4 time, played in D Major in standard fiddle tuning. It is considered a tour-de-force — one of the more difficult accordion instrumentals — and has long been a favorite at accordion contests in southern Louisiana.

Also known as: "Ardoin Two-Step" and "Two-Step des Perrodins."

The song is named for the Perrodin family. According to Marc Savoy, the Perrodins were two brothers who requested the tune frequently at dances. No single composer has been definitively credited — like many Cajun standards, it passed through oral tradition, gaining the name of those who loved it most.

It was first recorded in New Orleans in 1929 by Angélas LeJeune (b.c. 1890), Dennis McGee, and Ernest Frugé.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pickin' on the Ol' Banjo
description:
The tune appears on the 1990 album Galleynipper by J.P. and Annadeene Fraley, released on June Appal Recordings (catalog JA0058). This is the most documented recorded version of the tune.

A native of eastern Kentucky, J.P. Fraley was taught to fiddle as a child by his father. His roots in Appalachian old-time fiddle tradition ran deep — he learned the music organically through family oral tradition, which is how many tunes in this style were passed down.

Fraley and his late wife Annadeene entertained festivals and audiences here and abroad, including the American Folk Song Festival, Smithsonian Folk Festival, the National Folk Festival, and Brandywine Folk Festival.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Piedmont
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Tune name | Piedmont |
| Genre | American Old-Time / Schottische |
| Key | D Major |
| Form | AABB (cut time) |
| Tuning | Standard fiddle tuning |
| Named for | Likely Piedmont, Missouri (Ozarks) |
| Primary source fiddler | Art Galbraith (1909–1993) |
| Earliest known lineage | Uncle Tobe Galbraith (born 1853) |

The tune is probably named for Piedmont, Missouri, a small town at the eastern edge of the Ozarks.

It is classified as an American Schottische in cut time, in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pike's Peak
description:
"Pike's Peak" is an American breakdown in the key of C Major, rooted in the fiddle traditions of Arkansas and Texas. It is a staple of the old-time repertoire — a favorite for square dances and old-time sessions alike.

The tune was recorded under the title "Pike's Peak" in 1933 by fiddler Ted Sharp and his band, whom Richard Nevins (1972) suggests came from central-eastern Arkansas. Sharp hailed from the Arkansas Ozarks, and the recording was made by the band Hinman, Sharp and Hinman.

According to Paul Mitchell, both Ted Sharp and Clark Kessinger went into position playing on the violin for parts of the tune — an unusual classical-influenced technique that gives the tune some of its high, soaring character.

The tune has an even older documented life under a different name. It had previously been recorded in 1930 by Clark and Luches Kessinger under the title "Rat Cheese Under the Hill" — a corruption of the tune name "Natchez Under the Hill," although that title usually refers to a version of the venerable "Turkey on the Straw."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Piney Woods Gal
description:
The most vivid oral history of this tune comes from Galax, Virginia, fiddler Eck Dunford, who told folklorist Elizabeth Lomax in 1941 that "Piney Woods Gal" was the original title, not "Katy Hill" as it was sometimes called. His explanation was a classic piece of folklore transmission:

> "About a hundred years ago a man by the name of Bob Cox passed through Southwest Virginia here in Grayson County, and he played this tune. Well, [he] was a fiddler that was a young man then. He learned the tune, but he didn't learn the name. And later he was traveling in North Carolina with his fiddle, and he met a young lady, and she asked him to play the fiddle for her. And he played this tune, and she liked the tune so well that he played it again. And it was in the piney woods country in North Carolina. So when the fiddler got home, he just named the tune 'The Piney Woods Girl of North Carolina.'"

Corroborating this, Galax fiddler Charlie Higgins told Alan Lomax in 1959 it was "one of the first ones I ever heard," and that "Old Eck Dunford, back then, he could tell 'em just exactly who made that and where at. He met a girl back in the piney woods somewhere." Lomax noted "there sounds like a story behind that," but no further explanation was forthcoming from the informants.

The tune has been traced to seminal Galax, Virginia, fiddler Green Leonard (1810–1892) via Emmett Lundy (b. 1864) via Luther Davis, through successive generations of Grayson County, Virginia, fiddlers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pleasure House Rag
description:
The tune is attributed to Virginia fiddler Kelly Perdue, appearing in the collection Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Virginia, and is documented on Slippery Hill with a home recording by Perdue in the key of D, standard GDAE tuning.

It is also included in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John Lamancusa, credited to Kelly Perdue, in the key of D.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Plowboy Hop
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Genre | Country Rag / Old-Time String Band |
| Key | B |
| Form | AABB′ |
| Origin | Southeast Missouri (Bootheel region) |
| First Recording | Victor 23675 (78 RPM), 1930 |
| Composer | Ben Tinnon (1891–1975) |

The tune is sourced to fiddler Ben Tinnon (1891–1975), born in the village of Holcomb, New Madrid County, near the Missouri-Arkansas border. He had a local reputation as a dance fiddler and also as a fiddle repairman, according to music researcher Charles Wolfe.

Tinnon was not a professional musician — he was rooted in the agricultural working-class culture of the Missouri Bootheel. The tune's name, "Plowboy Hop," reflects this rural identity: a joyful, syncopated dance piece born from the life of a farming community.

Ben Tinnon recorded "Plowboy Hop" as part of the Grinnell Giggers, a string band from southeast Missouri. The Grinnell Giggers recorded only once, for Victor Records in Memphis, Tennessee, in November 1930, producing eight sides, most of them Tinnon originals.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Polly Put the Kettle On
description:
"Polly Put the Kettle On" is an English nursery rhyme. It is an old-time, breakdown fiddle tune derived from a well-known song and nursery rhyme from Great Britain dating back to the 1790s or early 1800s, with a Roud Folk Song Index number of 7899.

The underlying tune is even older than the rhyme itself. The tune associated with this rhyme, "Jenny's Baubie," is known to have existed since the 1770s. The tune, under the title "Jenny's Bawbee," is still used as a "Tea Call" in some regiments in the British army, and Scottish collector Herd seems to have known it as early as 1776.

A song with the title "Molly Put the Kettle On or Jenny's Baubie" was published by Joseph Dale in London in 1803, and it was also printed with "Polly" instead of "Molly" in Dublin around 1790–1810 and in New York around 1803–07.

The nursery rhyme is mentioned in Charles Dickens' Barnaby Rudge (1841), which is the first record of the lyrics in their modern form. Eric Partridge's A Dictionary of Slang and Unconventional English declares this to have been a catch phrase around 1870.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Poor Little Johnny's Gone To War
description: Poor Little Johnny's Gone To War is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Porter
description:
Porter's Reel is a square tune with two parts, typically played in the key of D. It is also known as Porter's Two-Step, and players have noted it sounds a bit like "Chinese Breakdown."

The tune comes from the playing of Stafford Stephen Harris (22 May 1927 – 15 September 2010) of Nacogdoches County, TX.

Harris was born in Laneville, Rusk County, TX, to Porter "Port" Stephen Harris (1903–1964) and Edna Faye Fryman (1911–1977).

Harris served as a pastor to numerous Missionary Baptist Churches, including Oak Grove in Garrison as well as Union Cross and Gravel Ridge in Nacogdoches. Stafford loved playing the fiddle, fishing, traveling, woodwork, and a good game of 42. He retired from Nibco in Nacogdoches.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Porter's Reel
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Also known as | Porter's Two-Step |
| Key | D (sometimes C) |
| Form | Two-part reel (square tune) |
| Origin region | East Texas |
| Primary source fiddler | Stafford Stephen Harris |
| Transcription | [Traditional Tune Archive](https://tunearch.org/wiki/Porter%27s_Reel) |

Porter's Reel (aka Porter's Two Step) comes from the playing of Stafford Stephen Harris (22 May 1927–15 September 2010) of Nacogdoches County, TX. Harris was born in Laneville, Rusk County, TX to Porter "Port" Stephen Harris (1903–1964) and Edna Faye Fryman (1911–1977).

Beyond music, Harris served as a pastor to numerous Missionary Baptist Churches, including Oak Grove in Garrison as well as Union Cross and Gravel Ridge in Nacogdoches. Stafford loved playing the fiddle, fishing, traveling, woodwork, and a good game of 42. He retired from Nibco in Nacogdoches.

The liner notes on the recording state: "Stafford Harris played on the Louisiana Hayride in his youth as a 'clown fiddler.' When he played Black Mountain Rag, he'd flip the switch and the fiddle would start smoking. Porter's Reel is a tune that was handed down to Mr. Harris from his grandfather."

title: Portsmouth Airs
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Genre | Old-Time Breakdown |
| Region | Kentucky / Ohio River Valley (USA) |
| Key | G Major |
| Tuning | Standard |
| Structure | AABB (also notated as AA'BB') |
| Named For | Portsmouth, Ohio |

The title references the Ohio River town of Portsmouth, Ohio. This is a regional tune firmly rooted in the West Virginia / Kentucky / Ohio border tradition, a corridor where fiddle styles and tunes traveled freely along river routes and railroad lines.

It was recorded on a 78 RPM for Brunswick in 1930 by West Virginia fiddler Clark Kessinger (1896–1975), who probably learned the tune as a boy in the Kanawha Valley.

The tune's most vivid origin story centers on Ed Haley, one of the most celebrated and influential blind fiddlers in Appalachian tradition:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Possum On A Rail
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Full Title | Possum on a (the) Rail |
| AKA | "Raccoon on a Rail" |
| Genre | American Reel / Old-Time Dance Tune |
| Key | G Major |
| Tuning | Standard (GDAE) |
| Structure | ABB (two-part) |
| Origin | Mississippi, USA |
| Composer | Lonnie Ellis (attributed) |
| First Recorded | 1930 (Victor 78 RPM) |

The tune is attributed to fiddler Lonnie Ellis, who shared fiddling duties in the Mississippi Possum Hunters with fellow fiddler John Holloway. On their 1930 recording, Ellis played fiddle, Pete Herring played guitar, and John M. Holloway played cello.

Ellis, who played fiddle on the recording of "Possum On The Rail," said he learned the tune from his brother, Homer.

Ellis and Holloway were from near Winona, Mississippi, which is north of Jackson.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Possum's Tail is Bare
description:
This version of the tune is most often sourced to Braxton County, West Virginia, fiddler Melvin Wine (1909–2003), albeit from field recordings and personal tutelage, as he never recorded the tune on his commercially released issues.

The notation is drawn from Wine's playing on a Berea College performance video, where he plays with a pronounced backbeat. His influence spread primarily through direct teaching and field recordings, making this one of those tunes that lived in the oral/aural tradition rather than on vinyl.

The tune is modal, with a C chord — giving it that distinctive, slightly haunting old-time feel typical of central Appalachian repertoire. It's set in standard GDAE fiddle tuning and played at a moderate tempo.

The song is a playful observation about animal anatomy — specifically tail variety. The Possum's Tail song is about the peculiarities of marsupial caudal anatomy. The core lyrical conceit contrasts woodland critters' tails:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Possum Trot 1
description:
The tune is attributed to fiddler Bill Shelor, recorded in D major, standard GDAE tuning, and sourced from the Old Originals Vol. 1 (Rounder LP 0057). Specifically, Bill Shelor was from Meadows of Dan, Patrick County, Virginia, and the recording appeared on Old Originals, Vol. 1 (1978).

Researchers Tom Carter and Blanton Owen (1976) reported that the tune had not been recorded outside of Patrick County, Virginia. They recorded it from Bill Shelor, who learned it from his uncle, Will Shelor, and who explained that the tune was titled because "it sounds very much like a possum trotting."

The tune is deeply local in origin — Carter and Owen note that it has not been recorded outside of Patrick County, Virginia — making it a rare, regionally specific survival rather than a widely traveled tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Possum Trot 2
description:
"Possum Trot 2" is listed in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes (compiled by John S. Lamancusa) in the key of D, with its source credited to the "Gettysburg Jam" — meaning it was collected from an informal jam session, rather than attributed to any single named fiddler. It sits alongside "Possum Trot 1," which is directly attributed to fiddler Bill Shelor.

The name "Possum Trot" itself has a clear folk explanation. Folklorists Tom Carter and Blanton Owen (1976) say the tune has not been recorded outside of Patrick County, Virginia. They recorded it from Bill Shelor, who learned the tune from his uncle, Will Shelor, and who said the tune was titled because "it sounds very much like a possum trotting."

Bill Shelor's recording of "Possum Trot" is documented in the key of D, in standard GDAE tuning, recorded in 1974, and released on Old Originals Vol. 1 (Rounder LP 0057). It is archived in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and the Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Virginia collection.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Possum Up A Simmon Tree
description:
"Possum Up a Simmon Tree" (sometimes "Possum in the Simmon Tree") is a traditional American old-time fiddle tune and folk song rooted in Southern Appalachian and African American musical traditions. A "simmon" is simply a colloquial shortening of persimmon — the wild fruit common across the American South that opossums are famously fond of eating.

The tune's roots are ancient by American folk music standards. There was a proliferation of folk songs with similar titles, including "Possum up a Gum Stump" and "Possum up a Simmon Tree," though the degree to which these songs share a common ancestor is not fully known.

A closely related tune, "Possum Up a Gum Stump," helps anchor the timeline: it was mentioned in chronicles before the year 1830, was cited as having been played in a 1914 Atlanta, Georgia fiddlers' contest, and was listed in a 1929 newspaper as one of the tunes likely to be played at an upcoming fiddlers' convention. The title also appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist and folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.

The song has deep connections to African American folk tradition. Lyrics were collected from Black informants in eastern North Carolina in 1908, with verses like: "A 'possum up a 'simmon-tree; I winked at him; he winked at me; I picked up a rock and hit him on de shin."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Betty Martin
description:
The story is that "Pretty Betty Martin" was born in England and when she came to this country, a young woman, had so many suitors on the ship in which she made the voyage that she could not choose among them, so, consequently, rejected all.

It has been said that she was a niece of the Duke of Marlborough, but even this reflected glory can add little to her fame as the heroine of the jingle.

Betty Martin's grandson was William Paca, one of the signers of the Declaration of Independence, and Chief Justice of Maryland, and Chief Judge of the U.S. Court of Appeals, besides filling other places of honor, and the ancestral home was on Wye Island, in one of the rivers tributary to the Chesapeake. Specifically, Elizabeth Smith, wife of John Paca, father of William, was a daughter of that "pretty Betty Martin" with whose name an old nursery rhyme is so free.

"Pretty Betty Martin" is an old and widespread song dating to the mid-18th century in America. The tune associated with it has numerous variations and titles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Little Indian
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Tune Type | American Reel (cut time) |
| Key/Mode | A Mixolydian (A Modal) |
| Tuning | Standard (GDAE) |
| Structure | AA'B or AABB |
| Regional Origin | Kentucky / West Virginia / Appalachia |
| Earliest Known Source | Ward Jarvis (1894–1982) |
| Most Famous Popularizer | Curly Ray Cline (1923–1997) |

The tune's origin, like most old-time fiddle tunes, is murky by nature. In old-time circles, saying "this is Pretty Little Indian, from Ward Jarvis" means he was the earliest source we know of, but it doesn't necessarily mean he actually wrote the tune himself.

Ward Jarvis (1894–1982), from Braxton County, West Virginia, who later moved to southeastern Ohio, is the primary attributed source. Jarvis is credited as the source for many old-time versions.

The tune also traveled through a parallel Kentucky lineage. Multiple recordings trace it back through Van Kidwell (a Kentucky/Ohio fiddler) and Buddy Thomas (a Kentucky fiddler):
The West Orrtanna String Band recorded it in 1978, having learned it from Kentucky/Ohio fiddler Van Kidwell.
Bob Carlin recorded it in 1980 on Fiddle Tunes for Clawhammer Banjo, having learned it from Van Kidwell via the Hotmud Family.
Roger Cooper recorded it in 2006 on Essence of Old Kentucky, having learned it from Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Little Shoes
description:
"Pretty Little Shoes" is actually the name applied to two distinct West Virginia old-time breakdown tunes that share a title but sound quite different from each other. Both are rooted in the Appalachian fiddle tradition of Clay County, West Virginia.
The source for this tune is Clay County, West Virginia, fiddler French Carpenter (1899–1965), passed down via Wilson Douglas. It is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in A Mixolydian.
The notated version comes from Jim Ketterman, and was printed in Silberberg's Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern (2002).
It was recorded by Wilson Douglas (West Virginia) on "Boatin' Up Sandy" (Marimac Recordings, 1989).

This is the version most commonly played today in old-time circles.
This week's tune is "Pretty Little Shoes" from the playing of James Warden "Ward" Jarvis (19 March 1894 – 18 September 1982). He was the son of Josiah "Si" Jarvis and Amanda Melissa Siers, and married Susie Ellen Fulks in 1920.
According to Milliner-Koken, Jarvis moved to Athens County, Ohio in the late 1940s to work in the timber industry. He played banjo with Ed Haley and John McIlwaine, frequently visited Henry Reed, and never recorded commercially — but was captured in various field recordings.
Jarvis's repertoire was typical of his West Virginia origin, with many archaic-sounding cross-tuned pieces as well as tunes popular in the 1920s and 1930s.
The tune was also played by West Virginia fiddlers Doc White and Lester McCumber.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Little Widow
description:
"Pretty Little Widow" is an old fiddle tune from Kentucky. It is classified as a traditional American tune with no known single composer — it belongs to the broader oral/aural tradition of Appalachian and Southern old-time music.

1. W. H. Stepp (1875–1957) — Magoffin County, Kentucky
One of the primary documented sources of the tune is W. H. Stepp (1875–1957), from Magoffin County, Kentucky. His version was recorded for and preserved by the Library of Congress, played in AEae cross-tuning (a reel in cut time).

2. John Ashby — Virginia
Another well-known version comes from John Ashby, recorded in the key of A with AEAE cross-tuning, sourced from the album Down on Ashby's Farm (County LP 745, 1974). This version is also referenced in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes: Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Virginia.

title: Pumpkin Vine
description:
"Pumpkin Vine" is rooted in northeastern Kentucky old-time fiddle tradition. It is classified as a two-step (in cut time, key of G), typical of the dance-driven instrumental tunes of the Appalachian highlands.

One of the primary documented sources for "Pumpkin Vine" (also called "Old Pumpkin Vine") is Alfred Bailey (1918–1996), from Fleming County, northeastern Kentucky, who was recorded in the field in 1986 by folklorist John Harrod. Bailey had the tune from Asa Neil, suggesting an older oral transmission chain reaching back at least a generation before Bailey himself.

Another significant carrier of the tune was fiddler Buddy Thomas (1935–1974), also from northeastern Kentucky, whose version was recorded and released on Rounder CD 0376: "Traditional Fiddle Music of Kentucky." Thomas is one of the most celebrated Kentucky fiddlers of his era, and his version helped bring the tune to wider audiences.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Puncheon Floor
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Full Title | Puncheon on the Floor (also known simply as Puncheon Floor) |
| Genre | Old-Time, Breakdown/Reel |
| Origin Region | Western North Carolina (Surry County / Dobson area) |
| Key | G Major (A part) → D Major (B part) |
| Tuning | Standard (GDAE) |
| Structure | AABB |

The name has deep Appalachian roots. The title refers to the old practice of building cabin floors out of trees split down the middle and set in the ground flat side up. More precisely, a puncheon floor is a floor made of logs split lengthwise which are pegged, flat side upward, to joists to make floors in log houses.

The word "puncheon" also has a second meaning — a puncheon is a barrel of liquor — which adds an amusing double meaning to the tune's title, and may even explain the alternate version "Puncheon on the Floor."

The most well-documented lineage of the tune traces to western North Carolina:
The reel is sourced to Dobson, North Carolina, fiddler Esker Hutchins, who learned it from an influential local fiddler, Crawley Hamlin.
Hutchins was a neighbor to Frank and Oscar Jenkins and was a fiddle mentor to Benton Flippen of nearby Round Peak. (Benton Flippen himself became one of the most celebrated figures in Round Peak–style old-time fiddling.)
Recorded by Ray Alden in 1972, Hutchins learned from "the grand old fiddler of the Dobson area, Crawley Hamlin."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Purcell's Reel
description:
The primary documented source for Purcell's Reel in the old-time tradition is Bob Walters, a Nebraska fiddler. Robert E. "Uncle Bob" Walters was born on June 16, 1889, in Decatur, Burt County, Nebraska. His grandfather, Ike Walters, and his father, William Wilson "Wilse" Walters, were both noted fiddlers — meaning Bob came from a deep multi-generational fiddling family.

Purcell's Reel is attributed to artist Bob Walters, played in the Key of A with standard GDAE tuning, recorded around 1950, and later released on the Old Time Fiddlers' Repertory University of Missouri LP (1976). It appears in the collections The Old Time Fiddler's Repertory and Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Nebraska.

Bob Walters was a titan of the Midwestern old-time fiddling scene. He won a number of contests sponsored by KFNF in Shenandoah, Iowa — so many that other contestants protested and he was eventually hired as a judge and "guest artist." He competed in radio contests in Omaha and Sioux City, and his last regular radio stint was on KMMJ out of Grand Island, Nebraska, where he played from the mid-1940s until around 1954. He was a consistent winner in local contests, at one point having won 34 out of 38 he had entered. His biggest win was the 1931 Tri-State Championship held in Sioux City, Iowa, where he took first prize along with a silver cup.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Queen Of France
description:
"Queen of France" is a tune that exists in the broader old-time American fiddle tradition, but — like many tunes in that canon — its precise composer and origin story are murky or lost to oral tradition. This is extremely common. Old-time fiddle style originates from the colonization of North America by immigrants from England, France, Germany, Ireland, and Scotland, who brought their native fiddling traditions with them, mixed with influence from African-American music.

The title "Queen of France" fits a naming pattern that was common in early American fiddling. The American Revolution period saw the cultural influences of the emerging new nation blended into a sound of its own, and many patriotic or politically themed fiddle tunes were coined during this era — including Washington's Reel, Bennington Assembly, and Jefferson and Liberty. Titles referencing royalty or foreign powers — like "Queen of France" — were often whimsical, ironic, or aspirational, sometimes commemorating political events or figures of the day.

The "France" in the title likely reflects the real French musical influence baked into old-time fiddling, particularly from Québécois immigrants. Québécois brought to New England to work in lumberyards and factories brought the distinctive rhythms and joie-de-vivre of Québec fiddle, heavily influencing the native country or contra dances of the area.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Quince Dillion's High D
description:
A beautifully layered story sitting at the intersection of Civil War fife music, Appalachian fiddling, and 1960s folk revival fieldwork. Here's everything known about it.

| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Type | American Reel (whole or cut time) |
| Key | D Major, standard tuning |
| Region | Southwestern Virginia / WV border |
| Structure | Commonly 2 parts (AABB); original may have had 4 parts |
| Defining feature | A high D note on the fiddle's E string |
| Library of Congress | [AFC 1999/016 — Henry Reed Collection](https://www.loc.gov/item/afcreed000178/) |

His full name was Quincie Perry Dillion, also known as "Uncle Quincy," and his date of birth in Franklin County, VA is variously reported as between 1810 and 1827.

"Uncle Quincy," as he was popularly called, was a noted man in the Civil War as a fifer. He belonged to Edgar's Battalion of Infantry, C.S.A., and was reportedly honored by both the Southern and Northern Armies for his music on the fife.

title: Rabbit in the Grass
description:
The original composer is unknown. The tune was made popular in 1928 by Luke Hignight's Ozark Strutters, a string band from Arkansas. Despite that early commercial recording, the tune's roots run deeper into the folk tradition.

The tune circulates under at least one well-known alternate title. In Marion Thede's The Fiddle Book (1967), it appears as "Soapsuds Splash", sourced from fiddler Emmett Newman of Delaware County, Oklahoma. It also appears in R.P. Christeson's Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, Vol. 1 (1973), sourced from Bill Driver of Missouri.

One of the most celebrated versions comes through the lineage of James Bryan and his mentor Mack Blalock. Mack Blalock was Bryan's source for many tunes. Growing up in northeast Alabama near Mentone, Bryan was influenced by the fiddling of Blalock and his family, who were all noted fiddlers in the region.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rachel
description:
The title "Rachael" or "Rachael's Hornpipe" has been attributed to Rachel Donelson Jackson (1767–1828), wife of President Andrew Jackson, according to the Texas Old Time Fiddling Association's website. However, there is no corroborating evidence for this assertion and it is purely conjectural.

Some have speculated that the tune might pre-date the Civil War, if you believe some of the associations with the "Rachel" title.

The tune is an American reel in 2/4 or cut time, known in Missouri, West Virginia, North Carolina, and Virginia, played in D Major in standard fiddle tuning. It's considered a square tune with two parts. The key of D is note-dense, but the notes mostly follow the three chord tones of the tune's three chords.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Railroad Runs Thru Georgia
description:
"Railroad Runs Through Georgia" is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown originating from Oklahoma, played in the key of A Major in AEae cross-tuning (AEAE). Its form is AABB.

The melody was in the repertoire of Oklahoma's Pottawatomie County Collins family, whose older members (such as W.S. Collins) contributed to Marion Thede's foundational folk music book. The latter 20th-century representative of the family, fiddler Earl Collins, recorded several albums carrying the tune forward.

The canonical field recording most often referenced in the old-time community comes from Max Collins, captured in a field recording by Gary Stanton and Tom Carter, and is referenced alongside Marion Thede's Fiddle Book (page 42) as notated by Walter Baker. It is sometimes described as "a Max Collins tune from the Oklahoma Ozarks."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Railroading Thru the Rockies
description:
"Railroad Through The Rocky Mountains" is the official name of the tune. It is classified as an Old-Time breakdown from the USA, Kentucky. It is played in D Major in standard fiddle tuning.

Jim Bowles, from Kentucky, is the primary source of the tune. He was a great old Kentucky fiddler known for "lots of weird, awesome tunes... with plenty of blue notes to go around."

Jim Bowles (1903–1993) learned the tune from his uncle, Wash Carter, who called it "Goin' Down to Shirley's", according to Jeff Titon (2001). So the tune that the broader old-time community knows as "Railroad Through the Rocky Mountains" was passed down within the Bowles family under a completely different name — a common phenomenon in oral folk traditions where the same melody circulates under multiple local names.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rattlesnake Bit The Baby
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Genre | American Old-Time, Reel (cut/2-4 time) |
| Key | C Major |
| Structure | AABB |
| Tuning | Standard fiddle |
| Region | USA (Virginia, Missouri, Appalachia, California) |

The title "Rattlesnake Bit the Baby" appears to be mandolinist Kenny Hall's name for the tune, but it is better-known under the name that fiddler Lowe Stokes recorded it — "Take Me Back to Georgia."

The tune is also known under several other names: "Katy Did (2)," "Boston Boy," "Ladies in the Ballroom (2)," "Kill the Shanghai Rooster," and "Take Me Back to Georgia" (Lowe Stokes).

The tune's transmission chain in the oral tradition is well-documented in the Virginia fiddling community. Among the influences on legendary Virginia fiddler John Ashby was a local fiddler named Walter Graham and John Sinclair, from whom he learned "Rattlesnake Bit the Baby."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rebel Raid
description:
"Rebel Raid" is a fascinating case in old-time music because the title was applied to multiple distinct and unrelated fiddle tunes across the Appalachian region, each with its own source fiddler. Here's what's known:

A breakdown fiddle tune attributed to Kentucky fiddler Ed Haley, the title most likely refers to the Civil War raids of Confederate General John Hunt Morgan ("Morgan's Raiders"), whose soldiers moved through the mountains of Eastern Kentucky in June 1864.

Jim Taylor (1996) and Jeff Titon (2001) believe the title may refer to the 1864 Confederate incursions of General John Hunt Morgan and "Morgan's Raiders" into eastern Kentucky.

The title "Rebel Raid" was attached to several tunes at the turn of the century, remarks John Hartford.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Red Apple Rag
description:
Red Apple Rag is an American Country Rag in 2/4 time, in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning. It follows an AB (Christeson), AABB (Phillips), or AA'BB' (Devil's Box) structure depending on the source.

Red Apple Rag is a widely-known, frequently played and recorded tune, popularized by Tennessee fiddle legend Arthur Smith (1898–1971). The composition is often credited to him.

The tune is also documented from the playing of farmer and fiddler Sammie Dyer (1906–1983, Macon County, north-central Tennessee), recorded in the field in 1972. The canonical source in scholarly notation traces to Arthur Smith of Humphreys County, east Tennessee.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Red Bird
description:
There are actually at least two distinct old-time tunes called "Red Bird" documented in the Traditional Tune Archive, plus a related "Red Bird Reel." Here's what's known about each:
Red Bird [1] is an old-time breakdown from the USA, Oklahoma tradition.
The tune attempts to imitate the call of a bird in one of its sections, and features pizzicato (plucked) notes — a distinctive and unusual technique for a fiddle breakdown, suggesting the tune had a programmatic or novelty character from early on.
The primary source for the notated version comes from Jubal Anderson of Pottawatomie County, Oklahoma, and also from legendary Oklahoma fiddler Byron Berline.
It appears in print in *Phillips' Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1 (1994), p. 197, and in Thede's The Fiddle Book (1967), p. 152.
Scholar Guthrie Meade notes the tune is very similar to Uncle Jimmy Thompson's "Billy Wilson (2)," recorded for Columbia in 1926. Uncle Jimmy Thompson (1848–1931) was the legendary Tennessee fiddler who famously appeared on the first broadcast of the Grand Ole Opry in 1927.
It is also related in some parts to the separate tune known as "Red Bird Reel."

Red Bird [2] is considered a showpiece tune for West Virginia fiddler Clark Kessinger (1896–1975), who recorded it several times, albeit later in life.
The tune is in A Major, in cut time (reel), and is associated with Kessinger from Lincoln County, West Virginia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Red Haired Boy (Little Beggar Man)
description:
The tune "Red Haired Boy" traces back to a Scottish tune called Gilderoy, whose name comes from a very popular 18th-century song about a Scottish outlaw named McGreggor, nicknamed Giolla Ruadh — meaning "red-haired lad" — who was executed in 1636.

"Red Haired Boy" is in fact the English translation of the Gaelic title "Giolla Rua" (Englished as "Gilderoy"), and is generally thought to commemorate this real-life rogue and bandit. However, folklorist Baring-Gould also remarks that in Scotland the "Beggar" of the title is identified with King James V. The song was common under the Gaelic title and the alternate title "The Little Beggarman" throughout the British Isles.

There are 17th-century song versions of Gilderoy — both Scottish and English — that pre-date Rob Roy McGregor. Rather than being rollicking drinking songs, these early versions are laments, told from a woman's point of view, and are in different modes than the more familiar Red Haired Boy/Little Beggarman versions we know today.

The tune appears in Baring-Gould's 1895 London publication Garland of Country Song and in The Forsaken Lover's Garland, and in the original Scots in The Scots Musical Museum. A similarly titled song, "Beggar's Meal Poke's," was composed by James VI of Scotland (who became James I of England).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rhymer's Favorite
description:
The tune appears under two common spellings: "Rhymer's Favorite" and "Rymer's Favorite" — both refer to the same piece and are used interchangeably in the old-time fiddle community.

The tune is listed in old-time fiddle resources as "Rymer's (Rhymer's) Favorite" and is attributed to Allen Sisson — a fiddler documented in the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle archive, one of the more comprehensive online catalogs of obscure old-time tunes and their source players.
