Specific written documentation about this tune's deeper backstory is scarce — which is actually very typical for tunes of this type. The old-time fiddle repertoire is made up largely of tunes in the public domain that have no known authorship, though many of these tunes have rich historical significance.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Richmond
description:
"Richmond" is actually a family of related (and unrelated) old-time fiddle tunes that share the name. Here is a breakdown of the main branches:

"Richmond" modulates from the first strain to the second — from D major to A major, much like "Flop-Eared Mule." Such tunes are occasionally called "cotillions" in the Upper South, especially in southwestern Virginia, but the tune usually simply goes by "Richmond."

"Richmond" is a well-known tune in the Upper South but seems to have limited distribution beyond that area.

A story circulating in some areas holds that the tune acquired its name from being a mainstay at a debutante's ball called the Richmond Cotillion, though there seems to be little evidence to substantiate this.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Richmond Cotillion (Emmett Lundy's version)
description:
This tune was played by Dalhart (near Galax), Grayson County, southwest Virginia fiddler Emmett Lundy (1864–1953) and recorded for the Library of Congress in 1941.

Crucially, Emmett Lundy's "Richmond Cotillion" is an entirely different tune from the more widely known "Richmond Cotillion (1)." This version is unrelated to "Richmond Cotillion (1)" and was probably mis-named on the recording — to date, no one has discovered what the original title might have been. Some now call it "Emmett Lundy's Cotillion" or "Lundy's Cotillion" as a result.

Kerry Blech, who played the tune in 2001 drawing on Emmett Lundy's playing, states on the recording that this tune was misnamed by the Library of Congress — he calls it "Lundy's Cotillion."

title: Richmond Cotillion
description:
"Richmond Cotillion" begins in D major and modulates into A major for the second part. "Richmond" is a well-known tune in the Upper South, though it seems to have limited distribution beyond that area. Like "Flop-Eared Mule," it modulates from the first strain to the second — in this case, from D to A. It is a popular old-time tune for squares and contras in North America.

The title's origin is genuinely murky and debated among researchers:

1. The "Richmond Polka" Theory (most likely)
   The title may have derived from "Richmond Polka," which is said to have been printed in the 1850s. Kerry Blech and others have argued that the tune's original name was simply "Richmond" or "Richmond Polka," and that the word "cotillion" became appended through its appearance on some of the Gennett stencil labels of Da Costa Woltz's 1920s recordings, which read "Richmond" Cotillion. Blech and Gerry Milne take this to mean that "Richmond" was simply a vehicle for the cotillion — an old dance form.

2. The Debutante Ball Story (popular but unverified)
   A story circulating in some areas claims the tune acquired its name from being a mainstay at a debutantes' ball called the "Richmond Cotillion," though there seems to be little evidence to substantiate this.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rickett's Hornpipe
description:
The particular Rickett honored in the title was a circus promoter, one John Bill Ricketts (1769–1800), a Scottish immigrant who came from England in 1792 and flourished in America through the 1790s, until his Philadelphia enterprise was destroyed in a fire on December 17, 1799.

The circus first came to an American town on April 3, 1793, when Ricketts presented his "unparalleled Equestrian Performance" in Philadelphia. He had honed his trick-riding skills in London, inspired by the enormous success of Philip Astley's circus, and adopted Astley's formula of breathtaking stunts on horseback, comedy routines, and acrobatics — all performed within a 42-foot ring.

He reportedly delighted his audiences by dancing hornpipes on the backs of galloping horses, and toward the end of his career hired another famous American hornpipe dancer, John Durang, to produce pantomimes for him.

Alan Jabbour (in American Fiddle Tunes) notes that circuses under Ricketts's name appeared in New York City, Philadelphia, Norfolk, Charlestown, Albany, Boston, Hartford, and Montreal.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Road to Malvern
description:
"Road to Malvern" is a modern composition by West Virginia fiddler Jim Childress, named after the Arkansas town where his wife was raised. More specifically, the tune was named for his wife, who was born in Malvern, Arkansas. Jim originally recorded it on the *2004 CD Turkey Sag with old-time stringband Uncle Henry's Favorites.

The band's lineup at live performances has included Pete Vigour, Mark Beall, Jim Childress, and Ellen Vigour.

The tune is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in the key of A Major, played in AEae cross-tuning on the fiddle, with an AABB structure.

Jim plays it cross-tuned (AEAE), but it works very well in standard tuning too.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Roaring River
description:
There are two distinct traditional fiddle tunes that go by the name "Roaring River," each with its own fascinating origin story. Here's a breakdown of both:

The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist and folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954. The Roaring River is a 14.9-mile-long river in Barry County, Missouri, in the Ozarks — suggesting the tune may be named after this actual waterway in the region.

This version has one of the most remarkable origin stories in all of American folk music:
Composer: Composed by Solomon Northup, an African-American fiddler and carpenter originally from Saratoga, New York.
His story: Northup was tricked into going to Baltimore to play for a circus, but was captured and sold into slavery. He had a variety of masters and endured various conditions and mistreatment, including time on several Louisiana plantations.
The tune's origin: He was, for a time, responsible for timber cutting and extraction on a river — perhaps his "Roaring River" was inspired by this experience.
Published source: "Roaring River" is transcribed and appears in Northup's memoir Twelve Years a Slave (1853). It is one of the very few American fiddle tunes with a known named composer and a datable manuscript source.
Date & form: The tune dates to approximately 1840–1850. It is an American reel in 2/4 time, in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

title: Robinson County
description:
The tune is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown, also known by the alternate title "Robertson." Its geographic association is central Arkansas, played in D Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB two-part structure.

"Robinson County" is a great old-time dance tune that was recorded in the 1920s by Sharp, Hinman, and Sharp.

The most documented early recording is by Ted Sharp, Hinman & Sharp, captured in 1933, which appears on Echoes of the Ozarks Vol. 1 (County CD 3506), part of the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rochester Schottische
description:
There are at least three distinct tunes known by the title "Rochester Schottische." This has led to substantial confusion among scholars and players alike. The most commonly played version in old-time circles today isn't even a schottische — it's a breakdown.

A schottische (pronounced "shotish") is a widely popular dance, supposedly somewhat like a slow polka, that probably originated in Bohemia.

The original composition behind the name traces to upstate New York:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rock that Cradle Joe
description:
Rock the Cradle Joe is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown, rooted in the traditions of Patrick & Franklin Counties, Virginia; North Carolina, and West Virginia. It's played in D Major, in standard tuning, with an AABB structure.

The tune's conceptual ancestry is surprisingly old. A song entitled "Rocke the Cradle, John" was licensed by Laurence Price in 1631 in England, and there is also an Irish song called "The Old Man Rocking the Cradle." These are not directly related in words or music to the American fiddle tune, but they demonstrate that the "man rocking the cradle" theme was an early and widespread one.

Most modern "revival" versions of the tune trace back to the playing of J.W. "Babe" Spangler of Meadows of Dan, Virginia, who recorded it in the late 1940s. His recordings are considered the primary source from which contemporary players learned the tune. Roger Howell has also recorded a notable version, learned directly from Babe Spangler, and a 1940s field recording of the Spanglers playing the tune survives. Roane County, W.Va., fiddler Franklin George (1928–2017) also recorded a version captured in a 2008 field recording.

The traditional lyric runs: "What'll we do when the baby cries, I don't know / What'll we do when the baby cries, Rock that cradle Joe."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rock the Cradle Lucy
description:
"Rock the Cradle Lucy" (also known as "Rock That Cradle Lucy" or "Rock That Baby Lucille") is an old-time breakdown rooted in north Georgia and Oklahoma. It is played in D Major, in ADae cross-tuning on the fiddle, and follows the standard AABB form.

Various sets of floating lyrics have been associated with the tune, some of which are shared with the similarly-titled "Rock the Cradle Joe." The song may have derived in part from an older minstrel-era song called "Miss Lucy Long," if only to retain the name "Lucy Long"; however, both music and words are significantly different, and a direct association is elusive.

The tune is also similar in melody to "Soldier's Joy." In fact, "Soldier's Joy" is listed as an AKA (or close relative) alongside "Rock the Cradle Lucy" in tune indexes.

The most influential recording of the tune came from Gid Tanner and His Skillet Lickers. The Skillet Lickers recorded it for Columbia Records (Columbia 15538-D, 78 RPM) in 1929.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rocky Mountain Goat
description:
"Rocky Mountain Goat" is a tune well-known in America but not clearly traceable beyond its shores. It is classified as an American reel (cut time), played in D Major, documented across Texas, Missouri, Virginia, Kentucky, and West Virginia. Its structure follows a standard AABB form.

A highly influential version — and the first to use the name "Rocky Mountain Goat" — was recorded for Paramount in 1927 by Doc Roberts and his band the Kentucky Thoroughbreds (with "Dick" Parman and "Ted" Chestnut), and later redone by him for Gennett (1929).

The recording sold 8,000 copies on the Gennett label and Roberts collected royalties.

Roberts claimed to have learned the tune from "an 80-year-old fiddler named Dude Freeman from Beattieville on the Kentucky River." As his son James Roberts recounted: "Daddy claimed Dude was one of the best hornpipe players he ever heard in his life — Daddy ran into him at a fiddle contest when he was young" (Charles Wolfe).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rocky Road To Jordan
description:
"Rocky Road to Jordan" is an American reel in D Major. It's a fairly obscure tune, and yet it has been popping up on players' tune horizons from a number of connected sources. It is one of the "100 Essential Missouri Tunes" listed by Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden.

The most vivid account of how the tune got its name comes from a story embedded in Illinois folk memory. The tune was mentioned by name in Edgar Lee Masters' (1868–1950) 1942 contribution to the Rivers of America series, The Sangamon, Chapter 6 — an examination of the common folk of Menard County, Illinois. In it, he recalled a visit in 1914 to an old friend of Masters' father, by the name of John Armstrong, of Oakford, Illinois, during which Armstrong was asked to play the fiddle.

Masters relates that in 1914, he and Theodore Dreiser took the train from Chicago to the town of Oakford, Illinois to visit John Armstrong. John Armstrong was one of the two sons of Jack and Hannah Armstrong, and was also a well-known fiddler, and among the long list of tunes in Masters' account is "Rocky Road to Jordan."

Armstrong recounted the tune's backstory — a great story of how the tune went through multiple name changes before landing on "Rocky Road to Jordan":

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rocky Pallet
description:
"Rocky Pallet" is an American reel (cut time) associated with the traditions of north Georgia and North Carolina, played in C Major in standard fiddle tuning (GDAE).

The title, somewhat obscure, probably refers to the use of "pallet" to mean a hard, narrow bed, as in the song "Make me a pallet on the floor." The imagery evokes the rough, rustic sleeping arrangements of rural Southern life — entirely in keeping with the earthy humor of the old-time string band tradition.

Most modern versions stem from the north Georgia band The Skillet Lickers' 78 RPM record, recorded in Atlanta for Columbia Records just before Halloween, on October 19th, 1927.

The Skillet Lickers also recorded the tune as part of their "Possum Hunt on Stump House Mountain," where "Rocky Pallet" is introduced as "Possum and Taters" — "Whoo," exclaims fiddler Gid Tanner, "do I love possum and taters!" as he leads the others on the hunt.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rodes' Division
description:
The tune is most canonically catalogued as "Rose Division" in the Traditional Tune Archive, and it circulates under several closely related names. It is also known as "Rowe's Division" and "Row's Division." The form "Rodes' Division" is a more recent and increasingly popular variant of the title (see below).

It is an American reel in cut time, rooted in North Carolina, typically played in C Major or B-flat Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

Most "revival" musicians learned the tune from a 1974 recording by the Hollow Rock String Band, although the band credits their version of the tune to fiddler John Lewis of Walnut Cove, Stokes County, northwest North Carolina.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Roger Sprung's #2
description:
Here is everything the available sources can tell us about Roger Sprung and the tune bearing his name, along with an honest accounting of where the record goes quiet.

Roger Sprung (August 29, 1930 – July 22, 2023) was an American banjo player and teacher best known for introducing authentic bluegrass banjo picking styles to the folk music community in the north and for the eclectic manner in which he adapted bluegrass banjo techniques to music of other genres.

Often called the "Godfather of Progressive Bluegrass" and the "Father of East Coast Bluegrass," he expanded the instrument's repertoire beyond traditional bluegrass to incorporate jazz, ragtime, classical, pop, and international influences.

He was introduced to folk music as a teenager in 1947 when his older brother took him to hear musicians perform in New York's Washington Square. After taking up the guitar, Sprung next took up the banjo, teaching himself to play by ear with the aid of 78 rpm records by Earl Scruggs. He was also influenced by Pete Seeger and Paul Cadwell, as well as Tom Paley, from whom he took several banjo lessons.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rolling the Logs
description: Rolling the Logs is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Root Hog or Die
description:
"Root hog or die" is a common American catch-phrase dating at least to the early 1800s, coming from the early colonial practice of turning pigs loose in the woods to fend for themselves — making it an idiomatic expression for self-reliance. The phrase can be parsed as, "Root (search for roots to eat), hog, or [you will] die."

The phrase spread rapidly through frontier culture. By 1829, the Vermont Gazette recorded: "In Ohio, they have a vulgar proverb which runs thus — 'Root, hog, or die.' It is usually spread in staring capitals among idlers and it is said often has an admirable effect in promoting habits of industry." By 1834, Davy Crockett used it in his autobiography: "We therefore determined to go on the old saying, root, hog or die" — from A Narrative of the Life of David Crockett, of the State of Tennessee.

The phrase resulted in several songs with the same theme, and several songs of unknown authorship were published before the Civil War, including patriotic and minstrel songs.

Scholar Charles Wolfe, commenting in his 1991 edition of African-American collector Thomas Talley's Negro Folk Rhymes, says the song "has obscure origins in the pre-Civil War minstrel stage."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rosebud Hornpipe
description:
Seattle fiddler, researcher, and publisher Vivian Williams discovered the tune in George Saunders' tutor New and Scientific Self-Instructing School for the Violin (Providence, R.I., 1847), set in the key of C major. This is considered the earliest documented appearance of the tune. The description of this as "an old tune dug up by Vivian Williams" confirms her key role in bringing it back into circulation in the modern old-time fiddle community.

The tune became closely tied to the Missouri Valley old-time fiddle tradition. It appears on the album Cyril Stinnett - Grey Eagle in C (MSOTFA 103), released by the Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association, performed by Cyril Stinnett on fiddle and Lena Hughes on banjo. The Bb arrangement used in Missouri old-time circles comes from Cyril Stinnett and the great Missouri Valley fiddlers.

The tune is classified as Old-Time, and the title appears in a list of Ozark Mountain fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Roscoe
description:
Roscoe is an old-time breakdown/reel in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning.

The tune was in the repertoire of fiddler and banjo player Kyle Creed (1912–1982), who learned it from Roscoe Russell; Creed couldn't remember the name of the tune and simply called it after his source.

The tune comes from the fiddling of Kyle Creed, who learned it from his guitar-playing friend Roscoe Russell. It may be that the tune didn't have a name, so Creed named it "Roscoe." It's possible Russell himself made it up.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rose in the Mountain
description:
"Rose in the Mountain" is a "crooked" tune from the Salyer Family of Magoffin County, Kentucky. Musicologist Jeff Titon (2001) believes the tune might have once been a march, although the primary source, John Salyer (1882–1952), played it as a reel/breakdown.

The tune is attributed to John Morgan Salyer (1882–1952, Salyersville, Magoffin County, eastern Kentucky), and the foundational recording comes from a 1941/42 home recording made by his sons, Glen & Grover.

This recording was later released on Berea College Appalachian Center AC003, "John M. Salyer: Home Recordings, 1941-42" (1993).

It is classified as an American Reel (cut time), from Kentucky, in the key of D Major, playable in standard or ADae tuning, with an unusual AABC structure — making it a distinctly "crooked" tune from the Salyer family tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Round The Horn
description:
"Round the Horn" was composed by New York fiddler and mandolin player Jay Ungar. It is a G major reel in 4/4 time, copyrighted in 1978 by Swinging Door Music/BMI.

Despite sounding deeply traditional and being widely absorbed into the old-time and Irish session repertoire, this is a modern composition — not an anonymous folk tune passed down through generations, though it circulates as one.

The title refers to making the trip around Cape Horn (the southern tip of South America) — the tune is played with "Off to California" and "Road to California" as a medley called "Bound for California" on a James Galway, Jay Ungar, and Molly Mason CD, which confirms the title's nautical/westward journey meaning.

It is an American reel in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB / AA'BB' structure.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rundown Boot
description: Rundown Boot is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Run Rebel Run
description: Run Rebel Run is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rush and the Pepper
description:
This tune is documented on the Indian Delta Creek Boys, Vol. 1 album, where the liner notes describe it as follows: "RUSH AND THE PEPPER (Key of D): Jesse James Abbott of rural Toledo said that he learned this hornpipe as a young boy in Missouri."

J.J. (Jesse James) Abbott turned 82 in the Fall of 1975, placing his birth around 1893 and his learning of the tune likely sometime in the early 1900s in Missouri.
The tune is documented from the playing of Jesse James Abbott, and was collected by Gary Harrison — one of many fine tunes Harrison collected in Illinois.
The tune is catalogued in old-time tune directories as "Rush And The Pepper, D-ADae — Jess Abbott via G. Harrison", referencing the non-standard ADAE fiddle tuning used to play it.
Key of D, played in ADAE cross-tuning (also written D-ADae)
Classified as a hornpipe — hornpipes are typically in 4/4 time and played somewhat slower than reels, often involving melodically complex and elaborately arpeggiated tunes.

| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Tune title | Rush and the Pepper / Rush in the Pepper |
| Type | Hornpipe |
| Key / Tuning | D / ADAE cross-tuning |
| Source fiddler | Jesse James Abbott (b. ~1893, rural Toledo, IL) |
| Geographic roots | Learned as a child in Missouri, collected in Illinois |
| Collector | Gary Harrison |
| Documentation | Indian Delta Creek Boys, Vol. 1 (liner notes, ca. 1975) |

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rustic Dance
description:
The tune was composed by Cyrus R. Howell (1836–1920), a schoolteacher and artist in Ontario, Canada. It was first published in Toronto in 1887 as a piano piece, and appeared in many editions and arrangements in the U.S. and Canada thereafter. It was originally in the key of C, with two more parts and a couple of key changes — quite different from the simplified versions that spread through American fiddle tradition.

It is a common, though widely varied dance tune in the East, Midwest, and other parts of the country. It can be heard rendered in various rhythms, including a schottische, although some maintain that it is actually a difficult tune to perform that dance to.

Musicologist Jim Kimball reports the tune is commonly played for a schottische for community dances in western New York, and that fiddler Mark Hamilton plays a two-part version in C which he calls "Humpty Dumpty Schottische" — he thinks his dad learned it when visiting the Toronto World's Fair in 1902.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ruth's Rag
description:
The tune was composed by fiddler Ben Tinnon and named for his wife, Ruth (1894–1982), who had a local reputation for her skill as a buck dancer and whom Tinnon married in 1910.

The group consisted of Tinnon (1891–1974) on fiddle, Melvin Paul (1905–1970) on banjo or mandolin, and Grover Grant (1897–1971) on guitar, and they hailed from Mississippi County, southern Missouri.

It was recorded by his group, the Grinnell Giggers, for Victor Records on Friday, May 30th, 1930, in a session in Memphis, Tennessee, and they went back to the studio in November of that year and cut another seven sides for Victor.

The recording was released on Bluebird 8182 (a 78 rpm record, now out of print), with Ben Tinnon on fiddle, Melvin Paul on banjo, and Grover Grant on guitar.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rye Straw
description:
"Rye Straw" is a shortened form of "Dog in the Rye Straw," which in turn is bowdlerized — it refers to a cycle of vulgar jingles. To put it plainly, the tune's true, unprintable title is scatological. As Missouri fiddle tune collector R.P. Christeson noted, "Title given here is a polite substitution for use in mixed company. The correct title is unprintable. Ford [Traditional Music of America, 1940] solved the problem by calling his version 'Rye Straw.'"

Part of the humor of the tune's many names seems to reside in coy titles that allude to the true meaning while appearing innocent enough to the uninitiated.

The melody was known throughout the South and Midwest under a variety of (mostly related) titles, but appears to have first been published in the 1876 collection by blackface minstrel performer and composer George H. Coes of Boston, Mass., as "Whoop from Arkansas (A)" and later by Missouri physician W.H. Morris (Old Time Violin Melodies, 1927, No. 28) as "Acrobat."

Marion Thede published Ozarks region versions as "Preacher's Favorite" and "Ladies Fancy (4)" in her The Fiddle Book (1960).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Saddle Old Kate
description:
"Saddle Old Kate" is an American reel in cut time, rooted in Missouri and Arkansas, played in A Major in standard fiddle tuning. Its structure follows an AA'BB' form.

The most colorful and widely repeated story behind the tune's name comes from Ozarks fiddler Fred Stoneking, who heard it from Bill Mustain. As retold in Stoneking's liner notes for his Rounder album:

Fred Stoneking says: "Back in the 'twenties, there was a guy by the name of Lum Varner and he had a younger brother called Jim. When Lum was about twenty years old, he made up this tune and called it 'Saddle Old Kate.' But those brothers had a little fall-out on account of being jealous of each other's fiddling ability. So they parted company. The problem was that Jim loved that tune too. He was so mad at his brother that he called the tune after his own horse which was Spike. A friend of mine named Joe knew Jim and that's how it came down to me as 'Saddle Old Spike.'"

In short: Lum Varner composed the tune around the 1920s, naming it after his horse Kate. His brother Jim feuded with him over it and renamed his version after his horse, Spike — giving rise to the closely related sibling tune "Saddle Old Spike."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Saddle Old Paint
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Name | Saddle Old Paint |
| Type | Air / Lament / Listening Piece |
| Key | G minor |
| Time Signature | Alternates 5/4 and 4/4 (unusual mixed meter) |
| Origin | United States (Ohio / Cherokee tradition) |
| First Known Recording | Heritage XXXIII, Forest Pick – "Visits" (1981) |

This unusual tune was in the repertoire of Forest Pick (1911–1979), a fiddler from West Portsmouth, southern Ohio, who said he had learned it from a full-blooded Cherokee Indian fiddler named Chief Red Bird, who played dances in the area.

So the chain of transmission is: Chief Red Bird → Forest Pick → the wider old-time world.

Chief Red Bird was a Detroit-area bandleader and dance fiddler who played on the radio and even recorded 78rpm records with Otto Gray's Oklahoma Cowboys from 1927 to 1933. He was born William A. Sanders in 1899 and died in 1978.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sadie At The Back Door
description:
The tune was composed by Seattle old-time musician Jere Canote, and was originally written as a banjo tune. Jere and his twin brother Greg are known as the Canote Brothers — Greg plays fiddle, and Jere plays guitar, banjo, and melodeon. They are renowned for their off-the-beaten-track tunes, both traditional and modern.

Sadie was Jere's cat, who would meow at the front door to get out, and then meow at the back door to get in. This quirky behavior — always leaving by the front and only returning through the back — directly inspired the tune.

It is described as a "delightful, fairly recent American old-time tune" — and notably a crooked tune (meaning it has an irregular or unexpected phrase structure). The piece has a mixolydian feel, driven by the toggling between the D and C chords. It is considered an excellent vehicle for exploring variations, especially in rhythm — swing, syncopations, anticipations, and rag rhythms.
Genre: Old-Time Breakdown / Reel
Key: D major
Form: AA'BB' (two-part, with variations)
Fiddle tuning: ADae (cross-tuning) — Greg Canote's fiddle is tuned ADAE. While you can play it in standard tuning, you'll miss that distinctive cross-tuned resonance from the sympathetic low A string.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Safe Harbor Rag
description:
The tune was composed by the late Dick Walton, a musician from Safe Harbor, Pennsylvania — a small community ironically situated on the Susquehanna River, right between two nuclear power plants at Peachbottom and Three Mile Island.

The tune takes its name directly from that town, which gives it a charmingly ironic geographic identity in the old-time world.

Also known as "Safe Harbor Reel," it is classified as an American Country Rag in cut time, played in F Major in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB' structure.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sail Away Ladies
description:
'Sail Away Ladies' has deep roots in south-central Kentucky and middle Tennessee, with the melody tracing back to the 'Sally Ann' family of tunes and their British Isles antecedents. The earliest recorded version is Uncle Bunt Stevens's 1926 instrumental fiddle recording — purely instrumental, no lyrics. Uncle Dave Macon's 1927 recording added the song's most famous lyrics: 'Ain't nobody's business but my own / Sail away ladies, sail away.' Macon — the 'Dixie Dewdrop,' one of the original Grand Ole Opry stars — gave the tune its commercial identity, but it was already a community property well before he touched it. The image of 'sailing away' in the context of a Kentucky or Tennessee mountain song is striking: the nearest navigable water was far enough away that sailing was a metaphor for escape and liberation rather than a description of actual travel. That distance between the lyric and the physical reality gives the song its particular flavor of longing. The tune has been recorded by Flatt and Scruggs, the New Lost City Ramblers, and dozens of revival-era artists.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: G major with a driving, optimistic rhythm that belies any sadness in the lyric. The four-part structure (AABBCCDD in some versions) gives the tune more variety than a standard two-part breakdown. Sing it while you play: 'Sail away ladies, sail away.' Uncle Dave Macon's banjo version is the canonical reference for the song tradition; for fiddle, Bunk Stevens's clean instrumental version is the starting point. Good tune for set openings because the rhythm is immediately engaging.

title: Sailing Over England
description:
The tune comes from the playing of Fitzhugh Lee Triplett (6 July 1897 – 24 January 1981) of Clay, Clay County, West Virginia. He was the son of William Hedgeman Triplett (1845–1906) and Elizabeth "Bettie" Louisa Mullins (1859–1932).

Triplett was a beloved figure in the West Virginia old-time music community. The Digital Library of Appalachia notes that he was "a mainstay at the West Virginia State Folk Festival in Glenville, WV, where he kept up a friendly rivalry with fiddler French Carpenter."

It is classified as an American Reel (cut time), in the key of D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB' form. The tune, played by Triplett as an uptempo reel, perhaps derived from a ballad air — suggesting it may have older, possibly British Isles roots that were reshaped into a driving instrumental. The title implies the singer (or narrator) is sailing over to England, we presume. Some players also take a tuning liberty: fiddlers can tune that G string up to A.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Saint Ann's Reel
description:
There is quite a lot of confusion about the origins of this tune. It is played in sessions in Scotland, Ireland, New England, Canada, and other spots around the world, and has been claimed as a Shetland tune, an Irish reel, a contra-dance tune, a French-Canadian and American old-time piece. Despite this ambiguity, the historical trail points clearly toward Québec, Canada.

St. Anne's Reel, also known as "St. Agathe" and "La Reel de la Baie Ste. Anne," was originally a Canadian reel played in Québec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and Cape Breton.

Allard researcher Jean Duval believes the title refers to the municipality of Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue at the western end of the island of Montreal. Alternatively, there are at least two bays by this name in eastern Canada, though it is not known if those geographic features explain the origin of the tune's title. There is a French community called Baie Sainte Anne, on St. Anne's Bay, near the mouth of Mirimichi Bay, New Brunswick.

Folklorist Father Stanislas Paulin also noted that New Brunswick's historically large Catholic population plays into St. Anne's Reel's popularity, because the song's namesake is a crucial figure of faith — "Saint Anne would be the mother of Mary and Mary, of course, the mother of Jesus." Paulin said Saint Anne has always been revered by all of the cultures in New Brunswick.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: St. Joe Hornpipe
description:
"St. Joe Hornpipe" is an American reel (played in cut time), associated with the states of Nebraska and Missouri, in the key of C-flat Major, in standard fiddle tuning with an AABB form.

The title of the tune "likely refers to the northwest Missouri city of St. Joseph." St. Joseph (commonly called "St. Joe") sits on the Missouri River and was a major hub of American westward expansion, giving the tune a distinctly regional Great Plains identity.

"The St. Joe Hornpipe" is considered one of the 100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes according to Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden, and was popularized by Missouri Valley fiddlers such as Bob Walters and Cyril Stinnett.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sally Ann Johnson
description:
Before diving in, it's essential to know that "Sally Ann Johnson" is actually two distinct tunes that scholars and players have long conflated:
"Sally Ann Johnson" [1] — A reel in D Major, rooted in Virginia/West Virginia, most famously associated with fiddler Henry Reed
"Sally Johnson" [1] — A reel in G Major, sometimes also called "Sally Ann Johnson," associated with Texas/Midwest fiddlers and nearly identical to "Katy Hill"

The title is sometimes confused with "Sally Johnson (1)" ("Katy Hill" family), a different tune altogether but which is also sometimes called "Sally Ann Johnson."

The broad dissemination and widespread variants of this melodic tune family, both in America and Ireland, point to a melodic theme of some age, appearing in print at least as far back as the first half of the 19th century. The name "Sally Ann Johnson" seems to be a regional Virginia/West Virginia one, however.

The most celebrated recording of "Sally Ann Johnson" is by Henry Reed, captured in D tuning in 1967 by folklorist Alan Jabbour as a field recording for the Archive of Folk Culture. Henry Reed (1884–1968) lived in Glen Lyn, Giles County, Virginia, and his recording is preserved at the Library of Congress as AFS 13703B10.

title: Sally Cooper
description:
"Sallie Cooper" comes directly from John Morgan Salyer, an Eastern Kentucky fiddler who was recorded by a family member in the 1940s. The notated version traces back to John M. Salyer of Salyersville, Magoffin County, Kentucky.

Salyer was one of the staunchest traditionalists in Appalachian fiddling. Many Kentucky fiddlers like John Salyer and Hiram Stamper cared little for new music and stayed with the old-time tunes — even as younger players were drawn toward the commercial sounds of the Grand Ole Opry era.

"Sallie Cooper" is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown, originating in Kentucky, played in G Major in GDad tuning.
Also known as: "Sally Cooper", "Sallie Cooper"
It is an old-time, breakdown fiddle tune.

"Sallie Cooper" is played in GDAD tuning, in which the high string is tuned down to D. It has two parts, but the second part is played only once. This gives it an unusual and somewhat haunting formal structure compared to the typical AABB old-time breakdown.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sally Will You Marry Me
description:
Most versions of the tune are sourced to Braxton County, West Virginia fiddler Melvin Wine (1909–2003). Wine is considered the definitive source for this tune in the old-time community, and virtually all modern versions trace back to him.
Also known as "Sal, Won't You Marry Me", it is classified as an American Reel (cut time), rooted in West Virginia, in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

The most referenced recording is by Melvin Wine on the album Hannah at the Springhouse (August Heritage CD AHR 021, 1989), collected by Gerry Milnes.
"Sandy River Belle" is considered a related melody.
West Virginia/East Kentucky fiddler Ed Haley had his own "Sally Will You Marry Me? (2)" — but it is a different tune entirely.
One well-known arrangement is by Rayna Gellert and the Brothers K — a gentler take on Melvin Wine's version, with Kevin Kehrberg on guitar and Jeff Keith on mandolin.
Fiddler Erynn Marshall (with guitarist Carl Jones) has also recorded a version, explicitly citing Melvin Wine of Braxton County, WV as the source fiddler.

Notated versions appear sourced to Pete Sutherland (Vermont) and Melvin Wine, published in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes (2011, pp. 578–579) and in Phillips' Traditional American Fiddle Tunes Vol. 1 (1994, p. 213).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sal's Got Mud Between Her Toes
description:
The tune is sourced to southern Kentucky fiddler Pat Kingery, whom collector and fiddler Bruce Greene recorded in the field in 1976. Kingery (ca. 1912–c. 1976) was from Nobob, Barren County, southern Kentucky, and performed with a group called Pat Kingery and the Kentuckians.

It's a three-part tune in the key of D, and the only known recording of Kingery playing it is that 1976 field recording made by Bruce Greene.

On that recording, Kingery did not sing words, but later told Greene the words that were traditionally sung to the tune: "Here comes Sally down the road, She's got mud between her toes, Though her face is pretty as a pear, She's got a yellow ribbon in her hair."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Salt Sack Behind the Door
description: Salt Sack Behind the Door is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Salt Spring
description:
"Salt Spring" is not an ancient traditional tune — it's an original composition by John Reischman, a West Coast mandolinist. Reischman's tune "Salt Spring" has become a modern standard, played at jam sessions by many people who think it's a traditional old-time fiddle tune.

John Reischman released his original tune "Salt Spring" on the debut album of his band John Reischman and the Jaybirds in 2001, and the tune has been a mandolin-player favorite ever since.

John Reischman is an acclaimed West Coast mandolinist who recorded "Salt Spring" with his band John Reischman and the Jaybirds. He is a Juno-nominated and Grammy award-winning artist known for his exquisite tone and original compositions.

A veteran of The Good Ol' Persons, the Tony Rice Unit, and many other seminal acts of his generation, Reischman knows firsthand the value of cross-generational knowledge sharing.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Salty River Reel
description:
Here is a thorough breakdown of everything known about "Salty River Reel" — its origin, associated fiddlers, and relationship to the broader "Salt River" tune family.

"Salty River Reel" (or "Salt River Reel") is not the same tune as "Salt River" or "Salt Creek" — experienced fiddlers are clear that these are distinct pieces. The similar-sounding names cause frequent confusion in the old-time community.

The tune "Salty River Reel" is most closely identified with Cyril Stinnett, a northwest Missouri fiddler who became one of its most celebrated carriers:
Cyril Stinnett was born near Savannah, in northwest Missouri, on January 27, 1912. His dad was a farmer and a fiddler. The family moved to southwest Missouri for a while, but Cyril eventually returned to the Filmore area where he spent the rest of his life.
Cyril began playing fiddle around age eight, practicing secretly in the basement on his dad's fiddle for months before surprising his dad with his new ability. Within a couple of years he was playing for dances.
His tremendous memory for tunes and precision in playing led some folks to refer to him as a "fiddling computer," but his playing was far from being mechanical. Although Cyril's renditions were melodically complex, they were in a sense, quite simple — no bow effects (double shuffles, etc.) other than the occasional use of 32nd notes, and little double string playing. Most of his tunes were two-part reels and hornpipes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sam and Elzie's
description:
It is believed that the tune was named for Sam and Elzie Crutchfield, father and son, who ran square dances in the early 1900s near Omega, Illinois. This gives the tune a clear community dance context — it wasn't a composed parlor piece, but a living dance tradition tied to a specific family and place.

The tune is strongly associated with Illinois fiddler Wilson Bray, whose biography was documented by Voyager Records (run by Phil & Vivian Williams):
Wilson Bray was born in Illinois in 1918, the first of eight children of Montie and Hallie Bray. His father was a fiddle and banjo player, and Wilson learned to play dance tunes on the fiddle from him at an early age, playing at the many square dances his parents put on. He also became a classical violinist and at age 14 played a weekly radio broadcast over station WILL in Champaign, Illinois.

This dual background — vernacular dance music at home and formal classical training — was not unusual for rural Illinois fiddlers of his generation, and it likely shaped the tune's character.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sam Hill
description:
"Sam Hill" is considered an Alabama tune, placing it firmly in the Southern Appalachian / Deep South old-time tradition. Detailed written documentation of its origins is sparse, which is typical of many old-time tunes passed down through oral tradition.

It is described as a "crooked tune" — meaning it has an irregular or asymmetrical phrase structure (e.g., bars that don't fall into a strict 8+8 form), a hallmark of many older Southern fiddle pieces.
Ralph Whited — The tune is attributed to Ralph Whited, as documented on Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource, transmitted via James Bryan.
James Bryan — James Bryan, a celebrated Alabama fiddler, plays "Sam Hill" on the CD Cricket's Lullaby with Carl Jones. Bryan is Norman Blake's longtime fiddler and is known for his smooth, immediately recognizable personal style — his playing on Bob Carlin's album Banging and Sawing is considered especially exemplary.

The phrase "what in the Sam Hill" is a recognized American euphemism — Sam Hill was reportedly a prominent man of the Northwest known for his prolific profanity, and his name came to be used as a substitute for foul language. Whether the tune's name connects directly to this folk etymology or to a specific person named Sam Hill in Alabama fiddling tradition is not definitively documented.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sand Mountain Drag
description:
"Sand Mountain Drag" is an American Country Rag in 2/4 or cut time, in the key of C Major, played in standard fiddle tuning.

The tune was recorded by Dilly & His Dill Pickles in Atlanta in March, 1930, for the Brunswick record company, released on their subsidiary label, Vocalion.

The group consisted of Atlanta fireman, guitarist, and singer John Dilleshaw (1896–1941), with a young Harry Kiker on fiddle, Shorty Lindsey on tenor banjo, and Pink Lindsey on bass.
Harry Kiker (the fiddler) was from Hiram, Georgia.
John Dilleshaw was born at Pumpkinvine Creek, New Hope, Paulding County, Georgia. The band was also known as "Seven Foot Dilly & His Dill Pickles" — a nickname referencing Dilleshaw's tall stature.

The tune is attributed directly to fiddler Harry Kiker, making him the primary creative source of the melody as it was committed to record.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sandy Boys
description:
The fiddle tune "Sandy Boys" comes from the great West Virginia fiddler Edden Hammons, who was born in 1875 and recorded in 1947 for the archives of West Virginia State University. Edden Hammons (1875–1955) was a colourful character and the source of many tunes. It is a tune from the repertoire of Pocahontas County, West Virginia.

Hammons was recorded in 1947 by a collector named Louis Chappell. His playing has a Scottish influence, with strongly detailed phrases and an old-fashioned style of intonation.

The colorful lore around Hammons is well-documented. He supposedly said, "Pon my honor, I'll lay my fiddle down for no damn woman" shortly before his divorce — this was in reference to whether it was time for him to get a real job.

While Hammons is the tune's most celebrated carrier, its roots go back much further. The original can be found in the American minstrel show repertoire — a similar version appears in *Phil Rice's Correct Method for the Banjo (1857), a period tutor, and also in an 1844 minstrel songbook (reproduced by the Harvard Theatre Collection, Cambridge, Mass.).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Santa Anna's Retreat
description:
"Santa Anna's Retreat" is an old-time tune thought to date from the Mexican War. It is also known as "Santa Anna's March" and is classified as an American reel from southwestern Virginia, in the key of A Mixolydian/Dorian, in standard fiddle tuning.

To most Americans, Antonio López de Santa Anna (1794–1876) is best known as commander of the Mexican forces at the Alamo in 1836. At the time of the conflict with Texas he was not only general of the army but the president of Mexico. During the Mexican-American War of 1846–47 he again commanded the Mexican forces opposing the United States army.

Henry Reed said — presumably on the authority of his fiddling and fifing mentor Quince Dillon, who was a fifer in the Mexican War — that this march was used by Santa Anna's army to retreat from the American forces during the Mexican War.

Reed's collection contains marches such as "British Field March" and "Santa Anna's Retreat," learned from Quince Dillon, a fifer in the Mexican War and an old man when Henry Reed was a boy.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sarah Armstrong's Tune
description:
Sarah Gray Armstrong (March 18, 1883 – August 12, 1957) was a well-known fiddle player in Pennsylvania. She was born in Gray Station, Derry, Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania.

She grew up in a musical family descended from Ulster-Irish immigrants; her grandfather was a fiddler, and his sons Charley (Sarah's father), Laney, Abe, Joss, and Dan were all musicians who played a variety of instruments and were accustomed to playing for dances.

Sarah began learning fiddle at the age of five, mentored in particular by her uncle Laney, who was the most accomplished fiddler in the family. Uncle Laney, Sarah's father Charley, and their three brothers — Dan, Joss (Joshua), and Abe (Abraham) — were in a band called "The Gray Boys," and Sarah would join them on cello.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Satisfied
description: Satisfied is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Saturday Night Breakdown
description:
This ragtime-influenced reel was originally recorded in 1929 by fiddler Wil Gilmer with his group The Leake County Revelers, all of whom resided in and around Sebastopol, Mississippi.

The quartet also included Dallas Jones on guitar, R.O. Mosley on mandolin and banjo-mandolin, and Jim Wolverton on banjo. They formed in 1926 and made some forty recordings from 1927 to 1930.

They were already regionally popular when they recorded in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1929, and had accompanied Louisiana politician Huey Long on his campaign for governor in 1928.

Their record sales, propelled by live broadcasts from the 1000-watt WJDX (Jackson, Mississippi) in a coveted 6PM–7PM Saturday night spot, made them sought-after performers across the Southeast.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Scotland Yard
description: Scotland Yard is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Scott #1
description: Scott #1 is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Setauket
description:
The most historically significant connection between the name Setauket and fiddle music is William Sidney Mount (1807–1868) — a celebrated American painter and an avid fiddler who lived in Setauket, Long Island, New York.

Mount's music manuscripts — now held at the Long Island Museum — include an untitled hornpipe written in A major, alongside "Roscommon's Hornpipe" and an untitled country dance. Mount is one of the best-documented American fiddler-painters of the 19th century, and his manuscripts are a primary source for early American fiddle repertoire.

Other tunes in his collection were noted as being learned from specific sources — for example, one melody was entered into his mid-19th century manuscript collection from a "Miss Spinola." This suggests Mount was an active collector and adapter of tunes circulating in his community.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shag Poke
description:
The tune is sourced to Dwight Lamb (b. 1934, Moorehead, Iowa), and its notation was transcribed by Andrew Kuntz for the Traditional Tune Archive.

It is played in the key of G, in standard GDAE tuning, and was recorded in 1999 on the Rounder CD Joseph Won a Coated Fiddle (Rounder CD 0429). It is also known under the alternate spelling "Shagpoke."

The tune is catalogued in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and the collection Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Iowa.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shenandoah Falls
description:
"Shenandoah Falls" is a peppy little reel in the old-time/breakdown tradition. It is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in A Major, standard tuning. It is also sometimes catalogued as a hornpipe or reel depending on the source and regional tradition. It is also known as "Shannandah Falls" and "Shannandoah Falls."

The tune's origins are a fascinating folk-transmission chain spanning California, Vermont, and beyond. Here's the documented lineage:

1. The Anonymous "Cookie" — The tune's earliest known source is a mandolin player known only as "Cookie," once a fellow student at Sonoma State College.

2. Carol Robinson — West Coast musician Carol Robinson, originally from Sebastopol, California, learned it as an untitled reel from that mandolin player named 'Cookie.'

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ship in the Clouds
description:
"Ship in the Clouds" is an American reel (cut time) rooted in Virginia. It is in D Major (A part) and D Major/Mixolydian (B part), playable in standard or ADae tunings on fiddle.

From Virginia fiddler Taylor Kimble comes this "pretty and crazy little tune" — it's in D and has a meandering, lyrical melody.

It is a well-known, crooked tune played by both Galax fiddler Uncle Norm Edmonds (1889–1976) and Laurel Fork fiddler Taylor Kimble (1892–1979).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shippingport
description:
Shippingport (also spelled "Shippensport") was a small town in the northeast part of Kentucky, now absorbed by the city of Louisville, located at the foot of the Louisville and Portland Canal.

A town grew up around the falls, catering to the river boat traffic between the upper and lower Ohio River, including a number of taverns — one of which was run by the Kentucky giant Jim Porter (1811–1859). Eventually a dam was built with locks for river traffic, and that, along with the construction of the canal, destroyed the livelihood of the community. All that remains of Shippingport today is in the name of nearby Shippingport Island.

The tune's name is a direct nod to this lively river-town culture — the kind of rough-and-tumble portage community where fiddling would have flourished.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shoes and Stockings
description:
Folklorist Alan Jabbour recorded that his source — Glen Lyn, southwest Virginia fiddler Henry Reed (1884–1968) — said that "Shoes and Stockings" was a tune of his elderly mentor, fiddler Quince Dillion, who had been a fifer in the Civil War.

This gives the tune a remarkable oral lineage: from a Civil War–era fifer → to Reed, a southwest Virginia mountain fiddler → to Jabbour, a folklorist who carried it into the revival era.

"Shoes and Stockings" entered the old-time canon by way of Alan Jabbour's recordings of Virginia fiddler Henry Reed, and it is one of a handful of tunes Reed is said to have learned from his mentor, Quince Dillion (or Dillon, as the family now spells it).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shoo Fly
description:
"Shoo Fly" (also known as "Shew Fly, Don't Bother Me") is an American reel and air in cut time. It is the tune associated with the "Shoo fly don't bother me" lyrics and has the feel of a lively dance tune in the melodic style of the later nineteenth century.

The song's origins are genuinely murky — multiple people and traditions have staked a claim:

A competing and perhaps stronger claim is made for "Shew fly don't bother me" as the work of Thomas Brigham Bishop, who hailed from the village of Wayne, Maine. By his own account, he wrote the song during the Civil War while assigned to command a company of black soldiers. He overheard a casual conversation in which one soldier dismissed the remarks of his fellow soldiers, saying "Shoo fly, don't bother me" to indicate his disdain — all the inspiration Bishop needed to fashion a song (in which he included the designation of the unit, Company 'G').

It became almost immediately popular and several versions were published about the same time. Bishop published his in 1869, rather too late, and tried to recapture his claim by proclaiming that his published sheet music was the "Original Copy and Only Authorized Edition."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shooting Creek
description:
Shooting Creek is a popular and common tune in the Franklin/Floyd County area of southwestern Virginia. Shooting Creek rises at the Blue Ridge, along the Floyd County–Franklin County line, and flows down the eastern flank of the mountain into Franklin County in the Virginia Piedmont. The hollow along Shooting Creek had a reputation for moonshining in the earlier twentieth century.

The name "Shooting Creek" refers not only to a post village, but to a waterway that runs through some of the steepest terrain in the county. The bootlegging connection was significant: the area was once referred to as "the moonshine capital of the world," and during Prohibition, agents destroyed 3,900 moonshine stills in Franklin County.

The Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org) classifies three separate tunes under the "Shootin' Creek" title:

An American reel in cut time, associated with West Virginia and southwestern Virginia, played in D Major, in ADae or standard tunings. This is the canonical old-time version most fiddlers know. The primary sources for notated versions are Oscar Wright (Princeton, Mercer County, West Virginia) and Bruce Reid.

title: Shucking The Brush
description:
When asked directly, fiddler Earl White confirmed he was told the tune is called Shucking the Brush and has always called it that — though he acknowledged that names and versions of old-time tunes can be, as he put it, "fluid."

One competing theory holds that the original name is "Shuck in the Bush" — as in a corn shuck stuck in a bush — a story passed down from someone who supposedly spoke directly with the fiddler who composed the tune.

The variant title "Chuck in the Bush" also appears in Silverberg's Tunes I Either Did or Did Not Learn at the Tractor Tavern and the Phillips collection, and may have also been published in The Devil's Box, which some believe is the original title.
Earl White (SF Bay Area) is the most-cited player associated with the tune's wider spread. The tune was first heard by at least one community member around 1980, likely played by Billy Hornung fiddling with the Jubilo String Band from the Philadelphia area, and later circulated widely through Earl White and his Bay Area band.
A fancier, multi-part version also exists in the Texas-style fiddle tradition, performed under the name "Shuck in the Bush," with fiddler Tashina Clarridge noted for a particularly spectacular rendition.
The tune has had a revival in sessions in the Albany, NY area, where players also debated its name.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Shuffle About
description:
Shuffle About (also known as "Shuffling Back") is an American reel in cut time, played in D Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB' structure.

The tune's traceable origin leads back to a single Kentucky fiddler:
The tune originates from Everett Kays (1905–1996) of Lawrenceburg, Anderson County, north-central Kentucky (between Lexington and Louisville).
Kays himself called the tune "Shuffling Back."

While most modern "revival" sources can be traced to a 1970s recording by Vermont fiddler Pete Sutherland, Sutherland himself learned the tune from Bruce Greene, who in 1975 recorded Everett Kays in Lawrenceburg, Kentucky.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Silver Bells
description:
> ️ Note: There are actually two completely different tunes called "Silver Bells" — a Tin Pan Alley / old-time fiddle tune from 1910, and the Christmas song from 1950. You asked about the old-time fiddle version, which has a rich and well-documented history. Here's the full story:

The tune was originally a 1910 Tin Pan Alley song, with words by Edward Madden and music by Percy Wenrich — the latter born in Missouri but who had moved to New York City two years before the song was published, marking the beginning of an important career on Tin Pan Alley.

The original composition was written in the keys of F and B by Percy Wenrich, with words by Edward Madden.

The earliest sound recording of the song was by Ada Jones and Billy Murray, for Edison in 1910 (Ed 10492).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Silver Lake
description:
"Silver Lake" is not a single tune but a name shared by several distinct old-time fiddle tunes, each with its own regional tradition and fiddler lineage. The Traditional Tune Archive catalogs at least six separate tunes under this name, reflecting how commonly place names like "Silver Lake" were borrowed by fiddlers across different regions of Appalachia and the broader American folk tradition.

This version comes from the playing of Emory Bailey of Shock, Calhoun County, West Virginia, recorded in the field in 1953 by Malvin Artley. It is in a basic AB form, with each section 8 measures long — though sometimes Bailey played the B part as 12 measures. The recording is in the key of D with AEad cross-tuning (also written as AEAD), and is included in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and the anthology Old Time Fiddling From The State Of West Virginia.

Bailey (also spelled "Emery Bailey") was a traditional West Virginia fiddler, and his version stands out for its non-standard cross-tuning and its occasional extension of the B part — a hallmark of highly individualized regional playing styles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sleepy Eyed Joe
description:
"Sleepy Eyed Joe" is a genuine piece of the American old-time fiddle canon, though — like many tunes in that tradition — its origins are hazy, its authorship unknown, and it exists in multiple distinct versions. Here's what is known:

Several different tunes share this (or similar) title. The two main versions documented in the Traditional Tune Archive are:

| Version | Key Source Fiddler | Region | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sleepy Eyed Joe (1) / "Sleepy Joe" | Bob Walters (1889–1960) | Burt County, eastern Nebraska | Key of A, fast reel |
| Sleepy Eyed Joe (2) | John Ashby (1915–1979) | Fauquier County, Virginia | Key of E, recorded 1978 |

Version 1 ("Sleepy Joe") is drawn from the playing of Bob Walters (1889–1960) of Burt County, eastern Nebraska, transcribed by Andrew Kuntz.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Slippin' Around
description: Slippin' Around is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Smith's Reel
description:
"Smith's Reel" is the name by which this tune has evolved in North America, though in Ireland it is known as "Kitty's Wedding." It is a favorite among fiddlers spanning the whole gamut of regional and stylistic persuasions and has been widely recorded.

It is classified as an American/Canadian breakdown or reel (cut or 2/4 time), in D Major, standard fiddle tuning, in AABB form.

Seattle musician Vivian Williams discovered "Smith's Reel" in George Saunders' New and Scientific Self-Instructing School for the Violin, a tutor first published in Providence, R.I., in 1847 (reprinted by Oliver Ditson in the 1850s). Saunders claimed to be a "Professor of Music and Dancing" on the frontispiece, and in that volume he claims to have composed the tune himself.

Whether that compositional claim is true — or perhaps not — further research may yet clarify.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snake Chapman's Tune
description:
Owen "Snake" Chapman (1919–2002) was a lifelong resident of Chapman's Hollow, Canada, Pike County, in northeastern Kentucky. His personal story is almost an archetype for the experience of Kentucky mountain people in the 20th century — born and raised in a log cabin, he worked as a coal miner from his late teens to middle age, retiring early with black lung, and working briefly in the auto plants of Detroit before returning to the family home in Chapman's Hollow in the late 1960s.

Snake knew as many melodies as any fiddler his peers had ever met, ranging from very old tunes learned from his father to modern bluegrass fare. Growing up in an isolated mountain hollow, Owen developed an astonishingly accurate ear for the nuances of a fiddle tune and could diagnose very sharply how the playing of certain popular fiddle tunes had evolved over his own lifetime.

Among all the melodies Snake played, the most astonishing were the tunes he learned as a boy from his elderly father, "Doc" Chapman, who had been born in 1850 — Doc's own father, according to family tradition, split logs with Abraham Lincoln before the family resettled in Kentucky.

Doc Chapman was born around 1850 (he was 67 when Snake was born) and thus learned his music from the antebellum generation. Snake learned fiddle when he was "eleven or twelve" from a father who must have been around 78 by then. If Doc had done the same, he would have been learning from someone born in 1783 — a mere seven years after the Declaration of Independence!

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snake River Reel
description:
The original was composed by musician and dance caller Peter Lippincott (formerly of St. Louis, now living in Arkansas). The tune has a contemporary composition date of 1985. He is described as a fiddler and potter from Missouri.

Lippincott himself described the tune's creation: "I just came up with it noodling around one day, oh so long ago. String bands, in St. Louis where I lived, took it to Galax and other fiddle venues and it caught on. Who knew? I named it after the Snake River, but other than sounding like a cool name there is no added significance. I also wrote an influential contra dance by the same name at about the same time."

He named it after the Snake River, but noted that "other than sounding like a cool name there is no added significance." Despite this, some in the old-time community have drawn colorful associations — it is described as a tune that "changes mode whilst keeping the same tonal centre," and at least one player hears it in the context of the Lewis and Clark expedition, pairing it in medleys with Over the Waterfall due to their shared mixolydian character.

The tune is described as an old-time reel "that changes mode whilst keeping the same tonal centre" — it begins in D-Major, then switches to D-Mixolydian in the second part. This modal shift between parts is part of what makes it distinctive and memorable in jam settings.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snake Winder
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Full name | Snakewinder (also written "Snake Winder") |
| Type | American Reel (cut time) |
| Key | G Major |
| Structure | AABB |
| Region | Northeastern Kentucky, USA |
| Source fiddler | Morris Allen → Buddy Thomas |

The tune was in the repertoire of northeastern Kentucky fiddler Buddy Thomas (1935–1974), who attributed it to his mentor, Morris Allen. That chain of transmission — from Morris Allen to Buddy Thomas — is the primary documented source for the tune as it is known today.

The canonical recording is credited as Morris Allen via Buddy Thomas, and appears on Rounder 0372, Buddy Thomas – Traditional Fiddle Music of Kentucky, Vol. 1 (1997). It is classified as an American reel in cut time from Kentucky.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snouts and Ears of America
description:
This tune is one of thirty-seven tunes collected in 1943 by musicologist Samuel Preston Bayard, from Derry, Pennsylvania fiddler Sarah Gray Armstrong (1883–1957). The source is Sarah Armstrong of Derry, Westmoreland County, PA, from Samuel Bayard's collection Hill Country Tunes: Instrumental Folk Music of Southwestern Pennsylvania (1944).

Although there is evidence that Sarah Armstrong's fiddle playing was recorded by her family, no such recordings have yet come to light.

Bayard was born in Pittsburgh, and spent a good deal of time as a child at his uncle's farm in Greene County, in the southwestern corner of the state. He was originally inspired to learn and preserve folk music on a trip to Ireland with his family at age 20, when he heard traditional Irish music in the town of Connemara. Bayard never made a tune-collecting trip to Ireland, since upon returning to the U.S. he discovered that his home region of Pennsylvania had a rich musical tradition of its own.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snow Deer
description:
Despite its rustic, evocative name, "Snow Deer" is a little confusing as a title. The tune is not about snow or deer — it is actually a Tin Pan Alley song from the early 20th century, written by Percy Wenrich, who composed it around 1910.

It was in the repertory of Arizona fiddler Kenner C. Kartchner, who said it was a "pioneer song of long ago." In actuality, it was a Tin Pan Alley song by Percy Wenrich, composed around the end of the first decade of the twentieth century during the craze for ethnic American Indian songs.

This is a song (words and music), and the story is about a cowboy who fell in love with a Native American woman named Snow Deer. The fiddle tune began life as a song which actually has nothing to do with deer or snow, at least not directly — instead it tells of a cowboy's love for an Indian maiden named Snow Deer.

The tune was captivating enough that it soon got picked up by fiddlers all over North America. It quickly found itself in fiddle repertoires all over the US and Canada, notably in Michigan, Texas, Arizona, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, and New Brunswick.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snowflake Breakdown
description:
"Snowflake Breakdown" (also known as the Snowflake Reel) was composed in 1959 by Canadian fiddler Wally Edward Traugott (1934–2010). The tune gained currency with American fiddlers, particularly along the Canadian border and in the Mid-West (Missouri).

Traugott was originally from Kitchener, Ontario, and recorded in Canada throughout the 1950s and 1960s, frequently appearing on the popular Canadian country music show "The Tommy Hunter Show." He played with Hunter on the Grand Ole Opry at the Ryman Auditorium. He eventually became disillusioned with the recording industry in Canada and relocated to the United States in the late 1960s.

Traugott was said to have been the highest paid fiddler in 1950s Canada as the fiddle player on The Tommy Hunter Show.

The tune is classified as a Canadian (originally) and American Breakdown/Reel, played in cut or 2/4 time with irregular measures in some versions, in D Major, in standard fiddle tuning. It has had currency in New England, northern New York, and Missouri.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Snow Shoes
description:
"Snow Shoes" is an American reel in cut time, played in D Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB form.

"Snowshoes" was popularized by Nashville, Tennessee, session fiddler Tommy Jackson (1926–1979), who recorded it in 1962. Jackson played with many of the greatest country-and-western Nashville stars for forty years and was one of the most sought-after session musicians of his era.

His definitive recording appeared on *Dot DLP-3454, Tommy Jackson – Swing Your Partner (1962).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Soapsuds Over The Fence
description:
"Soapsuds Over the Fence" is a traditional American old-time fiddle tune (breakdown/reel) with deep roots in Appalachian and Southern folk music. It takes its place in a longstanding tradition of "naming the tune whatever is actively happening within eyesight at the time of writing." No single composer is credited — like most old-time tunes, it evolved anonymously through oral tradition across multiple regions.

The title (as "Pouring Soapsuds over the Fence") appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.

The tune's name appears even earlier in historical dance records. It was listed alongside tunes like "The Arkansas Traveler," "Cotton Eyed Joe," and "Great big 'taters in sandy land" as music played at old-time dances and barn parties in Missouri.

The tune goes by several alternate titles:
AKA "Pouring Soapsuds Over the Fence," "Soap Suds," and "Throw the Soap Suds in the Corner of the Fence."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Somebody's Buried in the Graveyard
description: Somebody's Buried in the Graveyard is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Soppin' Up the Gravy
description:
"Soppin' Up the Gravy" is an alternate name for the old-time breakdown "Sopping the Gravy," rooted in the fiddle traditions of Missouri and Texas. It is played in the key of D and is considered an advanced-level fiddle contest breakdown.

The tune clearly sounds like it is derived from "Year of the Jubilo" (a Civil War-era song). Stacy Phillips, in his fiddle transcription books, also notes connections between related tunes from this family. In the broader world of old-time music, many tunes share common ancestral material — essentially one "amoeba-like" tune that over generations split into various discernible but related pieces.

There are at least three distinct traditional versions documented:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Speed Of The Plow
description:
This tune has a surprisingly rich and documented history, unusual for a piece of folk music. It also exists in several distinct, melodically unrelated versions that share the same name, which causes considerable confusion. Here's a full breakdown:

What is most unusual about this tune is that we do know who composed it — unlike many older tunes whose origins are typically unknown. Captain Francis O'Neill researched the melody and reported his findings in Irish Minstrels and Musicians (1913), tracing it to one John Moorehead (also spelled Morehead or Muirhead), of County Armagh, Ireland.

Moorehead was an Englishman who emigrated to Armagh, Ireland, in 1782. A talented young violinist, he became employed by London's Covent Garden Theatre in 1798 and wrote the tune the following year, originally entitling it "The Naval Pillar" after a military victory. It spread rapidly throughout Great Britain and the English colonies, and the melody was later used in a theatrical play, Speed the Plough, which led to the song's current title.

Francis O'Neill (1913) believed the tune to be Irish in character and stated it was regarded as English due to its being first heard in English theaters, though he regretfully determined it too associated with England to include in his Dance Music of Ireland (1907).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Speed The Plow
description:
"Speed the Plow" (sometimes "Speed the Plough" or "God Speed the Plough") is a well-traveled tune, popular with fiddlers for over 200 years. Although it is considered a chestnut in many circles, it has a deserved place in the core fiddle repertoire in several genres, for it seems to flow off the fiddle yet is melodically interesting in both its parts. The reel is extremely widespread in English-speaking traditions and can be found in the repertoires of fiddlers throughout North America, Ireland, Scotland, and England.

What is most unusual is the fact that we do know who composed "Speed the Plow," unlike many older tunes whose origins are typically unknown. Captain Francis O'Neill researched the melody and reported his findings in Irish Minstrels and Musicians (1913), basing his remarks on entries from the British Musical Biography. Therein he found that the reel was the work of one John Moorehead (whose name has also been given as Morehead or Muirhead), of County Armagh, Ireland.

A talented young violinist, Moorehead became employed by London's Covent Garden Theatre in 1798 and wrote the tune the following year, originally entitling it "The Naval Pillar" after a military victory. The melody was then used in a theatrical play called "Speed the Plough," leading to the song's current title.

The phrase "God speed the plough" goes back at least to the 14th century as a prayer for a successful crop and as a song sung by gangs of mischievous revelers on Plough Monday rampages at the end of the Christmas season.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Spotted Pony
description:
One of the most popular tunes in the Missouri Ozarks tradition, 'Spotted Pony' has roots in the late 19th century — fiddlers of the early 20th century reported learning it from their grandparents' generation. Folklorist Vance Randolph documented it in his 1954 list of traditional Ozark Mountain fiddle tunes, the most comprehensive survey of the regional repertoire. At least three distinct tunes share the name 'Spotted Pony,' circulating across Missouri, Arkansas, and Texas, which suggests the title was applied to multiple melodies in different communities rather than tracing back to a single source. The image of a spotted pony — piebald, pinto, colorful — was a common metaphor for something lively and unpredictable in Southern rural culture. The tune's rhythmic drive and clear structure made it a staple of Midwestern dances and contests, and it remains one of the tunes most likely to appear in an Ozark-style old-time session.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: C major with a rolling, confident structure. The tune sits well under the fingers in first position and has a natural momentum that carries dancers. Multiple versions exist — some with slightly different A parts, some in different keys — so it's worth knowing which version your band plays before the jam. The rhythm should feel light-footed, like the pony of the title. A bright, up-bow stroke on the strong beats gives it energy.

title: Spring Creek Gal
description:
| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Genre | Old-Time, Breakdown |
| Key | D Major |
| Structure | AABB (standard tuning) |
| Form | Reel / 2-part |
| Also known as | "Spring Creek Girl," "Spring Creek" |

The origin of "Spring Creek Gal" is a fascinating case of oral transmission across the Midwest, with the story preserved in remarkable detail thanks to the fiddlers themselves.

The tune's strongest association comes from Al Murphy, an eastern Iowa fiddler. The reason the tune became so closely tied to him is that Alabama fiddle player James Bryan heard Murphy's band, Grasslands (Murphy, John Purk, and Bob Black), jamming on the tune at a festival near Burlington, Iowa, at Seven Ponds Park, in September 1981.

James Bryan was playing there with Norman and Nancy Blake in The Rising Fawn String Band. Bryan learned the tune immediately after hearing it just one time.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Springfield
description: Springfield is a reel in the key of D from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Spring In The Valley
description:
"Spring in the Valley" was composed in the mid-1970s by fiddler Tom McCreesh, who played with the Hotmud Family for several years.

The band's leaders, Dave and Suzanne Edmundson, resided in Spring Valley, Ohio, and McCreesh's title may be a word-play on the town they lived in. Tom McCreesh played in the band for a couple of years in the mid-1970s and is on the record Buckeyes in the Briarpatch.
