The tune is an American Reel (cut or 4/4 time), in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB form.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Squirrel Hunters
description:
The "Squirrel Hunters" was the name for a group of civilians who assisted regular federal forces in defending Cincinnati, Ohio from a Confederate attack in 1862. The nickname was given to militiamen who came to the defense of Cincinnati when it was threatened by Confederate forces victorious in Kentucky. There were not enough regular Union forces to spare, so Governor Tod called for volunteers — and over 15,000 men showed up. The Confederate force, upon learning the size of the opposition, turned back and retreated.

Army paymaster Major Malcolm McDowell assigned these backwoods volunteers the nickname of "Squirrel Hunters." The term allegedly comes from the report of a Confederate scout who said words to the effect that they looked like a bunch of squirrel hunters. In 1863, a piece of music was published titled "The Squirrel Hunters March," but it's not this tune.

It's an Allegheny tune — from Western Pennsylvania down the spine of the mountains into West Virginia. This tune was known in Pennsylvania primarily as a fife "stop-beat" piece, though Bayard identified it as a member of "one of the most widespread and ramifying of our British Isles melodic families."

Samuel Bayard collected the tune named for these irregulars along the Ohio border in southwestern Pennsylvania. Bayard (1908–1997) specialized in Pennsylvania folklore, especially fiddle and fife tunes from the state. Bayard mostly heard "The Squirrel Hunters" tune from fifers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Star Of Bethlehem
description:
"Star of Bethlehem" is classified as an American march in 2/4 or 4/4 time, rooted in southwestern Pennsylvania, and played in D Major in standard fiddle tuning.

Don't be fooled by the name — it is not a Christmas tune. The word "star" in the title is used in the Irish sense, meaning a beautiful woman.

The tune's roots are genuinely murky, stretching across the Atlantic:
Scholar Samuel Bayard (1981) believes the tune to be Scottish, though he finds it "a little hard" to trace.
The tune is considered "traditional" (no known author), but the first part of the tune shows up in several melodies from Ireland, Scotland, and England — including the Irish "Centenary March" and "Comhra Donn (An)", and the Scottish "Caledonian March" (printed by George Willig in Philadelphia in 1837 and by Elias Howe in his Musician's Companion of 1842).
One researcher, Barry Callaghan (2007), says the core tune was current as a military march during the Peninsular War, and probably even earlier.
Forms of the tune also appear as the air for hymns in shape-note hymnals.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Steamboat Round The Bend
description:
"Steamboat 'Round the Bend" is an American reel (whole or cut time), rooted in the Missouri and Nebraska tradition, played in G Major in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB form.

The tune is most closely associated with a specific regional fiddler. The primary recorded source is Bob Walters, captured playing it in 1956, later released on the Old Time Fiddlers' Repertory University of Missouri LP (1976), part of the collection Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Nebraska.

Nebraska old-time fiddler Elvin Campbell also played the tune — described as a "Bob Walters tune" — in the Missouri Valley style. This firmly places the tune within the Missouri-Nebraska regional fiddling tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Step to the Music Johnny
description: Step to the Music Johnny is a reel in the key of A from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stillhouse Branch
description:
"Stillhouse Branch" is most closely associated with Buddy Thomas, a fiddler from Lewis County, northeast Kentucky (1935–1974), who recorded the tune under that title but also knew it alternately as "Brown Stream" — a mondegreen (a mishearing) of "Brown's Dream." Thomas believed the "Brown Stream" title referred to the stream of whiskey that emerges from a moonshine still, according to folklorist Mike Yates (2002).

Thomas knew the tune as "Stillhouse Branch," and learned his version from his cousin, Perry Riley (1893–1973).

"Stillhouse Branch" is the name given to several Appalachian rivulets — there are Stillhouse Branches in southwestern Virginia near the town of Pound, in Nicholas County, West Virginia, and in Rowan County, Kentucky — but the name undoubtedly referred to any number of mountain streams that provided water used for distilling liquor. The name thus carries a distinctly Appalachian moonshining flavor, connecting landscape, livelihood, and music.

"Stillhouse Branch" belongs to a large family of related tunes that includes "Brown's Dream," "Brownstream," "Herve Brown's Dream," "Jimmy Johnson Pass that Jug Around the Hill / Johnny Bring the Jug Around the Hill," "John Brown's Dream," "Little Rabbit," "Pretty Little Gal," "Table Mountain Road," and others.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stonewall Jackson
description:
Here's a comprehensive breakdown of the old-time fiddle tune "Stonewall Jackson" — covering multiple distinct tunes sharing that name, their origins, and the key figures behind them.

Most tunes bearing this name are believed to honor Confederate General Thomas "Stonewall" Jackson (1824–1863), one of the most celebrated military figures of the Civil War. The title of related Jackson tunes may or may not refer to the famous flanking march made by the Confederate general Stonewall Jackson at Chancellorsville in 1863. It was extremely common in the post-Civil War era for American fiddlers — especially in the South and Midwest — to name tunes after celebrated military and political figures, resulting in multiple unrelated tunes sharing the same name.

It seems presidents and fiddle tunes go together, as a quick check of old-time tune titles reveals quite a few named after presidents (and generals).

The Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org) catalogs at least three separate, unrelated old-time tunes all called "Stonewall Jackson." This is not unusual in the folk tradition — the same name could be independently attached to different melodies in different regions.

title: Streak O' Lean Streak O' Fat
description:
"Streak O' Lean, Streak O' Fat" was recorded in the late 1920s by Seven-Foot Dilly and His Dill Pickles, led by guitarist John Dilleshaw. The recording is catalogued in the key of C (standard GDAE tuning) and dates to around 1930.

There is some debate about exactly who played fiddle on the recording. The fiddler was most likely Harry Kiker, who was the earliest fiddler in Dilleshaw's band. However, YouTube documentation of the 1930 recording attributes the fiddle to A.A. Gray — a seven-time Georgia fiddle champion. It's possible both men played on different sessions under the Seven-Foot Dilly banner.

The tune's roots go back well before the 1930 recording. It belongs to a family of closely related Southern fiddle tunes:
"Streak O' Lean, Streak O' Fat" is closely related to a tune by Gid Tanner and His Skillet Lickers called "Hell Broke Loose in Georgia," but "Streak O' Lean" has some extra parts — four parts in all.
The melody is also related to other tunes including "Big Footed Nigger (2)" and "Possum up a Gum Stump (2)."
The parent melody has deep pre-20th-century roots: researcher Cauthen (1990) found reference to a Georgia fiddler, Ben Smith, who served with the 12th Alabama Infantry in the Civil War and was known to have played the related tune during that conflict.
The tune was also used in 1899 in a Gallatin, Tennessee fiddle contest as a "category tune" — where each contestant played their own version, with the best rendition winning a prize, a formerly common way of structuring fiddle contests.
A.B.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stumptail Dog
description:
"Stumptail Dog" is one of several variant titles for the same tune family, which also goes by "Stumptail Dolly," "Stump-Tailed Dolly," and "Stumptown," among others.

The tune's unusual name traces back to a real working dog breed and a piece of Appalachian folk legend:

A century and a half ago, if you asked a sheep farmer in the areas of Southern West Virginia or Eastern Kentucky what the best sheepdog was, he would have said without hesitation, "a Stump-Tailed Dolly!" — described as having long, tangled hair and a docked (stubbed) tail, believed to have originated from the Briard breed, introduced to the region by Johann Dahle, a Hessian mercenary who served with the British against the colonists in the Revolutionary War.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stumptail Dolly
description:
"Dolly" is generally considered a regional eastern Kentucky tune. It is an old-time breakdown/reel in G Major, and goes by the aliases "Stumptown Dolly" and "Stumptailed Dolly" and is classified as an American Reel. The tune's authorship is unknown, but it was widely played among the fiddlers of this area beginning as early as 1830.

The most famous carrier of this tune. Kentucky fiddler William Hamilton Stepp was recorded in 1937 by Alan Lomax of the Library of Congress, and this tune "Stump-Tailed Dolly" (or just "Dolly") was part of that recording session. His recording is held in the Library of Congress archive as AFS 568 and remains the version most modern players learn from.

Jeff Titon (2001) says John Salyer (1882–1952) recorded a similar version of this local tune as "Stumptailed Dolly." John lived not far from the home of Stepp, and the two played together frequently, sharing repertoire. Salyer's home recording of "Stumptailed Dolly" from 1940/41 is archived at the Berea Sound Archives.

According to Magoffin County fiddler Glen Fannin (1901–1978), who played a version for collector Bruce Greene, the original title of "Dolly" may or may not have been "Stumptailed Dog," named so by Salyer's father Morgan, who had a bob-tailed dog named Dolly.

title: Sugar In Coffee
description:
Here's a full research summary drawn from the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), the most authoritative source for North American fiddle tune annotations.

The tune goes by several names, including "Sugar in My Coffee-O" and "I Like Sugar in My Coffee-O," and is also related to the tune known as "Cornstalk Fiddle."

It is an American reel (in 2/4 or cut time), documented across Arizona, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Missouri. Its strongest association is with the Ozarks and surrounding Southern/Midwestern regions.

The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist and folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.

title: Sugarbaby
description:
"Sugar Baby" is a traditional old-time fiddle tune that has circulated widely in the American folk and string band repertoire. It is sometimes listed under variant titles and appears in multiple regional traditions across Appalachia and the broader American South.

One of the most celebrated early recordings associated with "Sugar Baby" comes from Dock Boggs, the Virginia banjo player and singer. Boggs recorded "Sugar Baby" in the late 1920s, and his version — marked by his distinctive modal, mournful style — became one of the defining recordings of the piece. Boggs drew on older ballad and blues traditions in the region, blending them into something uniquely his own.

The tune is often played in a minor or modal key, giving it a haunting, melancholic quality that is characteristic of many old-time Appalachian tunes. It sits at the intersection of fiddle tradition and banjo repertoire, and has been adapted by both.

During the American folk revival of the 1960s and 1970s, Dock Boggs was rediscovered by folklorists and enthusiasts, and "Sugar Baby" gained a new audience. Mike Seeger was instrumental in bringing Boggs back into the spotlight, recording and performing with him, which helped re-introduce the tune to younger generations of old-time musicians.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sugar Hill
description:
Music researcher Mike Yates (2002) reports that "Sugar Hill" is "believed to have been composed by George Washington Dixon some time prior to 1827," a version of which was published in New York in 1855 in Christy's Negro Songster, a mid-19th century collection of blackface minstrel songs.

Yates also finds it related to a Kentucky tune called "Jenny Get Around," suggesting the melody circulated widely across Appalachian oral tradition long before any formal documentation.

The title's meaning is debated, with at least three competing theories:
Sugaring-off parties: Davidson (notes to Folkways 2477) thought it probably referred to drunken binges during "sugaring-off", or the process of heating collected sap to make maple sugar.
African-American slang: Another observation is that the song has African-American roots and "Sugar Hill" is said to signify the "wild part of town," the red-light district.
Geographic/cultural resonance: "Sugar Hill" also refers to a famous section of Harlem, NYC, said to refer to "the sweet life" that went on there.

The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954, and the tune is sometimes found in that region under the title "Bunker Hill (4)." The tune has come to be identified with Galax, Va., style string bands and has also been described as a classic Surry County, North Carolina, number.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Sunflower Hornpipe
description:
"Sunflower Hornpipe" is an old-time American fiddle tune in the hornpipe genre. The hornpipe of earlier British tradition in 3/2 time is a different genre — the modern American hornpipe (as played in old-time and country fiddle styles) is a distinct form. American hornpipes are typically played in 4/4 time with a characteristic dotted rhythm, often swung for dancing.

The old-time fiddle style originates from the colonization of North America by immigrants from England, France, Germany, Ireland, and Scotland, who brought their native fiddling traditions with them, mixed with influence from African-American music.

Many old-time instrumental tunes have precedents in British tradition dating back to the late eighteenth century — tunes such as "Leather Britches," which began life as a Scottish reel. Other tunes seem to have circulated primarily in America in the same period, like "Ricketts' Hornpipe," named after a late eighteenth-century circus entrepreneur.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sunnyside
description:
"Sunnyside" is a traditional old-time fiddle tune that appears in multiple tune databases and session repertoires. It is sometimes listed under variant names depending on regional tradition.

The tune's exact composer is not definitively documented, which is common for old-time fiddle tunes that were passed down orally through Appalachian and rural Southern communities. Like many tunes of the genre, "Sunnyside" likely emerged from the folk tradition rather than from a single identifiable composer.

The tune is typically played in a major key and follows the standard AABB two-part structure common to old-time fiddle music. It has a bright, upbeat character consistent with its name.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet 'Bama
description:
The tune traces directly to fiddler Stanley Bailey (1914–1988) of Nashville, Berrien County, in south Georgia. A photo from the Nashville (GA) Historical Society captures Bailey around 1923 or 1924 with a cigar-box fiddle that he made himself — a vivid glimpse into the deep, self-taught rural tradition he came from.

Bailey reportedly learned the tune from his uncle, placing its roots at least one generation further back into Georgia folk tradition.

Bailey was the Georgia State Fiddle Champion in 1932 and 1934 — a credential that speaks to how highly regarded he was in the Southern contest fiddling world of his era.

Bailey was "rediscovered" in the 1980s, several years before his death, and was recorded in the field by Ohio fiddler Joe LaRosa, as well as Alice Gerrard, Bob Carlin, Jim and Joyce Cauthen, and others.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Bundy
description:
Sweet Bundy is an American reel in cut time, played in the key of D Major in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB' structure.

The known provenance of this tune traces a fascinating chain of oral transmission through rural Indiana:

According to Paul Tyler, who recorded Dickey several times in the latter 1980s, source fiddler Lotus Dickey had this tune from his brother, Cyprien, who learned it "from a fellow by the name of Lee Trinkle, down around Rego, Indiana, in Orange County."

So the known chain is:
> Lee Trinkle (Rego, Orange County, Indiana) → Cyprien Dickey → Lotus Dickey

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Dixie
description:
The instrumental tune "Sweet Dixie" was composed by Bill Emerson, a renowned bluegrass banjo player. It has become a bluegrass classic since it was first recorded with Jimmy Martin and the Sunny Mountain Boys around 1964.

Bill Emerson explained the origin of the title: Jimmy Martin actually suggested it. Emerson had already written the tune and had a different title long before he went to work for Martin. When he played it for Martin, Martin wanted to record it right away but didn't like the original title. While they were discussing what to call it, Emerson pointed out that it shares the same chord changes as "Home Sweet Home" — and Martin said it needed to have the word "Sweet" in the title. Emerson suggested "Sweet Dixie," and so it became.

The tune was recorded in the Key of D because Emerson consulted fiddler Vernon Derrick about whether C or D would work better. Derrick preferred D, and Emerson was glad he did — noting it "wouldn't have had the same sound in C."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Jenny
description:
Here is a deep dive into the history and origin story of "Sweet Jenny Jones" — a tune with a remarkably rich trail spanning Wales, England, Ireland, and ultimately the American old-time tradition.

The melody originates as "Cader Idris", an 1804 composition by the 19th-century Welsh harper John Parry (1776–1851), known by his bardic name "Bardd Alaw" ("Master of Melody"), and named by him after the mountain in Meirionnydd, Wales.

Parry did much to promote and popularize Welsh music in England in both music hall and fashionable society settings, and he was very successful with this air, which was immensely popular in 19th-century England. It was first published by him in The Welsh Harper, being an Extensive Collection of Welsh Airs (1839).

The Jenny Jones of the title was said to have been a dairymaid at Pontblyddin Farm, who fell in love with a ploughman named Edward Morgan. Edward went to sea and spent twenty years in the Navy; however, he returned to marry Jenny.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Little Julie
description:
Here's everything the historical record tells us about "Sweet Little Julie" — a rare and regionally specific old-time fiddle tune from the Blue Ridge mountains of southwest Virginia.

"Sweet Little Julie" is classified as a Reel (single/double) from the United States, played in the key of D. It is typically played in cross-tuning (ADAE), a hallmark of the southwest Virginia fiddle tradition.

It is considered one of the "local" Blue Ridge tunes in D — not a common tune, played by only a few musicians in the Southwest Virginia Blue Ridge, and rarely heard these days.

The tune's most well-documented source is Norman Edmonds, a fiddler from southwest Virginia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Marie Sheet Music 1893
description:
"Sweet Marie" was a popular song written and composed by Cy Warman (words) and Raymon Moore (music) in 1893.

Warman, a journalist and versifier, wrote the lyric in honor of his wife and approached Moore, a popular variety stage singer, asking him to perform it. Moore came up with the tune and sang it as part of the *musical comedy Africa (1893), which opened at the Euclid Opera House in Cleveland.

The sheet music, with words by Cy Warman and music by Raymon Moore, was published by W. Paxton, ca. 1893. The original sheet music is held at both the Library of Congress and the Levy Sheet Music Collection at Johns Hopkins University (public domain).

Ironically, the song received only a lukewarm reception after Moore sang it — but when the singer left the show as it moved to Pittsburgh, his replacement, Charles Hopper, made it a widespread hit.

title: Sweet Marie (NC version in D)
description:
"Sweet Marie" was originally a popular song written and composed by Cy Warman (words) and Raymon Moore (music) in 1893. Warman, a journalist and versifier, wrote the lyric in honor of his wife and approached Moore, a popular variety stage singer, to perform it. Moore came up with the tune and sang it as part of the musical comedy Africa (1893), which opened in the Euclid Opera House in Cleveland.

Ironically, the song received only a lukewarm reception after Moore sang it, but when the singer left the show and his replacement, Charles Hopper, took over, it became a widespread hit.

As with many songs that attained a measure of popularity, many parodies were written — not least because the rhythmic meter scans the same as a limerick.

Sweet Marie apparently didn't start out as a traditional fiddle or banjo tune. Instead, the tune seems to have started life as a slow, sentimental ballad in the late 1800s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Marie (WV version in A)
description:
"Sweet Marie" was a popular song written and composed by Cy Warman (words) and Raymon Moore (music) in 1893. Warman, a journalist and versifier, wrote the lyric in honor of his wife and approached Moore, a popular variety stage singer, asking him to perform it. Moore came up with the tune and sang it as part of the musical comedy Africa (1893), which opened in the Euclid Opera House in Cleveland.

"Sweet Marie" is like the tune "Redwing" in the sense that while it was originally written in 1893, it is not technically an "Old Time" tune in the strict sense, but morphed into one — similar to "Redwing," which was also a pop tune that came out of Tin Pan Alley in New York City. Both tunes now make for great-sounding "Old Time"/Bluegrass tunes.

Sweet Marie apparently didn't start out as a traditional fiddle or banjo tune. Instead, the tune seems to have started life as a slow, sentimental ballad in the late 1800s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sweet Nell
description:
"Sweet Nell" is a modern old-time fiddle tune, written by Rob Pine and Jim Mullany. Both are fiddle players now based in the Southwest. The story passed around the community is that one of them wrote the A part and the other wrote the B part.

Despite sounding like a traditional tune named for a sweetheart, the origin of the name is a charming and quirky one. The cover notes reveal that the eponymous track is not named for a wife or lover, but for Nell Newman, daughter of the actor Paul Newman.

As the album notes put it: "We send this tune out to Paul Newman's daughter, Nell Newman, whose smiling face adorns the bags of pretzels and chips we often devour between playing tunes." The notes also cheekily add that "a small portion of the proceeds from the sale of this CD goes toward the purchase of a bag of Newman's Own Pretzels or a package of Fig Newmans for our next practice."

In short: they used to eat Newman's Own brand snacks at their jam sessions, and Nell Newman's image was on the packaging — so they named the tune after her.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sycamores Along The Brandywine
description:
"Sycamores Along The Brandywine" is a relatively obscure old-time fiddle/string band tune. The most concrete documentation found is its appearance in the discography of Walt Koken (b. 1946), a prominent old-time banjo player and figure in the revival scene. It appears as track 060 on an album attributed to Walt Koken and Clare Milliner (Milliner on fiddle, Koken on banjo), recorded around 2003 in Pennsylvania, released on the Millstream Music label (MM 0030). Koken was also a member of The Original Fat City String Band and the influential Highwoods Stringband.

No composer credit, earlier recording, or direct oral-history account for this tune title surfaced in available records — which is actually very typical for the genre.

The tune's name almost certainly references the Brandywine Valley of southeastern Pennsylvania/northern Delaware, a historically rich area for old-time music. The Brandywine Valley Friends of Old Time Music (BFOTM) was founded in 1972 by Carl Goldstein and Shel Sandler, two Delaware lawyers and musicians, along with local autoharp player Mike Hudak, a protégé of the brilliant Virginia autoharpist Kilby Snow.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sycamore Shoals
description:
Sycamore Shoals is a real historical location — a state park in Elizabethton, Tennessee, situated along the Sycamore Shoals of the Watauga River. It is a National Historic Landmark where a series of events critical to the establishment of the states of Tennessee and Kentucky, and the settlement of the Trans-Appalachian frontier, took place.

There is a lot of history in the area, and the fort at the Shoals holds re-enactments of the muster of the Overmountain Men as well as old-time music jams each month.

The tune is connected to the Revolutionary War — specifically the "Overmountain Men," the militia force that famously mustered at Sycamore Shoals before the Battle of Kings Mountain (1780). Some in the old-time community have suggested the tune dates to that era, though its exact age is debated.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tar River
description:
"Old Tar River" (also seen as "Ole Tare River") is one of the earliest documented American banjo/fiddle tunes, with roots firmly planted in the antebellum minstrel stage of the early 1840s. Here's everything known about its origin and history:

The original song was written and composed by Joel Sweeney (1810–1860) around 1840. Sweeney — sometimes called the "Elvis" of the 19th century — wrote and popularized the tune, performing it under the title "Old Tar River, or the Serenade of My Lovely Dinah."

Sweeney was a Virginia-born banjoist and minstrel performer, widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in early American popular music and the popularization of the five-string banjo.

The song was sung by the Virginia Minstrels in New York a year later, described as "Old Tar River — or the incidents attending a Coon Hunt." A member of the troupe, Frank Brower, was credited with introducing the playing of the bones onstage during a Fourth of July, 1841 performance in Lynchburg, Virginia, when he accompanied Dan Emmett in the then-new song "Tar River."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tater Patch
description:
Like many old fiddle tunes, the exact origins of "Tater Patch" are a bit of a mystery. But thanks to the oral tradition, a remarkably vivid story has been preserved.

Tommy Jarrell, an old-time fiddler whose performances of the tune are the most-often quoted source for it, credited it to a banjo player named Ike Leonard.

Mt. Airy, western North Carolina, fiddler Tommy Jarrell told musician and folklorist Mike Seeger: "There was a fellow by the name of Ike Leonard…he was a working in the potato patch and this tune come in his mind. And he just throwed down whatever he was a doing and went to the house and got his banjo and played it." This must have happened around 1910 — before 1920.

Jarrell explained that he got it through his uncle Charlie Barnett Lowe in the 1920s — and that Charlie Barnett's brother had married Ike Leonard's widow, giving him what he called "the straight story" to the Tater Patch tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Taylor's Quickstep
description:
Taylor's Quickstep is an old-time quickstep fiddle tune, first recorded by fiddler Leonard Rutherford and his partner, guitarist John D. Foster (billed as Rutherford & Foster), on January 14, 1929.

The tune was recorded in 1929 for Gennett Records in Richmond, Indiana, by fiddler Leonard Rutherford (1898–1951) paired with Kentucky singer John D. Foster (1896–1984). It was released on Gennett as "Taylor's Quickstep" and simultaneously on the budget Supertone label as "Monroe County Quickstep."

The Supertone release used a pseudonym: it appeared under the artist pseudonym "Fox and Davis."

"Taylor's Quickstep" was named for Dennis Taylor, Gennett's talent scout in central Kentucky. This is confirmed by Rick Kennedy's book "Jelly Roll, Bix, and Hoagy: Gennett Records and the Rise of America's Musical Grassroots" (2013), which agrees with Tony Russell, who also described Taylor as Rutherford & Foster's manager.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Temperance Hall
description:
"Temperance Hall" is a traditional old-time fiddle tune found in the American folk repertoire. Like many old-time tunes, its precise origin is difficult to pin down with certainty, as it was passed down orally through generations of fiddlers before being formally documented.

The name "Temperance Hall" is a direct reference to the temperance movement in 19th-century America, which advocated against the consumption of alcohol. Temperance Halls were physical meeting places — community buildings — where temperance societies gathered. It was common practice in old-time music to name tunes after local landmarks, events, or community institutions, and many tunes were played at dances held in such halls (somewhat ironically, given the halls' anti-alcohol mission).
Key & Mode: Typically played in A major or D major, depending on regional tradition.
Time: Standard 4/4 (or cut time) dance feel.
Style: Falls in the category of hoedown/breakdown — a lively, rhythmically driving tune well-suited for square dancing and old-time sessions.
Structure: Standard AABB 32-bar form, common to the old-time repertoire.
The tune appears in old-time jam and session repertoire lists, particularly in the Appalachian and Midwestern traditions.
It has been referenced in online old-time tune databases such as [The Session](https://thesession.org) and [ibiblio's tunebooks](https://www.ibiblio.org), though its documentation is sparse compared to more widely known tunes.
Like many tunes of its era, no single composer is definitively credited — it is considered a traditional tune of unknown authorship.

title: Ten Cents
description: Ten Cents is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tennessee Politics
description:
"Tennessee Politics" is not a traditional anonymous folk tune — it has a known and celebrated composer. "Tennessee Politics" is a tune by American fiddler John Hartford, transcribed directly from the manuscript in his personal tune notebooks, and presented by fiddler Matt Combs.

John Hartford was a prolific composer, multi-instrumentalist, and newgrass pioneer. Over 2,000 original and unrecorded fiddle tunes were discovered in his archive after his passing — amassed in sixty-eight music notebooks and composed during the last eighteen years of his life — demonstrating the breadth of his writing style, with hints of bluegrass, old-time, folk, country, and even classical music.

One of the most respected musicians in Nashville history, Hartford is considered a cornerstone of the newgrass movement due to his 1971 masterpiece Aereo-Plain. He won four Grammy Awards, including two for his 1967 recording of "Gentle on My Mind."

Hartford's journals date back to 1983, essentially coinciding with the sessions for his 1984 album Gum Tree Canoe, recorded at the legendary Cowboy Arms Hotel and Recording Spa in Nashville.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Texas
description:
The tune known as "Texas" in the old-time fiddle repertoire has a remarkably well-documented, if slightly tangled, origin story — rooted in a single Appalachian fiddler, a traveling stranger, and a folklorist's naming decision that stuck.

The tune traces directly to Henry Reed (1884–1968), a fiddler from Glen Lyn, Giles County, in southwestern Virginia. It is a "crooked" tune — the first strain always has 17 beats, the second has 13 — from fiddler Henry Reed of Glen Lyn, Virginia.

Alan Jabbour dubbed it "Texas" because Reed told him he had no name for it, but had learned it from "a fellow either going to Texas or from Texas." At some point Reed also told Jabbour the man who played the tune was a Mr. Drummond(s).

The Library of Congress recording confirms the story: Henry Reed called it "Texas" and said he learned the tune from a Mr. Drummond(s) from Texas, but during a later performance he was certain that the title was "New Castle," after the county seat of nearby Craig County, Virginia.

title: Texas Barb Wire
description:
The tune was popularized by West Coast mandolinist, singer, and entertainer Kenny Hall (1923–2013). In the Traditional Tune Archive's notation, the tune is credited directly to Kenny Hall as composer.

Hall learned the tune in the late 1930s from a schoolmate, Warren Raley, whose family was from Oklahoma and Louisiana — and Raley himself had the tune from his father. This gives the tune a clear oral-tradition lineage: from an unnamed earlier source → Raley's father → Warren Raley → Kenny Hall → the wider old-time community.

The tune is an American Reel in cut time, in the key of G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB' form.

The title connects to a defining moment in Western American history. On November 24, 1874, Joseph F. Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, was granted a patent for fencing material — barbs wrapped around a single strand of wire and twisted around another. His original double-strand design, "the Winner," became the most commercially successful of the hundreds of eventual barbed wire designs.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Texas Gals
description:
"Texas Gals" is sourced to Alonzo Elvis "Tony" Alderman (1900–1983), a fiddler from western Virginia, playing with The Hill Billies. It was recorded on Vocalion 5021 (78 RPM) in 1927.

The recording is noted as being in the key of C, standard GDAE tuning, with Tony Alderman and Charles Bowman on fiddle, and is referenced in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Virginia.
Tony Alderman was a central figure in The Hill Billies, one of the earliest string bands to record commercially. He was from the mountain region of western Virginia.
Charles Bowman was a co-fiddler on the recording. Both were key contributors to preserving and popularizing old-time string band tunes in the early recording era.

The tune is set in cut time (C|) in the key of C, and has a lively, driving character consistent with the old-time reel/country rag style. It features three distinct melodic parts, a somewhat unusual structure for old-time tunes of the era.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Texas Quickstep
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Tune Name | Texas Quickstep |
| Alternate Titles | Rachel's Hornpipe / Rachel / Texas Galop / Spanish Polka / Missouri Quickstep |
| Key | D Major |
| Form | Reel (single/double), also listed as a Polka in some sources |
| Most Famous Recording | Red Headed Fiddlers, Brunswick 285 (78 RPM), 1928 |

The tune carries one of the most storied attributions in American fiddle music. It was also known as "Rachel's Hornpipe," and is attributed to Rachel Jackson, wife of President Andrew Jackson. This makes the tune's roots stretch back to the early 19th century, long before it was commercially recorded — though whether Rachel Jackson actually composed it or merely inspired its name is unverifiable, as with many folk attributions.

The tune is also listed under the alternate titles "Missouri Quickstep" and "Texas Quickstep," with "Rachel" sometimes used as the primary title.

The tune's most important popularizer was Albert L. "Red" Steeley, the anchor of the Red Headed Fiddlers, a Dallas–Fort Worth duo.
The canonical recording is credited to the Red Headed Fiddlers (Dallas–Ft. Worth, Texas), specifically A.L. "Red" Steeley (1893–1969) and J. Warner "Red" Graham.
The Red Headed Fiddlers featured fiddler A.L. "Red" Steeley and Red Graham on banjo, and they had a radio program in Ft. Worth for about 10 years during the 1920s up to about the time of the Depression. The program was almost entirely fiddling.
Steeley and Graham recorded "Texas Quickstep" in 1928, and it stands as a prime example of a very tight and unified fiddle and banjo duet.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Third of July
description:
It is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown, played in G Major, with an AA′BB′ repeating structure.

The primary source for the tune is the Red Brush Rowdies, a West Virginia string band featuring fiddler Miller Wikel, who recorded in the 1930s.

The tune is also known as — or closely related to — "Cornshucker's Frolic."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Thread The Needle
description:
Here's what's known about the old-time fiddle tune "Thread the Needle" based on available sources:
Classification: Traditional old-time fiddle tune. No single composer is credited — like many tunes in the old-time canon, it was passed down orally through regional playing communities.
A catchy tune that fiddler Carl Jones first heard in Alabama in the 1970s, played by Joe Sharp. This is one of the clearest documented transmission stories for the tune — connecting it to the Deep South old-time tradition.
The tune has been recorded and performed by Erynn Marshall, a prominent figure in the old-time world. Erynn Marshall is an old-time fiddler who resides in Galax, Virginia, and has played for over 30 years, performing and teaching at music camps and festivals across North America, Europe, Australia, and China.
She won 1st place in fiddle at both the Clifftop and Mt. Airy Fiddlers Conventions.
The recording was released as a traditional track on the album Old-Time Sweethearts - Vol. 1 & Vol. 2, performed by Erynn Marshall, Carl Jones, Rachel Eddy, and Em Hammond.
On that recording, Rachel Eddy plays a Slim Jim banjo.
"Thread the Needle" is also a well-known play-party and square dance figure in American folk tradition, where participants form an arch and "thread" through it — strongly suggesting the tune's title and character are tied to this social dance tradition. The lively, rhythmic nature of the melody fits perfectly for calling such figures.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Three Forks of Cheat
description:
The Cheat River forms in the Allegheny mountains of West Virginia and runs north into Pennsylvania where it empties into the Monongahelia River. The river forms in Parsons, West Virginia, from the confluence of Shavers Fork and Black Fork.

However, Black Fork itself is fed by the Blackwater River and by the Dry, Glady, and Laurel Forks — these are traditionally referred to as the five Forks of Cheat. This raises an interesting question the tune's name hints at: why "three" forks? The number likely reflects an older naming convention from before all tributaries were formally surveyed.

The Cheat was so important for travel in that remote region that in 1870 it was declared a public highway.

There is a traditional fiddle tune called "Three Forks of Cheat" that is known throughout the country, and even in other countries, thanks to a family of West Virginians. This folk song is most commonly associated with the Hammons Family from Pocahontas County, a multi-generational line of musicians who helped pass on some of the best-known traditional songs from West Virginia.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Three Thin Dimes
description:
According to Seattle fiddler and old-time music expert Kerry Blech, the source for the tune is Barnesville, Ohio, fiddler Old John Hutchison (1915–1979), who never formally recorded.

The tune comes from the playing of this east Ohio fiddler and was captured in 1977 by field recorder Jeff Goehring.

Celebrated multi-instrumentalist Tim O'Brien first heard the tune as played by the Hutchison Brothers band on their Vetco Records release around 1976. John and Zeke Hutchison's father (Old John) wrote the tune and taught it to the band's fiddler, Greg Dearth.

The tune spread further through the West Coast old-time scene as well. One player traces his source for "Three Thin Dimes" to Seattle fiddler Armin Barnett, though the specific chain of transmission is murky — it almost certainly led back to Ohio fiddlers.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tie-Hacker Hoedown #1
description:
According to folklorist Howard Marshall, a "tie-hacker" was an itinerant worker who cut ties from the north Missouri forest for the railroads in the late 1800s, following the Civil War. The term refers specifically to folks who made railroad ties from timber, chopping them into shape with an axe.

Tie-hackers typically worked in two-man teams. Hard-working teams could hew about twenty hardwood railroad ties in an 11-hour workday, earning each man about a dollar. Some men worked full time as tie hackers, but tie-hacking was also a way for Ozark farmers to earn much-needed cash during the winter.

In 1912, over 15 million hand-hewed railroad ties were made by tie-hackers in the forests of southeastern Missouri. By the early 1930s, the market had changed — white oak became more valuable for barrel staves than railroad ties, and in the 1930s, creosote chemical treatment and portable sawmills that could saw ties cheaper effectively put an end to the Ozark tie-hacker's way of life.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tie-Hacker Tune #2
description:
The name of the tune is rooted in a forgotten chapter of American labor history. A "tie-hacker" was an itinerant worker who cut ties from the north Missouri forest for the railroads in the late 1800s, following the Civil War. These tie-hackers helped construct the railway across northern Missouri by cutting railroad ties from the once abundant stands of white oak in the region. They were often Irish or Scots-Irish who lived in camps in the white oak woods, and some of their music was preserved in the playing of the Wilson family of Linn County, north-central Missouri.

Tie-Hacker Hoedown No. 2 comes from the playing of Nile Wilson (1912–2008), of Linn County, north-central Missouri. Wilson was the key figure through whom this tune family survived. The tunes come from the repertory of this northern Missouri fiddler, who played them (some in the form of a country rag) as fast breakdowns. Nile played a lot of tunes in C, a desirable key for square dance music, as the fiddle rings out nicely in that key.

Tie-Hacker Hoedown No. 2 is a Reel in cut time, in the key of C Major, played at a "Moderately Quick" tempo. It is part of a small family of related tunes — there is also a Tie-Hacker Hoedown #1 and a Tie-Hacker's Rag — all traced back to Wilson.

> ️ Note on labeling: The tune has been mislabeled on at least one compilation — appearing as Tie Hacker #2 on the Now That's A Good Tune: Masters of Traditional Missouri Fiddling CD when it is actually a different tune ("Old Reunion").

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tilden to the Whitehouse
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Key | G major |
| Source Fiddler | Ernie Carpenter |
| Transcribed By | Sandy Hofferth |
| Published In | The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John S. Lamancusa |

The tune "Tilden to the Whitehouse" is listed in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes in the key of G, attributed to Sandy Hofferth from Ernie Carpenter — meaning Hofferth learned and/or transcribed it from the playing of Ernie Carpenter.

Ernie Carpenter (1909–1991) was a celebrated West Virginia old-time fiddler, one of the most important traditional source fiddlers of the 20th century. He is widely regarded as a master of the West Virginia fiddle tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tippy Get Your Hair Cut
description:
The story of "Tippy Get Your Hair Cut" is one of the most charming transmission tales in all of Appalachian folk music. The tune was learned by Braxton County, West Virginia, musician Bob Wine, father of fiddler Melvin Wine, who heard mulatto fiddler Jilly Grace play it but once.

According to Gerry Milnes (1999), the elder Wine "could not even bribe Grace to play the tune a second time, but he managed to learn it anyway." Grace was a fiddler in the Burnsville area who occasionally played for horse-drawn traveling merry-go-rounds.

So in one remarkable act of musical memory, Bob Wine plucked the tune from a single fleeting performance and passed it down to his son.

Melvin Wine (1909–2003), a Braxton County, West Virginia fiddler, became the primary carrier of this tune — his version being the one usually referenced today, recorded in the 78 RPM era alongside the Kessinger Brothers (also from West Virginia).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tomahawk
description:
Bob Holt got this tune from the great Nashville fiddler Tommy Jackson. It appears on the LP Square Dance Tonight! — one of those "square dances without calls" LPs that made Tommy a favorite of fiddlers all over North America back in the 1950s and 60s.

So the tune's traceable commercial origin lies with Tommy Jackson, a prolific Nashville session and square-dance fiddler who recorded extensively in that era.

The tune appears to have traveled into the old-time world via (at least) two distinct routes, creating two related but distinct branches:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tom Fuller's Reel
description:
Tom Fuller (1890–1979) was born and raised in Indian Territory before Oklahoma became a state. Orphaned as a child, he made his way through life guided by a strong work ethic, a love of music, and a kind heart. He worked as a farmer, cowboy, and oilfield worker in southern Oklahoma and west Texas.

In his early teens, about 1905 or a little before, Tom sold bluing (a product used to whiten laundry) to earn extra money to buy his first fiddle. He taught himself to play by ear initially, watching and listening to other fiddlers in the area. He played quite a few dances as a teenager and into his early twenties.

Eager to improve his skills, he took some lessons from a music teacher in Hulen, Oklahoma in the early 1920s. He was proud of learning to play "by note," and afterwards enjoyed playing music from the church hymnal. He used to joke that he played fiddle for dances and violin for church.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Tune The Old Cow Died On
description:
The tune for the original comic song was written by Joseph Eastburn Winner — composer of the famous "Little Brown Jug" — with words by George Russell Jackson, and published in 1880 by John F. Perry & Co., Boston. The original full title was "The Tune that the Old Cow Died On." The sheet music is preserved and viewable at the Library of Congress: [loc.gov/item/sm1880.05588](https://www.loc.gov/item/sm1880.05588/).

The song tells of old Farmer John who came home one summer afternoon, sat beneath a maple tree, and sang himself a tune — drawing all the cows running up to form a ring around him, for they had never heard him attempt to sing before.

The oldest cow in the herd tried hard to join in the song, but she could not strike the melody, though her voice was loud and strong. The farmer laughed until tears ran down his cheeks, but the cow was so determined that she tried to sing until she dropped down dead.

A separate, older folk variant of the story features a fiddler instead of a singer:

title: Turkey Buzzard Laughed at Crow
description: Turkey Buzzard Laughed at Crow is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Turkey in the Pea Patch
description:
"Turkey in a Peapatch" is an American Reel (cut time) tune, rooted in the tradition of northeast Kentucky and southern Ohio. It is played in D Major, in standard or ADae fiddle tuning. Its form is AABB' (two repeated parts, with a variation on the second).

It is a separate and distinct tune from the more famous "Turkey in the Straw," despite the similar name. It belongs specifically to the Appalachian/old-time tradition of the Kentucky-Ohio border region.

The tune is credited as [Traditional] and was first recorded and released by Uncle Dave Macon and His Fruit-Jar Drinkers in 1927. Like most old-time fiddle pieces, its exact compositional origin is unknown — most tunes in the old-time fiddle repertoire are in the public domain and have no known authorship, though many have rich historical significance.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Turkey Sag
description:
"Turkey Sag" is a composed old-time fiddle tune, not a tune of anonymous folk tradition — though it has spread so widely through the old-time community that many players assume it to be traditional.

Jim Childress wrote the tune in 1977 or 1978, and considers it the tune that made him take composing seriously. Remarkably, it came to be very widely played years before he ever officially recorded it — prompting him to finally record it so he could have some say in how the tune actually goes.

The tune was finally released on Childress's 2004 CD also titled Turkey Sag, a collection of 16 original fiddle tunes composed over roughly 25 years. Several of these tunes have become widely known and played by old-time musicians around the world. The original versions were performed by Uncle Henry's Favorites, Rick Epping, Jimbo Cary, and Barbara Payne.

The tune is catalogued in the Traditional Tune Archive as a Reel in D major, played in standard GDAE tuning, attributed to Jim Childress (as sourced from Eric Zorn's YouTube performance).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: 28th of January
description:
Modern revival fiddlers source the tune from Bluefield, West Virginia, fiddler Franklin George, who learned it from his mentor Jim Farthing, who called the tune "28th of January."
Franklin George — William Franklin "Frank" George (6 October 1928 – 15 November 2017) was from Roane County, WV.
Jim Farthing — Farthing was a fiddler from Virginia near the North Carolina border who had moved to West Virginia for mining-related jobs and who performed carpentry with George's father.

The title was curious to George, who did not know what it referred to, nor had Farthing been forthcoming with an explanation.

Additionally, Steve Goldfield interviewed Franklin George for Fiddler Magazine (vol. 21, No. 2, Summer 2014) and was told that George had heard the tune played on an LP by "a French fiddler who played it almost identically, under a different name, a French name." George could not recall either the fiddler nor the French title.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: 22nd of February
description:
Composed by Zeke Backus and first released by Snuffy Jenkins and The Hired Hands in 1962, '22nd of February' takes its name from George Washington's birthday, which was designated a federal holiday in 1879 and remained a major celebratory occasion in rural American communities well into the 20th century. Folklorist Alan Jabbour theorized that the closely related tune '28th of January' — named for the Battle of New Orleans anniversary — shares common roots with '22nd of February,' and that calendar-named tunes may represent a tradition of commemorating civic occasions through fiddle music. This connection between patriotic holidays and fiddle repertoire was more common in the 19th and early 20th centuries, when local celebrations often included community dances. Also known as 'Miller's Reel,' the tune demonstrates how the same melody could accumulate multiple titles as it moved through different communities and contexts.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: A major with a bright, celebratory quality suited to its patriotic title. The tune has clear AABB structure and a rhythm that suggests lively dancing. Related tunes '28th of January' and 'Miller's Reel' are worth knowing if you learn this one — the family resemblance is clear once you play all three. Snuffy Jenkins's banjo recording is the primary reference; the tune has a slightly different energy in fiddle arrangements.

title: Twinkle Little Star
description:
Here is a comprehensive history and origin story of "Twinkle Little Star" as an old-time fiddle tune — tracing the melody from 18th-century France through American parlors, stage plays, and fiddle contests.

The tune is originally from France and was first seen in print in Paris in 1761 — though "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" as a song didn't exist back then. The tune is an old French melody titled "Ah! Vous Dirai-Je, Maman" ("Shall I tell you, Mother?") that first appeared without words in Les Amusements d'une Heure et Demy by M. Bouin in Paris in 1761.

We have to travel to England in 1806 to find the origins of the lyrics. That's when Jane Taylor and her sister Ann published their second book of poems for children, called Rhymes for the Nursery. Jane wrote the poem "The Star" for the book.

It's a bit of a mystery when the poem and the tune came together. It seems the first time they're seen in print as a song was in 1838, in a book called The Singing Master.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Twinkle Twinkle Little Star
description:
The tune is actually an old French melody titled "Ah! Vous Dirai-Je, Maman" ("Shall I tell you, Mother?") that first appeared without words in Les Amusements d'une Heure et Demy by M. Bouin in Paris in 1761. Who actually wrote the original melody? No one really knows.

The lyrics come from a poem titled "The Star" written by the English poet Jane Taylor (1783–1824), published in her book Rhymes for the Nursery in London in 1806. While the first stanza of "The Star" is usually heard in the lullaby, there are actually five stanzas of the poem that can be sung to the melody.

The combination of the lyrics and tune first appeared in print in 1838 in The Singing Master: First Class Tune Book. Jane Taylor, who died in 1866, is unlikely to have seen any proceeds from her creation, and certainly had no idea of the millions of children she would end up delighting.

In 1781–82, Mozart wrote his Variations on "Ah vous dirais-je, Maman." Many people think he wrote the tune to "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" — he didn't. He just created a wonderful piece based on the existing tune. Historians believe Mozart would have likely heard and composed on the French melody while he was in Paris between April and September of 1778.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Twin Sisters
description:
"Twin Sisters" is one of the most fascinatingly tangled titles in the old-time repertoire — it's actually a floating title attached to several distinct tunes, making its history layered and complex. Here's a full breakdown:

"Twin Sisters" is a floating title that is appended to a variety of tunes, perhaps in association with dance figures. The Traditional Tune Archive catalogs at least five separate tunes under this name. The two most commonly encountered in old-time circles are:

1. The "Boys of Bluehill" derivative — a D-major reel/hornpipe (the most widely played today)
2. The Sidna Meyers modal tune — a Carroll County, Virginia banjo tune with a completely different character

Twin Sisters is closely related to and possibly a descendant of the Irish hornpipe "The Boys of Bluehill," also published as "Beau of Oak Hill" among other titles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Two Bits
description: Two Bits is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Uncle Frank's Piece
description:
According to The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John S. Lamancusa, "Uncle Frank's Piece" is played in the key of D, and its known transmission chain is: Bill Wellington ← Wilber Terry ← Frank Vance. This is the clearest documented lineage for the tune — it was passed down through oral/aural tradition from fiddler Frank Vance to Wilber Terry to Bill Wellington.

The violinist.com blog "Uncle Frank's Fiddle" offers a richly detailed portrait of a real-life "Uncle Frank" fiddler that provides context for how tunes with this kind of name originate:
A cousin named Lee Williams, an accomplished fiddler, taught Frank "a few chords and the tune of 'Old Dan Tucker'" around 1907–1908, and another cousin, Harvey Walker, later taught him to tune his instrument and play by ear.
Frank recalled: "I kept the folks away at night, practicing on that fiddle." He would work in the fields all day, whistling tunes he'd heard, then try to play them after supper into the night.
Frank eventually wrote down the names of 120 songs he could play and sing from memory, including at least 40–50 old-time fiddle tunes. His repertoire included "Arkansas Traveler" (in D), "Whistlin' Rufus" (in G), and "Ft. Smith" (in G).
Frank played his fiddle until he was 90 years of age, then gave it up at 91.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Uncle Pink
description: Uncle Pink is a reel in the key of G from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Valley Forge
description:
The tune is named for George Washington and the Continental Army's Pennsylvania encampment in the winter of 1777–78. It belongs to a tradition of American fiddle tunes named after historical events.

The known lineage of "Valley Forge" runs through three key figures in the Arkansas Ozarks:

Jimmie Driftwood learned "Valley Forge" from fiddler Absie Morrison, whose repertoire contained numerous pieces named for events in American history. Where Morrison obtained the tune, or if the title "Valley Forge" is even his own, is unknown.

Morrison's dad and uncles also played the tune — it was an old tune known throughout the Ozarks by many old-timers. While the Morrison family knew it well, it likely didn't spread widely into the hills through them directly.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Vince Crawford's Tune
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Full Name | Vincent Crawford's Tune |
| Genre | Old-Time, Quadrille |
| Key | G Major |
| Tuning | Standard (GDAE) |
| Structure | AA'B (three-part form) |
| Source | Traditional Tune Archive ([tunearch.org](https://tunearch.org/wiki/Annotation:Vincent_Crawford%27s_Tune)) |

The tune comes from the playing of Vincent Crawford of Avenstoke, Anderson County, Kentucky, and was first recorded in 1979 by Gus Meade and John Harrod, then recorded again in 1985 by John Harrod.

Crawford's repertoire is also documented on the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and the album Traditional Fiddle Music of Kentucky, Vol. 2: Along the Kentucky River (Rounder Records). Another tune attributed to him, "Sand Riffle", was recorded during the same April 8, 1979 session by Guthrie Meade and John Harrod.

title: Wagoner
description:
Despite what the name conjures, "Wagoner" has nothing to do with Conestoga wagons. The title honors a Tennessee thoroughbred horse that competed in a hugely popular Louisville, Kentucky, horse race in 1839. John Hartford accepted that the tune "Grey Eagle" melody was once known as "Miller of Drone," and that the "Grey Eagle" title became attached to it in America following this famous late 1830s race between horses known as Grey Eagle and Wagner — a race that took place at the Oakland Racetrack in Louisville in 1838. The tunes "Wagner" and "Grey Eagle" both commemorate those two competing horses. Wagner was the smaller of the two; Grey Eagle stood 16 hands high and was legendary. The race attracted national attention — and Wagner beat Grey Eagle not once but twice.

These other "Wagoner/Wagner" tunes in the key of C descended from a "Wagner" tune first published in 1838 or 1839 under that title, in honor of the racehorse "Wagner."

The tune's melodic DNA is older than its American name. The first part is thought to be derived from "Billy in the Lowland/Lowground," while the second is a strain from an old Scottish air "Gaberlunzie," the earliest version of which can be found in Thompson's Orpheus Caledonius, 1725. This second strain has an old and venerable history in folk process; the second half of both "Wagoner" and "Gaberlunzie" greatly resemble the Scots tunes "Johnny Cope" and "Keep Off the Grass." Even the second half of the well-known "Mississippi Sawyer" may be derived from this element.

The tune was published as "The Hero" in George P.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wagoner One Step
description:
"Wagoner" is a very popular fiddle tune and a square dance favorite of the old days — likely every old-time fiddler knows a version of it. It's a tune in the key of C, a key less commonly played than the regular A, G, and D, but if a fiddler knows one or two tunes in C, it's probably "Wagoner" or "Billy in the Low Ground."

The title honors a Tennessee thoroughbred horse named "Wagoner" that competed in a hugely popular Louisville, Kentucky, horse race in 1839. The tune appears in historical manuscript collections alongside similarly race-horse-named tunes like "Grey Eagle," suggesting both were celebratory dance pieces composed around the same era.

The earliest known notated appearance is in the G. McMillan music manuscript collection (1843), where it appears directly alongside "Grey Eagle" in the score — the tune was notated in William C. Peters' "Grey Eagle Quadrilles" (1840).

The tune spread across the South and Midwest and was adopted by local fiddling communities who renamed it after their own region:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waiting for the Boatsman
description:
The melody was in the repertoire of fiddler Melvin Wine (1909–2003), of Copen, Braxton County, West Virginia, who played it quickly, almost at dance tempo. It is Wine's derivation of a hymn that he learned from the singing of his mother.

Drew Beissewenger, a Wine biographer, says that the fiddler would sometimes sing the hymn's lyrics before playing the tune. They began: "Oh, I'm waiting for the boatman, he is driving o'er and o'er."

The story told in old-time circles is that Melvin played the song based on his memory of a hymn that his mother sang to him as a child.

As Drew Beisswenger noted in his thesis "Fiddling Way Out Yonder: Community and Style in the Fiddle Music of Melvin Wine", he had seven references to hymns with the title "Waiting for (or without 'for') the Boatman." A Stamps hymn book notes: "Theme suggested while waiting at Ferry on Tennessee river, midnight, July 3, 1917, near Section, Alabama."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waldorf Reel
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Tune Name | Waldorf Reel (AKA "Waldorf's Reel") |
| Genre | American Old-Time Reel |
| Key / Tuning | G Major / Standard (GDAE) |
| Form | Two-part (AB) |
| Time | Cut time |
| Year Recorded | 1974 |

The tune is sourced to Guthrie "Gus" Meade and is said to be named after Waldorf, Maryland. It is thought that Meade recorded the tune and named it — though he did not compose it.

More specifically, legend says the tune is named after Waldorf, Maryland, where it was written down by Guthrie Meade, a computer programmer who collected Kentucky tunes on reel-to-reel tapes at the Library of Congress.

So the tune's name has a double meaning: it refers to both the town of Waldorf, MD, and quite literally to the reel-to-reel tapes Meade used in his fieldwork.

title: Walk Along John
description:
"Walk Along John" is an American reel (cut time), rooted in the states of Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas, played in G Major with standard fiddle tuning. It is also known as "Come Along John" and "Johnny Walk Along with Your Paper Collar On."

The tune's story begins on the antebellum American stage. A minstrel song called "Walk Along John" or "Come Along, John" was published in 1844, with music and words attributed to J.P. Carter of the Virginia Serenaders in their published songbook, though it also states it is "an Old Southern Refrain" — possibly based on an African-American corn (shucking) song called "Shock Along John."

The tune quickly entered popular culture: it was popular enough to be employed in the 1844 Presidential race between Henry Clay (Kentucky) and James K. Polk (Tennessee), with each side sculpting the lyric to their political advantage.

Remarkably, an early version also appears in print far from America's South: there is a close version of the tune in The Boston Collection of Instrumental Music (1910), and it appears in the J. Roose manuscript from Manchester, England (1850). The tune was also notated in Thomas Briggs' Instructions for the Banjo (1855).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Walk Along John to Kansas
description:
"Walk Along John to Kansas" comes from the playing of fiddler Kenner "K.C." Kartchner. Kenner was born in Snowflake, Arizona in 1886 and is considered an important figure in the old-time music world.

The tune was reportedly written by Kartchner, earning him the nickname the "Frontier Fiddler" — also the title of the 1990 book about him published by the University of Arizona Press (Frontier Fiddler, edited by Shumway).

Arizona fiddler Kartchner himself identified the tune as having come from the South, suggesting he may have adapted or preserved a melody with older Southern roots rather than composing it from whole cloth.

Walk Along John to Kansas was recorded in the field by Alan Lomax from the playing of Frank Goodwyn (guitar) and Mrs. F.E. Goodwyn (fiddle), of Hebbronville, Texas, in 1941. This recording is preserved in the Library of Congress American Folklife Center collection.

title: Walk Chalk Chicken with a Necktie On
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Also Known As | "Walk Chalk Chicken," "Walk Chalk Chicken With His Head Pecked Off," "Walk Talk Chicken With His Head Pecked Off" |
| Genre | American Reel (cut time) |
| Key / Tuning | Key of A, cross-tuned fiddle — specifically AEae (cross/sawmill tuning) |
| Primary Source Fiddler | Melvin Wine (1909–2003), Braxton County, West Virginia |
| First Major Recording | Cold Frosty Morning, 1976 |

The tune comes from the playing of Copen, Braxton County, central West Virginia fiddler Melvin Wine (1909–2003). He is the sole known source for this tune in the old-time canon.

He learned the tune from his father, who was the only person he ever heard play it. This makes it essentially a Wine family heirloom — passed down privately for at least two generations before being recorded and shared with the wider folk community.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Walking in My Sleep
description:
A Blue Ridge breakdown from the Round Peak heartland of Surry County, North Carolina and Patrick County, Virginia, 'Walking in My Sleep' carries the loose, ragtime-inflected quality that characterizes some of the most interesting tunes in the Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham repertoire. The tune has a 'rag-like' melody — syncopated, slightly swinging — that suggests the influence of early 20th-century popular music on the mountain tradition, a reminder that Appalachian fiddlers were not isolated from commercial music but absorbed and transformed it constantly. The dreamlike quality of the title — walking in one's sleep, moving without full consciousness — resonates with the tune's slightly off-kilter rhythm, which seems to hover between full wakefulness and something looser. Collected from the Round Peak tradition, it appears in fiddle recordings and instructional material associated with the Surry County musical community.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
notes: G major with a rag-like syncopation that requires careful rhythmic attention — the accents don't always fall where you expect them. Play it with Round Peak bow weight: pressure, commitment, drones ringing. Don't iron out the syncopation trying to make it 'regular.' The irregularity is the charm. Medium tempo where the rhythmic interest is audible; too fast and you lose the rag-like feel that makes this tune distinctive.

title: Walking Uptown
description: Walking Uptown is a reel in the key of F from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Washington Courthouse
description:
Here is everything the web sources were able to surface about the old-time fiddle tune "Washington Courthouse", combined with the broader context that helps explain how a tune like this gets named, circulated, and preserved.

"Washington Courthouse" is named after Washington Court House, Ohio — the county seat of Fayette County in south-central Ohio. This type of place-name title is extremely common in old-time music; tunes were frequently named after the towns, counties, crossroads, or landmarks where they were popularized or first heard.

The most documented thread connecting this tune to a specific person and place comes from a 1983 field recording. A field recording from 1983 captures Jeff Goehring playing the tune, with Goehring citing his source as Estill Adams of Washington Courthouse, Ohio. This suggests Adams was a local traditional fiddler from Fayette County, Ohio, who preserved and transmitted the tune — a classic example of the oral folk transmission chain. The Canote Brothers (Greg and Jerry) also recorded the tune with the Small Wonder String Band, helping bring it to a wider old-time audience.

The story of "Washington Courthouse" reflects patterns common to the entire old-time canon:
The titles of many fiddle tunes "conjure up people and places, incidents and functions" that are part of the texture of Appalachian frontier culture.
The first fiddle tunes were passed from one generation to the next; as settlers spread out and mixed with other immigrant cultures, their different fiddle tunes and techniques began to mingle.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Washington's March
description:
"Washington's March" is a celebrated old-time Appalachian fiddle tune most closely associated with the Hammons family of West Virginia — one of the most storied fiddling dynasties in American folk music history. Despite its title, the tune is played in reel tempo, and may possibly be a very distant derivative of "Washington's Grand March," though there were many melodies in America that carried the Washington name — an indication of his influence even in backwoods areas.

The tune's definitive custodian was Edden Hammons (born Edwin Hammons, 1875–1955) of Pocahontas County, West Virginia. Allan Jabbour, in his 1984 liner notes to the Edden Hammons recording, says this is one of the tunes in the Hammons family repertoire that has special family associations — it was considered to have been composed by early family members, "or at least uniquely preserved by them."

Its original composer is unknown, said to have been written or simply collected by someone further down the Hammons family tree.

One of the most vivid pieces of lore around this tune comes from a 1947 field recording session. The folklorist Louis Watson Chappell stated that Edden Hammons won the 1939 Greenbrier Valley fiddle championship playing "Washington's March," and that he had learned it "59 years ago and first played it on a gourd covered by a deer skin."

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Waterloo
description:
The Battle of Waterloo (June 18, 1815) spawned a whole family of fiddle and pipe tunes across the British Isles and North America. The battle was fought in 1815, some two years before the printing of Gow's 4th Repository, and in the context of the times, the heroic event was still quite topical.

One key "Waterloo" tune — "Highland Brigade at Waterloo" — was composed by John Gow (1764–1826), the youngest son of the famous Scots fiddler-composer Niel Gow. John moved to London, and with his brother Andrew established a publishing firm, becoming the English distributor of the Gow family publications.

Gow included two other tunes in the same collection referencing the battle: "Lamentation for the Fallen Heroes of Waterloo" and "Royal Highlanders Welcome from Waterloo."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waverley
description:
The tune "Waverley" (also spelled "Waverly") comes from the playing of fiddler Art Galbraith (1909–1993), originally from Greene County, Missouri, in the Ozarks region, later of Springfield, Missouri.

Missouri fiddler Art Galbraith had a very soft, sweet style of fiddling. "Waverley" comes from him — it's in the key of G, played in standard tuning, and has a nice vocal quality.

Art Galbraith originally had the tune from his Uncle Tobe, but since it wasn't part of his ongoing repertoire, he had to remember it and re-learn it later in life.

A similar tune is "Hell Agin' the Barn Door (2)." Beisswenger & McCann remark that Galbraith family lore has it that the tune is an old Scottish tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Waynesboro
description:
"Waynesboro" is an American version of the Irish reel perhaps best known as "Over the Moor to Maggie." The Irish original includes a third part not usually played in the old-time version. The transformation of an Irish dance tune into a staple of the Appalachian fiddle tradition is a classic example of how immigrant music took root and was reshaped on American soil. Considering that the majority of settlers in lower Appalachia, and all across the South, were of Scots and Irish origin, it's no surprise that such tunes traveled and transformed across the Atlantic.

Doc Roberts (Kentucky) is the central figure in the tune's documented American history:

The tune was popularized by Kentucky fiddler Doc Roberts, who attributed his version — learned from his brother Liebert — to African-American fiddler Owen Walker, a source of many of Roberts' tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ways of the World
description:
It's important to know there are two unrelated tunes both called "Ways of the World" in the old-time tradition. They are not related to each other. Here's a breakdown of both:

This is the version most players know today, and it has a well-documented origin story.

"Fiddling Bill" Stepp (1875–1947) was from Lakeville, Magoffin County, Kentucky. When the index cards for his Library of Congress recording were typed up, the name "Wm." (for William) was rendered "W.M." — and this error was repeated for many years. His actual name was William Hamilton Stepp.

The source for modern versions of the tune is Magoffin County, Kentucky, fiddler William Stepp (1875–1947), who was recorded by Elizabeth and Alan Lomax for the Library of Congress in 1937. He was the last fiddler to be captured on disc machine by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax during their Kentucky song-collecting expedition. He was a close friend of fiddler John Salyer.

title: The Week Before Christmas
description:
The name "The Week Before Christmas" is deeply rooted in Appalachian holiday tradition, not just a tune title. In the mountains, fiddlers and dancers would travel from house to house holding dances night after night. The week before Christmas and the week after were considered "the big time," a festive period of roughly two weeks usually winding up around New Year's.

This tradition was closely tied to a related tune and custom called "Breakin' Up Christmas" — the tune played at the last dance of the Christmas season. This account comes from Lawrence Bolt, a fiddler born in 1894 in Galax, VA.

The tune itself is not of great antiquity. It may have been composed by Preston "Pet" McKinney, a fiddler and Civil War veteran from Lambsburg, VA. Mt. Airy, NC fiddler Tommy Jarrell — a 1982 NEA National Heritage Fellowship recipient — was strongly associated with this song and cited McKinney as one of his early influences.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Weller's Reel
description:
I'll be upfront: "Weller's Reel" is a tune with very sparse documented history, which is common for many old-time fiddle tunes. Here's everything that can be established, along with broader context:

"Weller's Reel" appears in the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), catalogued as an American reel in 2/4 time, key of D major, with a standard two-part (A/B) structure. The archive holds the ABC notation for the tune but lists no composer and provides no annotation or historical notes — meaning no specific origin story, fiddler attribution, or regional provenance has been formally documented in this primary reference database.

The tune is also accessible at abcnotation.com, where it appears with sheet music, a playable MIDI file, and ABC/MusicXML code, sourced from the Traditional Tune Archive collection.

The old-time fiddle repertoire consists largely of tunes in the public domain with no known authorship — yet many of these tunes have rich historical significance. "Weller's Reel" fits squarely in this category.

title: Wes Muir's Tune
description:
"Wes Muir's Tune" is an American reel in C Major, rooted in the Missouri old-time fiddling tradition. Here's everything known about its origin:

The tune comes from the repertoire of Missouri fiddler Nile Wilson (1912–2008), and is named for a contemporary of his fiddle-playing father, William Randolph "Dolph" Wilson, who lived around New Boston, Linn County, Missouri.

Born August 6, 1912, in New Boston, Linn County, Missouri, Nile Wilson spent his youth on the farm. His paternal grandfather Wilson came from western Indiana after the Civil War, with family roots in Virginia and Kentucky. Many of his maternal Davis relatives had been in Missouri for many generations, also with roots in Virginia.

As a child, Nile was surrounded by traditional violin players — his brother Orley, his uncle Lester Wilson, his great uncle Charlie Davis, and numerous neighbors and friends. His grandfather Davis sang songs while Nile played fiddle tunes.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
