title: Western Country/Susanna Gal
description:
"Susannah/Suzanna Gal" is an American reel (cut time) in D Major, known also as "Blue Eyed Girl/Gal," "Fare Thee Well My Pretty Little Miss," "Fly Around My Pretty Little Miss," "Goin' Back to Georgia," and "Western Country," documented in North Carolina, West Virginia, and Virginia.

It is a popular dance tune in the Galax (Grayson County, VA) / Mt. Airy (NC) region — "a Galax standby" — known under several titles in the same area, and well-known in several variants throughout the upland South.

The tune's name shifted dramatically depending on where you were. As dulcimer player and researcher Wayne Jordan explained at the 2012 Union Grove Old Time Fiddler's Convention:
In North Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia, it's primarily known as "Fly Away My Pretty Little Miss." In Kentucky, Tennessee, and Ohio, it's known as "Shady Grove." In Texas and nearby states, it's "Susanna Gal." And when you hit Colorado and move west, it's known as "Western Country." It's known by different names, played in slightly different ways in all these places.

Like a lot of tunes that are really old, it started off in England. The first time it was written down was in 1658, in a publication called Wit and Drollery.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Whistling Rufus
description:
"Whistling Rufus" was written by Kerry Mills (né Frederick Allen Mills), an American ragtime composer and music publishing executive of the Tin Pan Alley era, whose stylistically diverse music ranged from ragtime through cakewalk to marches. Mills trained as a violinist and was head of the Violin Department of the University of Michigan School of Music when he began composing, later moving to New York City in 1895 to start his own music publishing firm, F. A. Mills Music Publisher.

The tune was composed in 1899, at the beginning of the ragtime era, with words later supplied by Murdoch Lind. Mills also composed other enduring American folk standards including "At a Georgia Camp Meeting" and "Red Wing."

The original sheet music came with a colorful backstory printed above the title. It was described at the time of its publication as a "characteristic march," with the addition that it "can be used effectively as a two-step, polka or cakewalk." The first page of the original sheet music also records that: "No cakewalk given in the Black Belt district of Alabama was considered worth while attending unless 'Whistling Rufus' was engaged to furnish the music."

Unlike other musicians, Rufus always performed alone, playing an accompaniment to his whistling on an old guitar, and it was with great pride that he called himself the "one-man band." Scholar Joyce Cauthen (1990) calls it a minstrel composition that passed into fiddling tradition, perhaps referring to Mills's "coon-song" period cakewalk. The full song title was originally "Whistling Rufus, or, The One Man Band."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White Creek
description:
"White Creek" comes from the playing of fiddler Earl Collins (1911–1975), who was based in Oklahoma and southern California, and whose musical family had roots in Missouri.

The tune is attributed to the Collins family, and was passed along through the old-time tradition via fiddler and collector Rafe Stefanini, who is well known for learning and transmitting tunes from older regional players and recordings.

It is classified as a reel, played in the unusual AEae tuning (also called "cross-A" or high-bass tuning), and is documented in the Library of Congress field recordings under AFS 14458 (Dave Ricker collection). It is also available via the Slippery Hill archive.

title: Whiteface
description:
"Whiteface" is a mercurial old-time tune composed in the 1980s by North Carolina fiddler/luthier Joe Thrift, who named it after a favourite calf. More specifically, the tune was written by Joe Thrift about his cow named Whiteface.

Joe Thrift is an American "progressive old-time" fiddler and luthier from Dobson, Surry County, North Carolina. As well as being a wonderful fiddler, Joe Thrift is an acclaimed luthier working in Dobson, North Carolina.

He composed the tune in the 1980s as a member of the band The Red Hots.

The tune was composed in the 1980s and first recorded by Joe's band the Red Hots in 1989, released on their album Ready to Roll.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White's Polka
description: White's Polka is a reel in the key of C from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White River
description:
There are actually two distinct old-time fiddle tunes associated with the name "White River" — an Ozark breakdown simply called "White River", and a related ragtime piece called "White River Stomp". Both are deeply rooted in the Ozarks region, but have different lineages. Here's the full picture:

The White River flows through southern Missouri and northern Arkansas and into the Mississippi River at Scrubgrass Bend, above Rosedale, Mississippi. The tune takes its name from this river and is rooted in the communities along its banks.

The tune probably originated in Missouri and was played by Howe Teague, Gene Goforth, and John Hartford.

The tune was described as "a special tune" played in the Goforth family repertoire for generations, according to the liner notes of Gene Goforth's album. However, John Hartford (2001) called it "one of those ancient Ozark tunes that nobody seems to know its origin."
Howe Teague (1913–2005, Dent County, Missouri): Teague learned it when he was young, and said he thought he had learned it from influential fiddler Roy Wooliver, and also cited another local fiddler, Buck Sullivan, as someone he remembered playing it.
Gene Goforth: His family treated it as a treasured heirloom piece, recorded on Eminence Breakdown (Rounder, 1997).
John Hartford: Recorded it on Hamilton Ironworks (Rounder, 2001), helping bring it to a wider audience.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White River Bottoms
description:
"White River Bottoms" is an old-time breakdown in D Major from Indiana, USA. It is played in standard fiddle tuning and follows an AABB structure.

The tune is most closely associated with Lotus Dickey, a fiddler from Orange County, Indiana. The primary notated version is sourced from Lotus Dickey (1911–1989, Orange County, Indiana), recorded on Marimac CS 9030, Lotus Dickey – Fiddle Tunes from Orange County, Indiana, Vol. 2 (1992).

The tune was known among older fiddlers in central and southern Indiana — including Noble Melton, Frank Wisehart, Ken Smelser, as well as Lotus Dickey and Jimmy Campbell of Dolan Heights — according to researcher Paul Tyler.

Dickey told Paul Tyler that "It's a local song from down in Orange County all the old-timers played at square dances, a good square dance piece."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: White River Breakdown
description:
"White River Breakdown" (also known simply as "White River") is a venerable old-time fiddle tune rooted deep in the Ozark Mountain tradition of Missouri and Arkansas. The tune probably originated in Missouri and was played by notable fiddlers including Howe Teague, Gene Goforth, and John Hartford.

The tune was recorded for the Library of Congress by musicologist and folklorist Vance Randolph, from the playing of Ozark Mountain fiddlers in the early 1940s. The White River flows through southern Missouri and northern Arkansas and into the Mississippi River at Scrubgrass Bend, above Rosedale, Mississippi.

The true authorship of "White River Breakdown" is genuinely unknown. The tune was described as "a special tune" played in the Goforth family repertoire for generations, according to the liner notes of Gene Goforth's album. However, John Hartford (2001) called it "one of those ancient Ozark tunes that nobody seems to know its origin."

Howe Teague learned it when he was young and said he thought he had learned it from influential fiddler Roy Wooliver. He also cited another local fiddler, Buck Sullivan, as someone he remembered playing it (Beisswenger & McCann, 2008). Teague is the primary source for the tune's notated version.

title: White River Stomp
description:
"White River Stomp" is an American country rag in 4/4 time (also used as a set dance tune), played in F Major in standard fiddle tuning.

The tune was first recorded by Jack Cawley's Oklahoma Ridge Runners for Victor Records in 1931. Cawley (1898–1968) was originally from Bonham, Fannin County, Texas, but moved across the border to the Oklahoma town of Bonham around 1914. The original 78 RPM disc was released as Victor 23521.

The title perhaps refers to the White River in Arkansas and Missouri — originating in the Boston Mountains of northwest Arkansas, it arcs northwards through southern Missouri before turning back into Arkansas, flowing southeast to its mouth at the Mississippi River.

The tune's origins are tangled up with at least two closely related pieces:
The tune is related to "Oklahoma Rag" and "Beaumont Rag" — it shares two parts with the latter.
The now-popular "Beaumont Rag" was recorded by the Texas-based Smith's Garage Fiddle Band in 1928, predating the Ridge Runners' recording. Which of the similar tunes was actually composed first is unknown, but it does indicate the melodic and rhythmic material was in circulation among fiddlers in the Texas/Oklahoma area in the late 1920s.
The tune has been recorded and performed under other titles, including "Bob Mitchell" and "Possum Rag." The origin is uncertain, but it was suggested by Mr. Walter Mears of Alvarado that Samuel Peacock, the fiddler in Smith's Garage Fiddle Band, may have been the composer.
Peacock and his two brothers, John and Charlie, were the musicians that comprised that group.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Who Hit Nellie with the Stovepipe
description:
This tune is primarily known as a curiosity of old-time fiddle nomenclature — one of the wonderfully absurd, humorous names that pepper the old-time repertoire. Wayne Erbsen, a well-known figure in old-time music circles, was collecting funny or interesting fiddle tune names and cited "Who Hit Nellie With the Stove Pipe?" as his personal favorite. It circulates in old-time communities mainly as a conversation piece alongside other memorably strange tune titles.

The tune most likely related — or even the same tune under a different regional nickname — is "Crooked Stovepipe," a well-documented old-time/Canadian fiddle standard. This kind of alternate naming is extremely common in the tradition. Tunes with different names sharing the same melody is a widespread phenomenon — for example, "Brushy Fork of John's Creek" is also known as "Poor Man's Trouble," "Chinquapin," and also the name of Crooked Stovepipe.

Authorship of Crooked Stovepipe is usually attributed to Jim Magill, a fiddler from Toronto and leader of Jim Magill and the Northern Ramblers, but it was most likely composed around 1932 by John Burt, piano player for George Wade and his Cornhuskers (a dance orchestra from Toronto). Jim Magill was one of the fiddlers in this orchestra for a time.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Who Shit in Grandpa's Hat
description:
The tune is catalogued in the Traditional Tune Archive as a barn dance from the United States.

The tune is credited to Sandy Hofferth, a fiddler who apparently composed it as an original piece in the old-time style. Some sheet music databases list the author as unknown, suggesting that attribution is not universally agreed upon and the tune may have drifted into the broader "traditional" repertoire over time — a common fate for old-time tunes.

The tune has circulated widely in the American old-time fiddle community. Notable recordings and performances include:
The New Southern Cowtippers recorded a version, documented on AllMusic.
The Dust Settlers (Tanner & Alex) recorded it for their album "Who Will Sing My Song".
Tanner Brethorst and Alex Meine are two musicians from Southeastern Minnesota who play in the old-time and bluegrass style.

Its humorous, irreverent title is a hallmark of a certain strain of old-time fiddle culture — many traditional tunes carry bawdy, outrageous, or comical names (e.g., "Who Stole My Cheese?", "Old Molly Hare") that were part of the social, informal context of barn dances and kitchen junkets.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wild Goose Chase
description:
"Wild Goose Chase" is not a single tune but a family of related old-time fiddle tunes sharing a name, a general character, and roots deep in the Appalachian and mid-South tradition. Here's a full breakdown of what is known:

"Wild Goose Chase" is classified as an American Reel (cut time), also known under the alternate titles "Flight of the Wild Geese (1)" and "Geese Honking." It is documented from the USA, primarily Virginia and Kentucky. The tune name covers at least four distinct melodic variants catalogued by the Traditional Tune Archive.

Collector R.P. Christeson, who collected one version of the tune in his home town in Missouri, noted that the original title for the melody is unknown, but that it was the tune most often played for a popular square dance figure called "The Wild Goose Chase." This is likely how the name stuck — the tune was named after the dance, not the other way around. An ex-street player named Joe Johnson, of Lincoln, Nebraska, told Christeson in the 1950s that the tune was called "Wrecker's Daughter," though it is unlike the tune of that name printed by Howe.

The tune was one of the few recorded by legendary Sparta (near Galax), Grayson County, Virginia fiddler Emmett Lundy (1864–1953), who played a somewhat irregular version that varies with each repeat.
Lundy learned much of his repertoire from an older fiddler named Greenberry Leonard, born around 1810. That puts the tune's transmission back to the early 19th century.
Lundy was recorded by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax for the Library of Congress (AFS 04940 A03) in August 1941.

title: Wild Rose Of The Mountain
description:
"Wild Rose of the Mountain" was popularized via the playing of Kentucky fiddler J.P. Fraley (1924–2011), and is a moderately paced reel, played deliberately almost as a listening tune. It is considered one of the most prominent modern fiddle tunes in the old-time tradition, alongside pieces like "Blackberry Blossom" and "Orange Blossom Special."

The tune is the title track of one of Kentucky fiddler J.P. Fraley's albums of the 1970s, performed along with his wife Annadeene. It is considered J.P. Fraley's signature tune.

Fraley learned the tune from two local sources: a woman named June Rice and a fiddling blacksmith named Bun Oney (who occasionally fiddled for the American Folk Song Festival), when Fraley was in his late 20s in Rush, Kentucky.

The tune was formally documented and released on Rounder Records 0037 as J.P. and Annadeene Fraley — "Wild Rose of the Mountain" (1974), which became the primary vehicle for spreading it to a wider audience.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Willits or Wontits
description: Willits or Wontits is a reel in the key of E from the Appalachian tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Willow Creek
description:
"Willow Creek" is a three-part reel composed by fiddler Ralph Whited (1919–1994), from Oneonta, Blount County, north-central Alabama.

Whited was a bachelor farmer who lived all his life in the house he was born in, below Sand Mountain at the foot of the Appalachian foothills — a farm inherited from his grandfather. He was also an avid fisherman and netted a 48 lb. catfish on Willow Creek, a favorite fishing hole for which he named his reel.

The earliest known field recording of the tune was captured in 1983 by field recordist Bob White and is referenced in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Alabama.

It was later formally released on the Field Recorders Collective FRC 717, "Ralph Whited: Old Time Alabama Fiddling" (2015).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wilson's Clog
description:
"Clog" tunes are a class of dance tunes drawn from a popular nineteenth-century dance form associated originally with Lancashire, England, and with wooden-soled shoes ("clogs") worn by the dancers to accentuate the rhythm of the steps. In some areas of the Appalachians, "clog" has come to signify both the tune and the dance step for which it is intended. The tune circulates as both a hornpipe and a clog depending on region and player.

The tune is most properly known as "Fred Wilson's Clog," and the Fred Wilson in question was a real, well-documented minstrel performer. Edward Le Roy Rice, in his book Monarchs of Minstrelsy (New York, 1911), describes Fred Wilson as having made his first appearance about 1843, spending four or five years with the various minstrel companies that sprang up at that time.

In 1848 he joined 'Bije' Thayer's Minstrels, a prominent Boston company. While Mr. Wilson was not the first to do clog dancing in this country, he was undoubtedly the first to do so in a minstrel company.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wilson's Hornpipe
description:
The earliest and most academically documented version traces to Scotland in the early 1800s.

"Mr. Wilson's Hornpipe" was composed by Edinburgh fiddler-composer Robert "Red Rob" Mackintosh (c. 1745–1808), a Scottish violinist and composer active in Edinburgh at the end of the 18th century, originally from Tullymet, near Pitlochry, Perthshire. He moved to London in the last decade of his life.

The tune was printed in his Fourth Collection of New Strathspey Reels, also some Famous old Reels (c. 1804, p. 24), dedicated to the Duchess of Manchester.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Winder Slide
description:
"Winder Slide" is a modern old-time tune composed around 1980 by Joe LaRose of Kent, Ohio, written in the style of Gus and Theodore Clark, who recorded two sides in North Georgia around 1930 — "Barrow County Stomp" and "Wimbush Rag."

Despite being a relatively recent composition, it still sounds as if it could've been around for a century or so.

One of the most fascinating parts of this tune's origin is how it was initially presented to the world. Joe's original recording was double-tracked guitar and fiddle, with 78rpm surface noise overlaid, and the first version he sent around was jokingly titled as being by "Gus and Theo Clark" — the real North Georgia duo that inspired the style. This was intentional misdirection; according to the Fiddler's Companion, "Winder Slide" was composed as kind of a spoof.

The tune's spread involves a great piece of old-time folklore. Kerry Blech (a key figure in the old-time community) described the chain of transmission:
Bruce Molsky first heard it on a tape sent to him by a friend. Joe's original recording was double-tracked guitar and fiddle, with 78rpm surface noise overlaid.
The tune was left alongside the other two real 78rpm cuts of the Clarks, and was at the end of a taped interview with Bert Layne. Bruce later found out the untitled tune was called "Winder Slide," but in the meantime he had started calling it "The End of the Layne.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wink the Other Eye
description:
"Wink the Other Eye" is classified as an American Reel in cut time, played in G Major with standard fiddle tuning, and found primarily across Kentucky, Tennessee, and Missouri. It is a ragtime-influenced reel meant to be played at a tempo slower than that of a standard breakdown.

Music historian Charles Wolfe described it as a "fine old Sequatchie Valley (Tenn.) fiddle band tune known to area fiddlers as diverse as Tom Douglas and Curly Fox" (The Devil's Box, Vol. 15, No. 4, Dec. 1981).

The tune appears to be well-known in the states just west of the Mississippi River, as well as in Tennessee and Kentucky.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wolf Creek
description:
The sole source for the tune is fiddler Roy Bennett (born c. 1895), who in the 1940 census was living on Wolf Creek Road in Meade County, Kentucky, with his wife and five children. The tune's name almost certainly derives directly from that road and the creek it was named for — a classic example of how old-time tunes were often named after the literal landscape surrounding the fiddler who played them.

Old-time fiddle music frequently identifies with the region through tunes that celebrate geographical places — rivers, creeks, mountains — showing a distinct connection to the land and a sense of place characteristic of Appalachian tradition.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Type | American Reel (cut time) |
| Key | D Major (Bennett's version); G Major (Phillips's transcription) |
| Tuning | Standard fiddle tuning |
| Form | AB (Bennett's version); AABBBB (Phillips's version) |

It is classified as an American Reel in cut time, played in G Major (per Phillips) or D Major (per Bennett), in standard fiddle tuning, with an AB structure (Bennett) or AABBBB (Phillips).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wooden Nickel
description:
"Wooden Nickel" is a modern composition, written around the late 1970s by Mark Gaponoff (also spelled Gapanoff) of Seattle, Washington.

This makes it a relatively recent entry to the old-time canon — composed in the tradition of classic old-time reels rather than being a truly antique tune passed down through oral tradition.

It is classified as an Old-Time Reel in cut time, in the key of D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wrassled With A Wildcat
description:
The tune is associated with fiddler Earl Collins (1911–1975). Collins was born in Missouri, grew up in Oklahoma, and lived most of his adult life in California. He started playing fiddle when he was just 4 years old. His first instrument was constructed from a cigar box, but he progressed rapidly and his father gave him a regular fiddle when he was seven.

The tune is documented in the key of A, played in AEAE cross-tuning, and Collins's recording is preserved at the Library of Congress, Archive of Folk Culture (AFS 14458), from the Dave Ricker collection. It also appears in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and in the collection Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Oklahoma.

The Milliner-Koken book lists all cross tunes in the key of A (AEAE) regardless of the actual cross-tuned pitch the fiddler may have been using.

title: Yellow Barber
description:
"Yellow Barber" (also known as "Arthur Berry") is an American reel in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, originating from Kentucky, West Virginia, southern Ohio, and Pennsylvania. It is a fairly notey reel in the key of D, usually played quickly, and initial research shows it was being played in the early to mid-1800s under at least two different names.

The origin of the name is genuinely contested and unresolved. There are three main theories:

Some historians claim this is a Kentucky tune likely named for a mixed-race fiddler named William Taylor, identified as "mulatto" in an 1850 census, who was born in Kentucky in 1821 but had moved to St. Paul, MN. Taylor was a barber by trade, but also led a popular small orchestra that was in demand for balls and parties in Minnesota. He was known for his big, booming voice and called the dances as he played. He died in 1862.

Researcher John Heine found a reference to this mulatto barber named William B. Taylor, a fiddler born in Kentucky in 1821, who called the figures as he played — Taylor's Band, composed of barbers, played for hundreds of balls, banquets, and steamboat excursions in the Minnesota territory from 1849 until his death in 1862.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Yellow Gals
description:
"Yellow Gals" (also "Yellow Gal") is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in A Mixolydian, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

"Yellow" was a term applied to light-skinned African Americans or those with mulatto coloring, and "Yellow Gal" is a phrase that dates back to at least the mid-19th century, where it appears in blackface minstrel songs.

There is a tune by this name that is cognate with "Buffalo Gals", popularized by Eugene Edwards. In fact, "Yellow Gals" belongs to a large family of regional "Gals" tunes — related tunes include "Alabama Gals," "Louisiana Gals," "Roundtown Girls/Gals," "Cincinnati Girls," "Jimtown Gals," and many others — all sharing a common melodic DNA. The popular "Buffalo Gals" melody has been set in a variety of musical forms and genres.

The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Yellow Jacket
description:
"Yellow Jacket" was composed by midwestern fiddler Garry Harrison. He is widely credited as the tune's author across multiple old-time music communities. Fellow fiddlers at Fiddle Hangout have remembered him with praise: "Nobody could compose fiddle tunes [like] Garry Harrison RIP" — suggesting he has since passed and is remembered fondly in the old-time scene.

The tune was composed by Harrison and spread through direct transmission — for example, The Tallboys string band requested permission from his daughter, Genevieve, to record the tune they had learned from his playing. This is a hallmark of how newer old-time compositions travel: person-to-person, with respect for living composers and their families.

The tune is typically played in cross A tuning (AEAE), though some players have adapted it to cross G.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Yew Piney Mountain
description:
"Yew Piney Mountain" is part of the canonical Appalachian music tradition and has been highly influential in American fiddle tradition generally, including its old-time fiddle and bluegrass fiddle branches. It is an archaic-sounding, slightly irregular ("crooked"), modal melody that fluctuates between Dorian and Mixolydian modes (or sits in a mixed mode, depending on the player), and was in the repertoire of several older central West Virginia fiddlers.

The tune's name history is surprisingly tangled. According to Alan Jabbour at the Digital Library of Appalachia, the tune was originally called "Blackberry Blossom" — until that title was taken over by a different (now more famous) tune. The earlier "Blackberry Blossom," as played by Sanford Kelly from Morgan County, is what is now known as "Yew Piney Mountain."

Andrew Kuntz's Fiddler's Companion, however, asserts that the two tunes are actually related rather than wholly distinct. John Hartford himself calls it "a cousin to" the breakdown "Old Time Blackberry Blossom" or "Garfield's Blackberry Blossom."

The tune was reportedly also played by well-known Kentucky fiddler J.P. Fraley, the more obscure Owen "Snake" Chapman, as well as by Sanford Kelly and others.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Zack Wheat's Piece
description:
"Zack Wheat's Piece" is another instance of a tune known only by the name of a man who played it. Zack Wheat was an earlier fiddler of some renown who lived near Argyle, Missouri. According to Christeson (1973), this fiddler was an earlier musician who lived in that area. The tune belongs to the broader Missouri/Ozarks old-time tradition, a regionally rich fiddle culture.

There is an intriguing and unresolved overlap with a famous athlete of the same name. There was a baseball player named Zack Wheat whose career spanned 1909 to 1927. He was born in the north Missouri town of Hamilton in 1888. Wheat played primarily for the Brooklyn Dodgers and was proficient enough to have been elected to the Hall of Fame in 1959. His batting was prodigious — he won the National League batting title in 1918 (.335) and batted over .300 a total of fourteen times, compiling a lifetime average of .317.

It is unknown whether there is any connection between the ballplayer and the tune; however, there is a small state park dedicated to Zack Wheat (the ballplayer) in the Camden/Morgan County area of Missouri, not far from Osage County, where the town of Argyle — home of Christeson's fiddler — is located; a strange coincidence.

The tune was first formally documented by R.P. Christeson in his landmark 1973 collection. The source for the notated version is George Helton (Maries County, Missouri), as documented by Christeson, and Ike Helton (1907–1983, Maries County, Missouri) as documented by Beisswenger & McCann.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Batchelder's Reel
description:
BATCHELDER'S (REEL). AKA and see "Atlanta Hornpipe," "Quigley’s Reel," "Quig's Reel." American, Canadian; Reel. F Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune has sometimes been credited to the fiddler and instrument maker of the title, Alvah Batchelder (1879-1968) of Frankfort, Maine, but is also associated with Batchelder's friend and pupil Albert Quigley (1891-1961, New Hampshire), whose name also became attached to the reel.  Both were noted dance fiddlers from the beginning through mid-2oth century, and Batchelder was leader of the Batchelder Orchestra that played the Knights of Pythias Hall dances in Frankfort for some forty years. 

The reel predates Batchelder, however, and was printed in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883) and its succesor, Cole's 1000 (1940), as the "Atlanta Hornpipe." The tune has been a staple among North American contra dance circles, particularly associated with New Hampshire, but can be found in the Pacific Northwest as well as New England. "Ross's Reel No. 4" is often played as a change tune. 

Sources for notated versions: - Jane McBride with Strathspey Phillips; accordion player Laurie Andres (Seattle) Songer. 

Printed sources: - Miller & Perron (New England Fiddlers Repertoire), 1983; No. 130. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 19. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 24. Tolman (Nelson Music Collection), 1969; p. 9.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: La Belle Catherine
description:
La Belle Catherine is one of the most popular Québécois fiddle tunes you will hear. It is classified as a French-Canadian Reel in D Major, and it is a fine example of a "crooked" tune — a distinctly Québécois form where the parts are not played an even number of times. In Boudreault's version, for example, the structure is: AAABBAAACCAAABBAACCAAABB.

The tune's roots stretch back centuries and cross multiple cultures:

La Belle Catherine is the name of a longways formation dance that was popular in Québec, one of the grandes danses of the region. The dance itself may date from the 1700s and has been attributed by ethnomusicologist Marius Barbeau to French origins.

A settler's firsthand account from the 1880s illustrates just how embedded it was in Québec social life: "Throughout the evening I danced the cotillon, the cardeuse, the brandy, the quadrille, the belle Catherine."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Brenda Stubbert's Reel
description:
BRENDA STUBBERT'S REEL. Canadian, Reel. Canada; Cape Breton, Prince Edward Island. A Dorian (Cranford/Holland, Fiddler Magazine, Martin & Hughes): A Minor (Songer). Standard tuning (fiddle). AAB (Songer): AABB' (Cranford/Holland, Fiddler Magazine, Martin & Hughes, Shears). One of the most famous compositions by Inverness, Cape Breton, fiddler, teacher and composer Jerry Holland (originally from Brockton, Mass.) in honor of another Cape Breton fiddler and composer, Brenda Stubbert.

Source for notated version: - Carl & Jackie Webster (Cardigan, Central Kings County, Prince Edward Island) Perlman.

Printed sources: -  Cranford (Jerry Holland's Collection), 1995; No. 40, p. 12. Fiddler Magazine, vol. 3, No. 2, Summer 1996; p. 17. Martin & Hughes (Ho-ro-gheallaigh), 1990; p. 18. Perlman (The Fiddle Music of Prince Edward Island), 1996; pg. 91. Shears (Gathering of the Clans Collection), 1986; p. 61 (pipe setting). Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 40.

Recorded sources: - BM-91, Buddy MacMaster - "Glencoe Hall." Boot Records, Jerry Holland - "Master Cape Breton Fiddler" (1982). Green Linnet SIF 1077, Capercaillie - "Crosswinds" (1987). Green Linnet SIF-1109, Altan - "The Red Crow" (1990). Green Linnett SIF1156, Jerry Holland - "Fiddlesticks Collection." SG155, Alasdair Fraser - "The Road North." Smithsonian Folkways SFW40491, Kinnon & Betty Beaton - "The Heart of Cape Breton" (2002, various artists).  Patty Furlong - "Traditional Irish Music on the Button Accordion" (1999).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Campbell's Farewell To Red Gap
description:
The American old-time tune is a direct descendant of a Scottish march. The tune is a setting of the Scottish march "Campbell's Farewell to Redcastle."

Despite mention of the existence of a melody by that name early in the 18th century, Glen (1891) finds the first printed version of the melody not to have been until Robert Bremner's 1757 collection Scots Reels, although it also is said to appear in James Oswald's Caledonian Pocket Companion (c. 1750). Another printing with the Campbell title appears somewhat later in the 1768 Gillespie Manuscript from Perth. Further to the south in Britain, the title was included in Henry Robson's list of popular Northumbrian songs and tunes, which he published c. 1800.

The melody is even older than those sources suggest. The melody is to be found as a country dance called "Hob or Nob" in collections earlier than Bremner — in Walsh's Caledonian Country Dances (4th book, c. 1745), in Johnson's Collection of 200 Favourite Country Dances (1748), and other contemporary dance books.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Charlie MacKerron's Reel (Islay Rant)
description:
Charlie McKerron is widely regarded as one of Scotland's finest fiddle players, having won the Daily Record Golden Fiddle Award. He first joined the Scottish Celtic supergroup Capercaillie in 1985 and has toured extensively throughout the world with the band.

Beyond Capercaillie, McKerron is an award-winning performer in his own right, leading his own fiddle supergroup Session A9. He is also an accomplished composer whose music has been widely recorded.

An accomplished composer, Charlie's music has been widely recorded and he has contributed to the film Rob Roy. Over the years he has performed with a wide variety of artists including Fish, The Pearl Fishers, and Fred Morrison.

The tune is a composition by Charlie MacKerron, the fiddler with the band Capercaillie. The dramatic and lyrical melody of the tune definitely comes from the northern [Scottish] tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Chorus Jig
description:
CHORUS JIG [1]. AKA - "The Chorus Reel." AKA and see "Glen Road to Carrick (The)," "On the Road (2)." English, Irish, Scottish, American; Reel. USA, New England. D Mixolydian (Bowman, Miller & Perron/1977 & 2006): D Major & G Major (Brody, Burchenal, Miller & Perron/1983, Silberberg): G Major {Ditson, Miller & Perron}: D Major ('A' & 'C' parts) & G Major ('B' part/Phillips: 'B' and 'D' parts/Sweet}. Standard tuning (fiddle). One part (Burchenal): AB (Silberberg): ABCC or ABAC (ending on the A or B part)[Brody]: AABC (Ditson, Miller & Perron/1977): ABCD (Sweet): AABCCB (Kaufman): AA'BCC'B (Phillips): AABCCD (Miller & Perron/1983): AABCC'DD (O'Neill). Despite the title, the tune is a reel, with long histories both in Ireland and the United States. Linscott (1948) explains: "The 'Chorus Jig' has always been a favorite with pipers. It is an Irish melody whose author and date are unknown. Jigs were originally tunes sung after a play by the clowns. During the 17th century everyone sang them, and the dances were performed by persons of all ranks. They are generally thought of as Irish, but jigs were common in England and Scotland. The word 'jig' applied to a form of rhyme and is of uncertain derivation." 

Perlman (1996) suggests the contra-dance reel called "Chorus Jig" originated from the jig form of the tune (see "Chorus Jig (3)"). In non-modal versions (as Randy Miller points out) it is the companion tune for a country dance of the same name in New England, and although the tune is Irish, the dance figures seem English according to experts. It was commonly included in dance and tune books by the 1850's, and can be found in an 1822 American collection called The Musical Cabinet (Charlestown, Mass.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Culburnie Cottage
description:
Culburnie Cottage is a reel in the key of D, composed by Alasdair Fraser, as catalogued in ABC notation on Folk Tune Finder.

Fraser (fiddle) and his collaborator Paul Machlis (piano) began working together in 1983, first recording their acclaimed album Skyedance — tracks from which appeared on Celtic compilations with nearly 2 million in combined sales.

Fraser has gained international fame as a performer and musical contributor to hit films such as The Last of the Mohicans and Titanic, and has been featured on over 150 TV and radio programs worldwide, including U.S. national broadcasts of CBS Sunday Morning, the Kennedy Center Honors, A Prairie Home Companion, and NPR's Morning Edition.

The duo has been described as having "kickstarted the Celtic-New Age fusion that exploded in popularity in the '90s" (All Music Guide).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dancing Bear
description:
"The Dancing Bear" was composed in February 1978 by Bob McQuillen (1923–2014), a piano and accordion player from Peterborough, New Hampshire. Despite being a pianist and accordionist rather than a fiddler, McQuillen was a prolific composer deeply embedded in the New England contra dance tradition.

The tune carries two intertwined dedications:
The "Oso" story: McQuillen's own note in his notebook reads: "I have a wonderful friend who is a Bear named Oso and this tune is for him because he likes it." He also dedicated it to Barry Nielson, "with love from Mac."
The clumsy dancer story: The story goes that Bob McQuillen wrote this tune for a rather clumsy dancer. This lore adds a charming layer — the lumbering, bear-like quality of the tune's repetitive melodic motif mirrors the image of someone dancing with more enthusiasm than grace.

| Attribute | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| Type | American Reel |
| Key | E Minor |
| Tuning | Standard fiddle |
| Form | AABB |
| Date composed | February 2, 1978 |
| Source book | Bob's Note Book 3, #21 |

Played on solo fiddle, the tune can feel repetitive, but adding chords — especially a C chord at the beginning of the fourth line — transforms it into something wonderful.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Dick Gossip's
The Earl's Chair
description:
Irish Reel | Also known as: Cathaoir an Iarla (Irish) | Down Between the Two Derryoobers (original working title)

The tune's origins lie with an East Galway flute player by the name of Pakie Moloney (who was an uncle of Galway-born New Jersey flute player Mike Rafferty), as related by historian and concertina player Gearóid Ó hAllmhuráin.

The composition is attributed to Patrick ("Pakie" or "Patto") Moloney, of Woodford, East Galway, likely in the 1940s or 1950s.

Moloney is said to have composed "The Earl's Chair" while sitting on a large rock in the Derrycrag Wood, East Galway.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Eddy's Reel
description: Eddy's Reel is a reel in the key of G from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Frenchie's Reel
description:
FRENCHIE'S REEL. Canadian, Reel. B Flat Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB (Hinds): AA'BB' (Songer). Composed by Canadian fiddlers Ward Allen and Mel Lavigne, recorded by Allen in 1957. It has been a New England contra dance staple for decades. According to Lavigne's widow, the tune was written by her husband, although popularized by Allen.

Source for notated version: - Todd Silverstein [Songer].

Printed sources: -  Hinds/Hébert (Grumbling Old Woman), 1981; p. 15. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 81.

Recorded sources: - Banff SBS 5296 (reissued on Canadian Cavalcade CCLP 2010), "Graham Townsend and His Country Fiddle." Folkways 8826, Per's Four--"Jigs and Reels." Rounder 0216, John McCutcheon - "Step by Step" (1986). Front Hall FHR029, The Fourgone Conclusions - "Contra Dance Music of Western Massachusetts."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Homage a Belle Gaspesie
description:
Hommage à la Belle Gaspésie is a French-Canadian Reel in the key of A Major, composed in the early 1980s by Québécois accordion player Marcel Messervier, born in Montmagny, Québec, in 1934. On fiddle it is played in standard tuning. The tune follows an AA'BB' structure.

Marcel Messervier is a world-class button accordionist and tunesmith. Other tunes he composed that are often played in the folk/trad community include:
La Belle Époque
La Grande Traversée
Hommage à Edmond Parizeau
Hommage à nos Musiciens
Hommage à Roc Prou
Reel Arthur
Reel des Accordéonistes
Reel Joseph
Reel Ti-Mé
Valse Bernadette

The title itself — Hommage — is a recurring theme in Messervier's compositional style, as he regularly wrote tribute pieces honoring musicians and places dear to him. His tribute to la Belle Gaspésie (the beautiful Gaspé region of Québec) reflects a deep cultural affection for that iconic coastal area.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Homage a Edmund Parizeau
description:
"Hommage à Edmond Parizeau" is a French-Canadian reel in A Major, played in standard fiddle tuning. It is one of the most beloved tunes to cross over from the Québécois tradition into broader old-time and Celtic session circles.

Edmond Parizeau (sometimes spelled Pariso or Pariseau) was a fiddler from Sainte-Foy, Québec. The tune bearing his name was in the repertoire of fiddler Jules Verret, and a notated version was sourced from Montréal fiddler Richard Forrest (Gemme).

Parizeau recorded "Danse du Procureur" / "Reel du Commonwealth" on a 78 RPM recording, Bluebird 55-5488 — a label for which he made a number of recordings. That original recording dates to 1953.

The tune is sometimes attributed to accordion player Marcel Messervier, who arranged and popularized it after an air recorded in 1953 by Edmond Parizeau — who called it "Reel du Commonwealth."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Joys of Quebec
description:
The tune is also known as "Les Joyeuses Québécoises", "Les Joyeuse Québécoise," and "Les Joyeuses Quebequoises." It is classified as a French-Canadian Reel or Polka (playable in 2/4 or 4/4 time), in A Major, in standard fiddle tuning.

The reel was popularized by — and is perhaps the composition of — influential Saint-Sauveur, Québec, fiddler and traveling salesman Fortunat Malouin (1870–1935), who recorded in the 1920s for the Starr and Columbia labels.

His recording of "Les Joyeuses Québécoises" appeared on Columbia 34144-F (78 RPM) in 1928.

The tune's true origin is genuinely disputed. A rival fiddler named A.J. Boucher published a competing version under the title "Variations sur un air canadien" — in five elaborate parts, the last two requiring position playing on the violin. Researcher Jean Duval believes that Boucher and Malouin were rivals or competitors, and that Boucher may have been trying to point out that "Les Joyeuses Québécoises" was not Malouin's composition, but rather a part of the older Québécois repertory that Malouin appropriated. Boucher may also have been trying to "show Malouin up" by printing a version with "fairly acrobatic variations" as the first piece in his collection, perhaps to demonstrate his musical superiority.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Reel Laurentides
description:
"Reel Laurentides" (also encountered as Quadrille des Laurentides, Reel des Laurentides, or just Laurentides Reel) is a French-Canadian fiddle reel named after the Laurentian region of Québec — the rolling hills and river valleys north of Montréal. It belongs to the rich musique traditionnelle québécoise repertoire, the same tradition that produced Saint Anne's Reel, Reel de Montréal, and dozens of other reels de [place name] tunes.

The most historically documented version of the tune is the "Quadrille des Laurentides, 4ème partie" (4th part of the Laurentides Quadrille):

The tune is transcribed from the playing of fiddler Isidore Soucy (1899–1963, Montréal, Québec), and was recorded on Starr 15736b (78 RPM) in 1930.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: MacLeod's Farewell
description:
MACLEOD'S FAREWELL. AKA - "Wedding Reel (The)." Scottish, Reel. E Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. Composed in the late 1980's by Donald Shaw, a Scottish musician, composer, producer, and one of the founding members of the group Capercaillie. The tune was written for another founding member of the group, fiddler Martin MacLeod, who had left the group for other pursuits. Shaw is known for his accordion and keyboard playing with the group. "The Wedding Reel" title for the tune comes from the group Lunasa, who miss-named it on their album "Merry Sisters of Fate." 

Source for notated version: 

Printed sources: Songer (Portland Collection, vol. 2), 2005; p. 121. 

Recorded sources: Green Linnet SIF-1094, Capercaillie - "Sidewaulk" (1991). Lunasa - "The Merry Sisters of Fate."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: McQuillen's Squeezebox
description:
McQUILLEN'S SQUEEZEBOX. New England, March (4/4 time). C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. Composed by New Hampshire dance caller and musician Ralph Page [1] (1903-1985), in honor of New Hampshire caller, keyboard player and composer Bob McQuillan. 

Source for notated version: 

Printed sources: Miller (Fiddler's Throne), 2004; No. 347, p. 203. Page (Ralph Page Book of Contras), 1969; p. 5. Page (Northern Junket), vol. 10, No. 6, 1971. Page (Northern Junket), vol. 13, No. 3, October 1978; p. 27.

Recorded sources: EFDSS RP 500, Southerners Plus Two - "Southerners Plus Two Play Ralph Page" (1969). Great Meadow Music, Randy Miller & Bob McQuillen - "Pure Quill" (2000).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Reel de Montreal
description:
"Reel de Montréal" is a French-Canadian/New England reel in cut time, with an 'A' part in G Major and a 'B' part in D Major. This unusual two-key structure — shifting from G to D within a single tune — has led some players to jokingly call it "the GD reel." The form is AABB or AA'BB' depending on the variant.

Tunes by the name "Reel de Montréal" were recorded by harmonica great Henri Lacroix (1895–c. 1962) in 1928, and by Montreal fiddler Joseph Allard in 1930; however, Allard's reel by this title is a different tune — catalogued separately as "Reel de Montréal (2)."

For "Reel de Montréal (1)" — the widely-played tune most people know today:
Montreal fiddler Joseph Allard (1873–1947) recorded the tune in 1930 as "Set de Vaudreuil 3ème partie," as part of a suite of country dances, with figures voiced by a caller on the recording.
Montreal fiddler J.O. LaMadeleine (1880–1973) recorded the tune for Starr Records in 1937 as "Reel de Vaudreuil."
In 1945, accordion player Gaston Dufresne recorded it under the title "Reel de Sherbrooke (2)."

This reel has travelled under a remarkable number of aliases across the Québec region and New England:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mouth of the Tobique
description:
The tune was composed by a New Brunswick "native Canadian" (First Nation) fiddler named Francis Sowish, probably sometime between 1910 and 1930. Alternate titles that predate the current name include "Grumbling Old Woman / Growling Old Man," as well as "French Mary" — the latter being the title used by Sowish himself.

The tune's provenance was first documented in the late 20th century. During a National Endowment for the Arts research project in 1977 into fiddling styles, New Brunswick fiddler Clarence Langen shared that "Mouth of the Tobique" (named after the Tobique River in New Brunswick) was better known locally as "Grumbling Old Woman / Growling Old Man." Clarence's aunt was the music teacher of the composer, Francis Sowish.

The piece "was common in the Perth-Andover (N.B.) area and had been composed by a local named Francis Sowish."

The famed Canadian radio fiddler Don Messer, in his tunebook, mistakenly switched the names of two Sowish compositions and published Sowish's tune "French Mary" under the name "Mouth of the Tobique." It is unclear whether Francis Sowish formally published his tunes or simply composed them and let them pass into oral tradition — and Don Messer got hold of them somehow.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Gray Cat
description:
"Old Grey Cat" is a popular tune at North American contra dances, borrowed from Scottish repertoire, although claims have also been made for an Irish provenance. Its origins are genuinely murky, making it one of the more delightfully contested tunes in the Anglo-Celtic tradition.

The tune sits at the crossroads of Scottish and Irish tradition. Scholar Charles Gore identifies "the old grey cat" as Sean Liath — an Irish cat — suggesting Irish roots. However, he finds Scottish printings only as far back as the 1880s, where it is listed as an Irish tune, and does not find it in the listings of Great Highland Bagpipe repertoire.

The tune is also known as "The Smuggler's Reel," adding further mystery. There seems to be no bagpipe music for it before 1800, yet it was printed as Scottish music but called an Irish tune.

The earliest known printed source is *Kerr's Merry Melodies, vol. 1 (c. 1880s, No. 8, p. 28) — a Scottish collection, where the tune appears in E Minor / E Dorian.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pays du Haut
description: Pays du Haut is a reel in the key of D from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pointe Au Pic Reel
description:
Pointe-au-Pic is a small town on the St. Lawrence River near Charlevoix, northeast of Quebec City. It sits in one of the most storied regions for traditional Québécois fiddling, where French-Canadian folk music thrived for centuries in relative geographic isolation, preserving older modal styles and dance forms.

The Reel du Point-au-Pic is a Québécois fiddle tune written by Joseph Bouchard. Joe Bouchard was a great fiddler from the Charlevoix region, which is the region east of Quebec City.

Jos Bouchard started on the violin at the age of 8, probably with some classical training, as well as coaching from Huron fiddler Élie Sioué; by 14 he was playing dance. Fiddling was a sideline for Jos, who worked for the CNR railroad for 32 years, but he participated in local festivals.

Pointe-au-Pic was Bouchard's hometown — the tune is essentially a musical tribute to the village where he was born and raised. Bouchard had the habit of renaming tunes from his repertoire, so it is possible that the Reel de Pointe-au-Pic exists under another name somewhere.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Prince Charlie
description:
The name "Prince Charlie" in fiddle music is not a single tune but a cluster of related tunes across Scottish, Canadian (Cape Breton, PEI, New Brunswick), American old-time, and English traditions — all orbiting the towering historical figure of Prince Charles Edward Stuart (1720–1788), better known as "Bonnie Prince Charlie."

Prince Charles Edward Stuart was indeed "over the water," in France with a price on his head should he return to Britain, growing old, fat, and alcoholic, while his air was advancing in popularity through the 18th century. His 1745 Jacobite uprising — and its defeat at the Battle of Culloden — became one of the most romanticized events in British/Scottish history, and fiddlers commemorated it prolifically.

In 1745, as Bonnie Prince Charlie was raising his standard to begin his ill-fated campaign, Niel Gow, then only 18, won a competition in Perth and was crowned "Champion of Scotland." Gow is regarded as the father of Scottish fiddle music and was a legend in his own lifetime, having played for Bonnie Prince Charlie in 1745 and being visited by Robert Burns during his highland tour.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Quickstep in the Battle of Prague
description:
Here is the full history and origin story of "Quickstep in the Battle of Prague" — a tune with a remarkably rich lineage connecting a battlefield, a Bohemian composer, a Northamptonshire poet-fiddler, and a sprawling network of 19th-century folk musicians.

The Battle of Prague took place on 6th May 1757, between the forces of Austria and Frederick the Great's Prussia. It was one of the bloodiest engagements of the Seven Years' War and became a touchstone of European cultural memory for decades afterward.

The piece is a programmatic sonata composed by František Kocžwara (Franz Kotzwara), a Bohemian instrumentalist and composer (c. 1750–1791). Born in Prague, Kocžwara spent much of his musical career in England.

He had been born in Prague, in the land of Bohemia, in 1730, and may well have witnessed the event in 1757 — Prussia vs. Austria, in one of the bloodiest battles of the time. He roamed around Europe as a double bass player for hire, and by 1775 had ended up in London where he composed prolifically.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Reconciliation
description:
Known formally as "The Reconciliation" (Irish: "An Reiteacad" or "An Reidteact"), the tune also goes by "Humphrey's Hornpipe (2)," "Humphrey's Reel," and "Olive Branch Hornpipe." It is classified as Irish, Canadian, and American, and can be played as either a hornpipe or a reel.

It is in A Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure.

Francis O'Neill — the legendary Irish-American collector of traditional music — most likely sourced this tune from Boston publisher *Elia Howe's Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883), where it appeared as a hornpipe under the title "The Olive Branch." As researcher Paul de Grae points out, "The Olive Branch" is the direct source for O'Neill's renaming of the tune to "The Reconciliation" — both titles carrying the same peacemaking symbolism.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Reel des Jeunes Maries
description:
(English: "The Newlyweds' Reel" or "The Young Marrieds' Reel")

The tune is catalogued as "Réel des Jeunes Mariés, Le" (also known as "Newly Weds Reel"), a French-Canadian / New England Reel in D Major, standard tuning, with an AABB form (Miller & Perron) or AABBA'A'BB form (Page).

"Le Réel des jeunes mariés" was recorded in 1931 (released January 1932) by harmonica player Louis Blanchette (1905–1969), who produced several marriage-themed reels among his many recordings in the 78 RPM era, among them "Reel des noces de diamant" (Diamond Wedding Reel, 1936), "Reel des fiançailles" (Betrothal Reel, 1932), and "Reel des noces d'or" (Golden Wedding Reel, 1935).

The second part of Blanchette's original recording is "crooked" (metrically irregular), and was "made square" for New England contra dancing in the 1960s, perhaps by musician and dance caller Ralph Page — and this is the version almost universally played today.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Road to Skye
description: Road to Skye is a reel in the key of A from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ross's Reel (#4)
description:
Here's everything reliably documented about this tune, sourced from the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), which is the authoritative reference for North American fiddle tune provenance.

Ross's Reel No. 4 is a New England reel from the USA, played in F Major with standard fiddle tuning in AABB form.

It became a favorite staple of the latter 20th century New Hampshire contra dance repertory.

It also goes by an alternate title: the alternate title "Lady's Walpole Reel" probably comes from association of the tune with the dance Lady Walpole's Reel.

title: St. Ann's Reel
description:
"St. Anne's Reel" has quite a lot of confusion surrounding its origins. It is played in sessions in Scotland, Ireland, New England, Canada, and other spots around the world, and has been claimed as a Shetland tune, an Irish reel, a contra-dance tune, and a French-Canadian and American old-time tune.

The tune is of French-Canadian origin and is now in the traditional repertoire of Canada, the USA, and Ireland. It is played in D Major with standard fiddle tuning.

The reel was first recorded by Montreal fiddler Willie Ringuette as "Quadrille du loup garou - 4ème partie" (1927), followed by a 78 RPM issue by another Montreal fiddler, Joseph Allard (1873–1947), in 1930.

Somewhat confusingly, Victor Records released Allard's recording with two separate titles, "Reel de Ste-Anne" and "Reel des esquimaults." Still another Montreal fiddler, Isidore Soucy (1899–1962), soon after recorded a version as "Reel lune de miel" (Honeymoon Reel).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Thomas Tourish's Tune
description: Thomas Tourish's Tune is a reel in the key of D from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Trip To Pakistan
description:
"The Trip to Pakistan" was composed by Niall Kenny, a flute player from Lanarkshire, Scotland. Kenny is a flute player from Edinburgh, and the tune has since become a traditional, with at least 26 known master recordings.

> Note: Sources vary slightly between "Lanarkshire" and "Edinburgh" — he is associated with both (Lanarkshire-born, Edinburgh-based).

The oldest known source for this tune dates to 1998. It is therefore a relatively modern composition — late 20th century — despite feeling and being treated like an ancient traditional tune.

It is classified as a Scottish Reel in E minor (also commonly played in B minor). It is described as "one of those really hypnotic tunes that works well fast or slow."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Crabs In The Skillet
description:
"Crabs in the Skillet" (Irish: Portáin Annsa Sgileid) is an Irish Double Jig (or Air) in 6/8 time. Despite its colorful American-sounding name, it is firmly rooted in the Irish traditional music canon.

The tune belongs to the coast of County Clare and County Limerick in Ireland — as noted by George Petrie in 1855: "This tune belongs to the coast of Clare and Limerick."

The source for the notated version traces to "J. Buckley (via) Mr. Joyce" [Stanford/Petrie]. P.W. Joyce states he noted the tune in 1854, and that James Buckley was "a Limerick piper, who stated his belief that the tune belonged to the county Clare."

So the tune was transmitted orally through a Limerick uilleann piper, collected mid-19th century — the original composer is unknown, as is common for tunes of this era.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Holm Band Tune
description:
"The Holm Band Tune" is a traditional jig originating from Orkney, the archipelago off the northern tip of Scotland. It is not an Appalachian old-time tune in the American sense — rather, it belongs to the North Atlantic / Orcadian fiddle tradition, a distinct regional folk music heritage.

As an Orcadian commenter on The Session folk music forum noted, the pronunciation of "Holm" is "ham" (as in the Orkney parish of Holm). The composer of the tune is unknown — it is presumed to have been written by one of The Holm Band, a local Orcadian band which no longer exists.

So the tune's name is essentially a dedication or association to that local ensemble, and with the band gone, detailed biographical records of its members have not been widely preserved in accessible online sources.

The tune is in the key of A major and takes the jig form (6/8 time).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: I Buried My Wife and Danced on Her Grave
description:
Back to I Buried My Wife and Danced on Her Grave

I BURIED MY WIFE (AND DANCED ON HER GRAVE). AKA – “I Buried My Wife and Danced on Top of Her.” AKA and see "Brístín Mire (An),” "Cunla," "Friar's Breeches," "Friar's Britches," “Frieze Breeches (1), Frieze Britches (1),” “Gallagher's Frolic (3),” “O'Gallagher's Frolics,” “On St. Patrick's Day I was Gay,” “Trumlo (The).” Irish, Air (6/8 time). D Mixolydian. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The air is the vehicle for the song of the title. Gearóid Ó hAllmhuráin says the tune is associated with Inagh, West Clare, piper Garret Barry (1847-1899). O'Neill (Irish Folk Music, 1910) thinks it “closely resembles” his “Frieze Breeches (1)” and “O'Gallagher's Frolics.”

Source for notated version: - New Jersey flute player Mike Rafferty, born in Ballinakill, Co. Galway, in 1926 [Harker].

Printed sources: -  Corfield (Tunes from New Brunswick), 2024; p. 163. Harker (300 Tunes from Mike Rafferty), 2005; No. 213, p. 66. Prior (Fionn Seisiún 3), 2007; p. 22.  Susan Songer with Clyde Curley (Portland Collection vol. 3), 2015; p. 101.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Joanie's Jig
description:
JOANIE'S JIG. American, Jig. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Composed by Nancy Martin of Vancouver, Washington. Danny Hathaway communicates that the jig was composed for his wife, Joan Hathaway, who played piano and whistle in various bands with the Martins.  

Source for notated version: 

Printed sources: Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 110.

Back to Joanie's Jig

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Kerfunken Jig
description:
Despite often being labeled an "old-time fiddle tune" in American folk circles, the Kerfunken Jig is actually a composed Irish traditional jig with a well-documented and charming origin story.

The tune was composed by flute player and flute maker Hammy Hamilton, born in Belfast in 1953, although he makes his home (and his flutes) in County Cork, Ireland. He is not a fiddler by trade — the tune was composed by Hammy Hamilton and performed by him on flute.

On his album The Moneymusk, Hammy tells us that he was teaching a flute workshop in a suburb of Quimper in Brittany and named the tune after the place, but says that "the spelling got mixed up somewhere along the way."

The correct spelling of the place is Kerfeunteun. Until 1960 it was run by a separate authority even though only a short distance from the centre of Quimper. Quimper Kerfeunteun is also the name of the local football club.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Burnt Potato
description:
LITTLE BURNT POTATO. AKA - "Burnt Potato," "Frank's Two-Step." American, Canadian, English, Irish; Single Jig. USA; New England, New York, Missouri. Canada; Maritimes, Ontario. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Begin): AABB (Brody): AA'BB' (Barnes, Bayard, Carlin, Messer, Miller & Perron, Perlman, Phillips). "Little Burnt Potato" was popularized by Canadian Maritime radio and TV fiddler Don Messer. The tune has been characterized as Irish in origin, although in fact it is the composition of Canadian fiddler Colin J. Boyd, who was himself of Scottish descent. Boyd was born in West Lakeville, Nova Scotia, in 1891, and learned to play the fiddle as a child, inspired by his uncle Hughie MacGillivary (whose fiddle he inherited). Like many in the community, he learned and spoke Gaelic. Due to a declining ecomony, Boyd found work in 1909 in Ontario, then moved to Boston for the years 1911-1916 where he studied violin and learned to read music. It was during his Boston years that he composed "Little Burnt Potato." Boyd had the distinction of being the first Nova Scotian fiddler to record in 1932, in Montreal for the Brunswick label. He later settled in Ontario, and passed away in 1975. 

"Little Burnt Potato" is Boyd's adaptation of an old Scottish jig passed on to him by Dan “The Ridge” MacDonald, formerly of Mabou, Cape Breton, and then Antigonish, Nova Scotia, according to Mary Boyd (liner notes to Shanachie Records, CB-1). His jig proved popular and has been widely disseminated, and has been interpreted in a number of styles. It has been a staple of New England contra dances.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Da Lounge Bar
description:
Da Lounge Bar is named after the famous bar in Lerwick, Shetland, and was written by Norwegian fiddler Annlaug Børsheim. It is sometimes called "Da Lerwick Lounge Bar" in session circles, but its official title is simply Da Lounge Bar.

Da Lounge Bar is the pub for tunes in Lerwick, Shetland — a legendary session venue. One regular recalled working in Lerwick in the late 1970s and spending many happy times there — including one memorable occasion when snow grounded all flights off the island and everyone retreated to Da Lounge.

The bar was frequented by the late, great "Peerie" Willie Johnson (10 December 1920 – 22 May 2007), who was respected as an influential and innovative musician in the Shetland folk scene. Since 2005, a "Peerie Willie Guitar Festival" has been held annually on the islands. Aly Bain was also a regular player there whenever he wasn't touring.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: One Horned Sheep
description:
The title is almost certainly not about a literal one-horned sheep. An old Scottish fiddler's explanation holds that "one-horn sheep" is a slang term for a still used for making illicit whiskey — the coil of wire on the still being the "horn." This fits the fact that the tune is well known throughout the Scottish Borders and Northumberland, where illicit distillation of whisky was carried out at least down as far as Durham up until around 1900. There are a number of Scottish tunes that celebrate illicit stills, such as "The Ewie With The Crooked Horn."

The tune has roots that are genuinely disputed:
Some believe it is Scottish, from Aberdeenshire or around the Buchan area, and it is very well known throughout the Scottish Borders and down into Northumberland.
However, some scholars are doubtful of claims that it's a Scottish jig, though it has been known in Scotland for some time.
The strongest case points to an Irish origin. The melody appears to be an amalgam of two old Irish tunes — "The Humours of Donnybrook" and "Sweet Biddy Daly" (the A and B parts, respectively).

The tune was first printed in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883) under the title "The Boss." It later appeared in O'Neill's collections in the early 20th century.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paddy Fahy's Jig
description:
Paddy Fahey (also spelled "Fahy," 17 August 1916 – 31 May 2019) was an Irish composer and fiddler considered one of the finest living composers of tunes in the style of traditional Irish music.

Born in the year of the Rising, 1916, and a native of Kilconnell in east Galway, Paddy Fahey grew up on a farm in Killaghbeg House. From a musical family, he began playing the fiddle at the age of five. His father, Jack Fahy, was a notable fiddle player and founder of the Aughrim Slopes Céilí Band. Paddy became a member of the band in the 1940s and toured throughout the UK and America — but the bright lights of the city weren't for him, and he chose to remain in his beloved East Galway, living and working as a farmer.

Paddy Fahy's Jig [1] (Irish title: Port Phádraig Uí Fhathaigh), also known simply as "Paddy Fahey's," is an Irish Double Jig in G Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an ABB (or AA'BB') structure.

It is a modern composition of Kilconnell, east County Galway, fiddler Paddy Fahey that has gained wide currency. Written by Paddy Fahey, it is one of his most popular tunes and is considered an Irish standard today — a must-know tune for any Irish fiddle session player.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: R. Aim's Compliments to J. Craigie
description:
Here is everything that can be reliably traced about "R. Aim's Compliments to J. Craigie" (also written as "Ronnie Aim's Compliments to Jimmy Craigie"):
The full title in ABC notation sources is "Ronnie Aim's Compliments To Jimmy Craigie" — a jig in D major (6/8 time).
The naming convention — "Person A's Compliments to Person B" — is a classic Scottish/Orcadian tradition of dedicating a tune to a friend, colleague, or admired musician as a musical gift or tribute.
The tune appears on the recording "Mither o' the Sea" by Jennifer & Hazel Wrigley, two prominent fiddle players from Orkney, Scotland — strongly suggesting the tune is Orcadian in origin.
It is frequently paired as a set with the "Holm Band Tune", and the pairing has been played by members of the Vermont Fiddle Orchestra.
The Holm Band Tune is specifically Orcadian — a comment on The Session notes that "the pronunciation of Holm is 'ham'" (the village in Orkney).
The title indicates that someone named Ronnie Aim composed or dedicated the tune to Jimmy Craigie, both almost certainly Orcadian musicians. This is a well-established tradition in Scottish fiddle music — composers would title a tune as a compliment to a peer.
However, it is not known who composed the "Holm Band Tune" — presumably one of The Holm Band, which no longer exists. A similar obscurity surrounds "R. Aim's Compliments" — no written biographical records for Ronnie Aim or Jimmy Craigie appear to survive in publicly accessible sources.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Strayaway Child
description:
"The Strayaway Child" is a 6-part traditional Irish jig composed by Michael Gorman, rooted in the Sligo area of Ireland. It is a dance tune in compound time (6/8 or 9/8), with a characteristic lilting rhythm.

The tune has one of the most romantically unusual origin stories in Irish traditional music. It was composed by Margaret Barry around 1956, with the help of Sligo fiddler Michael Gorman (who lived in London most of his life). Parts of the tune came to Barry in a dream, which was then developed by Gorman.

From the sleeve notes of Portrait: Margaret Barry — Margaret's jig "The Strayaway Child" is now well known among Irish musicians. She describes how it came to her in a dream. In its final form, it was too complex to tackle on the banjo, and it was left to her collaborator Michael Gorman to popularize it.

In her own words, Barry said: "Now and again, I do dream, of music all the time. And there's music coming into my head, when I'm dreaming, that I've never heard in reality. It's just one of those things that even — I composed a jig of me own. It was true, a bit of dreaming that I got the parts of that dream. I only remembered a couple of parts of that."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Swelkie
description: Swelkie is a jig in the key of G from the Celtic tradition. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tripping Up the Stairs
description:
"Tripping Up the Stairs" is a traditional Irish jig (in 6/8 time), one of the most widely known and recorded tunes in the Irish and old-time fiddle traditions. It has nineteen settings and twenty-six comments on The Session alone, and has been added to over 2,500 tunebooks.

The tune is not anonymous. According to David Taylor (1992), it is the composition of the great Co. Mayo and New York fiddler John McGrath (1900–1955), who originally entitled it "The Jew Jig" (though Paul de Grae thinks that title may have been used for "Banish Misfortune"). Taylor wrote about McGrath after being inspired by several conversations with McGrath's nephew, Vincent McGrath of Drogheda, who presumably passed along the original title.

This jig is a textbook example of how Irish and old-time tunes accrue alternate titles across regions and generations. It is also known as Paddy O'Flaherty, Plains of Kilkorkery, The Pride of Kildare, Roscabury, Sacho's, Sackow's, The Syracuse, Trippin' Up the Stairs, and Tripping Upstairs.

Even more names appear in research databases: It has been documented under titles including Sacko's Jig, Sackow's, The Jew Jig, Syriacus, The Pride of Kildare, and appears in tune sets like Sliabh Luachra Set and Out on the Ocean.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The White Petticoat
description:
"The White Petticoat" (Irish: An cota-beag ban) is an Irish double jig in 6/8 time. It is a well-known two-part traditional Irish jig played out of the key of E minor. The tune follows an AABB structure in standard fiddle tuning.

This is where things get interesting. Unlike many Irish tunes with clearly traceable roots, The White Petticoat's origins are genuinely murky:
The provenance of the tune is not known — many have remarked on its unusual nature in the context of the bulk of O'Neill's collection, and the melody is only sourced to Francis O'Neill himself (a very loose source attribution, as O'Neill often put his name to tunes he learned from in the course of years of playing with Irish musicians from Chicago and other areas).
It is one of the few tunes in O'Neill's in aeolian minor — nearly all minor-sounding tunes in that collection are in dorian. This alone makes it stand out as something of an outlier in the Irish traditional canon.
It's a very eerie, pretty tune with a bit of a Spanish/Mediterranean feel in the second half due to the D# implying the harmonic minor.
It kind of feels like a Morris Dance tune to some, but no such link has been found.

The earliest printed source is Francis O'Neill's landmark 1903 collection:
It appears in O'Neill's Music of Ireland (1903), also known as O'Neill's 1850.
It was also reprinted in O'Neill (Krassen), 1976, p. 74, and Knowles' Northern Frisk (1988), No. 38.

Captain Francis O'Neill (1848–1936) was Chicago's chief of police and an obsessive collector of Irish traditional music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: DeDannan Polka Set (Julia Clifford's/O'Keefe's Polka/Johnny I Do Miss You)
description:
This polka medley is rooted deep in the Sliabh Luachra tradition — the small, rugged border region between Counties Kerry and Cork in southwest Ireland, widely regarded as the heartland of Irish polkas and slides. The set brings together three tunes intimately connected to the most celebrated fiddlers and music masters of that region.

The set was recorded by De Dannan in 1980. It appears as track 6 on their album The Mist Covered Mountain, running 3:18.

The tune known as "Julia Clifford's" (polka) is also known as Johnny Leary's, Johnny O'Leary's, and Tarrant's.

This polka is named directly after one of the great Irish fiddlers. Recordings from the 1970s, such as those captured at the Listowel Arms Hotel, showcase spirited renditions of polkas like "Julia Clifford's" (also known as "Johnny O'Leary's"), illustrating the lively ensemble traditions of Kerry music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ducks of Magheralin
description:
DUCKS OF MAGHERALIN.  Irish, Polka (2/4 time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Magheralin (pronounced 'Maralin') is a village and parish in the barony of Lower Iveagh, townland of Moira, County Armagh. It has been the site of a church and monastic settlement since the 8th century. The 'Ducks of Magheralin' was the name for the weavers of the town because they used duck grease to lubricate their looms. The poet James Malcolmson wrote a poem called "The Ducks of Maralin":

It is just about a year ago that I went to see the King,

And on my voyage in Ulster my troubles they were twin;

He decorated me with medals, and they were made of tin,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Em Polka
description: Em Polka is a polka in the key of Em. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: I'll Buy Boots for Maggie
description:
I'LL BUY BOOTS FOR MAGGIE. Irish, Polka (2/4 or cut time). A Minor. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB.

Source for notated version: - the Kansas City group Scartaglen [Black].

Printed sources: -  Black (Music's the Very Best Thing), 1996; No. 294, p. 158.

Recorded sources: - Scartaglen - "Scartaglen." Patty Furlong -"Traditional Irish Music on Button Accordion" (1999. Learned from the playing of Paddy "Offaly" O'Brien).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Johnny I Do Miss You
description:
"Johnny I Do Miss You" is an Irish polka in 2/4 time, originating from West Kerry, Ireland — the heartland of the Kerry polka tradition. It comes from County Kerry and is usually played either in D major or G major.

This tune is a fascinating case of folk music's fluid naming conventions. It is also known as "Aidan Coffey's," "All Along the River Bank," "Fr. Jones," "Gleann An Tuairín Ghairbh," "Johnnie I Do Miss You," "Johnny I Do Love You," "Tureengarbh Glen," "Tureengarriffe Glen," and "What Thadgh Said to Biddy," among others.

One of the most colorful origin stories comes from community discussion on The Session. When Denis Doody (a Kerry fiddler) made his record, he had a stock of tunes he had no names for — called "Gan Ainms" (Irish for "untitled"). The recording company insisted they all had to have names, so he made them up on the spot — which created problems later when taking requests at concerts.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Julia Clifford's Polka
description:
Back to Julia Clifford's Polka (1)

JULIA CLIFFORD'S (POLKA) [1] (Síle Uí Chlúmháin). Irish, Polka (2/4 time). D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle) (fiddle). AABB'.

Source for notated version: - melodeon player Denis O'Keeffe (Rathmore, County Kerry) [Breathnach].

Printed sources: -  Breathnach (Ceol Rince na hÉireann vol. V), 1999; No. 101, p. 51.
