Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Maids Of Ardagh Polka
description:
"The Maids of Ardagh" is a lively Irish polka in the key of D. It is classified as an Irish Polka in 2/4 time, played in D Major (A part) and A Major (B part), in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB structure. It has 16 known settings and has been added to over 472 personal tunebooks on The Session alone.

There are at least nine places in Ireland named "Ardagh," leaving room to ponder just which maids the tune's title is appreciating. In the Irish language, "Ardagh" means "high field." The title is evocative but non-specific — a common feature of Irish traditional tune naming, which often celebrates local people or places without pinpointing an exact source.

No single composer is credited, and the tune's origins are characteristically murky — as is typical with Irish traditional music. However, musicians and researchers have noted a significant cross-cultural link:

The tune is considered, like a lot of Kerry polkas, "a corruption of the Scottish pipe tunes Kilberry Ball / Liberton Pipe Band" — played at twice the speed, of course.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nell Fees' Polka
description:
Nell Fees' is classified as an Irish polka in 2/4 time, set in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning, with an AA'BB' structure.

This is one of those tunes where the title shifts depending on who taught it to you. As is typical with many polkas, the tune is called by various titles based on from whom it was learned, including "Dan Callahan's," "Johnny O'Leary's," "Sean Henneghan's Polka," and "John Brosnan's."

The name "Nell Fees'" almost certainly follows the same folk convention — it likely refers to a specific fiddler or musician named Nell Fees from whose playing the tune was learned and transmitted, though detailed biographical records for her/him have not surfaced in publicly available archives.

One known recorded source is Máire O'Keeffe on Gael-Linn CEFCD 165, titled "Cóisir/House Party" (1994). Another is Patty Furlong on "Traditional Irish Music on Button Accordion" (1999), who learned the tune from New York fiddler Patrick Ourceau.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: O'Keefe's Polka
description:
The tune is part of a family of Irish polkas associated with the O'Keeffe surname, and several distinct (though related) tunes bear this name. The most famous figure connected to these polkas is Pádraig O'Keeffe (1887–1963), the legendary fiddle master of the Sliabh Luachra region of Ireland.

The polka is one of the most popular traditional folk dances in Ireland, particularly in Sliabh Luachra, a district that spans the borders of counties Kerry, Cork, and Limerick. This is the geographic home of "O'Keefe's Polka" and most of its associated variants.

Introduced to Ireland in the late 19th century, there are today hundreds of Irish polka tunes, most frequently played on the fiddle or button accordion. The Irish polka is a dance music form in 2/4 time, typically 32 bars in length, subdivided into four parts played AABB. Irish polkas are typically played fast, at over 130 bpm, and are characterized by an off-beat accent.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Patchwork Polka
description:
The "Patchwork Polka" is a three-part polka composed by Scottish fiddle and bagpipes player Iain Peterson (1934–2006) from Ardnamurchan (a remote peninsula on the west coast of Scotland). It got its name because his wife was working on some patchwork at the time he wrote it.

One documented version comes from Willie Taylor, sourced from the CD "An Audience With the Shepherds" (Veteran – VT159CD).

The tune notes were provided by John Howson, drawn from that recording.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Toormore Polka
description:
The Toormore Polka (also spelled Tournmore, Tuar Mór, or Crosaire De Bhalis) is a traditional Irish polka, not an American old-time tune. It is part of the rich polka tradition of Munster (southwest Ireland), closely associated with the West Kerry / Sliabh Luachra region. There are actually two Toormore Polkas — a First and a Second — both circulating widely in Irish traditional sessions and fiddle instruction.
"Toormore" is the anglicized form of the Irish Tuar Mór, a place name in County Cork, on the Mizen Peninsula in West Cork. The tune takes its name from this locality — a common naming convention in Irish traditional music where tunes are named after the townland, parish, or area where they were played or collected.
It is also known by alternate titles including Tuar Mór Polkas 1, The Tuar Mór, and Wallace's Cross.

The tune belongs to the broader Irish polka tradition:
The polka (polca in Irish) is one of the most popular traditional folk dances in Ireland, particularly in Sliabh Luachra, a district spanning the borders of counties Kerry, Cork, and Limerick. Many figures of Irish set dances, developed from Continental quadrilles, are danced to polkas. Introduced to Ireland in the late 19th century, there are today hundreds of Irish polka tunes.
The Irish polka is a dance music form in 2/4 time, typically 32 bars long, subdivided into four parts played AABB. Irish polkas are typically played fast, at over 130 bpm, with an off-beat accent.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Poppy Leaf (Hornpipe)
description:
"Poppy Leaf Hornpipe" is an American, Canadian, and Irish hornpipe in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning. Its structure follows an AABB form (as notated by Cole, McNulty, Miller & Perron, and Mulvihill), and an AA'BB' form in Cranford's transcription. It was noted as something that "can be used as a Clog" (according to Cole).

The tune first appeared in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883), and its direct successor, Cole's 1000 Fiddle Tunes (1940), from which it was picked up by both Irish(-American) and Canadian fiddlers. Ryan's Mammoth Collection was one of the most influential early American tunebooks, and its inclusion there firmly roots "The Poppy Leaf" in the 19th-century New England / American dance music tradition.

The identical tune was also printed as a clog or hornpipe in A.S. Bowman's J.W. Pepper Collection of Five Hundred Reels, Jigs, etc. (Philadelphia, 1908) under the title "Mulberry Leaf." On The Session, the tune is also listed under the aliases Ballyvoe #2, The Ballyvoe, Keane O'Neary's, and Poppyleaf.

The tune circulated across USA (New England) and Canada (Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton). From there, it spread into Irish traditional music circles, making it a genuinely transatlantic tune with American origins.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stack Of Barley
description:
The title supposedly refers to that part of the barley harvest that was kept aside for the making of Irish poitín (literally, "small pot," also spelled poteen or potheen). In Ireland, barley has long been used to make porridge and bread, but it is also the key ingredient for making whiskey and beer. In Irish it is known as An Staicín Eórna (or Stáicín Eórnadh) — "the little stack of barley."

The tune has no single known composer — like most traditional Irish tunes, it evolved communally over generations. One of the first appearances of "Stack of Barley" in print was in O'Neill's Music of Ireland (1903); it subsequently appeared in The Roche Collection of Irish Traditional Music (1912), and Allan's Irish Fiddler (c. 1920s).

However, manuscript evidence predates even O'Neill. The tune appears in the James Goodman music manuscript collection from mid-19th century County Cork, and also in the P.D. Reidy music manuscript collection, London, 1890s, attributed to "Michael O'Grady, Castleisland, Co. Kerry" — collected by "Professor" Patrick Reidy of Castleisland, a dancing master engaged by the Gaelic League in London to teach dance classes.

The tune also carries a rich web of aliases. It is also known as "Coming Down to Jerry's with a Bucketful of Berries," "Evening Was Waning," "Little Mary Cassidy," "New Bedford Reel (2)," "Patrick Condon's Vision," "Stack of Barley," and "Stacks of Barley."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Haughton House
description:
"Haughton House" is a Scottish march, not an American old-time tune in the traditional Appalachian sense — but it has traveled widely across traditions and appears in Irish, Shetland, and folk revival repertoires, making it feel like a shared old-time/traditional tune today.
Haughton House is a manor in Aberdeenshire, near the village of Alford on the banks of the River Don, and the tune was composed by a James Mitchell, published on a single sheet with variations by James Scott Skinner.
It is classified as a Scottish March in G Major, in standard tuning, with an AABB structure.
The tune was played in the Shetland Islands (especially Uist) as a wedding march and was sometimes labeled a Shetland tune; however, the melody is mainland Scottish in character and appears to have been originally called "Haughton House."
The tune was known for a time as "Auchadon House" (probably a mishearing), and was thought to be from Shetland — but it was composed by James Mitchell and published as a single sheet with variations by James Scott Skinner.
Shetland fiddler Debbie Scott confirmed this confusion: she knew nothing about the tune's history "other than it is not a Shetland tune," was not aware of it being used as a wedding tune in Unst, and speculated "maybe someone used it once and it got picked up on" — agreeing it is "probably plain Scottish."
A related tune, "R.O.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Johnny and Dorothy Livingston (March)
description:
The composer of this tune is Mairi Campbell herself. Mairi Campbell is a Scottish fiddler and singer known for her distinctive, lyrical playing style rooted in the Scottish folk tradition.

The tune is named for Johnny and Dorothy Livingstone, who farm Balure on the island of Lismore in Argyll, Scotland. This is a tune written as a personal tribute — a common tradition in Scottish and Celtic music where composers honor friends, family members, or community figures with a dedicated tune.

This is not a reel but a Scottish march, transcribed from the playing of Mairi Campbell on a YouTube video. It circulated in sessions including among fiddlers who learned portions of their tunes at sessions in Edinburgh.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Niel Gow's Lament on the Death of His Second Wife
description:
Niel Gow (22 March 1727 – 1 March 1807) was a Scottish fiddler active in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. He was born in Strathbraan, Perthshire, as the son of John Gow and Catherine McEwan, and the family moved to Inver in Perthshire when Niel was an infant.

In spite of being something of a musical prodigy, he originally trained as a plaid weaver, but eventually gave up that trade to become a full-time musician. He started playing the fiddle when very young, and at age 13 received his first formal lessons from one John Cameron of Grandtully.

He was widely considered the best fiddle player in Perthshire — the story goes that at age 18 he entered a competition judged by John McCraw, a blind musician, who awarded him first prize and claimed he "would ken his bow hand among a hunder players." This attracted the attention of the Duke of Atholl, who became Gow's patron, and also ensured his employment for balls and dance parties put on by the local nobility.

In 1787, Gow was visited by Robert Burns during the latter's tour of the Highlands. He was the most famous Scottish fiddle player of the 1700s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sarah's Song
description: Sarah's Song is a march in the key of D. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Da Slockit Light
description:
Tom (Tammy) Anderson MBE (1910–1991) was a Scottish fiddler, teacher, composer, and collector of traditional tunes. He has been described as "the most prominent personality in the entire history of Shetland fiddling."

Born on 29 August 1910 on the "Moorfield" croft at Eshaness, Shetland Islands, he was brought up in a musical home and learned to play the fiddle from his grandfather; as a teenager he played in local bands for weddings and dances in the Northmavine area.

From an early age, Tammy was composing fiddle tunes, and throughout his life produced over 300 melodies, the earliest in 1936, the last dated July 1988.

From 1970, Anderson campaigned to have the fiddle taught in Shetland schools as part of the curriculum, and when successful, he became the first official fiddle teacher in the Shetland school system. Aly Bain was the first of his many pupils.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Crested Hens
description:
"Crested Hens" was composed in 1983 by French national and hurdy-gurdy (vielle à roue) player Gilles Chabenat, who remarks that some bars of a Debussy composition served as inspiration for the germ of the tune.

Although this tune is often mistakenly thought to be an ancient Breton tune, it was actually written by Gilles Chabenat in 1983. He wrote it on a hurdy-gurdy as a bourrée à trois temps (3/8 time), and thus was originally played much faster than most people play it now.

"Crested Hens" is a translation of the French Poules Huppées. According to Gilles himself: "I was 15 and couldn't decide on a title, one day we were playing at oxymorons and my friend said 'Poules Huppées' — we all laughed at it for a long time, so I decided to name the tune that."

So the name is essentially a playful, nonsensical inside joke between teenage friends — not a reference to any particular chicken breed or folk symbolism.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Jackie Donnan's Mazurka
description:
JACKIE DONNAN'S MAZURKA. AKA and see "Joe O'Dowd's Mazurka." Irish, Mazurka (3/4 time). D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. A version of this tune appears in the Roche Collection (vol. 3, 1927) as a redowa called "Barnacle Waltz (The)," while another was entered into the mid-19th century music manuscript collection of uilleann piper and Church of Ireland cleric James Goodman [1] as "Limerick Waltz (2) (The)." 

Source for notated version: fiddler Jackie Donnan (Co. Down) [Boys of the Lough].  

Printed sources: Boys of the Lough, 1977; p. 15.

Recorded sources: Transatlantic TRA 311, Boys of the Lough - "Lochaber No More."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Sonny Brogan's Mazurka (#1)
description:
Mazurkas originated in Poland and spread across Europe in the 1800s, both as tunes and as a dance form. They found their way to Ireland in the mid-1800s and became a traditional tune form there, particularly in County Donegal.

"Sonny's Mazurka" is perhaps the most well-known of all Irish mazurkas.

Patrick Joseph "Sonny" Brogan (4 July 1906 – 1 January 1965) was an Irish accordion player from the 1930s to the 1960s, and was one of Ireland's most popular traditional musicians. He was one of the earliest advocates of the two-row B/C button accordion in traditional music and popularized it in the 1950s and '60s.

Sonny was born in Dublin on the 4th July 1906, the eldest of three children born to Andrew Brogan and Alicia Brown. It has been suggested that Sonny first developed an awareness of Irish music as a young boy while on holidays in Kildare and heard his uncle Thomas Cleary playing the accordion. He taught himself to play the accordion and as a young man attended piano lessons for a while.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sonny Brogan's Mazurka (#2)
description:
"Sonny's Mazurka" is perhaps the most well-known of Irish mazurkas. It is in D Major, in 3/4 time, and typically follows an AABB structure. The "#2" designation (vs. #1) refers to the fact that two distinct mazurkas circulate under Brogan's name — these two are often played together, and it is suspected they were both in Sonny Brogan's repertoire, which accounts for them both being tagged with his name, despite their differences and similarities.

Mazurkas originated in Poland and spread across Europe in the 1800s, both as tunes and as a dance form. They found their way to Ireland in the mid-1800s, and became a traditional tune form there, particularly in County Donegal.

Patrick Joseph "Sonny" Brogan (4 July 1906 – 1 January 1965) was an Irish accordion player from the 1930s to the 1960s, and was one of Ireland's most popular traditional musicians. Despite the tune being closely associated with fiddle playing, Brogan was actually an accordionist, not a fiddler.
He was one of the earliest advocates of the two-row B/C button accordion in traditional music, and popularised it in the 1950s and 60s. He originally played on a single-keyed Hohner melodeon, and later the two-row Paolo Soprani, which he used until he died.
Sonny Brogan was born in Dublin, the eldest of three children. On a holiday trip to Kildare as a young boy, he first heard Irish music played on the accordion by his great uncle, Thomas Cleary.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: April Waltz
description:
The tune was composed by Selma Kaplan (Altamont, N.Y.) in 1982; "written for a friend, during a huge unexpected snow storm in April '82." Selma has worked for many years at WAMC, an NPR station serving Vermont, Massacusetts and New York, and is an occasional on-air personality.

Printed sources: Matthiesen (Waltz Book), 1992; pg. 12.

title: Black Hills Waltz
description:
Kenner Kartchner was a fiddler born in Navajo County, Arizona in 1886, who grew up in a Mormon settlement in a musical family. He is important in the old-time music world in many ways.

His early career as an itinerant fiddler — which began around the time his father was serving a Mormon mission — made him a sort of "rock musician" of his day.

He is the central figure associated with the Black Hills Waltz, and the tune's transmission to modern players runs entirely through him.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cherry Blossom Waltz
description:
The Cherry Blossom Waltz is credited to Homer Lee "Pappy" Sherrill of South Carolina, documented from a 1989 field recording in the collection of Ashley Carder.

The tune is played in the key of D, in standard GDAE tuning, in waltz (3/4) time, and the archived recording features Snuffy Jenkins on washboard.

The notation was later published in Fiddler Magazine, Vol. 8, No. 1, Spring 2001.
1989 — Captured via field recording, preserved in Ashley Carder's personal collection
2001 — Notation published in Fiddler Magazine (Vol. 8, No. 1, Spring 2001)
The tune is catalogued in the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org) under Waltz/Valse/Vals, United States

title: Clayhole Waltz
description:
"The Clayhole" was an old camping spot near the Arizona-Utah border where lumberers, freighters, and cowboys would rendezvous. In the liner notes for Powder River, Skip Gorman recalls Larkin Gifford telling him that a "clayhole" was a camp on the Arizona-Utah border where lumber freighters and cowboys would meet. The name evokes the rough-and-tumble world of the American West — a gathering place for working men far from town.

The tune comes from the playing of the Gifford Family, who were for several generations musicians in the southern Utah area, beginning with Moses Elias Gifford in the late 1800s. Samuel Kendall Gifford later formed the Gifford Family Band in the first half of the 20th century, and musical descendants of the family continue to entertain.

The waltz comes to us primarily from the playing of Larkin Gifford of Springdale, Utah. Larkin learned it from his father, Moses Elias Gifford, who brought it with him to Utah in the late 1800s. Moses's original source for the tune is unknown, but no sources suggest he composed it himself.

The chain of transmission is remarkably well-documented for an old-time tune:

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Country Waltz
description:
The tune simply called "Country Waltz" is one of those old-time gems whose precise origins are somewhat murky — a common fate for tunes that traveled through oral tradition across North America. Here is everything the research turns up:

The most detailed paper trail for "Country Waltz" leads to Canada. Missouri fiddler and researcher Charlie Walden first heard this waltz on the old K-TEL record 25 Old-Tyme Fiddle Hits, which was actually an American reissue of a Canadian record on the Arc label (FH-2). On the U.S. K-TEL version none of the fiddlers were identified, but the Canadian issue told the names — and the fiddler playing "Country Waltz" on that album was Ned Landry of New Brunswick.

Ned Landry (1921–2009) was one of the most celebrated Maritime Canadian old-time fiddlers, known for his smooth, melodic style. The K-TEL/Arc record was a major vehicle by which the tune spread southward into American old-time circles.

Several of the old-time fiddlers around Mid-Missouri picked up this tune — Taylor McBaine being among them. This mirrors the pattern of many Canadian tunes filtering into Midwestern fiddle communities via records and radio.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cowboy Waltz
description:
COWBOY WALTZ.  American, Waltz (3/4 time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BA'.  The tune is from a recording of the playing of fiddler Tilman Pyeatt (1933 - 2007), his second wife Molly Pyeatt (guitar), and Moon Mullins (banjo). Tilman was in the Air Force for many years, stationed in Texas. His family band, consisting of Tilman and his children Marilyn, Gene and Lehman, played bluegrass weekly on KMAC radio, San Antonio, and at local venues. The family moved back to Tilman's native Arkansas in 1970 where they continued to perform at local events.

title: Don't You Remember The Time
description:
"Don't You Remember The Time" appears in the repertoire catalogued at Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource, listed among a broad collection of traditional G-tuning fiddle tunes. Unlike many neighboring tunes in that same list — such as Dandy Jim (attributed to Clyde Davenport), Double File (Gaither Carlton), or Devil In The Strawstack (Tommy Jarrell) — "Don't You Remember The Time" is listed without a specific attribution or source fiddler, which is common for tunes that have entered the general old-time commons without a traceable single originator or collector.
Regional tradition: The tune sits comfortably in the Southern Appalachian and Upper South old-time tradition, a genre where tunes passed orally through communities over generations, making pinning down a single composer or "inventor" nearly impossible.
Naming convention: The title follows a classic old-time pattern of question-phrase titles (e.g., "Did You Ever See the Devil Uncle Joe", "Don't You Mind the Weather"), often connected to older songs or dances that predated formal recording.
No commercial recording credit: Unlike tunes recorded in the 1920s–30s commercial hillbilly era (e.g., by Fiddlin' John Carson or Henry Gilliland), this tune does not appear to have a well-documented early 78rpm recording tied to a named fiddler.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: El Paso Waltz
description:
The tune is credited as written by Dave Richardson of the Boys of the Lough, a well-known British/Irish folk group. The transcription in circulation comes specifically from the playing of Alabama fiddler James Bryan.

This cross-cultural lineage is key to the tune's identity: it was written by a Celtic folk musician but adopted and popularized in the American old-time fiddle scene through Bryan's interpretation.

The canonical recorded version is preserved in MP3 format on the Digital Library of Appalachia, where Bryan plays it with Carl Jones.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Eye Of The Beholder
description:
The tune "Eye of the Beholder" is an original composition by Jim Childress, a fiddler and old-time musician from Virginia. Jim is a long-time resident of Free Union, Virginia.

As well as performing with the band Uncle Henry's Favorites for over 40 years, Jim has written tunes such as The Road to Malvern, Turkey Sag, Shadowdragon, and Halfway Pond that have become widely known and played in the old-time music community.

"Eye of the Beholder" appears on a 2014 recording — the second collection of original fiddle tunes by Jim Childress. It is from the album Free Union.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Flat Water Fran
description:
"Flat Water Fran" was composed by Edinburgh-born Phil Cunningham, apparently for a relative who enjoyed flatwater canoeing.

Phil Cunningham is a celebrated Scottish musician and composer, best known for his work as an accordionist with the band Silly Wizard, and his long-running duo with Shetland fiddler Aly Bain.
It is catalogued on The Session as a waltz (3/4 time) by Phil Cunningham, also known as "Flat Water Fran."
The tune was written for "some relative who goes rowing on… flat water."
It is written in G major and has a lyrical, flowing quality well suited to its water-themed inspiration.
The tune appears on the album "Portrait" by Aly Bain & Phil Cunningham (2010), as Track 2.
On that recording, the players take the tune up into A major after the second time through.
Kevin Crawford also recorded this tune on his album Carrying the Tune under the track name "Phil & Rory's," performing it in B with John Doyle on accompaniment.
The oldest indexed source for the tune dates to 2012.
Flat Water Fran has become a popular session tune in Edinburgh over the past several years.
On The Session, it has been added to 560 tunebooks — a strong indicator of widespread adoption in the Celtic/Irish session community.
It gained early attention as a "Transatlantic Sessions" tune, the famous BBC/RTE TV series that pairs Scottish and Irish musicians with American roots artists.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Gisele Valse
description:
Valse Gisèle was composed by fiddler Yvon Cuillerier of Saint-Bruno, Québec, Canada. The composition is dated to 1994.

It is a French-Canadian waltz in 3/4 time, in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning. This places it squarely within the rich Québécois fiddle tradition — a distinct branch of North American folk fiddling with deep French roots.

The tune was published in print in Fiddler Magazine, Vol. 9, No. 2, Summer 2002, on page 41.

The tune has been recorded by Alycia Putnam on her album Fiddle Storm, and by André Proulx on his self-titled album André Proulx. It can also be heard performed by Calvin Vollrath on YouTube. It has additionally been performed by fiddler Katherine Moller (a YouTube recording exists from 2017).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Green Valley Waltz
description:
GREEN VALLEY WALTZ. American, Waltz. USA; east Tennessee, Oklahoma. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Phillips): AABB (Thede). Most sources trace back to Tennesse's Fiddlin' Arthur Smith. "Green Meadow Waltz" is a related melody. Mike Seegar is quoted as saying: "I know of no other fiddler who uses Arthur Smith's device of singing in harmony with the fiddle on the last lines as he does in 'Green Valley Waltz'" [Florence Times, July 28, 1968]. The waltz was recorded by east Tennessee fiddler Jimmy McCarroll with the Roane County Ramblers for Columbia Records in October 1928, but the side was unissued.

Source for notated version: - John Lewis (Heavener, Oklahoma) [Thede]; Skip Gorman [Phillips].

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 265. Thede (The Fiddle Book), 1967; p. 146.

Recorded sources: - Folkways FA 2379, "McGee Brothers and Arthur Smith" (1964. Originally recorded 1957). Marimac 9008, The Lazy Aces - "Still Lazy After All These Years" (1986. Learned from an Arthur Smith recording).

title: Inishowen
description:
Great — the general searches didn't surface a dedicated article about the specific tune "Inishowen." Let me pull together what is well-documented from both the old-time and Irish traditional music worlds about this tune, synthesizing what's known.

Inishowen (Irish: Inis Eoghain, meaning "Island/Peninsula of Eoghan") is a peninsula in County Donegal, in the northwest of Ireland — the northernmost point of the entire island of Ireland. It has a distinctive and ancient fiddling tradition that is considered one of the most locally flavored in all of Irish music.

The tune titled "Inishowen" is most commonly associated with Irish traditional music, not specifically American old-time, though it has crossed over into old-time repertoire — a common pathway, since old-time music originates from immigrants from England, France, Germany, Ireland, and Scotland who brought their native fiddling traditions with them, mixed with influence from African-American music.

The Inishowen Peninsula itself has a distinctive fiddle tradition. Grace Toland is from Inishowen, Co. Donegal, where the English-language singing tradition is particularly varied — and the instrumental tradition is similarly rich. The area is known for a raw, unembellished fiddle style that pre-dates many of the more ornamented Sligo or Donegal styles.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Isabelle Waltz
description:
The tune is associated with Warren Helton, whose father, Vernon Helton, often played it at dances in Brinktown, Missouri. This places its roots firmly in the central Missouri old-time dance tradition, where waltzes were a regular feature of community social dances.

The "Isabelle Waltz" is related to an untitled central Missouri melody known as either "Kemp's Waltz" or "Norma Lou's Waltz," suggesting a small cluster of closely related regional waltz variants, likely passed down informally through local fiddling families and communities — a very common pattern in old-time music.

The tune was recorded by David Cavins and was included on the compilation CD "Play Me Something Quick and Devilish."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Julia Waltz
description:
The most specific attribution found comes from the fiddle community itself. A member of the Fiddle Hangout forum notes that the tune was written by Jeff Kaufman of Free Raisins, and that "Julia" is believed to be his wife or daughter. The poster also mentions loving the way "Audrey (the Fiddler)" plays it. This suggests the tune is a composed waltz by a known modern author, rather than an anonymous traditional piece passed down through generations.

European dance styles that became popular in the United States during the 19th century — including the quadrille, polka, schottische, two-step, and waltz — provided new tunes and additional fodder for original compositions. New types of fiddle tunes emerged in the US, including breakdowns, blues, and rags.

Despite the fact that the majority of the old-time fiddle tradition consists of very old tunes with no known authorship, new fiddle tunes have always been written and are still being written today. The Julia Waltz fits squarely into this category of newer original compositions in the old-time style.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kansas Waltz
description:
"Kansas Waltz" is credited to Elias Howe, dated to 1861, and can be found in Howe's Musician's Omnibus No. 2, published in 1862.

While Howe was himself a fiddle player, he was primarily a collector and publisher of dance tunes popular in the mid-19th century — so it seems probable that Howe collected rather than composed the tune, meaning it may genuinely be considered "traditional."

In 1885, W.F. Shaw published a separate Kansas Waltz composed by Fred Hoffmann for piano. A copy of that publication resides in the U.S. Library of Congress Notated Music Collection.

title: Keys To The Kingdom
description:
"Keys to the Kingdom" is an old-time fiddle tune that appears in various old-time and American folk music collections. It is sometimes listed under alternate titles and is part of the broader Appalachian and American fiddle tradition.

The tune is associated with the old-time fiddle repertoire of the American South and Appalachian region. Like many old-time tunes, its exact composer and precise origin are difficult to pin down definitively, as the tradition was largely oral and passed from fiddler to fiddler across generations rather than through formal composition or publication.

The title "Keys to the Kingdom" reflects a strong thread of sacred and gospel-influenced imagery that runs through old-time fiddle music, particularly tunes from the American South, where religious life and community music-making were deeply intertwined.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kiss Me Waltz
description:
The tune is widely known under the titles "Kiss Waltz," "Kiss Me," or "Kiss Me Waltz" — note that "Kiss Me Again Waltz" is a different tune. It is an old-time waltz in G Major (A part) & D Major (B part), played in standard fiddle tuning.

Seattle fiddler Vivian Williams finds that the tune was derived from a classical composition called Il Bacio by the Italian composer Arditi in the mid-19th century. The title Il Bacio means "The Kiss" in Italian — a fitting ancestor for a tune that traveled from the European concert hall into Southern and Midwestern fiddle tradition.

The melody became widely known throughout the South and Midwest under the titles "Kiss Me Waltz" or "Kiss Me." It is particularly associated with Missouri and the Ozarks region, though it was embraced across the American fiddle world.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Kiss Waltz
description:
KISS WALTZ [1], A. AKA - "Kiss Me Waltz." Old-Time, Waltz. G Major ('A' part) & D Major ('B' part). Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. Widely known under the titles "Kiss Waltz", "Kiss Me," or "Kiss Me Waltz" ("Kiss Me Again Waltz" is a different tune). The melody was recorded by Texas fiddler Captain McKinney for Okeh Records in 1929. North Carolina banjoist and singer Charlie Poole, with Roy Harvey and the North Carolina Ramblers around the same time as did McKinney, under the title "Kiss Waltz." The setting (led by the group's fiddler Posey Rorrer) was an up-tempo version of the tune, although the side was never issued commercially. Other early recordings are by W.T. Narmour and S.W. Smith (twice, in 1929 and 1934). Seattle fiddler Vivian Williams finds that the tune was derived from a classical composition called "Il Bacio" by the Italian composer Arditi in the mid-19th century. Kentucky mandolinist and bandleader Bill Monroe recorded a version on his "Uncle Pen" album under the title "Kiss Me Waltz" (the title Art Galbraith also used), with fiddle by Kenny Baker, and was presumably played by Monroe's uncle Pendleton Vandeveer. Galbraith's own "Down Home Waltz (2)" has a very similar first strain to "Kiss Waltz [1]."

Source for notated version: - Art Galbraith (1909-1993, near Springfield, Mo.) [Beissswenger & McCann].

Printed sources: -  Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 39.

Recorded sources: - Columbia 142644-1, Charlie Poole & the North Carolina Ramblers (1926). County 540, "Charlie Poole and the North Carolina Ranblers" (originally recorded 1926). County 3508, Charlie Poole and the North Carolina Ramblers, vol. 2. Historical Records HLP-8005, Charlie Poole (1926-1930) - "A Young Boy Left His Home One Day" (1975).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Lament Of The First Generation
description:
This tune was composed by Liz Carroll, one of the most celebrated Irish-American fiddlers of the modern era. It was released on Liz Carroll's album "Lost in the Loop" on February 1, 2000. The oldest known source for the tune, considering indexed recordings and transcriptions, dates to 2000.

Liz Carroll is a Chicago-born Irish-American fiddler and composer, widely regarded as one of the foremost composers of new Irish traditional music. She is known for writing tunes that feel deeply rooted in the traditional idiom while carrying a distinctly personal voice — the title "Lament of the First Generation" is widely understood to reflect themes of immigrant identity, the experience of first-generation Irish-Americans caught between two worlds.

It is a waltz (3/4 time) in G major, with four known settings documented in the Irish traditional music community. The standard transcription is an exact copy from Carroll's own handwritten sheet music, which was previously available on her website.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Life's Fortune
description: Life's Fortune is a waltz in the key of D. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Little Kid's Waltz

title: Lonely Bird
description:
There are actually multiple distinct tunes that travel under the name "Lonely Bird" in the fiddle tradition. The name is most famously associated with Aly Bain's 1996 album of the same name, which brought several of these pieces to wider attention. Here's a breakdown:

The most direct bearer of the title in the traditional sense.
It is a Finnish slow air, composed by Hatti Hintikka.
Shetland fiddler Aly Bain recorded it on his Lonely Bird album (Green Linnet GLCD 3105, 1996), having learned it from fiddlers at a festival in Finland.
It also appeared on Whirlie Records CD2, also credited to Aly Bain under the title Lonely Bird.
It is also known by the Irish title "Gan Tusa Beid Me Uigneac A Grad", and has an Irish air version in 6/8 time.

A separate, older tune of Scottish origin.
It is a Scottish slow air in 6/8 time, in B-flat major, with an AABB structure, described as "a Highland air" by Gow.
It appears in *Nathaniel Gow's Complete Repository, Part 3, published in 1806. This makes it one of the earliest documented uses of the title.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Marino Waltz
description:
MARINO WALTZ. Irish, Waltz. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. Composed by John Sheahan of The Dubliners. Marino is a "leafy suburb" of Dublin, the location of the architecturally significant 18th century building called "The Casino". The melody has sometimes been called the "Bord na Móna" waltz from association with that product in advertising. 

Source for notated version: 

See also listing at:

Hear/see the waltz played by John Sheehan and Andre Rieu on youtube.com [1]

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Mr. Fisher's Old German Waltz
description:
The tune's name is quite literal — it traces directly to a real person. "Mr. Fisher's Old German Waltz" was learned from a Mr. Fisher of Bowling Green, Missouri, who described the tune as "an old German waltz" — which became the basis for the title.

The fiddler who collected and popularized it was Lynn "Chirps" Smith, a celebrated Midwestern old-time fiddler from Illinois. Along with the waltz, Chirps also learned a tune called "Bowling Green" from Mr. Fisher.

Chirps Smith is the figure most responsible for preserving and spreading this tune. Described as "the Midwest's premier fiddler," Smith presents tunes that evoke memories of front-porch music-making on the Illinois prairie and dances in the hollers of Little Egypt, in a style he calls simply "Midwestern."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Monty's Waltz
description: Monty's Waltz is a waltz in the key of D. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mother Marc's Waltz

title: Mountain Grove Waltz
description:
The Mountain Grove Waltz is a traditional tune attributed to Al Murphy of Iowa City, Iowa.

Prominent fiddler Tricia Spencer — who teaches and performs the tune — learned it directly from Al Murphy, an Iowa City, Iowa fiddler.

Al Murphy was a fiddler and guitar player from Iowa City, Iowa who passed away recently. Tricia Spencer describes feeling like he was part of her fiddling family, as he knew people who had played with her grandfather.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Muscatatuck Waltz
description: Muscatatuck Waltz is a waltz in the key of F. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: My Pretty White Kitty
description:
John Dee Kennedy (1914–1997) was a self-effacing man who, in his prime, was considered by many to be the best breakdown fiddler in Pawnee and Osage counties, Oklahoma.

In a generation where most of his contemporaries were playing Western swing, bluegrass, or Texas contest style fiddle, John perpetuated an older family and community tradition that can be traced through the mountains of Arkansas all the way back to earlier roots.

"My Pretty White Kitty" is catalogued as a waltz, attributed to John Dee Kennedy, and appears in old-time fiddle tune indexes alongside similarly rare and regionally specific pieces.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nachusa Waltz
description: Nachusa Waltz is a waltz in the key of C. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Nancy's Waltz
description:
Nancy's Waltz was composed in 1980 by Chris Romaine of Silver Spring, Maryland, as a gift for Nancy Morris, described as "a good dance and music friend."

So unlike the vast majority of old-time fiddle tunes — which are anonymous and centuries old — this is a modern composition with a fully documented origin story and a known author.

The tune was played at Pinewoods (a music and dance camp) in 1981, where it was picked up by prominent fiddler Rodney Miller and others.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Norma Lou's Waltz
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Key | C major |
| Style | Old-time waltz (3/4 time) |
| Region | Mid-Missouri |
| Original Source | The Kemp family, Mexico, MO |
| Name Given By | Fiddler Charlie "Possum" Walden |
| Named For | Norma Lou Applebee |
| First Known Recording | Hoe-downs, Hornpipes & Hokum (Marimac Recordings, 1993) |
| Difficulty | Intermediate |

"Norma Lou's Waltz" is an old waltz from Mid-Missouri that fiddler Charlie Walden learned from the Kemp brothers of Mexico, MO — and they credited it to their grandfather, making it a genuinely old tune.

The story has a memorable twist: for a lot of years, Walden ran around claiming that he wrote the tune, as it had appeared in his head one day and he couldn't for the life of him remember where he got it — until Floyd Kemp and his brother corrected him at a contest.

As Walden put it on his blog, someone walked up to him and said, "That's my grandpa Kemp's old waltz."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Northern Lights Waltz
description: Northern Lights Waltz is a waltz in the key of G. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: The Old Man Waltz
description: The Old Man Waltz is a waltz in the key of G. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Old Rusty Mill Waltz
description:
The Old Rusty Mill Waltz is catalogued in the key of G, and is attributed to Melvin Wine, appearing on the recording Hannah at the Springhouse.

This is the most definitive known attribution. Melvin Wine (1909–2003) was a celebrated West Virginia old-time fiddler, widely regarded as one of the great traditional Appalachian fiddlers of the 20th century. The tune appears in the Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes compiled by John Lamancusa.

The "Rusty Mill Waltz (G)" is recognized among old-time fiddlers as a well-known, playable waltz in the standard repertoire, listed alongside tunes like Salyer's Waltz, Green River Waltz, and Over the Waves.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Olga Blom's Waltz
description:
Detailed historical documentation on this tune is sparse (as is common with many old-time fiddle tunes), but here is everything the available sources reveal:

"Olga Blom's Waltz" is catalogued in the key of C, and its source is cited as Across the Fields – Traditional Norwegian-American Music from Wisconsin.

This places the tune squarely in the Norwegian-American immigrant tradition of the Upper Midwest — specifically Wisconsin, which had one of the largest concentrations of Norwegian settlers in the United States during the 19th and early 20th centuries. The tune is named after a person — Olga Blom — almost certainly a Norwegian-American woman, likely either the composer of the waltz or a person it was dedicated to. This naming convention (a waltz named for a specific individual, often female) is extremely common in Scandinavian and Norwegian-American folk music.

The tune appears in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John S. Lamancusa, a book containing 522 traditional old-time tunes transcribed from jams, source recordings, festivals (Clifftop, Rock Bridge), and workshops (Rocky Mountain Fiddle Camp, Swannanoa, Augusta, Fiddle Hell).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Over The Waves
description:
José Juventino Policarpo Rosas was a Mexican composer and violinist, known worldwide for the waltz "Sobre las olas" ("Over the Waves"). He was born to an indigenous Otomí Mexican family in 1868 in a village in Guanajuato, which was later renamed in his honor in 1939 as Santa Cruz de Juventino Rosas.

His father, Juan de Jesús Rosas, had made a career playing harp in a military band and encouraged his children's talent. Taught by his father, Juventino became a violin prodigy and was joined by his brothers Manuel (guitar) and Patrocinio (singer) to form a traveling band. Together, with their father on harp, they performed at festivals and other celebrations.

In 1875, the family headed to Mexico City in search of better opportunities. Equipped with a simple fiddle, the child Juventino played folk tunes and popular songs in the streets of the densely populated barrio known as Tepito, then notorious for its poverty and crime.

The waltz "Sobre las olas" ("Over the Waves") is the best-known work of Rosas, who first published it in 1888. Casino owners Vicente Alfaro and Calixta Gutiérrez de Alfaro, important arts funders, commissioned Rosas to write a festival piece in the mid-1880s, which resulted in "Sobre las olas" (dedicated to Calixta). The specific origins of its inspiration are shrouded in lore.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ook Pik (Ootpik) Waltz
description:
Frankie Rodgers (1936–2009) was a British Columbian country fiddler and entertainer. Despite the rumors of antiquity and Native American provenance, the "Ookpik Waltz" was not derived from indigenous sources but rather is a latter 20th century composition of Mission, British Columbia, fiddler Frankie Rodgers, who published it in a tune book of his compositions.

The tune restores credit to Frankie Rodgers and his rich performing and recording career. His Ukrainian heritage colored his composition and performance of the Ookpik Waltz.

Sheet music of "Ookpik Waltz" was published with a 1965 copyright to Rodgers. His waltz was first recorded in 1973 (track #6 on the LP "Maple Sugar, Fiddle Favourites by Canada's Old Time Fiddle King"), although the copyright to his published book of compositions gives 1965 as a date.

The melody has been "folk-processed" since then, but is still recognizably derived from the original.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Orvetta Waltz
description:
There are actually two distinct tunes sharing the name "Orvetta Waltz," with separate origins that intersect through Missouri fiddling tradition. Here's the full story:

A popular and much-published waltz composed by E.B. Spencer, published in Boston by the Oliver Ditson Company on Washington Street in 1879.

The sheet music bears the dedication: "Composed and Dedicated to Miss Mary E.R. Johann by E.B. Spencer." It was published in Boston by Oliver Ditson in 1879.

The original piece is written in a Romantic style for piano, and was first published in the 19th century (1879). The original key was A in 3/8 meter. The sheet music is held at the Library of Congress and is freely viewable online.

title: Ozark Waltz
description:
"Ozark Waltz" was originally recorded in Memphis, Tennessee, in June 1930, by the Morrison Twin Brothers String Band of Searcy County, Arkansas, featuring the twin fiddles of Abbie (1876–1965) and Absie (1876–1964, sometimes "Apsie") Morrison, who were themselves twins, backed up on guitars by Abbie's sons Claude and Lawson.

The brothers got their break after a recording company representative heard them play in Little Rock.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Type | Old-time Waltz (3/4 time) |
| Key | F Major (also notated in D) |
| Tuning | Standard fiddle tuning |
| Structure | AA'BB' |
| Region | USA — Arkansas / Ozarks |
| First Recorded | June 1930, Memphis, TN |

Scholar Guthrie Meade believes the tune might have been adapted from the air of a popular song from around the turn of the 20th century, and identifies an early recording by Earl & Joe (1930) in addition to the Morrisons'. This suggests the tune may have been circulating in the region before it was formally recorded, and the Morrisons' version was simply the first to be captured on disc.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Paris Waltz
description:
"Paris Waltz" was composed by Arthur Smith (1898–1971), and named for the Henry County, Tennessee seat — the town of Paris — near where Smith was born and raised.

Henry County itself is named after American Revolutionary-era hero Patrick Henry of Virginia, while the town of Paris was named in honor of the Marquis de Lafayette. So despite its grand French-sounding name, this is very much a Tennessee tune with deep local roots.

Arthur Smith recorded the waltz for Bluebird Records in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1938, backed by the Delmore Brothers — Alton and Rabon — who both played guitar. This recording is the definitive version and showcases Smith's distinctive style, including his expressive note-bending technique.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Peek-A-Boo Waltz
description:
The waltz began as a song air, originally written and composed by William J. Scanlan (1856–1898), who published it in 1881. The "Peek-a-boo" is attributed to William J. Scanlan, an Irish-American from Springfield, Massachusetts.

Scanlan was a singer who began his career as a child, and by his early teens was accompanying lectures at temperance meetings to sing hymns and provide a musical interlude between sermons. The song "Peek-a-boo" was sung by him in Bartley Campbell's play Friend & Foe.

Two years after Scanlan's original publication, his publishers printed an arrangement (by L.A. Benjamin) of his song melody as part of a waltz medley entitled "Peek-a-Boo Waltz." The Library of Congress holds that published sheet music, attributed to W. J. Scanlan and published in New York by T. B. Harms in 1883.

In the original, the verse is in duple time and the chorus is in waltz time, and the words tell of a father who comes home from work to play with his young child.

title: Pinedale Waltz
description:
"Pinedale Waltz" comes from the fiddling of Kenner Casteel Kartchner and is named for the town of Pinedale, Arizona, dating to approximately c. 1900, with authorship attributed perhaps to Frank Pruitt (per Shumway, 1990).

The attribution "perhaps by Frank Pruitt" reflects the uncertainty common in old-time tune documentation — tunes were often passed orally and authorship blurred over generations.

The tune is most closely associated with K.C. Kartchner, and its primary printed source is the book Frontier Fiddler (University of Arizona Press, 1990). It is also referenced in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes and in collections of Old Time Fiddling from the State of Arizona.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Poor Girl Waltz
description:
The tune is classified as an American/Canadian waltz in 3/4 time, and goes by both "Poor Girl's Waltz" and "Poor Girl Waltz."

The waltz was recorded in May 1929 for Brunswick Records by fiddler Reese Jarvis (1900–1967, of Clendenin, West Virginia) and guitarist Dick Justice (1906–1962), in Chicago, Illinois.

It is described as "an uncommon tune" in early documentation, attributed to West Virginia fiddler Reese Jarvis.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Poughkeepsie Waltz
description: Poughkeepsie Waltz is a waltz in the key of F. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Pretty Waltz
description: Pretty Waltz is a waltz in the key of C. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Quabbin Waltz
description:
The tune associated with the Quabbin Waltz is called "Quabbin Moonlight Mikva," and was composed by Amy Rose. It was performed by Anna Patton, Karen Axelrod, and Kate Barnes on the album Summersweet.

The track "Quabbin Waltz" by Gary Roodman was released on July 18, 2024, and also appears on the album Summersweet.

The Quabbin Waltz is an English Country Dance, devised by Gary Roodman in 2023 and published in Countable Calculated Figures.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ranger's Waltz
description:
"Ranger's Waltz" was composed by Quentin Ratliffe, the saxophone player for The Mom and Dads, a four-piece dance band (drums, saxophone, piano, and accordion) from Spokane, Washington, who formed in the 1950s and who recorded the waltz in 1971.

Vivian Williams describes the group as playing "the basic 'Grange Hall Dance' repertoire of waltzes, schottisches, varsouvienne, three-step, foxtrots, and two steps," and notes that "their records were very popular regionally and in Canada in the 1970s."

The tune was later released on the album "20 Favorite Waltzes" (1980) by The Mom and Dads on Warner Special Products.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Red Fox Waltz
description:
"Red Fox Waltz" is an old-time waltz from the USA, rooted in the Missouri tradition, played in the key of D major. It is an AB two-part waltz in 3/4 time and is considered one of the most graceful pieces in the Midwestern fiddling repertoire.

The waltz has been attributed to fiddler Harold Allen (1925–2012), originally from Nebraska but who later lived in Oregon, where he was active in the Idaho and Oregon old-time fiddlers' associations. On his album Fiddling Around (American Heritage Music Corporation AH-4-1-4), Harold Allen is credited with composing the tune.

There is also a field recording of Harold Allen playing the waltz at the Weiser, Idaho national fiddle contest in 1966, preserved courtesy of Vivian & Phil Williams.

According to Vivian Williams, during the 1960s the tune became popular for a time at the Weiser, Idaho national fiddle contest, played and popularized by fiddlers originally from Missouri, where it is a frequently heard waltz.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rockin' The Babies to Sleep
description: Rockin' The Babies to Sleep is a waltz in the key of D. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rosalita Waltz
description: Rosalita Waltz is a waltz in the key of C. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Rose Waltz
description:
The name "Rose Waltz" actually encompasses several distinct tunes in the American old-time and traditional fiddle canon. Here's a breakdown of the most documented versions:

"The Rose Waltz" is sourced to Nebraska fiddler Uncle Bob Walters (1889–1960) and is considered one of the "100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes" according to Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden.

Bob Walters's version was documented by the Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers' Association and appeared in the landmark collection "Old Time Fiddler's Repertory" (1976).

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Sonny's Mazurka
description:
"Sonny's Mazurka" is perhaps the most well-known of Irish mazurkas. Despite its deep roots in the Irish traditional repertoire, the tune has a surprisingly tangled history of names, players, and attributions.

Mazurkas originated in Poland and spread across Europe in the 1800s, both as tunes and as a dance form. They found their way to Ireland in the mid-1800s and became a traditional tune form there, particularly in County Donegal.

Although the tune has gone by a number of names, it is today most often called after the County Dublin accordion player Sonny (Patrick Joseph) Brogan (1906–1965), originally from Prosperous, County Kildare.

Brogan made records in the 1930s with The Lough Gill Quartet and was a member of Ceoltóirí Chualann under the direction of Seán Ó Riada. Importantly, Brogan was an accordion player, not a fiddler — the tune just became strongly associated with his name through tradition.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Stars And Stripes Waltz
description:
"Stars and Stripes Waltz" is a tune that is not often heard today, placing it among the rarer gems of the old-time Missouri and Ozark fiddle tradition. Like most tunes in this tradition, it is considered traditional and public domain.

The tune is firmly rooted in the Missouri/Ozark fiddle tradition, not the more commonly documented Appalachian stream. It appears on two key historical recordings:

1. Lonnie Robertson — The tune is documented as performed by Lonnie Robertson, in the key of C (standard GDAE tuning), recorded in the Waltz style, sourced from Fiddle Tunes Ozark Style Vol. 2 on Caney Mountain Records (CLP 233 LP), learned by way of Luther Hampton, and referenced in Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Missouri.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Swedish Waltz
description:
"Swedish Waltz" is not a single tune — the Traditional Tune Archive catalogs at least five distinct fiddle tunes under that name, reflecting how immigrant communities brought Scandinavian dance music into the American old-time tradition. They are classified separately as Swedish Waltz [1] through [5].

This version is classified as American, waltz (3/4 time), associated with the states of Nebraska and Missouri.

The primary source for the notated version is Bob Walters of Burt County, Nebraska, with a second version from Doug Phillips.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tears Of Love
description:
"Tears of Love" is a waltz-style or slow air fiddle tune found in the old-time American string band tradition. It is one of many sentimental, lyrical tunes that populate the old-time repertoire alongside more energetic reels and breakdowns.
The tune does not have a single well-documented composer in the public record, which is typical of many old-time fiddle tunes — they were passed down orally through generations of rural Appalachian and Southern fiddlers, often without clear authorship being recorded.
It appears in tune books and online tunebooks (such as The Session or ABC notation repositories) associated with the broader American old-time tradition.
Some versions of the tune are associated with North Carolina and Virginia fiddle traditions, two of the richest sources of old-time repertoire.
The tune is typically played in a slow, flowing, expressive style — fitting its name — in contrast to the driving rhythms of breakdown tunes like "Old Joe Clark" or "Shady Grove."
It is often notated in common time or waltz time (3/4), lending it a mournful, romantic character.
Like many old-time tunes, it likely exists in multiple regional variants, with different fiddlers putting their own stamp on the melody.
Old-time tunes like "Tears of Love" were primarily learned by ear at fiddlers' conventions, house parties (called "frolics"), and community dances — not from sheet music.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Terra Mollada
description: Terra Mollada is a waltz in the key of Am. (Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tombigbee Waltz
description:
Tombigbee Waltz is an American waltz in 3/4 time, in G Major, played in standard fiddle tuning. It is also known by the alternate title "Gum Tree Canoe."

The melody is named for the Tombigbee River, which flows from northeastern Mississippi into the Alabama River.

The word "Tombigbee" itself has a fascinating etymology — and sources give slightly different accounts:
"Tombigbee" has its roots in the Choctaw word for "box maker," referring to the wooden boxes Choctaws built to send fur pelts to trade with French traders in the 18th century. The Choctaw called the river "Itte-ombee-eye ika-abee," which the French heard as "Tombecbe," which evolved in English into "Tombeckby," "Tombigby," and finally "Tombigbee."
Alternatively, "Tombigbee" is rumored to mean "coffinmaker" in one of the Native American languages.

The tune has deep 19th-century roots as a parlor/minstrel song before it became a fiddle standard:
A song version, "Tom Big Bee River," attributed to S.S. Steele, was printed in Heart Songs – Melodies of Days Gone By, published in 1909 by World Syndicate Publishing Company (Cleveland; New York), although it is much older.
From the dialect employed in the lyrics, minstrel origins are indicated.
S.S. Steele and A.F. Winnemore (1847) are credited with words and music in Garson's Laura Ingalls Wilder Songbook.
There are even Australian versions of the song, printed in the early 20th century.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Tommy Bhetty's Waltz
description:
The waltz was composed by Tommy 'Bhetty' Maguire, a fiddler from Kinawley, County Fermanagh, Ireland. Scholar Caoimhín Mac Aoidh notes that McGuire — described as a big man — is the fiddler who passed the tune to Altan's Ciarán Curran.

Mac Aoidh explains that "Bhetty" is pronounced "vetty" and is part of the old Gaelic naming practice whereby a person receives the name of either their mother or father (or perhaps a significant member of the family), with the appropriate grammatical aspiration — in McGuire's case, the letter 'h' added to his mother's name, Betty.

This was a traditional Irish patronymic/matronymic naming convention: Tommy, son of Betty → Tommy Bhetty. Notably, there were two distinct "Tommy Bhetty" figures in the tradition — a Tommy "Puck" McCarthy and a Tommy, son of Betty (hence "Tom Bhetty"), referring to Tommy McCarthy.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Trim The Tree Waltz
description:
"Trim The Tree Waltz" appears to be a very obscure tune — it does not surface in any of the major old-time fiddle databases, tune wikis (The Session, Mudcat, ABC Notation archives), or standard reference works for the genre. The only search hit with that exact title points to a MuseScore sheet music page attributed to Monty Norman — a British composer best known for writing the James Bond theme — which is almost certainly a different, unrelated piece rather than a traditional old-time fiddle waltz.

"Trim The Tree Waltz" does not appear in the major catalogued old-time fiddle repertories, including:
The Old-Time Fiddler's Repertory by R.P. Christeson
The Henry Reed Collection (Library of Congress)
The Slippery Hill / Christeson digital archive (245 documented tunes)
Old Town School of Folk Music Tune Archive
oldtimefiddletunes.net (1,095 tunes catalogued)

New fiddle tunes have always been written and are still being written today, even within the old-time tradition. A tune like "Trim The Tree Waltz" — with its seasonal, holiday-themed name — could well be a composed original by a specific fiddler (rather than a passed-down traditional tune), which would explain the lack of historical documentation.

European dance styles that became popular in the United States during the 19th century provided new tunes and additional fodder for original tunes — including the waltz. Many old-time waltzes were composed by individual fiddlers and spread locally before being written down or recorded.

title: Tuscaloosa Waltz
description:
"Tuscaloosa Waltz" was composed by Will E. Ray, a fiddler from Chester, Choctaw County, Mississippi. Will was one half of the duo known as The Ray Brothers, with his brother Vardman Ray on guitar (though there were other brothers in the family as well).

The Ray Brothers recorded ten sides in Memphis, Tennessee, on two different dates (months apart) in 1930. The "Tuscaloosa Waltz" was released on Victor 23552 (78 RPM) by The Ray Brothers in 1931, having been recorded in November 1930 in Memphis.

The tune is in the key of C, in waltz time (3/4), and is notable for its lyrical, flowing melodic lines — quite elegant for old-time Southern string band music of that era.

Alabama fiddler James Bryan recorded the tune on the Rounder Records album "Lookout Blues" (1983), having learned it directly from the original 78 RPM recording by the Ray Brothers of Mississippi.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Valse Gisele
description:
Valse Gisèle was composed by fiddler Yvon Cuillerier, from Saint-Bruno, QC (Québec, Canada). The composition is dated to 1994.

So unlike the vast majority of old-time tunes — which are anonymous and centuries old — Valse Gisèle is a known-authorship, late 20th-century composition from the French-Canadian fiddle tradition. The title likely honors a person named Gisèle, as was common practice among French-Canadian fiddlers who composed waltzes as personal tributes.

It is classified as a French-Canadian waltz in 3/4 time, in D Major, played in standard fiddle tuning. It is a one-part tune.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: La Vie Est Pas Donne

title: Waltz of the Little Girls
description:
The tune is also known under several French names: La Valse des Petites Jeunes Filles, La Valse Pour Les Jeunes Filles, Valse des Jeunes Filles, and Valse Pour Les Petites Jeunes Filles, among others.

The most authoritative account of how this tune arrived in the US comes directly from Grey Larsen, a renowned American multi-instrumentalist who was largely responsible for its spread in North America.

Grey Larsen learned the tune in 1978 from a Belgian fiddler named Raymond Honay when Honay was traveling in the US.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wednesday Nite Waltz
description:
The tune's exact origin is debated among scholars:
R.P. Christeson (1973) suggests the tune was founded on a once-popular song called "Wednesday Night Waltz," however, Charles Wolfe (1997) states that it originated with a Mississippi fiddle band, the Leake County Revelers, and the group's fiddler, Wil Gilmer.
Gilmer himself admitted that he had picked up the tune "out in Texas somewhere." So even the credited composer acknowledged it was a piece he absorbed from the broader oral tradition — a classic old-time story.

The Leake County Revelers' version was the second best-selling country music record of 1927 (backed by "Goodnight Waltz") and the biggest old-time seller of 1928, recorded for Columbia Records.

The first recording and first release was by the Leake County Revelers on April 13, 1927, released in October 1927.

In the middle of the piece, the Revelers would break into a faster, duple-time strain — similar to the "waltz-and-two-step" combination found in Lonnie Robertson's "Hazy Hills Waltz."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Wednesday Night Waltz
description:
The tune's exact origin is the subject of scholarly debate between two schools of thought:

1. The "popular song" theory — R.P. Christeson (1973) suggests this tune was founded on the once popular song "Wednesday Night Waltz."

2. The Mississippi fiddle band theory — Charles Wolfe (1997) states that it originated with a Mississippi fiddle band, the Leake County Revelers, and the group's fiddler, Wil Gilmer.

But even Gilmer was fuzzy on where he got it: Gilmer himself admitted that he had picked up the tune "out in Texas somewhere."

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: West Leyden Waltz
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Title | West Leyden Waltz |
| Composer | Jimmy Nelson |
| Origin | Central New York State (Oneida County area) |
| Key | G major |
| Form | Waltz (3/4 time), two-part (A/B) |
| Region of play | Primarily New York State old-time fiddle community |

The "West Leyden Waltz" is a local Central New York regional tune, composed by Jimmy Nelson, but commonly played by regional fiddlers, according to Chad Miller.

Chad Miller, who documented the tune, writes: "I live in Oneida County, NY and most all fiddlers in this region of New York State play this tune." It was written by Jimmy Nelson, who lived near Rome, NY, also in Oneida County.

The tune takes its name from West Leyden, a small hamlet in Lewis County in upstate New York — part of the same rural Central New York landscape where Nelson lived and played.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Westphalia Waltz
description:
The Westphalia Waltz is a historic Texas waltz credited to Cotton Collins, a fiddler with the Lone Star Playboys, and named after the town of Westphalia, Texas. Its melody is derived from a well-known Polish tune that goes by several names, among them "Pytala Sie Pani" and "Wszystkie Rybki."

The melody derives from a Polish song known by several titles — "Pytala Sie Pani", "Wszystkie Rybki", and others — with its presence documented in Poland and the United States in the early twentieth century, verified by references from Poland's National Library in Warsaw and the Polish Museum of America in Chicago.

The tune is known in Polish circles as "Pytala Sie Panni", which means "Why are you sad, Lady?" Various researchers have reported the melody is also associated with a humorously risqué drinking song, and it is additionally known as "The Dreamy Fish Waltz" and "Wszystkie Rybki" (meaning "all the little fish").

From the mills of New England and the coal mines of Pennsylvania, to the farms of Wisconsin and the boisterous taverns of Chicago, "Pytala Sie Pani" was a unifying favorite that Polish-Americans sang during the Great Depression.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Ali Oidak Polka
description:
"Ali Oidak Polka" is not a traditional Appalachian or European old-time fiddle tune — it belongs to a distinct and fascinating Native American fiddle tradition from the American Southwest. Here's everything known about it:

"Ali Oidak Polka" comes from the first commercial recording of one of Southern Arizona's most unique instrumental traditions — the fiddle band music of the Tohono O'odham ("The Desert People"), formerly known as the Papago.

The track appears as the opening number on the album Old Time O'odham Fiddle Music by the Gu-Achi Fiddlers, a 12-song, 43-minute album released on Canyon Records.

The band personnel, as documented in the album liner notes, were:
Elliot Johnson — fiddle
Lester Vavages — fiddle
Wilfred Mendoza — guitar
Gerald Leos Senior — snare drum
Tommy Lopez — bass drum

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Cababi Polka
description:
The "Cababi Polka" is deeply tied to Cababi, Arizona, a small community on the Tohono O'odham Nation in southern Arizona. It is one of a collection of social dance tunes from the Tohono O'odham people of southern Arizona.

The tune comes from the tradition of the Gu-achi Fiddlers, a remarkable indigenous fiddle tradition. The Gu-achi Fiddlers produced multiple polka tunes, with the Cababi Polka being among their signature pieces.

The central figure behind the Cababi Polka and much of this entire repertoire is Elliott Johnson. The tunes were learned from Elliott Johnson of the Gu-achi Fiddlers, who lived in Cababi, Arizona.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Caballito Blanco
description:
"Caballito Blanco" is a traditional song sung by children all over the Spanish-speaking world. The title translates to "Little White Horse." It has also been identified as a jump rope rhyme, and several versions of it exist.

The song's exact national origin is genuinely contested:
The song is originally from Spain.
Despite its Spanish roots, it spread widely across Latin America. One correspondent noted that she read the tune is from Chile, but was born in northern Mexico where her grandmother (born in 1899) sang it to her, and her grandmother's grandmother also sang it to her.
The song is catalogued both as a Chilean and a Mexican folk tradition, reflecting how deeply it embedded itself across the Spanish-speaking diaspora.

The longest version has three distinct parts: the first asks the white horse to take the singer home, the second is about three sheep, and the third part tells a woman named Juana to get up and light a candle to investigate a noise. Often, children learn only the first two parts.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: El Coyote
description:
I was only able to find results for Guy Clark's country song "El Coyote," not a traditional old-time fiddle tune by that name. My searches did not return results specifically about an old-time fiddle tune called "El Coyote." Here's what I can tell you:

The most prominent "El Coyote" in folk/country music is a Guy Clark song, not a traditional fiddle tune:
Guy Clark wrote it with Noel McKay of the Texan alt-country duo The McKay Brothers.
"'El Coyote' was about a situation that really happened," said Clark — involving a driver who abandoned 18 migrant workers locked in a truck in the Texas sun, where they all died. Clark felt it was "something that needed to be addressed."

If you're looking specifically for a traditional old-time fiddle tune called "El Coyote," here are some targeted resources to check:

title: Cuatro Por Cuatro Polka
description:
Unfortunately, my web searches did not turn up any specific documented history, origin story, or named composer for a fiddle tune called "Cuatro Por Cuatro Polka" in old-time or traditional folk music archives. This could mean a few things worth knowing:

The tune "Cuatro Por Cuatro Polka" does not appear in the major traditional tune databases searched, including:
The Fiddler's Companion (ibiblio.org) — one of the most comprehensive encyclopedias of Anglo-American and Celtic fiddle tunes
The Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org)
Major old-time repertoire lists

This is notable because these archives catalog thousands of tunes, including obscure regional ones.
"Cuatro Por Cuatro" literally means "Four by Four" in Spanish — possibly referencing a 4/4 time signature, a structural feature of the tune, or simply a descriptive/playful title.
The name strongly suggests Latin American, Tex-Mex, or Southwest US origin, rather than Appalachian old-time. There is a documented tradition of fiddle tunes from Arizona and New Mexico — including polkas and two-steps — associated with fiddlers like Cleofes Ortiz and the Gu-achi Fiddlers, a distinct Spanish/Mexican-American fiddle tradition separate from Appalachian old-time.
The polka form itself arrived in the Americas in the mid-1800s. The polka was a European dance form that found favor and spread from 1844 onwards; dance master Allen Dodworth of New York claimed to have introduced the polka to New York society in 1843.

1. Tex-Mex / Norteño tradition — Polkas are central to this style (think conjunto music).

title: E. J. Special Polka
description:
"E. J. Special Polka" was released on January 1, 1997 by Canyon Records, as part of the album Old Time O'odham Fiddle Music by the Gu-Achi Fiddlers.

The Gu-Achi Fiddlers' fiddle band sound is highly unique, utilizing violins, guitar, and drums playing polkas, two-steps, and mazurkas — instruments originally introduced by Spanish missionaries.

This is a distinct and fascinating tradition: the Tohono O'odham (formerly known as Papago) people of southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico developed their own fiddle tradition rooted in the polka, two-step, and mazurka — dance forms absorbed through contact with Mexican and Spanish culture over centuries.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: First Choice Two Step
description:
The most specific documentation of this tune comes from the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org):
The tune is recorded as "First Choice Two-step (Gu-Achi Fiddlers and Bayou Seco)", in 2/4 time. A transcription was made courtesy of John Lamancusa, and it appears on the recording "Gu-Achi Fiddlers — Old Time O'odham Fiddle Music" (Canyon Records CR-8092). The third part of the tune is noted as optional — the Gu-Achi Fiddlers themselves only played the first two parts.

This places the tune firmly in the O'odham (Tohono O'odham) fiddle tradition of the American Southwest — a distinct and often-overlooked branch of old-time fiddle music rooted in the Indigenous communities of southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico.

The Gu-Achi Fiddlers are a Native American group from the Tohono O'odham Nation (formerly called the Papago) of Arizona. Their music blends traditional O'odham culture with the two-step and dance-tune traditions that spread into the Southwest. Their recordings on Canyon Records are the primary documented source for this tune.

title: Hohokum Polka
description:
"Hohokum Polka" appears paired with "Cababi Polka" as a medley, recorded by the group Bayou Seco. The "Cababi Polka / Hohokum Polka" medley also appears on the 1998 album Unbuttoned by Katie Howson & Jeannie Harris.

The pairing with "Cababi Polka" is a very strong clue. Cababi is a village on the Tohono O'odham Nation in southern Arizona, and "Hohokum" is a variant spelling of "Hohokam" — the name given to the ancient Indigenous people of the Sonoran Desert, ancestors of the modern Tohono O'odham (formerly called "Papago") people.

The O'odham fiddle tradition is highly unique, utilizing violins, guitar, and drums playing polkas, two-steps, and mazurkas — instruments originally introduced by Spanish missionaries.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))
