title: Libby Bird Song Mazurka
description:
The tune was recorded by the Gu-Achi Fiddlers and appears on their album Old Time O'odham Fiddle Music, released on Canyon Records (2001). This CD is considered one of the definitive releases of its kind. The leader of the Gu-Achi Fiddlers on that recording, Elliot Johnson, died approximately 30 years ago, and it remains the first and only commercial recording of this style.

The tune is believed to be named after a relative of one of the Gu-Achi Fiddlers — making it a deeply personal, community-rooted composition rather than a tune with anonymous folk origins.

The tune comes from the string band music of the Tohono O'odham people of Southern Arizona — a unique local style of the Southwest. These fiddle-driven bands created a distinctive sound playing polkas, two-steps, and mazurkas, utilizing violins, guitar, and drums. String bands provided music for religious festivals, community celebrations, and social dancing, likely through the 1950s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Lonnie's Polka
description:
The most concrete lead on "Lonnie's Polka" comes from The Fiddler's Companion, a comprehensive tune reference database. The source — Missouri fiddler Bob Holt — seemed to equivocate a bit on where he learned the tune and what the title was, but believed he picked it up from a radio broadcast of regionally famed fiddler Lonnie Robertson.

This places the tune squarely in the Missouri / Ozarks old-time tradition, transmitted through the oral/aural tradition of radio — a common vector for spreading regional fiddle tunes in the mid-20th century. The tune is named in honor of (or directly attributed to) Lonnie Robertson, a well-known regional fiddler in that area.
Form: AABB (two-part structure, each section repeated)
Genre: Polka, in the old-time tradition

Fiddle tunes are primarily instrumental melodies, though some have words that can be sung. Most originated as tunes for dancing. Most fiddle tunes consist of two melodic parts (A and B), frequently played in AABB form — the A part twice, then the B part twice.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Memories in Ajo
description:
"Memories in Ajo Polka" is a piece of Old Time O'odham Fiddle Music from Southern Arizona, associated with the Gu-Achi Fiddlers, a traditional Native American fiddle band from the Tohono O'odham Nation.

The Gu-Achi Fiddlers utilize instruments originally introduced by Spanish missionaries, with a highly unique fiddle band sound featuring violins, guitar, and drums playing polkas, two-steps, and mazurkas.

The tune "Memories in Ajo" is a polka, which is one of the core dance forms in the O'odham fiddle tradition. Ajo itself is a small town in Pima County, Arizona, near the Tohono O'odham reservation — so the title is a direct geographical and cultural reference to that region.
The Tohono O'odham (formerly known as Papago) people developed a rich fiddle tradition blending European missionary musical influences with their own indigenous musical sensibility.
This style is sometimes called "Waila" music (from the Spanish "bailar," to dance) — a uniquely Southwestern Native American genre.
The Gu-Achi Fiddlers are one of the most celebrated groups in this tradition, and their recordings are available on Canyon Records, a prominent Native American music label.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mi Suegra Aprietan Mis Botas Polka
description:
The tune's full title is "Mi Suegra Me Aprieta Las Botas", which translates from Spanish as "My Mother-in-Law is Tightening My Boots" — a comic, slightly absurdist image that perfectly captures the tune's playful personality.

The tune belongs to a medley of pieces from the repertoire of Gregorio Ruiz of Pecos, New Mexico. Gregorio called the core tune "La Polka de Eustaquio Ortiz," but it is more commonly known as "La Polka 'e la Suegra" (Mother-in-Law Polka), and it is one of the most popular Northern New Mexican polkas.

Cleofes Ortiz played a version of this tune which he called "Mi Suegra Me Aprieta Las Botas" — My Mother-in-Law is Tightening My Boots.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Valse de los Panos
description:
The tune is most directly associated with Cleofes Ortiz, a New Mexican Hispanic fiddler. He learned most of his tunes from his cousin, Emiliano Ortiz, a well-known fiddler who taught him both the local dance traditions and tunes he had picked up in lumber camps throughout New Mexico and Colorado. When he was 14, Cleofes began to play for local bailes (dances) and continued until his marriage.

The tune is notated in 3/4 time (a waltz), attributed to Cleofes Ortiz, in the key of G (A part) and D (B part). The title translates roughly to "Waltz of the Cloths/Shawls" (paños = cloths, handkerchiefs, or shawls in Spanish), suggesting it may have been associated with a particular dance gesture or local custom.

This tune belongs to the New Mexican Hispanic fiddle tradition, a distinct branch of the broader old-time fiddle world. It is documented in a free book titled 39 Fiddle Tunes of Arizona and New Mexico, drawn from recordings by the Gu-achi Fiddlers, Cleofes Ortiz, and others, transcribed by John S. Lamancusa.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: La Pecosita
description:
"La Pecosita" is a tune from the O'odham Indian tribe in Arizona. It belongs to a genre with several other tunes in that tradition — described as great music and fun to play. Importantly, it is not Mexican music — it is a genre all by itself.

The O'odham (also known as the Tohono O'odham, meaning "Desert People") are a Native American people of the Sonoran Desert in southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico. Their fiddle tradition — sometimes called "waila" or "chicken scratch" music — is a unique genre that blends:
Spanish colonial fiddle traditions introduced by Jesuit missionaries
Indigenous musical sensibilities of the desert Southwest
Later influences from polka, cumbia, and conjunto styles

This makes tunes like "La Pecosita" distinct from both mainstream old-time Appalachian fiddle repertoire and Mexican regional music. The name "La Pecosita" is Spanish for "The Little Freckled One" (pecosa = freckled, -ita = little/diminutive), a style of affectionate naming common in the Spanish-speaking Southwest.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Purple Lilies Polka
description:
"Purple Lilies Polka" is a tune that sounds almost like a Mexican polka, but it is actually a polka from the Native American Tohono O'odham tradition. The Tohono O'odham are an Indigenous people of the Sonoran Desert, straddling southern Arizona and northern Mexico.

It is a Tohono O'odham tune from southern Arizona, specifically associated with the Gu-Achi Fiddlers — a fiddle ensemble rooted in the Gu-Achi (Santa Rosa) community on the Tohono O'odham Nation.

The Gu-Achi Fiddlers are the primary source group for this tune. Their style blends Indigenous O'odham musical sensibility with the influence of Mexican norteño/polka rhythms — a natural result of the Tohono O'odham people's deep cultural and geographic ties to the Sonoran borderlands. A free collection of 39 fiddle tunes from Arizona and New Mexico — including tunes from the Gu-Achi Fiddlers and others — has been transcribed and compiled by John S. Lamancusa, making it one of the key documentary sources for this regional repertoire.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: El Quelite
description:
"El Quelite" is a traditional Mexican song that captures the essence of nostalgia and the bittersweet memories of love and place. It belongs to the ranchera tradition — the heartfelt, countryside-rooted genre of Mexican folk music. Lucha Villa, one of its most celebrated interpreters, is known for her powerful voice and emotive interpretations of ranchera music, bringing to life lyrics that speak of the beauty of the Mexican countryside and the pain of love left behind.

Credited composer: The song is attributed to Alfonso Esparza Oteo, a prolific Mexican composer from the early 20th century who wrote many beloved ranchera and popular songs.

The song is named after a real town. Some 19 miles from the port of Mazatlán, crossing the Tropic of Cancer, is the town of El Quelite — with cobbled streets and old colorful houses of rural architecture, surrounded by the Quelite River and fertile land. Small but packed with culture and tradition, the town was founded in the 1800s.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Redondo de Leyba
description:
"Redondo de Leyba" is recorded by Cleofes Ortiz, a New Mexican fiddler. The recording is catalogued in the Strachwitz Frontera Collection at UCLA, released on the Ubik label (catalog number C-3342) in cassette format, with accompaniment by Augustine Chavez and Jeanie McLerie, and is tagged as an instrumental featuring guitar, violin, and strings.

Cleofes Ortiz is featured in a free book of "39 Fiddle Tunes of Arizona and New Mexico" collected and transcribed by John Lamancusa, available at OldTimeFiddleTunes.net. This places the tune firmly in the New Mexico hispano fiddling tradition — a distinct regional strand of old-time fiddling rooted in Spanish colonial folk music rather than Appalachian or British Isles traditions.

"Leyba" (also spelled Leiba or Leyva) is a common New Mexican Spanish surname, and "Redondo" means round in Spanish — suggesting the tune is either named after a person from the Leyba family or a place associated with that name. "Redondo de Leyba" translates loosely as "the Leyba round dance" or "the Leyba circle tune." It sits alongside similar pieces in Ortiz's repertoire like "Redondo En Do" (Round in C), reinforcing the idea that "redondo" refers to a circular or round-dance form — a tradition with deep roots in Spanish colonial New Mexico.

title: Santa Rosa Processional
description:
Based on my research, here is what can be determined about "Santa Rosa Processional" as an old-time fiddle tune — along with important context for why a full origin story is difficult to pin down:

"Santa Rosa Processional" is an old-time fiddle tune associated with Southwestern / Native American and Mexican musical influences, rather than the more commonly known Appalachian old-time tradition. Its name and character suggest a ceremonial or parade-style piece — a processional being music composed or used for a formal procession, likely connected to a feast day or religious celebration associated with Santa Rosa (a common Catholic saint's day honored in many indigenous and mestizo communities of the American Southwest and Mexico).

The tune appeared as a Tune of the Week (TOTW) on Fiddle Hangout on September 12, 2010, and that discussion thread generated notable comments on Native American and Mexican music and influences. This places it firmly in a conversation about Southwestern and Mexican fiddle traditions, distinct from Appalachian roots.

The tune appears to be part of a broader tradition of fiddle music from the U.S. Southwest and northern Mexico. Examples of this tradition include Raweali/Huichol fiddling (documented on the CD Wood That Sings: Indian Fiddle Music of the Americas), and music compiled by ethnomusicologist Jack Loeffler in the three-CD set La Musica de los Viejitos (Music of the Old Men), recorded along the Rio Grande and heavily flavored with Mexican influence.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Uncle Charlie's
description:
The old-time tradition is full of tunes named after beloved local fiddlers, and "Uncle Charlie's" most plausibly traces back to one of two well-documented figures:

Charlie Barnett Lowe was Tommy Jarrell's father-in-law — Jarrell married Charlie's daughter Nina. He was a legendary figure in the Round Peak, North Carolina / Virginia old-time community. Charlie Lowe was the grand old legendary Round Peak clawhammer banjo player, and tunes attributed to him circulated under his name in that tradition.

A tune called "Charlie Lowe's Tune" was identified, and the fiddler playing it was Nick of the Flatiron Stringband. It also appeared on the album We'll Die in the Pigpen Fighting by "Tom, Brad, and Alice" — Tom Sauber, Brad Leftwich, and Alice Gerrard.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: La Vaquera
description:
La Vaquera (meaning "The Cowgirl") — also known as El Vaquero — is a chotis (schottische) that was popular in northern New Mexico. It belongs to a rich tradition of Spanish Colonial dance music that blended Old World and New World influences.

Cleofes Ortiz was born in 1910 on the Pajarito Plateau near Rowe, New Mexico. When he was eight years old, he made his first fiddle from a lard bucket, with screen wire strings.

He learned most of his tunes from his cousin, Emiliano Ortiz, a well-known fiddler who taught him both the local dance traditions and tunes he had picked up in lumber camps throughout New Mexico and Colorado.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Mabel Polka
description:
Direct historical documentation for "Mabel Polka" specifically is sparse in publicly indexed sources. Like many old-time fiddle tunes, it may belong to the large category of tunes with obscure or entirely oral origins. "Mabel Polka" is likely part of the old-time fiddle repertoire, most of which is in the public domain and has no known authorship — though many of these tunes have rich historical significance.

Polkas originated in Bohemia (Czech Republic) in the 19th century — a surprisingly recent period — but spread quickly in German and Polish folk music, throughout Europe, and were easily picked up by American fiddlers.

The polka's origin story first appears in the periodical Bohemia in 1844, attributed to a young Bohemian woman named Anna Slezáková. As told by Čeněk Zíbrt, music teacher Josef Neruda noticed her dancing in an unusual way to a local folk song in 1830, and he then put the tune to paper and taught other young men to dance it.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Storm Polka

title: Misirlou
description:
"Misirlou" is a folk song from the Eastern Mediterranean region. No verifiable single origin exists, but the melody is widely regarded as emerging from the multicultural milieu of the Ottoman Empire, where Greek, Armenian, Jewish, Turkish, and Levantine communities interacted extensively. It is a folk melody that emerged some time before 1920, though it's not unreasonable to assume it's much older than that.

Misirlou (Μισιρλού) is the feminine form of Misirlis (Μισιρλής), which comes from the Turkish word Mısırlı, formed by combining Mısır ("Egypt" in Turkish, borrowed from Arabic) with the Turkish -lı suffix, literally meaning "Egyptian." In short: "Egyptian Girl."

The original Greek lyrics of "Misirlou" tell a story of forbidden love between a Greek (Christian) man and an Egyptian (Muslim) woman. This theme was considered risqué in its time due to the religious and ethnic differences between the characters. While the lyrics don't explicitly mention religion, the nationalities of the man and woman imply the divide.

In the realm of Middle Eastern music, the song is a very simple one, since it is little more than going up and down the Hijaz Kar or double harmonic scale (E–F–G–A–B–C–D). Initially, the song was composed as a Greek tsifteteli dance, in the rebetiko style of music, at a slower tempo and a different key than the orientalized performances that most are familiar with today.

(Source: oldtimefiddletunes.net (John Lamancusa collection))

title: Devil's Dream
alternative_titles: De'il Amang The Tailors, De'il Amang The Taylors, The De'il Amang The Taylors, De'il Among Da Tailors, De'il Among The Tailors, The De'il Among The Tailors, De'il Among The Taylors, The De'il Among The Taylors
description:
One of the oldest and most widely-played tunes in the Anglo-American fiddle tradition, 'Devil's Dream' appears in printed collections from the early 19th century and was popular on both sides of the Atlantic. Its name may reference the tune's relentless, driving energy — fast-moving phrases that challenge the player. Documented in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883) and numerous New England and Southern fiddle collections, it crossed genre lines into contra dance, square dance, and later Western swing. Tommy Jackson, Doc Roberts, and the New England caller Ralph Page all used it.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Schroeder's Playboys, digitized by the Internet Archive.

notes: This tune demands clean string crossings and a relaxed right arm — tension kills the flow. The repeating B-part figures (bBbB, gBgB) are the signature: keep them even and light. Play it a notch faster than feels comfortable and trust the tune to do the work. Many New England versions stay close to the printed versions; Southern versions have more variation and ornament.

title: Flop Eared Mule
description:
A staple of Appalachian jam sessions, 'Flop Eared Mule' is a simple, good-humored G major reel that appears in Southern fiddle collections throughout the 19th century. The image of a mule with one ear flopped over — a common barnyard sight — gives the tune its personality: slightly ungainly but irresistibly charming. It was a popular contest tune in the Southeast and is still a standard at Old-Time camps because its simple structure makes it approachable for beginners while leaving plenty of room for variation.

The recording heard here is by Bev Baker and Norman Combs, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: A great first tune for beginners — the G major scale sits comfortably in first position and the structure is predictable. Don't rush the opening phrase; let each note speak. The 'flop' in the title suggests a slight looseness, not mechanical perfection. At sessions, this tune often signals a gear-shift to something lighter and fun.
audio_source: Baker, Bev; Combs, Norman via Internet Archive (1937)

title: Nine Pound Hammer
description:
A coal mining and labor song from the Appalachian coalfields, 'Nine Pound Hammer' references the heavy hammers used by miners and railroad workers to drive steel. Versions appear in Kentucky, Virginia, and Tennessee from the early 20th century. Merle Travis, Grandpa Jones, and Bill Monroe all recorded it. The song and fiddle tune became emblematic of the labor tradition in mountain music — hard work, solidarity, and the longing to lay down the burden and go home.

(Source: recording by stringband.mossyroof.com)
tags: labor song, coal mining, singable, beginner
notes: A song-tune — let the words shape your phrasing: 'This nine pound hammer is a little too heavy for my size.' The groove should feel relaxed and weighty, not hurried. G major with open strings gives it a full, resonant sound. Great for beginners because the form is simple and repeated. Many players add slight slides into the main notes for an authentic mountain feel.

title: Johnson Boys
description:
A courtship and dance song from the Southern Appalachians, 'Johnson Boys' appears in early 20th century field recordings and was a staple of the Round Peak and Blue Ridge fiddle traditions. The Johnson boys were the eligible bachelors in the community — a stock figure in mountain social humor. The tune's simple D major structure made it a natural vehicle for improvised verses at dances and community gatherings. Several versions were collected by folklorists in the 1930s–1940s.

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south), USA (Piedmont), USA (Southeast), USA (Ozarks/western tenn). First documented in New Lost City Ramblers's *Old-Time String Band Songbook* (1964). JOHNSON BOYS . AKA and see " Tennessee Girls ." Old-Time, Song and Fiddle Tune. USA; North Carolina, Virginia, Arkansas. D Major. ADae or Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. Paul Clayton identifies this as an old courting song, comic in nature. Some see similarity with the Gows' tune " Welcome Whisky Back Again ," and the Irish " Finnegan's Wake ." Gus Meade found "Johnson Boys" "an adaptation of [the Irish song] ' Doran's Ass ' (see Laws Q19), dating from around 1860. It was also used with other I… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south), USA (Piedmont), USA (Southeast), USA (Ozarks/western tenn).
tags: singable, beginner, courtship, mountain, round peak
notes: A song-tune with a driving D major feel. The melody stays in comfortable first position. Sing the words as you play: 'Johnson boys, they raised in the ashes / Didn't know how to court a maid.' The rhythm should bounce — this was dance music at mountain gatherings.

title: Way Downtown
description:
A blues-inflected Appalachian breakdown with roots in the string band tradition of the 1920s and 30s. 'Way Downtown' was popularized by Gid Tanner and the Skillet Lickers and has been recorded by Old Crow Medicine Show, Doc Watson, and many others. The song paints a picture of the Saturday night scene in small mountain towns — drinking, dancing, and finding a way home. Its minor-leaning melody within a G major framework gives it a distinctive ambiguity.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
notes: The G major setting has a bluesy quality — let the melody breathe and don't over-ornament. The 'downtown' feeling should come through in the phrasing: relaxed, loose, a little world-weary. Great tune for learning to play behind a singer.

title: East Tennessee Blues
description:
A breakdown with blues influence that emerged from the East Tennessee fiddle tradition in the early 20th century. The tune blends the driving structure of Southern breakdown fiddling with the blue notes and syncopation of the emerging blues style. Recordings by East Tennessee players from the 1920s–1930s capture the moment when the two traditions were actively cross-pollinating. The result is a tune that swings harder than a straight reel but has more structure than a pure blues piece.

Attributed to Charlie Bowman. Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). First documented in Miles Krassen's *Appalachian Fiddle* (1973). EAST TENNESSEE BLUES . AKA and see " Hey Mr. Muskrat ," " Honeysuckle ," " Honeysuckle Rag ," " Huckleberry Blues ," " Poca River Blues ," " Ten Cent Cotton ." American, Country Rag. USA, Va. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). One part (Christeson): AB (Beisswenger & McCann]: AA'BB' (Brody, Krassen, Phillips, Silberberg). The tune is credited (by biographer Bob Cox) to Tennessee fiddler Charlie Bowman (1889-1962), who is said to have composed it in the 1920's. Bowman, according to Cox, had no… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south).
notes: The blue notes are the key — let the 3rd and 7th scale degrees slide or bend slightly for the blues effect. Don't play it too rigidly; the swing feel matters more than note-perfect accuracy. D major gives you plenty of open-string resonance to work with.

title: Buffalo Gals
description:
Originally a minstrel song published in 1844 as 'Lubly Fan,' 'Buffalo Gals' was adapted and republished under dozens of regional titles — 'Pittsburgh Gals,' 'Louisiana Gals,' 'Alabama Gals' — by itinerant performers who localized it for each audience. The tune was ubiquitous at dances, circuses, and camp meetings throughout the 19th century. Its call-and-response structure (verse then chorus) translated naturally into fiddle instrumental form. Still played today at Old-Time sessions as a beginner-friendly crowd-pleaser.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Pickard Family, digitized by the Internet Archive.
notes: A cheerful, simple tune in C major. The first position sits naturally on the instrument. Sing 'Buffalo gals, won't you come out tonight' in your head to find the right phrasing — the melody should feel like a conversation. Great for learning to hold a steady tempo.

title: Camptown Races
description:
Composed by Stephen Foster in 1850, 'Camptown Races' was immediately absorbed into the fiddle tradition where it has remained ever since. The energy and forward drive of the tune — imitating the thunder of horses on a racetrack — made it a natural dance tune. Foster's songs crossed racial lines in a way that complicated the era's social divisions; 'Camptown Races' was performed by Black and white musicians almost from publication. The 'doo-dah' refrain gives it an infectious, participatory quality.

(Source: Internet Archive)
notes: Play it with forward momentum — the 'doo-dah' energy should be in every phrase. G major sits comfortably in first position. Keep the bow near the middle of the stick for a full, round tone. Great tune for practicing even 8th notes at a steady tempo.

title: Deep Elem Blues
description:
Deep Ellum (Elm Street) was the historically Black entertainment district in Dallas, Texas, where jazz, blues, and string band music converged in the 1920s. 'Deep Elem Blues' was recorded by the Lone Star Cowboys in 1933 and later by the Grateful Dead in 1970, bringing it to a new generation. The tune captures the danger and excitement of the district — 'When you go down to Deep Elem, keep your money in your shoes.' It lives at the crossroads of blues, country, and Old-Time string band music.

The recording heard here is by The Bansai Bills, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: blues, dallas, string band, grateful dead, singable
notes: The blues feel comes from the flattened 7th and the syncopated phrasing. Don't play this tune straight — it needs the swagger. The G position lets you use the open G string as a drone under the melody. Listen to Grateful Dead's version for the feeling, then bring it back to the fiddle tradition.
audio_source: The Bansai Bills via Internet Archive (2014)

title: Fox Chase
description:
A narrative fiddle piece that imitates a fox hunt — the horn calls, the chase through the woods, the baying of hounds, and the triumphant (or tragic) conclusion. 'Fox Chase' exists in multiple regional versions but is most associated with the Appalachian tradition where it served as a showpiece for virtuoso fiddlers. The tune is as much a performance as a piece — the fiddler calls out the action and mimics the sounds of the hunt. Tommy Jarrell and other Round Peak fiddlers played notable versions.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: narrative, showpiece, imitative, round peak, tommy jarrell
notes: Fox Chase is a piece, not just a tune — you're telling a story. The horn calls, the hound baying, the chase rhythm, the catch or escape — each needs a distinct character. Let the bow do the sound-painting: long sustained notes for the horn, choppy bow strokes for the galloping chase, bending notes for the hound calls. Every fiddler has their own version.

title: Little Maggie
description:
A Mixolydian-flavored Appalachian song and fiddle tune about a hard-drinking, hard-living woman — a stock figure of mountain social ballads. 'Little Maggie' was a staple of Stanley Brothers repertoire and became a bluegrass touchstone, but its roots are in the Old-Time fiddle and banjo tradition of the Virginia-North Carolina highlands. The Mixolydian mode (G major with a flatted seventh) gives it a distinctly archaic, modal quality that connects it to older British Isles traditions.

The recording heard here is by Alan F Brookes, preserved by the Internet Archive.

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). LITTLE MAGGIE. AKA - "Little Maggie with a Dram Glass in Her Hand." Old-Time, Bluegrass; Breakdown and Song. USA; western North Carolina, southwestern Virginia. A Mixolydian. A popular Appalachian song and breakdown that has been absorbed into core bluegrass repertory from its old-time roots, whose lyrics belong to the " Darling Corey / Country Blues / Hustling Gambler " family of songs, although the melody differs. It was recorded by the Stanley Brothers in 1946, when their music was more ol… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south).
tags: mixolydian, modal, stanley brothers, singable, bluegrass crossover
notes: The flatted 7th (F natural in G) is the key — don't accidentally sharpen it or you lose the modal color entirely. Sing the words to find the phrasing: 'Over yonder stands little Maggie / with a dram glass in her hand.' The tune should feel old, unhurried, and a little dangerous. Great for learning modal playing.
audio_source: Alan F Brookes via Internet Archive (1999)

title: Train 45
description:
A railroad song and fiddle tune from the Round Peak area of Surry County, North Carolina, closely associated with Tommy Jarrell and his circle. The number 45 refers to a specific locomotive route through the mountain South. Train songs were enormously popular in the pre-automobile era — the railroad was the most powerful machine ordinary people encountered, and its rhythms worked their way into music naturally. Tommy Jarrell's version is the definitive Old-Time rendering.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Sonny Osborn, digitized by the Internet Archive.

Attributed to G.B. Grayson. Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: railroad, tommy jarrell, round peak, singable, surry county
notes: Play it with the rhythmic drive of a train — steady, relentless, forward-moving. The D major setting is comfortable and open. Tommy Jarrell's version has a beautiful rolling bow stroke; aim for that momentum. The tune works well with open-string drones on the D string.

title: Stoney Point
description:
Named for Stoney Point, a community in Catawba County, North Carolina, this reel is closely associated with the Round Peak and Piedmont fiddle traditions. It was collected in multiple versions in the mid-20th century and is a standard at Southern Appalachian jams. Its driving G major structure and singable melody have kept it in active circulation. The tune exemplifies the 'long bow' style of Southern playing — sustained phrases with the bow engaged fully across the string.

(Source: recording by slippery-hill.com)
tags: north carolina, round peak, long bow, session standard
notes: Use a long, engaged bow stroke — don't chop the notes. The G major position allows open-string drones that fill out the sound. The melody has a strong sense of direction; follow it without forcing ornaments. At Southern sessions this tune can run for many passes without losing energy.

title: Bright Morning Star
description:
A Sacred Harp and Appalachian modal tune of great antiquity, 'Bright Morning Star' exists in both hymn and fiddle instrumental versions. The A minor (Dorian or natural minor) setting gives it an otherworldly, reverent quality. The tune was a staple of shape-note singing traditions in the South and crossed into the fiddle repertoire as an instrumental piece. Its simple, stepwise melody and modal ambiguity link it to a very old stratum of Anglo-American folk music.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: modal, sacred harp, ancient, reverent, dorian
notes: Play it slowly and with space — this is not a dance tune. The modal quality needs room to breathe. Avoid vibrato; let the notes speak plainly in the old Sacred Harp style. The A Dorian mode (natural 6th and 7th in A minor) gives it its distinctive, timeless sound.

title: Growling Old Man and Grumbling Old Woman
description:
A comic song-and-dance tune from the Appalachian tradition, this piece depicts a domestic argument between an old married couple — a staple figure of 19th-century rural humor. The alternating phrases imitate the voices of the two characters. It appears in Southern fiddle collections from the 19th century and was a popular clog dance tune. The humor is in the call-and-response structure: each phrase 'answers' the previous one in a different register.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: comic, dialogue, clog dance, 19th century, southern
notes: Play each phrase with a distinct character — the 'man' phrases strong and gruff, the 'woman' phrases higher and sharper. The humor lives in the contrast. D major is comfortable; focus on making the register shifts clear and dramatic.

title: Jawbone
description:
An antebellum song and fiddle tune that references the jawbone of a mule used as a percussion instrument in slave music — a precursor to the washboard and bones traditions. 'Jawbone' appears in Frederick Douglass's slave narrative as an example of the music he heard as a child. The tune was collected in multiple Southern fiddle traditions and represents the deep African American contribution to the Old-Time music vocabulary.

First documented in Miles Krassen's *Appalachian Fiddle* (1973). JAWBONE . AKA and see " Old Jawbone (1) ," " Walk Jawbone ." American, Reel/Song. G Major (Krassen, Phillips): A Major (Beisswenger & McCann). Standard or AEae tuning (fiddle). AB (Beisswenger & McCann): AABB (Krassen, Phillips). The tune has minstrel origins, with 'jawbone' probably referring to a stock character in such shows, says Charles Wolfe (1991). The jawbone was also a recognized percussive instrument in 19th century Aftrican-American traditional music and was employed by minstrel tr… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: african american tradition, antebellum, singable, percussion roots
notes: The groove comes from the jawbone percussion origin — keep the rhythm percussive and bouncy rather than smooth. D major sits naturally in first position. The tune's historical significance adds weight to playing it well; know its context.

title: Railroad Bill
description:
Based on the legend of a real outlaw — Morris Slater, an African American man who robbed Louisville and Nashville Railroad trains in Alabama in the 1890s before being shot by a sheriff in 1896. Railroad Bill became a folk hero in Black Southern communities, joining the pantheon of outlaws who stood against authority. The song and fiddle tune spread widely through the South. W.C. Handy and numerous folk collectors documented versions, and it was recorded in the 1920s–30s by string bands on both sides of the color line.

The recording heard here is by The Homesteaders, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: outlaw ballad, african american, alabama, singable, blues
notes: The tune has a bluesy swagger that matches the outlaw character. G major with flatted 7ths (F natural) gives it the blues quality. Don't play it neat and polished — let it have some grit. The cross-racial history of this tune is important; it belongs to everyone who plays it.

title: Charming Betsy
description:
An Appalachian reel with an Irish-influenced melodic structure, 'Charming Betsy' appears in Southern fiddle collections from the 19th century and was a dance hall standard in the mountain South. The 'Betsy' in the title is likely the classic courtship figure of American folk song. The tune's flowing D major melody and clean two-part structure make it representative of the Scots-Irish inheritance that shaped Appalachian fiddle music.

(Source: Internet Archive)
notes: A smooth, flowing reel — the bow should move like water. D major gives you open-string resonance to fill the sound. The A part and B part have similar contours; distinguish them with bow pressure and phrasing. Keep the tempo steady; this is dance music.
audio_source: D.D.Teoli Jr. A.C. via Internet Archive

title: Coal Creek March
description:
Named for Coal Creek, Tennessee (now Lake City), where one of the bloodiest labor conflicts in American history took place in 1891–92 — the Coal Creek War, in which miners rose up against the use of convict labor in the mines. The march rhythm of this tune carries the weight of that history. Tennessee fiddle tradition preserved the tune as a memorial to the conflict and as a piece of regional identity. It is rarely heard outside specialist Old-Time circles but carries enormous historical significance.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: march, labor history, tennessee, coal mining, historical
notes: Play it with gravity — this is a memorial as much as a tune. The march rhythm should feel purposeful, not militaristic. D major is bright but the subject gives it weight. Understanding the Coal Creek War context makes every note more meaningful.

title: Wake Up Susan
description:
A lively courtship breakdown from the Appalachian fiddle tradition, 'Wake Up Susan' calls out to a girl who has slept through the dance. The urgency in the title matches the tune's driving energy. Collected in multiple Southern fiddle traditions in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it appears in both song and instrumental forms. The simple D major structure and memorable A-part opening make it easy to learn and a crowd-pleaser at sessions.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
notes: The urgency of waking Susan should be in the bow: decisive, bright, forward. D major in first position is comfortable for beginners. The tune's strength is in its momentum — don't let it droop at phrase ends. Call out 'Wake up, Susan!' in your head to find the right energy.

title: Barlow Knife
description:
Named for the Barlow folding knife — a working-class staple of 19th-century American life — this reel appears in multiple Appalachian and Southern fiddle collections. The Barlow knife was so common it appeared in Mark Twain's 'Tom Sawyer' and was a standard trade item at country stores. The tune's G major structure and driving rhythm suggest a tune for dancing rather than sitting still. It circulated in the mountain South well into the 20th century.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
notes: A clean, driving reel in G. The key gives you open-string drones and resonance. Play the downbeats firmly and let the off-beats flow. Don't over-ornament — the tune has its own momentum when played cleanly.

title: Pretty Little Horse
description:
A gentle lullaby-song from the Appalachian tradition that doubles as an instrumental fiddle piece. 'Pretty Little Horse' (sometimes 'Hush Little Baby' variant) soothes a child with promises of a fine horse and saddle. The song was collected widely in the Virginia and North Carolina mountains in the 1920s–30s. As an instrumental, the lilting 3/4 or 4/4 feel (depending on the version) captures the rocking quality of the lullaby tradition.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
notes: Play it gently and let the lullaby quality come through. G major in a rocking rhythm. This is a listening piece, not a dance tune — slower and more expressive. The simplicity is the point; don't add complexity where the original is deliberately plain.

title: Roving Gambler
description:
A gambling ballad from the British broadside tradition that took root in the American South and Appalachia. 'Roving Gambler' tells of a card shark who moves from town to town, winning money and hearts. The tune was popular with string bands in the 1920s–30s and was collected by Cecil Sharp during his Appalachian field work. Its simple G major structure and verse-chorus form made it easy to adapt for both song and fiddle. Doc Watson, Pete Seeger, and many others recorded versions.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: gambling ballad, british origin, singable, cecilsharp, doc watson
notes: The roving gambler should sound confident and slightly swaggering. G major is the right key — open and resonant. Don't rush; the gambler takes his time. Great tune for learning to play behind a singer. Keep the rhythm steady like a card dealer's rhythm.

title: Ida Red (Canote Version)
description:
A second version of Ida Red featuring the Canote Brothers' definitive A major arrangement. While the Slippery Hill version focuses on the tune's connection to Chuck Berry, the Canote version emphasizes the older 1920s string band recording tradition. Collected in multiple Southern states, 'Ida Red' exists in several regional variants. The A major key gives it a brighter, more fiddle-forward character than some versions. This hypnotic tune inspired Chuck Berry to write 'Maybellene' (1955).

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: driving, A major, chuck berry, string band, 1920s
notes: Keep the groove tight and hypnotic — the whole point of this tune is momentum. A major in first position is comfortable. Let the open A string drone under the melody. Chuck Berry heard this and wrote rock and roll; channel that energy.

title: Cindy (Full Version)
description:
A fuller companion entry to the existing 'Backstep Cindy' and 'Cindy' entries, capturing the most widely-played G major version. 'Get Along Home, Cindy' is one of the most recorded American folk songs — appearing in shape-note hymnals, on 78s, and at every fiddle camp. The courtship story of 'Cindy' — a girl whose father keeps her from dancing — gave the tune its universal appeal. Burl Ives, Pete Seeger, and countless string bands recorded versions.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: courtship, singable, beginner, jam standard, appalachian
notes: Play the chorus bright and lifted — 'Get along home, Cindy, Cindy, I'll marry you someday!' G major in first position. A great first tune because the structure is simple and repeating. The verse should feel slightly more grounded, the chorus more urgent.

title: Hangman's Reel
alternative_titles: Reel du Pendu, Le Reel du Pendu, Reel of the Hanged Man
description:
One of the most dramatic tunes in the tradition, 'Hangman's Reel' carries two histories converging at the same gallows. The original is 'Le Reel du Pendu' (Reel of the Hanged Man), a French-Canadian melody documented in Quebec's Kamouraska region in the late 19th century — first recorded by Joseph Allard (1928) and Isidore Soucy (1927–1952), and later played with authority by Jean Carignan. The Appalachian old-time version was popularized by Albert Hash (1917–1982) of Rugby/Whitetop, Virginia, who learned it from a 1968 recording by Texas fiddler Bill Northcutt. Hash's version spread through the folk revival circuit and became a festival standard. Multiple folk legends tell of a condemned prisoner who earned his freedom by composing and playing the tune overnight on an out-of-tune fiddle — a story that explains the non-standard cross-tuning many fiddlers use. Some say that plucking the top three strings in the final part mimics the sound of a breaking neck.

Attributed to Bill Northcutt , Albert Hash. Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). First documented in Stacy Phillips's *Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 1* (1994). Additional notes Source for notated version : - Albert Hash via Liz Slade (Yorktown, New York) [Kuntz]; Tim O'Brien [Phillips]. Printed sources : - Phillips ( Traditional American Fiddle Tunes ), vol. 1, 1994; p. 108. Silberberg ( Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern ), 2002; p. 58 (appears as "Hanged Man's Reel"). Songer ( Portland Collection ), 1997; p. 92. Recorded sources : - County CO-CD-2711, Kirk Sutphin - "Old Roots and New Branches" (1994). June Appal 014, John McCutcheon - "The Wind Th… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south).
tags: cross-tuning, french-canadian, appalachian, dramatic, albert hash, festival
notes: Often played in AEae cross-tuning, which gives the tune its eerie, gallows quality — standard tuning loses something essential. The four-part AABBCCDD structure lets the drama build slowly. Albert Hash's Appalachian version drives harder than the Quebec version. Use your whole bow and commit to the story. This tune rewards players who let the narrative shape their playing.

title: Greasy Coat
description:
A signature tune of Edden Hammons (1876–1955), the legendary Webster County, West Virginia fiddler recorded in 1947 by folklorist Louis Chappell for the Library of Congress. Hammons played with old-fashioned intonation and Scottish-influenced phrasing that preserved a rapidly vanishing tradition. The Hammons family — including Burl and Currence — learned from both Scots-Irish and Black folk artists, including Grafton Lacy, making their repertoire a genuine multicultural archive. 'Greasy Coat' is a product of this layered inheritance: European modal scales over African-American rhythmic drive. The title comes from an 1849 humorous poem about a man too slovenly to find a wife — though other theories point to unwashed wool heavy with lanolin, or a Confederate soldier's worn field coat. A famous comic lyric goes: 'I don't drink and I don't smoke / and I don't wear no greasy coat / I don't cuss and I don't chew / and I don't go out with the girls that do.' Played in AEAE cross-tuning with A Dorian or Mixolydian tonality.

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). First documented in Stacy Phillips's *Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 1* (1994). GREASY COAT . AKA and see " Old Greasy Coat ." American, Reel. USA, West Virginia. A Dorian: A Mixolydian (Burl Hammons). Standard (Burl Hammons) or AEae (Edden Hammons) tunings (fiddle). ABCC. There are several meanings for the term 'greasy coat.' It said to have been an old-time euphemism for a condom (although verification of this in the literature is wanting), but it has also been suggested the term refers to an unwashed fleece (i.e. still retaining the lanolin), and a Confederate soldier… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south).
tags: cross-tuning, modal, west virginia, hammons family, dorian, edden hammons
notes: Cross-tune to AEAE before you start — the standard-tuned version loses its drone magic entirely. The G and D strings go up a whole step each, and the open strings must ring through every phrase. The modal quality (watch the flatted 7th) gives this tune its grit and growl. Edden Hammons played with deep bow pressure and unhurried phrasing. This is dance music with geological patience.

title: Old Buck
alternative_titles: Ol' Buck
description:
One of the most charming creation stories in the old-time repertoire. In the 1940s, Tommy Jarrell (1901–1985) of Round Peak, Surry County, North Carolina, was trying to learn 'Paddy on the Turnpike' from fiddler Rafe Brady, who played it twice for him. About a year later, Jarrell worked up what he believed was his version of it. When he played it for Brady, Brady said: 'Tommy, that ain't Paddy on the Turnpike, that's Old Buck.' Jarrell responded: 'Well, if there's a tune named Old Buck I don't know nothing about it — but that was all that was said, and that's what I called it from then on. So I made a tune I reckon.' The tune belongs to the double-tonic reel family, its two parts playing off each other with a shifting harmonic center. Tommy Jarrell and musical partner Fred Cockerham (1905–1980) became the most influential chroniclers of Round Peak style, and their recordings were central to the 1970s old-time revival.

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). First documented in *Old Time Herald vol. 3 No. 1* (August 1991). Will I was a trying to learn "Paddy On the Turnpike," Rafe Brady came down here one time and I got him to play it twice for me. Well that was back yonder in the 40's when I wasn't doing no fiddling much, you know, and I got to fooling with it...and about a year after that I come up with that tune that I play there and Rafe was down here again. I played it for him and he says "Tommy, that ain't 'Paddy on the Turnpike', that's Old Buck'. Well, if there's a tune named 'Old Buck' I don't know not… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south).
tags: tommy jarrell, round peak, surry county, folk process, double-tonic, north carolina
notes: Round Peak style: heavy bow close to the bridge, drones ringing, no excessive vibrato or prettiness. The tune has a restless, unresolved quality — a ghost of Paddy on the Turnpike filtered through Jarrell's memory. Rough edges are part of the deal. The A and B parts chase each other without fully catching. Available on Field Recorders' Collective recordings of Tommy Jarrell.

title: Honey Babe
alternative_titles: Red Rocking Chair, Ain't Got No Honey Baby Now, Red Apple Juice, Sugar Babe
description:
Part of one of old-time music's most sprawling song families, 'Honey Babe' travels under many aliases — Red Rocking Chair, Red Apple Juice, Sugar Babe, Ain't Got No Honey Baby Now — all carrying floating verses from the same vast reservoir of Southern folk song. Dock Boggs recorded a cousin version as 'Sugar Baby.' Norman Edmonds had a notable fiddle arrangement that Bruce Molsky later taught, combining the lyrical melody with verses drawn from multiple traditions. The emotional core is loss and longing: 'Ain't got no use for your red apple juice / Ain't got no honey baby now / Who'll rock the cradle and who'll sing a song / Who'll be your honey when I'm gone?' The tune's simplicity and ability to hold endless verses made it a staple of mountain social gatherings, singings, and front-porch music across Virginia, Kentucky, and the Carolinas. Played here by Darin Gentry's ensemble Danger Gently.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: song-tune, singable, beginner, floating verses, appalachian, dock boggs
notes: Sing it in your head while you play — this is a song-tune, and the phrasing follows natural speech. 'Ain't got no use for your red apple juice.' G major with open strings gives it warm resonance. Don't reach for complexity; the power of this tune is in its plainness. Works well as a rest between harder reels.

title: Squirrel Heads and Gravy
description:
The most successful practical joke in old-time music history. Around 1975, Missouri fiddler Chris Germain composed a tune and deliberately passed it off as an ancient Appalachian reel, claiming he'd learned it from an old West Virginia fiddler 'who died shortly after teaching it.' The inspiration came from friends who overheard a child at a music festival ask an elderly fiddler if he knew a tune called 'Squirrel Heads and Gravy' — no such tune existed, but the title was too perfect to waste. The hoax worked: the tune spread through Midwest jams and festivals, was recorded by multiple bands as 'Traditional' — including Bovee and Heil and the Piney Creek Weasels — and developed genuine regional variations in different keys and cross-tunings. Germain's original was in A with AEAE tuning; G major GDad versions followed. Germain eventually confessed, but by then the tune had completed the folk process on its own. The name may reference Missouri fiddler Taylor McBaine (1911–1994), who famously ate squirrel brains as a delicacy. It is now, by any measure, a traditional tune.

SQUIRREL HEADS AND GRAVY. American, Reel (cut time). G Major. Standard or GDad tuning (fiddle). AABB. "Squirrel Heads and Gravey" was composed by fiddler Chris Germain (originally from Ferguson, Missouri, then of Washington D.C.) around the year 1975, apparently as part of a joke. Ironically, the tune has entered tradition and is sometimes listed as a "traditional" melody. The rumor that there is an older tune by the same name only seems to be part of the joke. One story goes that Germain ask… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: modern composition, folk process, singable, beginner, jam standard, missouri
notes: The B part is the payoff and is meant to be sung: 'Squirrel heads and gravy, squirrel heads I say / Squirrel heads and gravy, I'm a-gonna eat them every day.' The simplicity is deliberate — Germain built it to sound convincingly old. Play it straight, without fussy ornament, and let the melody do its work. An instant crowd favorite at jams.

title: Reel des Esquimaux
alternative_titles: Reel des Eskimos
description:
First committed to record in 1939 when French-Canadian master Isidore Soucy pressed it to 78 RPM, 'Reel des Esquimaux' (Reel of the Inuit) is one of the more enigmatic pieces in the Quebec and Métis fiddle repertoire. Soucy's original version was 'crooked' — meaning it carried irregular phrase lengths that don't divide evenly into standard 8-bar strains — before later versions were smoothed out for square and contra dance. The tune circulates through both Québécois sessions and Métis fiddle gatherings, where it picks up the longer bow strokes and open-string drones characteristic of the Red River fiddle tradition. The title's reference to the Inuit people may evoke the geography of northern Quebec or simply the tune's slightly cold, modal quality in certain interpretations. Isidore Soucy (1899–1963) was among the most documented French-Canadian fiddlers of the 78 RPM era, alongside Joseph Allard and Jean Carignan — his recordings are foundational for anyone studying the Quebec tradition.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: french-canadian, metis, crooked, isidore soucy, 78rpm, red river
notes: In Métis style, use long bow strokes and let the open strings drone beneath the melody — the tune breathes differently than an Irish or American reel. In Celtic or old-time settings, more ornament and shorter bow. Try both and decide which fits your room. The crooked version is worth learning: the irregular phrase endings create a subtle surprise that the regularized version irons out.

title: Malheur County Blues
description:
Named for Malheur County in the high desert of eastern Oregon — a vast, remote ranching country bordering Idaho and Nevada, its name French for 'misfortune' or 'bad hour' after early fur trappers lost a supply cache to indigenous people — 'Malheur County Blues' belongs to the living tradition of old-time fiddle music expanding westward. Oregon developed its own fiddle culture through organizations like the Oregon Old-Time Fiddlers Association and through musicians who carried Appalachian, Cajun, and Scandinavian influences into the Pacific Northwest. The blues tonality in D connects it to a broad family of modal, minor-inflected breakdowns that describe landscape and labor rather than social dancing. This tune appears in Jason Chinchen's repertoire and represents the ongoing creative life of the tradition outside its Appalachian heartland.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: oregon, pacific northwest, blues, modal, contemporary, d mixolydian
notes: The D blues tonality means C-natural not C-sharp — the flatted 7th gives it the open-range, wistful feeling the title calls for. Let the bow travel slowly on long notes; this is not a driving breakdown but a contemplative one. Good for shifting a session's mood from high-energy reels toward something more spacious.

title: Turkey in the Straw
alternative_titles: Zip Coon, Natchez Under the Hill
description:
'Turkey in the Straw' began life in 1834 as 'Zip Coon,' a blackface minstrel number published in New York and Baltimore with disputed authorship among performers George Washington Dixon, Bob Farrell, and George Nichols. The character 'Zip Coon' was a caricature of a dandified free Black man — one of minstrelsy's ugliest stock figures. The tune's melody, however, drew from older fiddle and banjo traditions and proved so catchy that it outlived its original context by two centuries. The title 'Turkey in the Straw' emerged in the late 19th century, stripping the minstrel associations and attaching the melody to rural, agricultural imagery. By the early 20th century it was simply a folk tune, recorded by countless string bands and appearing in early country music catalogs. Its pentatonic structure and driving rhythm made it one of the most recognizable American melodies in the world — appearing in ice cream truck jingles, cartoons, and folk festivals with no trace of origin. The minstrel roots are historical fact, not a reason to avoid the tune, but a reason to know its full story.

First documented in Francis O'Neill's *Music of Ireland. 1850 Melodies* (1903). Well, I was—where we lived, we lived down on the Williams River, when the—when I saw this thing, and so--. And we always went to bed pretty early, my dad did, and—about eight o’clock we always went to bed—and I laid down and I, didn’t seem like I could go to sleep. And I laid there a while and just directly I heard the click, open come the door, and in walked this skeleton of a man, Lord, I’ve—he was really tall, a-must’ve been six or seven feet tall or looked like that. And he had—I noticed … (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
tags: beginner, pentatonic, minstrel origins, widely known, driving
notes: The melody is deceptively simple — pentatonic, symmetrical, relentlessly singable. Play it with a hard, driving bow stroke. The A part's opening phrase is one of the most recognizable in American music. The B part bounces before returning to the A. At fiddle jams, it's often used as a warm-up or a crowd-pleaser. The tune works well for call-and-response between fiddle and banjo. Tempo should feel like a brisk walk rather than a run.

title: Pretty Polly
alternative_titles: The Gosport Tragedy, William and Polly
description:
'Pretty Polly' is among the darkest tunes in the Appalachian repertoire, telling the story of a young woman lured into the woods by her lover — who digs her grave before bringing her there — and murdered. In many versions she is pregnant; in some she returns as a ghost. The ballad descends from the British 'The Gosport Tragedy' or 'William and Polly,' documented in English broadsides as early as the 17th century and carried to Appalachia by Scots-Irish immigrants. It was collected extensively by John Harrington Cox in 'Folk-Songs of the South' (1925) and by Cecil Sharp in the 1910s. Dock Boggs recorded a devastating banjo and vocal version in 1927 that became the American standard. The murder ballad tradition — 'Pretty Polly' alongside 'Banks of the Ohio,' 'Tom Dooley,' 'Omie Wise' — reflects real social conditions in isolated mountain communities: violence against women, absence of legal protection, and folk memory as reckoning. The tune is hauntingly simple; the words carry the weight.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)
tags: murder ballad, minor, appalachian, dock boggs, dark, british isles origin
notes: The minor key is non-negotiable — don't brighten it. The melody has a relentless forward motion that mirrors the lover leading Polly toward her fate. Play slowly and deliberately, especially on the long notes. Dock Boggs's 1927 banjo recording is the canonical reference; its archaic quality is worth studying. On fiddle, deep bow pressure on sustained notes honors the weight of the text. Don't rush the ending.

title: Falls of Richmond
description:
A bright D major reel named for Richmond, Virginia, the former capital of the Confederacy and one of the great Southern fiddle cities. The Falls of the James River at Richmond were a significant geographic landmark and transportation chokepoint that shaped the city's industrial history. The tune circulates widely in Appalachian and Southern old-time jam sessions and appears in multiple fiddle collections under variant titles including simply 'Richmond.' Walt Koken, banjoist and co-founder of Highwoods String Band, plays a definitive version in D major with a strong, straight rhythmic drive typical of Southern breakdown style.

Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). First documented in David Brody's *Fiddler's Fakebook (The)* (1983). FALLS OF RICHMOND . American, Reel. USA, West Virginia. A Aeolian or Dorian ('A'and 'B' parts) & A Major ('C' & 'D' parts). AEae (Brody, Phillips) or ADae tunings (Edden Hammons, Kuntz) {fiddle}. AABCB (Brody): AABBCCDDBB (Kuntz, Phillips, Songer). "Falls of Richmond" has been a popular piece among old-time revival musicians but its original associations apparently were solely with the Hammonds family of West Virginia. It is said that members of the family trace the tune back to "Old Uncle Pe… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)
notes: A clean, driving D major reel — all four open strings are available as drones. Two distinct parts: the A part climbs up the scale with confident strides; the B part has a satisfying descending run. Play it straight and hard. This is a dance tune and needs a locked groove more than ornamentation. Great for building right-hand bow arm consistency.

title: Lazy John
description:
A playful, driving old-time breakdown in G. A staple of Southern Appalachian sessions, 'Lazy John' has a laid-back groove that belies its rhythmic complexity. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

Attributed to Clyde Davenport. Geographic provenance: USA (Central). First documented in Gene Silberberg's *Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern* (2002). LAZY JOHN. American, Reel and Song (cut time). G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. A tune/song from the playing of Monticello, Kentucky (on the Cumberland Plateau), fiddler Clyde Davenport [1] (b. 1921), and a largely different tune (and song) from the similarly titled " Sleepy John / Sleepy-Eyed John ," with only small similarities in the chorus.

Davenport told interviewer Dr. Jeff Titon that he learned the tune from the radio, possibly, notes Titon, from the western swing band version b… (Source: Traditional Tune Archive, tunearch.org)

title: Last Chance
description:
A brisk old-time reel in D with a clean two-part structure common to the Southern Appalachian tradition. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Dry and Dusty
description:
One of the most beloved and accessible old-time fiddle tunes in the repertoire. 'Dry and Dusty' has a simple, satisfying melodic arch in G that makes it a favorite at beginner jams. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Policeman
description:
A driving Southern Appalachian breakdown in D with a martial, rhythmically propulsive character. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Elk River Blues
description:
A moody, bluesy old-time fiddle tune named for the Elk River in central West Virginia, with a modal feel and spacious phrasing. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

Attributed to Ernie Carpenter. Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). First documented in Claire Milliner & Walt Koken's *Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes* (2011). A mountaintop-removal coal mine sits adjacent to the headwaters of Elk River, and the mining process has caused rock overburden to fill the valley at the river's source. Acid runoff has also taken a toll on wildlife and fish in the area. The tune is played slower than a breakdown, at a very brisk walking pace.

title: Ruffled Drawers
description:
A classic Southern Appalachian reel in D with a colorful name and a satisfying melodic arc, prized for its drive at sessions. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

First documented in Stephen F. Davis's *The Devil’s Box vol. 23 No. 1* (Spring 1989). RUFFLED DRAWERS. AKA and see " New Five Cents (1) .” American, Reel (cut time). D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. See also closely related tunes " Buffalo Nickel (2) " and “ Robinson County .” This ditty was sung to the first strain of the tune (collected by John Hartford from fiddler Roy Acuff):

title: Brushy Fork of John's Creek
description:
Named after a tributary of Johns Creek in eastern Kentucky, this haunting two-part reel has a distinctly modal Appalachian quality rooted in the Eastern Kentucky fiddle tradition. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Tennessee Breakdown
description:
A high-energy Tennessee fiddle breakdown in G with a propulsive rhythm and clear melodic structure suited for square dances and open jams. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 1.

Attributed to Dudley Vance. Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). First documented in Stacy Phillips's *Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 1* (1994). This, or another tune with with the same name, may have been composed by Vance's contemporary, southwestern Tennessee fiddler Jess Young. The title "Tennessee Breakdown" appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954; there is no way of knowing whether this is the same tune or not.

title: Fall on My Knees
description:
A lyrical, expressive waltz-time tune in the old-time tradition with a hymn-like searching quality. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Benton's Dream
description:
A flowing two-part reel in G with a slightly dreamy, lyrical quality rooted in the Southern Appalachian tradition. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

Attributed to Benton Flippen. Geographic provenance: USA (Upland south). First documented in Stacy Phillips's *Traditional American Fiddle Tunes vol. 1* (1994). BENTON'S DREAM . American, Reel. USA, Surry County, western North Carolina. A Mixolydian. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. Composed by Mt. Airy, Surry County, N.C., fiddler Benton Flippin (1920-2011). Susan Songer notes that Flippen wrote the tune some time in the 1960's while at neighboring Mt. Airy fiddler Tommy Jarrell's house, just fooling around on the fiddle. Jarrell said "That's a good tune" and dubbed it "Benton's Dream."

title: Shove That Pig's Foot a Little Farther in the Fire
description:
An old-time breakdown in D with one of the most memorable titles in the fiddle canon — raw, earthy, and full of drive. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Josie-O
description:
A rhythmically compelling breakdown in G with the momentum and lift characteristic of the best Southern fiddle dance tunes. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Red Prairie Dawn
description:
A sweeping waltz-time tune that evokes the open landscape of the American prairie, with gentle arc and sustained melodic lines. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Train on the Island
description:
A well-traveled old-time reel found across the Appalachian fiddle tradition, with a clean two-part structure and forward drive. Featured on George Jackson's The Old Time 100, Vol. 2.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Dubuque
description:
Named for the Iowa city on the Mississippi River, a Midwestern old-time reel with the rolling feel of upper-Mississippi valley fiddle music. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Eighth of January
description:
A patriotic fiddle tune commemorating Andrew Jackson's victory at the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815. One of the oldest and most widely known tunes in the American fiddle canon. Also known as 'Battle of New Orleans.' Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Jack of Diamonds
description:
A traditional gambling song and fiddle tune found throughout the Appalachian and Texas fiddle traditions, recorded by many old-time artists. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Jeff Sturgeon
description:
A breakdown named for Jeff Sturgeon, a fiddler in the Southern Appalachian tradition. Composer-named tunes anchor repertoire to specific regional players and communities. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: John Brown's Dream
description:
A rolling modal reel in A with the haunting quality characteristic of eastern fiddle traditions. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

(Source: TuneVault editorial research)

title: Uncle Joe
description:
One of the quintessential old-time breakdown tunes, found in nearly every regional fiddle tradition across Appalachia and the South. Its simple two-part structure and momentum make it a perennial session favorite. Featured on George Jackson's Old Time 100, Vol. 3.

First documented in E.F. Adam's *Old Time Fiddlers Favorite Barn Dance Tunes* (1928). UNCLE JOE.
